title: Masterplan review – Stanley Tucci is wasted in Amazon’s smooth-brained heist caper | Action and adventure films | The Guardian
description: A ‘family’ of criminals attempt to steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in pulpy and forgettable thriller
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: A ‘family’ of criminals attempt to steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in pulpy and forgettable thriller
Content: Stanley Tucci in Masterplan.Photograph: Courtesy of Amazon MGM StudiosView image in fullscreenStanley Tucci in Masterplan.Photograph: Courtesy of Amazon MGM StudiosAction and adventure filmsReviewMasterplan review – Stanley Tucci is wasted in Amazon’s smooth-brained heist caperA ‘family’ of criminals attempt to steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in pulpy and forgettable thrillerOwen MyersFri 16 Oct 2026 15.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the last half-decadeStanley Tuccihas been a source of near-inexhaustible on- screen delight, whether making friends with nonnas in his delightfulcookingshowsor smartly judged supporting turns inConclaveandThe Devil Wears Prada 2. He is an actor well placed for a star vehicle of his own, and this one,Masterplan, sounds good on paper: an art heist fronted by the actor at his most debonair, flanked by a grandson of a French New Wave legend (Victor Belmondo, related toBreathlessstar Jean-Paul) and a buzzy breakout of The White Lotus (Simona Tabasco, winning inseason twoof Mike White’s comedy).‘It’s all I think about’: Stanley Tucci on love, grief and pastaRead moreThere’s a good bit of pulpy fun to have here, with double, triple and quadruple crossing, silly spy gadgetry which has been updated to include retina scan cloning and something called “VR intrusion”. As British criminal mastermind Roger, Tucci is game to send up aristo archetypes, even if his character often veers into parody. “I’m English,” his character says at one point. “‘Not bad’ is what I say when I orgasm.”“Not bad” is what I say about Masterplan, a straight-to-streaming Amazon Prime offering that the studio is burying this weekend, seemingly choosing to focus on its just-released romantic dramaLove of Your Life. Cybersecurity hacker Chiara (Tabasco) and explosives expert Jay (Belmondo) are Europe’s leading young criminals, working together remotely under aliases and using some kind of dark web app to sign up for new gigs. When they meet for the first time while breaking into a mansion on the shores of Italy’s Lake Geneva, sparks fly. “Sixty seconds, in and out,” promises Jay before Chiara snaps back playfully: “Don’t you use that name on Tinder?”Just as you settle in for an evening of will-they-won’t-they hijinks, the film pulls a bait and switch. It turns out that the pair have been set up by Roger (Tucci), a veteran thief himself who has the “job of a lifetime” for them: a decade-in-the-making plan to make off with theMona Lisain a complicated scheme that involves drones, trickery, truffle-related espionage and a long-forgotten tunnel that conveniently exists under the Louvre. Also: they are in fact brother and sister, the result of an energetic mid-90s for Roger when he seduced their respective mothers.You would think the fact that they are now siblings would put the kibosh on Jay and Chiara’s flirtation, but the film seems to feel otherwise. As the makeshift family relocate toParisto put plans in motion for the heist, Chiara makes jokes about the size of her half-brother’s “hammer” and offers to settle squabbles through a round of strip poker, which strikes me as an unusual way for siblings to bond.View image in fullscreenVictor Belmondo and Simona Tabasco in Masterplan.Photograph: Amazon MGM Studios/PADespite the jokes that land with a thud, Masterplan is on safer ground when it sticks to the espionage. That is thanks to Thomas Vincent, the director, recapturing some of the juice he showed in the episodes ofBodyguardhe directed, and I would rate Masterplan as a hair better thanRole Play, the dull film he previously made for Amazon. When it isn’t trying to dazzle you with technology, Masterplan has a few twists on heist movie tropes (including a very clever use of a helium balloon) that avoids it feeling like a total retread of the Ocean’s 11 franchise, even if it doesn’t come close to matching the ingenuity of those films. And while the characters are too thinly drawn to make you care too much about them, I appreciated flourishes that nod to the female and gay male gaze, such as the diva moment where Tabasco’s character dons a platinum blond wig and the camera’s lustiness for Belmondo, who has a talent for losing his shirt.Everything isn’t as it seems, and while the film should really end 30 minutes before it does, it has a few final tricks up its sleeve in the third act, as the characters begin to learn who they can really trust and Chiara’s hacking skills are put to the test once more. Even as the plot becomes increasingly ridiculous, ample bangs and explosions ensure that the nearly two-hour runtime doesn’t totally drag. The best you can offer Masterplan is faint praise: it could breeze by as company to your Sunday night takeout even if you will struggle to remember it a week later.Masterplan is streaming onAmazon Prime VideonowExplore more on these topicsAction and adventure filmsStanley TucciAmazon Prime VideoMona LisaPaintingParisArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween | Television | The Guardian
description: The comedy smash is back – and now the standups aren’t allowed to laugh or shriek! Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Phil Wang and more reveal what made them crack – and what happened when they went too far
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The comedy smash is back – and now the standups aren’t allowed to laugh or shriek! Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Phil Wang and more reveal what made them crack – and what happened when they went too far
Content: Paranormal obsessive … Daisy May Cooper on Last One Laughing HalloweenPhotograph: Prime VideoView image in fullscreenParanormal obsessive … Daisy May Cooper on Last One Laughing HalloweenPhotograph: Prime VideoTelevision‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: HalloweenThe comedy smash is back – and now the standups aren’t allowed to laugh or shriek! Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Phil Wang and more reveal what made them crack – and what happened when they went too farBrian LoganFri 16 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat could be more disorientating for a comedian than not being able to laugh – for nine hours! – nor elicit laughter from anyone else in the room? I’ll tell you. Try all of the above on a sunny summer weekend while pretending it’s Halloween. Then force the comics to return to the scene of what one of their number, Phil Wang, calls “a cross between a gameshow and a psychological experiment”, and relive the whole ordeal for a man from the Guardian. Is it any wonder Wang, Lou Sanders, Tom Allen and others come across as a little punch-drunk 24 hours after emerging from televised captivity on the smash comedy hit Last One Laughing?It’s the day after filming, at Elstree Studios, the show’s Halloween special which sees a unique tweak to its winning formula: contestants must not only refrain from laughter but from screaming. “Which I thought might be a non-event,” says Wang, “but it’s actually harder. I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am.” The participating comics – including paranormal obsessive Daisy May Cooper and that maestro of comedy-horror, Reece Shearsmith – seek not only to amuse each other but spook them too. Which makes sense, says hostJimmy Carr. “Laughs and screams come from the same place. There’s surprise in a joke, and there’s surprise in a jump scare. Comedy and horror mess around in the same area. It’s the same bit of your brain.”View image in fullscreenThe cast of Last One Laughing HalloweenPhotograph: RAY BURMISTONNot that Last One Laughing is making serious moves into chiller territory: after all, why tamper with a format that’s given Prime Video such a huge hit? With over 2m people tuning in per episode, series one was the platform’s biggest ever UK launch. The show later won a Bafta for Best Entertainment Programme. “I don’t want to overplay the jump scares,” says Carr – who first persuaded the channel to develop a UK version of what was originally a Japanese hit. “There’s nothing that would trouble anyone. It’s not that kind of show. It’s just fun. It’s ‘event TV’ – especially when it’s tied around something like Halloween – that’s great for bringing people together.”And for bringing comedians together too – the more so now LOL has joined Taskmaster as the shop windowpar excellencefor standups making the leap from fringe to mainstream. Alongside national-treasure veterans (Bob Mortimer in series one; Mel Giedroyc in series two), Last One Laughing reserves places for up-and-coming acts – see recent Edinburgh comedy award winner Harriet Dyer here. Getting involved, she says, was “a whirlwind, to be honest. But it was a dream come true.” All the participating comics agree, mind you, that you can’t treat LOL like a career opportunity. “You can’t play it like that,” says Tom Allen. “You have to engulf yourself in the moment. And that reveals people’s true character. There’s something very vulnerable about laughing. We feel very open when we do it.”View image in fullscreen“Laughs and screams come from the same place” … host Jimmy Carr on Last One Laughing: Halloween.Photograph: AmazonFew comics are more oversharingly their own self than Lou Sanders, a late casualty (red-carded by Carr in episode six) in series one, now returning for series 2.5. There’s a strict embargo on spoilers today, but when I ask Sanders if previous experience gave her an advantage in the Halloween outing, her response does not suggest a triumphant comeback. “I thought I would be better,” she says. “But I was immediately on the back foot. And Reece got into my head early on.” Then there’s the knowledge that millions are watching. On series one, “Joe Wilkinson said to me ‘no one’s going to watch this,’ and I believed him. And then it did well. This time, you know there’s going to be eyes on it.”Sanders has been charged with giving me a tour of the LOL house, a bar cum living room cum art deco theatre, like a prefab 1920s ocean liner constructed in a ginormous Elstree hangar. Here is the fruit machine that’s used to prompt new challenges. There the stage on which contestants perform their ‘joker’ party pieces – around which more strictures circulate than you’d expect. (“I thought it would be funny to have a fire on my head,” says Harriet Dyer. “But I was told: no fire. Then I wanted long arms, but I wasn’t allowed them … ”) There are also creepy dolls, just for Halloween. Does it get claustrophobic in here, I ask Sanders? “I wasn’t in here long enough to know” comes her doleful reply.View image in fullscreenStraight face … Lou Sanders in Last One Laughing: Halloween.Photograph: AmazonBut if Sanders’ tactics proved inadequate, others enter Last One Laughing with sophisticated strategies all mapped out. “My tactic was to channel Dame Maggie Smith in Downton Abbey,” says Tom Allen. “Very aloof, very lofty. So I channelled everything through my eyebrows, rather than a lot of people, who try not to laugh by biting the inside of their mouth.” Wang had a more attacking approach. “My mantra was: a good defence is a good offence. Get on the front foot, try to get to people. Focus on those you know at first, because you know what makes them tick. And while doing that, watch the people you don’t know, to see what makes them laugh.”Dyer entered the house with an idea of whatnotto do. “I think Sam Campbell said on series two that he thought about, like, kids dying to stop himself laughing. So I thought: should I focus on the worst thing that’s ever happened to me? But I’m not sure watching someone be traumatised with what life’s thrown at them makes for very good telly.” Campbell is the maverick Aussie comic who tested the show’s conceit to breaking point last time around, by staying po-faced from start to finish. He eventually lost in a tie-break to David Mitchell. “We nearly broke David,” says Jimmy Carr. “At the end he was going, ‘I don’t think I’ll ever laugh again. I’ve lost that part of myself for ever’.”View image in fullscreenSerious matter … Reece Shearsmith competes in Last One Laughing: Halloween.Photograph: AmazonSeries two’s other breaking point was reached when – great controversy, this – the comic Amy Gledhill was red-carded by Carr for smiling rather than laughing. My own household can’t have been alone in its outrage at this disregard for the show’s core conceit. But Carr is unrepentant. “I mean, we’d got to that stage of the day,” he says: something had to give. “And it’s that water cooler thing: as long as people are arguing about it and having fun, so much the better.”To Carr, the show is as much sports as entertainment: the key, he thinks, to its success. “There’s a narrative to sports, whereby you’ve got to watch to the end because you don’t know what’s going to happen. And that’s the same thing with this show: it’s competitive, and you want to know who’s going to win.” “And each episode ends on a really effective cliffhanger,” adds Phil Wang, “which is quite hard to achieve with comedy.”The other clincher, for Carr and the comics, is how rigorously LOL is produced. Says Carr, “the other countries don’t do the set pieces we do”: the guest appearances, the challenges, the props and tricks contestants can bring to the table – much to Lou Sanders’ dismay. “Reece Shearsmith is Mr Halloween, isn’t he? He’s got all that stuff at home! It’s not fair. I haven’t got a severed hand at home, have I?”According to Wang, “shows that prepare more than they need always prosper. And this show definitely prepares more than it needs.” Every contestant has a camera trained on them throughout, and a dedicated “spotter” hanging on their every smirk. “I presented it in the room yesterday for nine hours,” says Carr. “But I haven’t seen it all yet. When you get in the edit, there’s a whole other show there. There’s all the conversations people have on the screens I’m not watching. I remember on series two discovering all these incredible moments with Diane Morgan we just didn’t know were there.”The lineup has already been announced for LOL series three, which broadcasts next year. Harry Hill, Katherine Ryan and Lee Mack all feature. What advice – or warnings – would the Halloween participants impart? “You end up in there for so long,” says Wang – lucky for some! – “that your mood goes from giddy and excited to paranoid and nervous. I was doing a lot of pinching, a lot of breathing, a lot of meditation and mindfulness.” It was, says Tom Allen, “an intense experience, trying to withhold two emotions and not let them out of the bag. It’s exhausting.”But it’s all in the service, says Allen, of something much needed in our not-always-joyful times. “The series speaks to a childlike sense of play, one that reminds us of being in assembly or in class at school and not being allowed to laugh. There’s nothing more exquisite than that burning desire to laugh while having to keep a lid on it, the steam cooker pressure that brings. Last One Laughing returns us to that youthful joy. I think it’s something people really crave.”Last One Laughing: Halloweenis onPrime Video from Friday.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionJimmy CarrfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Uncovering the secrets of New Zealand’s elusive ‘jungle penguins’  | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: The tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin, known for its prominent yellow eyebrows, has for years baffled scientists with its unusual habits
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: The tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin, known for its prominent yellow eyebrows, has for years baffled scientists with its unusual habits
Content: A tawaki on the Shelter Islands in Fiordland’s Doubtful Sound.   Photograph: Derek MorrisonThe tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin, known for its prominent yellow eyebrows, has for years baffled scientists with its unusual habitsByEva Corlettin Wellington. Photography Derek MorrisonFri 16 Oct 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDeep in the misty fjords of New Zealand’s South Island, a team of researchers is trying to catch one of the world’s most elusive penguins: the forest-dwelling tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin.For weeks, researchers stand sentry each day over a burrow on Eleanor Island, hoping to corner the female bird so they can retrieve data from its tagging device.But this penguin has developed a clever exit strategy – digging multiple tunnels to elude its captors.View image in fullscreenThe Tutoko I prepares for a research trip during its annual Fiordland crested penguin nest survey around Doubtful Sound“It took us about four days to recapture that bird,” says Dr Thomas Mattern, a research fellow at the University of Otago and chair of the Tawaki Project, a scientific initiative established to study the population.“We plugged all the holes around the nest so that it could not escape, until we finally could recover that device,” he adds.In a first for the species, Tawaki Project researchers are conducting long-term population counts, unlocking secrets about the bird’s breeding and foraging habits, and what threats they might face.The project is New Zealand’s most comprehensive mapping of tawaki nests. Over September, it mapped 93 nests across two islands in Fiordland, and has now mapped 1,200 nests across nine fjords in the past 12 years. Its mapping shows the tawaki population is roughly three times bigger than earlier surveys suggest, says Mattern, pictured below at Precipice Cove.View image in fullscreenDr Thomas Mattern searches for tawaki near Precipice Cove during a research trip with the Tawaki ProjectThe Māori name for crested penguins, tawaki, is a catch-all for several species aroundNew Zealandand the sub-Antarctic region, but the focus of this annual voyage is on the decliningspecies that inhabits remote Fiordland, New Zealand’s largest national park, which is Unesco heritage listed.Until German-born Mattern and his wife, Ursula Ellenberg, founded the volunteer research project in 2014, almost nothing was known about Fiordland’s tawaki, which stands half a metre tall, and features prominent yellow eyebrows.“Tawaki are a ghost,” Mattern says of the penguin’s enigmatic behaviour.But “they are the most amazing penguin species … They do not fit any penguin mould. What we know about penguins, you throw it all out of the window.”View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: A tawaki taking shelter. A research vessel at anchor near the Shelter Islands. Dr Thomas Mattern looks for penguins. A nest tag on Eleanor IslandUnlike most penguins, the Fiordland tawaki do not breed in colonies, preferring instead to build single burrows deep in dense rainforest, sometimes at high elevations. While some other species can nest in forests, tawaki are unique because they nest exclusively in forests, Mattern says, describing them as “proper jungle penguins”.Its hunting habits are also unusual. Some groups fish entirely within the fjords, while others hunt in the ocean.View image in fullscreenThe tawaki’s habits have baffled scientists“When you think you have them nailed down, you go to a different fjord, and they show behaviour that just does not conform to any of the ideas you have developed so far,” Mattern says.Myth or mystery: are moose roaming the isolated wilds of New Zealand?Read more‘Absolutely zero sense’Tawaki have also become infamous among scientists for their baffling journey to feed before they go through their annual “catastrophic moult” – the scientific term for when animals shed and replace all their feathers in one go.All penguins moult after breeding season and before they do, they eat vast quantities of food to put on weight. Despite an abundance of food around the fjords in December (when breeding season ends), tawaki undertake a 5,000 to 7,000km return trip to the sub-Antarctic region to feed.“These emaciated tawaki, that have just said goodbye to their chicks, hop in the water and travel halfway to Antarctica, which makes absolutely zero sense because there should be more than enough food in the water just outside their breeding area,” Mattern says.“They are running a marathon, while trying to gain weight.”View image in fullscreenResearchers Owen Dabkowski and Mandy Abernethy explore a nest on Eleanor IslandMattern believes tawaki are likely acting on ancient instinct, heading to grounds where all other crested penguin species feed.The Tawaki Project is funded by public donations and international grants, and supported by local volunteers, such as‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brinkRead moreRichard Abernathy, the owner of tourism company Fiordland Expeditions, who donates his boat and time to the expedition for several weeks a year.“Since 2018, we’ve been chasing penguins all over Fiordland,” says Abernathy whose ability to find nests in surprising places has earned him the nickname “sniffer dog”.Together, their efforts have “shed light on the most understudied species” in New Zealand, Mattern says.In 2020, the International Union forConservationof Nature’s Red List moved tawaki up in status from “vulnerable” to “near-threatened” because the researchers were able to develop a better picture of their populations, estimated to be in the region of 12,00 to 15,000 mature birds.View image in fullscreenA tawaki swims in Charles Sound in FiordlandBut risks remain, including from commercial fishing practices.“[We’re] looking at survival rates … to determine whether the population is stable,” says Mattern.“If they’re going down, then we need to kick into gear to improve the situation for them.”Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandPenguinWildlifeConservationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A direct cultural threat’: your questions on the rise of the right across Europe answered | Europe | The Guardian
description: With support for far right politics well established across Europe, how might upcoming elections shape its future? Europe correspondents Jon Henley and Ashifa Kassam answered Reddit users’ questions about their reporting from the continent
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: With support for far right politics well established across Europe, how might upcoming elections shape its future? Europe correspondents Jon Henley and Ashifa Kassam answered Reddit users’ questions about their reporting from the continent
Content: Guardian Europe correspondents Jon Henley and Ashifa Kassam.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenGuardian Europe correspondents Jon Henley and Ashifa Kassam.Composite: Guardian DesignConversationsEurope‘A direct cultural threat’: your questions on the rise of the right across Europe answeredWith support for far right politics well established across Europe, how might upcoming elections shape its future? Europe correspondentsJon HenleyandAshifa Kassamanswered Reddit users’ questions about their reporting from the continentJon Henley,Ashifa KassamandLucy O’BrienFri 16 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSupport for far-right parties has been growing across Europe, with radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France andGermany.The Guardian reported this year thatnearly a quarter of voters in Europe voted for far-right parties in their most recent national elections,a fivefold increase since 1995.In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland recently booked ahistoric state election victoryin Saxony-Anhalt. Elsewhere, though – in the Netherlands, in Hungary and in Sweden, where theSweden Democrats lost vote share– far-right parties have suffered defeats. But their ideas – and their influence on mainstream politics – are today clearly visible across the continent, notably on policies around immigration and law-and-order.The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing inFrance, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year.How might these elections shape the political future ofEurope? What is the impact of their policies – and what might prevent their continuing rise?The Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley has reported for the Guardian from 23 of the EU’s 27 member states, while Europe community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam was on the ground in Sweden and Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state to speak with people ahead of the elections.Jon and Ashifa answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below.View image in fullscreenGiorgia Meloni and Marine Le Pen have openly criticised Donald Trump.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersOne user asked: It’s no secret in Europe thatDonald Trumpand his allies are funding far-right parties all over the continent. Trump is unpopular enough in Europe that even the majority of people planning to vote for the AfD et al despise him. So how can so many Europeans who hate Trump still vote for the far right?Jon Henley:You’re absolutely right about the Trump administration’s efforts to promote far right parties in Europe. That was made very plain in the US National Security Strategy policy document last year – Iwrote about that here.But while there may be an ideological affinity between European far right and nationalist voters on issues like anti-immigration, hostility toward the EU, and softer stances on Russia, Trump’s “America First” policies (demands re Greenland, tariff threats, etc.) and constant unpredictability pose major problems for far-right leaders trying to look credible in Europe, because they scare all European voters – including far-right voters.Leaders including Giorgia Meloni in Italy andMarine Le Penin France have openly criticised Trump and distanced themselves from his more erratic pronouncements, conspiracy claims and hostility toward European security.European far-right voters’ support for Trump varies from country to country but is broadly low – clearly peace and security in Europe matter more than anti-immigration sentiment. Ultimately, nation-first means putting your nation first, and Trump has made clear that the US’s interests are not Europe’s interests.The evidence would seem to suggest that many of Europe’s far-right voters think their own far-right parties will be more responsible as regards (many of) those issues – though whether they actually will be or not is moot, of course.00000000000000000000asked: How do you measure when a grassroots movement represents a genuine structural shift versus an isolated vocal minority?Ashifa Kassam:Our jobs involve covering a wide range of community actions, whether it’s people fighting backagainst datacentres,protestsagainst tourism, or thevandalisationof mobile phone masts by people who seemingly linked them to the coronavirus pandemic.Oftentimes the reporting starts small and local. For example, perhaps it’s focused tightlyon a protestagainst tourists in Barcelona or a push to restrictcruise ship dockingsin Dubrovnik. From there, myself and the editors often continue to watch these movements and their reach; are politicians responding in any way? Are others joining in? Will the movements lead to policy changes? These are the kinds of questions that I tend to consider when deciding how much to make of the grassroots movements and how much coverage to give them.At times it’s been incredible to see just where these movements will go, whether it’s the housing protestsin Spain that led to snap general electionsor the opposition movementthat coalesced aroundPéter Magyar in Hungary in 2024 and which, more than a year later, saw him oust Viktor Orbán from power.Sign up for the This Is Europe newsletter: our free continental emailRead moreView image in fullscreenAs president, Marine Le Pen is unlikely to have a parliamentary majority, which will limit her room for manoeuvre.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersGramoun-kalasked: Can the EU survive the rise of the extreme right? What if AfD and RN get into power at the same time?Jon Henley:One of the very few upsides of Brexit is that hardly any European far right parties now want their countries to leave the EU. Instead, they want to “transform it from within”, turning it more into a looser “Europe of nations”.But that’s not to say the EU would not be considerably weakened by, say, a President Le Pen, who could paralyse decision-making, challenge the supremacy of EU law and push a “France First” agenda undermining the single market and Schengen free-travel zone and opposing EU expansion, climate action, etc.I’m not sure there’s any imminent risk of the AfD coming to national power in Germany (and if Le Pen wins France’s presidential election, which isn’t certain but looks highly plausible, she is also unlikely to have a parliamentary majority, which will limit her room for manoeuvre).Plus, the AfD is too extreme even for the RN – Le Pen’s outfit (which kicked the AfD out of its European parliament grouping a while ago over various issues including comments to the effect that not all Nazis were bad), has repeatedly made it clear it is not an ally of the German party and does not share its views on eg. “remigration” – the mass deportation of immigrants.But for sure – if Spain, Italy, France and Poland all see far-right parties in government after elections due over the next 12 months or so, the EU will face some major challenges. I don’t think it will collapse, but it will certainly find it even harder to reach agreement on many major issues than it already does, and so move (even) more slowly. Natalie Tocci wrotea great comment piece about this.OrangeSpaceMan5asked: Do you see Nato and the EU disintegrating if we see Far-Right victories across Britain, Germany and France?Jon Henley:No, I don’t see the EU and Nato disintegrating, just becoming a lot more complicated/difficult to run … The EU could be “eroded from within” above all by far right-led governments using their veto (as Orbán did with Hungary) in major decisions like the EU budget, EU enlargement, the green deal, etc. They may well also simply ignore EU law, as Orbán also did. And for Nato, see previous answer – it would survive but become more paralysed in terms of longer term decision making.Ashifa Kassam:I think we saw a glimpse of how complicated things can become in the European parliament after an EU vote earlier this year aimed at increasing deportations. The immediate aftermathlaid bare just how deeply polarisedthe EU has already become, as right-wing MEPs chanted “send them back” and centre-left and left-wing MEPs shot back with “Shame on you.”View image in fullscreenThe long-simmering anger over soaring housing costs in Spain burst into public view.Photograph: Daniel Gonzalez/EPAElendXasked: Why and how have the left and centre parties failed to respond to the concerns of the electorate? How do they now need to respond?Ashifa Kassam:What comes to mind immediately is the housing crisis in Spain and beyond. It’s been just over two weeks now since the Spanish protests and encampments over the housing crisisburst into public view,laying bare the long-simmering anger over soaring housing costs.I think it’s an issue that has long been overlooked by many left and centre parties across Europe, even as vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected, and analysts warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. Last year I spoke to Jaume Collboni, the Socialist mayor of Barcelona, who (along with 21 mayors across Europe) are urging the EU to treat the surging housing costs as a “new pandemic” by unleashing billions in funding to boost affordable housing and give mayors a seat at the table to ensure measures capable of tackling housing speculation. Speaking to me,Collboni warned:“We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse.”I also think left and centre parties have done little to address the precariousness of the labour market, ie. the rise of gig jobs and, in many cases, the deterioration of public services. If you keep aneye on the Eurobarometer,the cost of living constantly ranks among the top concerns for people across Europe, hinting at the idea that this could be fertile territory for politicians to focus on. Immigration, in contrast, was in 7th place in the most recent survey.Jon Henley:I think broadly speaking mainstream parties have failed to adequately address people’s concerns about the cost of living, declining public services (healthcare, education, transport), economic/job security, etc. – as I said above, fear of/anger at some kind of “loss of status” is one of the key drivers of the far right vote. (I’m not suggesting that’s easy – it clearly isn’t, economies are struggling.)I’d also add that far-right parties are clearly extremely effective at exploiting voters’ concerns politically, including by pointing the finger at the group they think are most to blame and promising to fix things by getting rid of them.And I’d also note that mainstream parties really have not helped themselves by adopting far-right parties’ framing on several issues in hopes of hanging on to disillusioned voters – electoral evidence shows that almost never works, mainly because, as Marine Le Pen’s father Jean-Marie put it, people tend to prefer the original to the copy.Dc740asked: Did you measure any change in online activity for extremist parties like Vox in Spain after the Yandex datacentre was targeted by Ukraine?Ashifa Kassam:Funny you should ask – earlier this week, I sent out queries on this to several research groups, so it’s something we’re looking into. It’s a really interesting question. Last week, inan interview with news site Eldiario.es, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez was asked whether he was worried about foreign interference in the elections given his high profile opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and the US-Israeli attack on Iran. His answer: “Yes, and not only by nations, but also by non-state actors.”View image in fullscreenSmoke billows from a Yandex datacentre, after a drone strike.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersCapitao_barbosaasked:How much foreign funding, especially from Russia and America, is being funnelled to these parties? And can we value how much indirect support (bots, disinformation by state actors, algorithm meddling on X, etc.) they are receiving?Jon Henley:Our data teamlooked at this question a couple of years ago, before the last European parliament elections. They concluded a quarter of all private money donated to political parties in the EU was going to far-right, far-left and populist movements – aided by the fact that only a quarter of EU countries require parties to identify private donors – with €97m (about one in every seven private donation euros across the EU) going to far-right parties.A European parliament report from 2023 estimated that about $1.18bn in funding towards organisations targeting LGBTQ+ rights and promoting traditional family policies flowed into Europe from 2019 to 2023, and a 2022 declassified US intelligence assessment found the Russian government had covertly funnelled at least $300m to foreign political parties, often in Europe, from 2014.Ashifa Kassam:We’ve also had some recent reporting on the flow of funds from the US. In July, the Guardianreported thatDonald Trump’s state department intended to allocate $12m to organisations in the UK founded by prominent conservatives. Of these funds, $7m was to go to 878, a thinktank that describes itself as being devoted to “the rediscovery of our ancient culture” and “ending mass migration.”In July, the state department issued a notice of funding, offering grants for organisations and institutions interested in promotingwhat it describedas “civilisational self-confidence in Europe”.While research out of Europe, such as the Munich-based Ifo Institute,has found“no correlation” between migration and higher crime rates, the US state department notice suggested it was hoping the grants would lead to outcomes including reports on the impact of mass migration on local safety and tools to analyse impact of mass migration on democratic institutions.One user asked: How serious would you describe the threat these far-right parties pose to democracy? And to what extent do you think there is a collaboration between them and powerful social media personalities or state sponsored online social media propaganda?Jon Henley:Some far right parties definitely pose more of a threat to democracy than others. Political scientists divide far-right parties into those that essentially operate within basic democratic norms (“radical right” parties), and those that seek to overturn the system, to the extent even of condoning violence (“extreme right” parties).If we take one example, AfD in Germany could be described as extreme right in some respects (and some local branches are indeed classified as such by German domestic intelligence). Some of its positions are in clear contradiction with liberal democracy: it is openly racist, homophobic, misogynistic. It believes citizens should be ranked by its own warped criteria, including ethnicity, gender and religious belief. It flirts continually with Nazi rhetoric, imagery and symbolism.On this question I recommendthis column by Cas Mudde, a top scholar of populism and the far right, after AfD won in the recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. He argues that mainstream parties have to wake up to the fact that they are not in a battle that’s about vote share and elections, it’s about democracy itself.Ashifa Kassam:I would add that we’ve seen some fairly high-profile examples of collaboration, from Elon Musk’s repeated endorsements of the AfD on X tohis 2025 X talkwith the party’s co-leader, Alice Weidel. The Guardian has also regularly explored the interplay between the far right and social media, such as a 2025 investigationthat looked at howa network of far-right Facebook groups had become an “engine of radicalisation” by exposing hundreds of thousands of people in Britain to racist and extremist disinformation.Will Trump’s economy sink Republicans in the US midterm elections? Our reporters take your questions liveRead moreView image in fullscreenElon Musk has repeatedly endorsed the AfD.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APKilmaSelthasked: Do you think the hard right parties tend to moderate as they approach power, or do they maintain their radicalism?Jon Henley:Based on Meloni and Le Pen, I would for a long time have said yes – Meloni basically struck a bargain to get elected in which she promised to be responsible on the economy, in the EU and as regards foreign policy, as long as she could do her culture-wars stuff domestically. Le Pen has spent years “detoxifying” the National Rally and kicking out over-radical undesirables. But if you look at AfD, they haven’t moderated their language at all – if anything, they’ve hardened it – and it manifestly is not doing them any harm. And as Meloni and Le Pen have moderated their positions, we’ve started to see them being outflanked on their right, by the likes of Roberto Vannacci and his National Future in Italy and Eric Zemmour’s Reconquête in France. So I think we may be heading into a period where the former far right is effectively now part of the political landscape, like “regular” parties that will sometimes win and sometimes lose elections, and will be increasingly challenged on their right by more extreme elements.Ashifa Kassam:Vox offers another way to look at this question, as the party was founded in 2013 bydisgruntled membersof the conservative People’s party (PP). Its leader, Santiago Abascal, is a career politician who was among those who saw an opportunity to push further on the right flank of Spanish politics when it came to Catalan separatism, immigration, abortion and LGBTQ+ rights. It was a hardline stance that was often (but not always) diluted when Abascal was part of the PP; now as a separate party, they’ve seized on their electoral momentum in some regions topush the partyto heed their agenda.What topic would you like to see a Guardian Conversation on? Email us at conversations@theguardian.com with your suggestions.Explore more on these topicsEuropeConversationsThe far rightFranceGermanySpainElon MuskDonald TrumpfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Of course Trump is helping Russia in Ukraine – he’s a master of the art of betrayal | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: The old certainties have gone. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in this new and dangerous world, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The old certainties have gone. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in this new and dangerous world, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago, Florida, 28 December 2025.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago, Florida, 28 December 2025.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpOf course Trump is helping Russia in Ukraine – he’s a master of the art of betrayalJonathan FreedlandThe old certainties have gone. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in this new and dangerous worldFri 16 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.37 EDTShareDonald Trump must find it oddly frustrating. He keeps showing the world exactly who he is, and yet the world keeps refusing to believe it. As clearly as he can, he is announcing that he is not the leader of the free world, that he is not even a reliable member of the democratic west, that he is in fact an ally of its enemies – but the west, including Britain, either doesn’t fully get the message or can’t quite bring itself to draw the obvious conclusion.Trump had another go this week, finding multiple ways to declare that in the war between Russia and Ukraine, he is no mediator or peace broker but a partner of Vladimir Putin. In fairness to him, the US president had loudly issued that declaration within weeks of his return to the White House when, in February 2025, he delivered anon-camera dressing down of Volodymyr Zelenskyyin the Oval Office, seeking to humiliate the Ukrainian leader by telling him “you don’t have the cards”, even as JD Vance demanded their visitor show gratitude. That should have made Trump’s position sufficiently plain, but in the past few days he has all but put it up in lights.Earlier this week Ukrainian forces found thatan essential piece of kit– a version of Elon Musk’s Starlink system used by Kyiv to guide its drones – was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph. That meant not only a sudden shrinking of Ukraine’s ability to strike behind the frontlines, but also the hobbling of an air defence system vital in protecting the capital from Russian jet-propelled drones. This was no technical hitch. Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, is owned and controlled by the US government – and,as Reuters reported, the order to limit its use in Ukraine came from the White House. Put simply, Trump actively intervened in the war to weaken Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. “The decision will bring a lot of human losses,” Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan. “Of course, people will die.”Trump’s move was hardly a bolt from the blue. This same week,Ukraineendured at least two nights of Russian bombardment without the usual advance warnings from the US of when or where Moscow was about to strike. Trump denied that he had broken off long-established intelligence sharing with Kyiv, but that’s exactly what it looked like.All this followed the US president’s decision to break the international sanctions regime on Moscow, by agreeing tobuy $4bn worth of Russian diesel oil. That volume will barely make asplash in the US market, where high diesel prices are imperilling the Republicans’ midterm chances in several rural states that rely on the stuff, but it will come as a welcome cash infusion for Putin’s war machine. Just asRussia’s military position was looking precarious, Donald Trump has come riding to the rescue. Throw in theUS invitation to Putin to attend December’s G20 meetingat one of Trump’s golf clubs in Florida, and you have a US president who might as well be skywriting his support for Russia and his betrayal of Ukraine.In Trump’s first term, much energy was spent trying to work out what dark secret lay behind this apparent affinity with Moscow. I tend to the view advanced by my expert colleagueLuke Harding, who, when asked if Trump is a tool of the Russian intelligence services, answers with a question of his own: if Trump were a Russian asset, in what way would he behave any differently from the way he behaves now?Whatever the motive, or whether, as Harding suggests, it’s some combination ofgreed, ideology, dictator envy andkompromat, the facts are unarguable. The most powerful member of the western alliance is, at best, an unreliable partner and, at worst, in league with the alliance’s chief enemy. Why this matters should not need spelling out, least of all in the week when the head of MI5 described Russia as“aggressor number one”. For years now, the Kremlin has demonstrated its willingness to attack Nato member states, usually in the form of hybrid or “grey zone” operations that are not overt acts of war but come instead with a patina of deniability. One study found that there have been than no fewer than“151 confirmed Russian-directed industrial sabotage incidents in Europe between February 2022 and February 2026”, while last weekend broughtcredible reports of a Russian intention to assassinate executivesof key European defence firms.What should the US’s erstwhile allies do about this new reality? The first task is to keep supporting Ukraine, all the more energetically given that Washington has, in effect, switched sides. The second is to avoid an error that is looming. The midterm elections, which are little more than a fortnight away, are expected to deliver big gains for the Democrats and a big blow to Trump. If Democrats retake one or both houses of Congress, plenty of European leaders will be tempted to exhale deeply, conclude that the orange storm has passed and that normal transatlantic service is about to resume. That would be a grave mistake.For one thing, while the US president has been unbound by congressional restraint for most of the past two years, it’s not certain that a constrained Trump will be a tamed Trump. On the contrary, one Washington hand warns that he could become a “cornered animal”, even more extreme in the area where a president is freest to act, namely foreign affairs. Of course, Trump will be gone eventually, but there too lies the danger of false comfort. “This shift is permanent,” one former UK cabinet minister tells me. If nothing else, Trump has proved that Trump and Trumpism can happen: now we know that the western alliance is neither guaranteed nor unshakeable, but vulnerable to a change in the US political weather.All of this means we are living in a newly dangerous world. Witness the richly reported new bookWar is Interested in Youby Gideon Rachman, which lays bare quite how seriously leading policymakers rate the risk of a third world war. It’s an age in which we can no longer rely on others to defend us. The chilling lesson of the Starlink episode for those who depend on US hardware or software is that the US always retains an off switch. In other words, Britain and the rest of Europe have to be able to defend ourselves, with our own armies and our own arms.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe best time for governments to have made this case was the night of that shocking Oval Office scene with Zelenskyy last year. But the second-best time is now. When John Healey delivers his first budget on 28 October, this is the argument he needs to set out. As a former defence secretary, he is especially well placed to do it. The Labour manifesto of 2024 was written before Trump was re-elected, before anyone knew that in the great clash of our time the US was about to align itself with authoritarianism against democracy. Things have changed and that document can no longer be treated as holy writ. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in a changed and perilous world. Trump is telling us that in a crude, loud voice. We must listen.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistUS midterms: Trump, war and America’s futureOn Thursday, 5 November join Jonathan Freedland, Devika Bhat, Professor Adam Smith in London and David Smith and leading US commentator Tara Setmayer live from the US to discuss the results and their implications for the future of Trump, the US and global politics.Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUkraineTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting | Film adaptations | The Guardian
description: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation
Content: What a novel idea … The Shining, The Godfather and The Silence of the Lambs.Illustration: Guardian Design/Maximum Film/Alamy; Allstar Picture Library/Alamy Stock Photo; Channel 5View image in fullscreenWhat a novel idea … The Shining, The Godfather and The Silence of the Lambs.Illustration: Guardian Design/Maximum Film/Alamy; Allstar Picture Library/Alamy Stock Photo; Channel 5Film adaptationsAn open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to TrainspottingNot every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptationLouise WillderFri 16 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey this summer, buying my ticket into the popular conversation along with everyone else. This year’s other divisive adaptation, Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights, had the world and his wife arguing about it before they had even watched the film. No doubt the makers of the recentSense and Sensibility movie werealso hoping for lots of people to go and see it to discover whether they hated it.After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: “That’s exactly how I pictured it in my head.” Or even less likely: “That was better than the book.” We’re more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year’s Thursday Murder Club debacle.But what makes agoodadaptation? Like Odysseus himself, and as every Nancy Meyers fan knows: it’s complicated. I have just written a book about the towering heights and profane depths of adaptation, The Book Was Better, for which I subjected myself to some of the worst viewing experiences possible, including the soft rock opera musical Heathcliff; 1996’s freakishly bad The Island of Dr Moreau; and a horrible three-part version of Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged. But I also saw plenty of masterpieces that equalled or sometimes surpassed the originals. Here’s what I learned.View image in fullscreenAll aboard … Trainspotting.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyThe first thing to say is that the quality of the source is irrelevant. I went into my research with some pretty fixed ideas: for instance, that “the brilliant adaptations are nearly always of fiction of the second or third class”, as Anthony Burgess wrote; that some works are “unfilmable”; that classics have more “room to breathe” on TV. Soon Irealised none of these were true. Yes, sometimes workmanlike novels, such as the late 60s and early 70s triumvirate Jaws, The Godfather and The Exorcist, can be tuned to a level of genius on screen. But great books can make great films, too: Trainspotting, The Go-Between, The Leopard and Burgess’s own A Clockwork Orange are just a few examples. And sometimes, in the case of The Da Vinci Code and Fifty Shades of Grey, a deeply silly book becomes a deeply silly film.double quotation markDon’t be too reverential ... an adaptation should never be a greatest hits albumIt is true that certain books lend themselves to the screen more readily.Jane Austen’s immaculate plots of love impeded are templates that can be dressed up in the clothes of any age, like the computer template Cher Horowitz uses to plan her outfits at the start of Clueless– thene plus ultraof free-handed adaptations. Austen’s novels contain the DNA of all romcoms, just as Robinson Crusoe is found in The Martian, the gothic novel in horror films, or A Christmas Carol in every single Christmas movie. Short stories, with their twisty shocks and rush towards the end point, seem made for cinema; my favourite film,Don’t Look Now, is based on a Daphne du Maurier novella. The murky origins and elasticity of myths and their close cousins, folk and fairytales, make them ceaselessly adaptable, because they leave gaps for a film-maker to fill with their own imaginations.Being unfaithful is usually helpful. Some of the best adaptations flirt with the source material, taking frightful liberties and then abandoning it like a tabloid love rat. “Steal the parts that you need, and then run as fast as you can,” advised Paul Thomas Anderson; Hitchcock claimed he read The Birds once before making his version, and never thought about it again. (One screenwriter I spoke to told me he was once asked not to read the novel he was adapting as the production company thought it would be a hindrance). Books and films are entirely different beasts, “apples and giraffes”, as author-screenwriter Dennis Lehane once said. Adaptation is an act of translation from the verbal to the visual. A film-maker needs to find their own language.View image in fullscreenYou’ve come a long way, baby … Children of Men.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyOne of my most beloved unfaithful adaptations is Alfonso Cuarón’s 2006 Children of Men, and not just because it stars Clive Owen at the peak of his physical perfection. It manages to transform a cerebral, theological novel by the Conservative peer PD James into a dystopian thriller about populism, terror and how we treat immigrants, one which – although now two decades old – feels fresher each year. (James was delighted with it.) Cuarón used the novel as a jumping-off point, then left it behind to follow his own adventure. What remained was the central conceit: what if we lived in a world without children? The “what if” high concepts of science fiction and speculative fiction are perfect for playing fast and loose with: a vessel into which a film-maker’s own preoccupations, and the anxieties of their age, can be poured.When writer-director Sally Potter reinvented Virginia Woolf’s time-travelling fantasia Orlando, she treated it “as if the book never existed”, turning it into a lavish nose-thumb to a UK establishment that had just passed section 28. She was, she said, cruel to the novel to be kind to the film. It’s the destruction-as-creation mantra. In the hands of the right writer and director, a source can, and should, be made to submit to their will: Stanley Kubrick betrayed Stephen King’s vision of The Shining but made a tour de force. Heart of Darkness mutated into a war epic with Apocalypse Now; Red Dragon became, well, a Michael Mann film, the hypnotic Manhunter. An adaptation should never be a hollow greatest hits album. Being too reverential towards a literary source can kill it, which is why I suspect films such as The Hunger Games and The Road, lovingly and stylishly made with few changes, felt slightly bloodless on screen to me.Can anything really be faithful anyway, and to what? No story is 100 per cent original. (As Alienscreenwriter Dan O’Bannon said: “I didn’t steal from anybody. I stole fromeverybody!”) I don’t even think you can be “true to the spirit” of a text, because the spirit is different for everyone. We all have our own little films running in our heads when we read. Many see The Great Gatsby as a death knell for the US; adapters tend to think: “parties!”. I think Heathcliff is a psychopath who likes to hang little dogs; successive directors clearly didn’t. I loved discovering that Jodie Foster lobbied hard for the part of Clarice Starling in The Silence of the Lambs because, for her, the novel was about a woman saving the life of another woman while “all these fucking men” get in the way. An adaptation may just be a glimpse into another mind’s eye, but their pictures seldom match the ones we had imagined.View image in fullscreenUp to date … Renée Zellweger as Bridget Jones.Photograph: Working Title/Sportsphoto/AllstarPerhaps the most obvious example of this is casting. As sure as night follows day, Hollywood casts a better-looking actor than strictly necessary, although not always reaching “Denise Richards in hotpants as a nuclear physicist in The World is Not Enough” levels. This can be deliberate: in Robert Bloch’s novel Psycho, Norman Bates is physically repellent; Hitchcock wanted the sweet-faced Anthony Perkins for the part to wrongfoot the audience. More often it’s because, as the critic Roger Ebert observed, cinema is a machine for generating empathy, so the thinking goes that leads should be “likable” – which backfired horribly when Bruce Willis was cast as a desiccated English journalist in the notoriously disastrous adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s The Bonfire of the Vanities. But sometimes an actor who is wrong on paper can make a role their own, whether it’s Margaret Rutherford as Miss Marple, Renée Zellweger as Bridget Jones or Michael Caine as Harry Palmer in The Ipcress File (in Len Deighton’s novels he’s a northerner and doesn’t have a name). Charisma goes a long way.Perhaps in the end, adaptation all comes down to emotions and sensations. “You’ve drunk the drink, and the taste that’s left in your mouth is what you go with,” as Anthony Minghella described adapting The Talented Mr Ripley. Irvine Welsh said you must smell the books. Hossein Amini, who reinvented The Wings of the Dove as “noir in costume”, wanted to recapture that ecstatic moment when “nobody else in the world understood or experienced that book exactly like I did”.Returning to The Odyssey, I wonder why, even though Nolan did the right things, subordinating it to his worldview and faithlessly reinventing it for our age by turning a wily trickster into a traumatised veteran, the film just made me feel as if I’d been in a war: long periods of boredom and waiting punctuated by violence. Perhaps, ultimately, he overthought it and should have felt it instead? Or maybe, as the late Hilary Mantel said of adaptation, you must “put down the text, and dream it”.The Book Was Better by Louise Willder (Oneworld, £14.99). To order a copy for £13.49 go to guardianbookshop.com Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFilm adaptationsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK police force pays out after claims it protected officers accused of abusing women | Police | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Devon and Cornwall police formally apologise to nine women and settle claim without admitting liability
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Exclusive: Devon and Cornwall police formally apologise to nine women and settle claim without admitting liability
Content: Devon and Cornwall police said none of the accused male officers were any longer in positions to do with protecting women from male violence.Photograph: Andrew Lloyd/AlamyView image in fullscreenDevon and Cornwall police said none of the accused male officers were any longer in positions to do with protecting women from male violence.Photograph: Andrew Lloyd/AlamyPoliceUK police force pays out after claims it protected officers accused of abusing womenExclusive: Devon and Cornwall police formally apologise to nine women and settle claim without admitting liabilityVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA police force alleged to have promoted and protected male officers despite knowing they were accused of domestic abuse has formally apologised and paid compensation to nine women, the Guardian has learned.The women allege they were subjected to a range of abuse including rape, assault, threats, harassment and coercive control while in relationships with male officers from Devon andCornwallpolice.Some of the officers served in positions protecting women from male violence, with one appointed after allegations were made, and another kept in the sensitive position after the force received accusations.The women allege that the force in south-westEngland“covered up” the serious crimes, which it denies. The force has vowed to improve how it protects women from police-perpetrated domestic abuse.Some women suffered for about 15 years, with their tormentors allegedly weaponising the force’s “reputation” for protecting male police abusers to break their victim’s will to seek justice.The nine women, some of whom served inDevonand Cornwall police, say their claims were mocked or disbelieved and investigations were bungled. Three of the women were arrested after accusations from their alleged abusers. One, a teacher, was cautioned, which was eventually erased from her criminal record.One senior source who served in the leadership of the force told the Guardian: “At best it was bad investigations, at worst it was collusion with the attackers.”The women say at least four of the officers who abused them are still serving. The force refused to answer that question. Four of the women served in the force but have now left.One of the male officers is accused of abusing and threatening his partner, who was then a serving police officer. The woman said: “I had my baby … in my arms. My other child was screaming as he rained punches on any area of my body he could get at. He cornered me in a room and repeatedly kicked me as he stood over me. I was terrified and was begging him to stop.”It is alleged the male officer was promoted twice after the force received the allegations, and was appointed to a leadership position in the force’s effort to tackle violence against women and girls.Starting in 2004, the woman complained to police for more than 14 years, and she says nothing was done.Devon and Cornwall police has agreed to pay compensation to all nine women who sued, and the chief constable, James Vaughan, has personally apologised for the failings, the force said.Police settled the women’s claim without admitting liability after atwo-year legal battle.View image in fullscreenThe Devon and Cornwall chief constable, James Vaughan, has personally apologised for the failings, the force said.Photograph: Zoe Head-Thomas/PAAnother of the accused male officers was known by colleagues as “Teflon” because nothing stuck to him despite repeated allegations, and known also as “rapey”, and was allegedly promoted.His former partner Sarah* told the Guardian the officer pursued a prolonged, deliberate and sustained campaign of abusive, controlling and coercive behaviour over 15 years. It included physical abuse, financial abuse, intimidation, manipulation of childcare arrangements and repeated harassment, intended to undermine, distress and exert control.Another woman, June*, a teacher, said of the officer with whom she had children: “Threats he’d made against me had been routinely dismissed, belittled and ignored. [He said] ‘you’ll lose your house, your job and the kids. Don’t make me angry, I’m about to load a gun.’“I will never under any circumstances cooperate with the police again. I have lost all faith in their willingness … to protect women from police-perpetrated domestic violence. He knows he has the full protection of the police.”Another, Freya*, said: “Absolutely it was a cover-up. The police harboured him until his retirement. I got called a liar by officers online.”Other male and female officers tried to help the women but still the force failed to act, according to the combined testimony from the women.The scandal comes after repeated promises by policing nationally to prosecute male officers who abuse women. Some of the women who received compensation and an apology say the reality was, and still is, different.Paula Kressinger, who served in the force for 30 years and has waived her anonymity, criticised the force’s refusal to admit liability. She said: “The police are always trying to cover up their mistakes … trying to protect their reputation. However, I believe we would have more respect and trust in them if they were to … take responsibility for their failings. I know they continue to fail victims of crime.”Sasha* said: “The police did cover up. Devon and Cornwall promoted my ex-partner … while the abuse continued. This gave a ticket to my abuser to continue his abuse post-separation.”The inaction by the force spurred on abusers, Sasha said. “During the course of the investigation my ex-partner said everyone in the police laughed at me, and the behaviour by the investigating officers made this seem to be a true statement. The continued disrespect and disregard by Devon and Cornwall police collectively became death by a thousand cuts.“I cannot express enough how much myself and my children have suffered over a period of 15 years, and to then be totally let down by the police …”The Devon and Cornwall force was placed into special measures a fortnight ago because of overall poor performance. The force declined to answer a series of questions from the Guardian.Asked what exactly the apology was for, the force replied that the chief constable met with the women in March 2026 and “apologised for the conduct of Devon and Cornwall police in its investigations of their reports of police-perpetrated domestic abuse”.Asked whether the nine women were regarded by the force as victims of a crime, it said: “In general terms, any allegations of criminal conduct or misconduct are considered through the appropriate investigative and legal processes. These are recorded and assessed and, where appropriate, subject to criminal and/or misconduct investigation.”The force also said: “No evidence has been identified to suggest that this was, in whole or in part, the result of a cover-up or misogyny.”It said none of the accused male officers were any longer in positions to do with protecting women from male violence.The legal case was brought by the Centre for Women’s Justice, a small charity.Debaleena Dasgupta, a solicitor for the women, praised their determination and courage and said: “Litigation should never have been necessary.Each of these nine women repeatedly tried to have their reports properly investigated but instead faced errors, indifference and incompetence at every turn. Some even faced contempt.“The similarities in the failures … indicate a broken system. And none of the safeguards one might expect to pick this up did. There have been endless reviews, inquiries and recommendations, and yet litigation remained my clients’ only option.”The force said: “Our processes have changed. All police-perpetrated domestic abuse will now be investigated by the force’s professional standards department. We are currently in the process of creating a bespoke advocate role for victims of police-perpetrated domestic abuse and similar offences to ensure their voices are heard and that they are provided with a gold-standard service.”* Names have been changed.Explore more on these topicsPoliceDevonCornwallViolence against women and girlsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House
Author: Jennifer Rankin
