Content: A Ukrainian soldier sets up Starlink satellite internet system near the frontline in DonetskPhotograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenA Ukrainian soldier sets up Starlink satellite internet system near the frontline in DonetskPhotograph: ReutersUkraineStarlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says ZelenskyyUkrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White HouseJennifer Rankinin Brussels andAndrew Rothin KyivFri 16 Oct 2026 14.01 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president,Donald Trump.Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’Read moreHours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having thebiggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant.Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttlingStarshield, the military versionof the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.View image in fullscreenFirefighters working at the scene of a Russian drone strike in a residential area in Kyiv on Thursday.Photograph: Vincenzo Circosta/Anadolu/Getty ImagesSpeaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that theSpaceXStarshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.Trump said on Friday he did not think either ⁠he or ⁠Elon ​Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starshield access and that any limits were not imposed by the US.Starshield is produced by Musk’s SpaceX butcontrolled by the US government.Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 ⁠across Ukraine on Friday, hitting two shopping centres and temporarily power to more than 1 million people, ⁠officials said.When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.View image in fullscreenZelenskyy with the presidents of the European Council, António Costa (left), and the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen (right), on Friday.Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty ImagesAccording to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with Zelenskyy that “it is clear that we have a gap of €70bn that has to be covered” for 2027, although she expected Ukraine’s other partners – which she did not name – to cover part of the sum.The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments froma €90bn funding plan agreed last Decemberthat was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyDonald TrumpSpaceXEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Healey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issue | Heathrow third runway | The Guardian
description: Chancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Chancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’
Content: Heathrow has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenHeathrow has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAHeathrow third runwayHealey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issueChancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’Heather Stewartin BangkokFri 16 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow despite the prime minister declining to back it.Healey’s predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves, put approval of the long-planned runway at the heart of her “growth speech” last year, saying it would“make Britain the world’s best-connected place to do business”.However, since arriving in No 10 in July,Andy Burnhamhas ducked the issue of whether the runway should go ahead, suggesting it should be “a matter for London and Londoners”.A recent Sunday Times report suggested the prime minister had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was “unconvinced” by arguments for the megaproject.Asked for his views in Bangkok this week, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation, which recently closed. He appeared to strike a markedly more positive note than Burnham, however.“I think in recent decades, and this is true in Heathrow and airports right across the UK, that they have been a big part of jobs and growth. And the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth,” he said.Healey has insisted economic growth is his and Burnham’s “number one mission” in government.Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support.“Our shareholders would like to do this,” he said earlier this week. “They do think that things are taking a long time, and so far they have decided to be OK with that … But of course we cannot wait for ever.”The airport’s owners include Qatar’s investment authority; the French private equity firm Ardian; Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission.Healey voted in favour of the third runway when the question was put to the House of Commons in 2018.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe chancellor was in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund annual meetings but has returned toLondonto put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.The UK was praised by the IMF this week for taking action to cut its deficit, while other large economies have opted not to do so. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged Healey to “stay the course” in his budget.On Thursday, official figuresshowedthe UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August.Explore more on these topicsHeathrow third runwayHeathrow airportAirline industryJohn HealeyAndy BurnhamAir transportTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oregon shooting victims: three boys and female teacher killed at elementary school | Oregon | The Guardian
description: Father of five-year-old Rhoam Summer says family ‘broken and lost’, while seven-year-old and 54-year-old in hospital
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Father of five-year-old Rhoam Summer says family ‘broken and lost’, while seven-year-old and 54-year-old in hospital
Content: A man puts down flowers at a memorial outside the Silver Rail elementary school.Photograph: Saj Sundaram/EPAView image in fullscreenA man puts down flowers at a memorial outside the Silver Rail elementary school.Photograph: Saj Sundaram/EPAOregonOregon shooting victims: three boys and female teacher killed at elementary schoolFather of five-year-old Rhoam Summer says family ‘broken and lost’, while seven-year-old and 54-year-old in hospitalMaya YangFri 16 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 18.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAuthorities are investigating a shooting at an elementary school in Bend,Oregon, where a 16-year-old shooter killed four people before being shot dead by a bystander.The shooting took place on Thursday afternoon at Silver Rail elementary school, about 125 miles (200km) south-east of Portland.Here is what we know so far about the four victims, including three children aged five, eight and 11, and a 25-year old teacher, as well as the two people injured.Rhoam SummerIn a Facebook group post, Rhoam Summer’s father Kelik Summer posted about his five-year old son’s death, saying that Thursday was “the worst day of my life.” He added: “My son Rhoam was killed in a school shooting. We are broken and lost, but are surrounded by friends and family who are keeping us safe.”Rhoam’s grandfather Bryan Jolly also confirmed his grandson’s death to the New York Times. Jollydescribedthe tragedy as “senseless and a shock”, adding that Rhoam was “in my house a lot and in my garden with me and wrestling with me on the couch”.View image in fullscreenRhoam Summer, who was killed in the shooting.Photograph: GofundMe“He was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear,” Jolly said.A separate GoFundMe page that appears to have been set up by friends of Rhoam’s family said: “In the wake of an unimaginable tragedy, the Summer family is grieving the heartbreaking loss of their sweet five-year-old son, Rhoam. There are no words that can ease the pain of losing a child, and no family should ever have to experience a loss like this.”Bend police also confirmed Rhoam’s identity on Friday afternoon.Eight-year old boyPolice are not releasing his identification at his family’s request.Eleven-year old boyPolice are not releasing his identification at his family’s request.Megan LambertTwenty-five-year old Megan Lambert, a teacher at the school, was identified as another victim killed in the shooting, Bend police said on Friday.In a statement shared with Bend police, Lambert’s family said: “Megan was a native central Oregonian. She grew up in Bend. She had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. She was a volleyball coach. She actually turned down pay for her first season as a coach, so families who couldn’t afford to participate could have the chance to play the sport she loved.”“Her goal was to be an educator, and teach in the school district she loved growing up in … Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher, though she subbed there for many years … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart,” her family added.The Central Oregon Volleyball Club website lists Megan as a local high school coach and describes her as a “blessing” who has done “so much for her team”.Saylor GrahamSeven-year old Saylor Graham was injured in the shooting, according to several GoFundMe accounts set up by co-workers and friends of her family. “The family is focused on being at the hospital while their child fights for their life,” one account said.“Right now, they are carrying the impossible weight of traveling to and from the hospital, staying near their child, caring for their other child, trying to keep up their household, and missing work during this crisis,” it added.View image in fullscreenSaylor Graham, who doctors said was in a ‘serious but stable’ condition.Photograph: GoFundMeA business partner of Saylor’s mother, Danielle Graham, declined to be interviewed but confirmed Saylor’s identity to the Guardian.Meanwhile, Bend police said on Friday that a seven-year old girl who was shot “is receiving life-saving care” at Oregon Health & Science University hospital in Portland, adding: “She is in serious but stable condition.”Becky DruryFifty-four-year old Becky Drury was also injured in the shooting, with her mother-in-law Yvonne Drurypostingon Facebook: “Our wonderful daughter-in-law, Becky was shot thr[ough] her left arm and right hand, and is recovering in the hospital after surgery this afternoon.”In the same post, Becky’s son Will Drury said: “Her left arm took a lot of damage so there’s a long recovery and more surgeries ahead. Her right hand took a hit as well, which also required surgery, but it is much less severe. The good news is she will be OK and we all get to keep that magnificent woman we love so much in our lives.”Bend police said on Friday: “The injured 54-year-old female teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and is currently receiving treatment at St Charles Bend [hospital].”Explore more on these topicsOregonUS school shootingsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Katie Zacharia fired after five days as White House press secretary | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Zacharia hosted widely panned first briefing on Tuesday and faced scrutiny after admitting she didn’t pass bar exam
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: Zacharia hosted widely panned first briefing on Tuesday and faced scrutiny after admitting she didn’t pass bar exam
Content: Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the press briefing room at the White House on 13 October.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenKatie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the press briefing room at the White House on 13 October.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APTrump administrationKatie Zacharia fired after five days as White House press secretaryZacharia hosted widely panned first briefing on Tuesday and faced scrutiny after admitting she didn’t pass bar examAriana BaioFri 16 Oct 2026 15.29 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia,was firedon Friday, just five days after she assumed the role, according to a White House official.Zacharia confirmed her departure from the White House on Friday evening.“President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to,” shewrote on social media. “It was an honor to work for him.”Zacharia, a little-known conservative political commentator prior to her selection as the president’s chief spokesperson, came under immediate scrutiny after a widely pannedinauguralbriefing on Tuesday. The 14-minute exchange was soon followed by a barrage of questions over her legal credentials after she admitted she did not pass the bar exam.In an interview on Thursday, Zachariadetailed her whirlwind sprintto the podium to replace Karoline Leavitt as the White House press secretary, stepping into the role as the president faces multiple headwinds just weeks before the midterm elections next month.Katie Zacharia’s five days as press secretary expose flaws in Trump’s TV-driven hiringRead moreOn Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia’s tenure would be short-lived, telling reporters thathe had askedhis embattled press secretary to “reconsider” the job.“I said: ‘Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don’t need it,’” Trump said, speaking outside the White House. “I said to her: ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider.’”During her first – and apparently only – press briefing, Zacharia stumbled through prepared remarks highlighting Trump’s accomplishments in his presidency. She made a notable gaffe when she called her husband “the president”.Members of the White House press corps were left puzzled when she departed the podium after only taking questions from three predominantly conservative media outlets.She spent the next hours and days trying to clarify swirling questions about her résumé, after reports emerged revealing thatZacharia, whom Trump has referred to as an “attorney”, had never passed the bar exam. She later confirmed that she took the bar once and failed.Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school in California, and repeatedly called herself a lawyer.She defended using the term to describe herself professionally, claiming there was a difference between a “lawyer” and an “attorney”, a title reserved for those licensed to practice law.She had previouslyshared social media postsidentifying herself as an “attorney”. And when the White House officially announced her appointment, the statementdescribedher as an “attorney”.Over the last few days, Zacharia has spoken with members of the media in an effort to try to move past the criticism and make the case that she was ready to take on the role as the president’s chief spokesperson.In an unexpectedly tough interview on Thursday evening,Fox host Sean Hannity grilled Zachariaabout her first press briefing, asking bluntly: “What happened?”Zacharia sought to explain that she had had little time to prep in the days betweenaccepting the job and holding her first press briefingand argued that the conservative Daily Mail, one of only three outlets she took questions from, was “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Hannity, a Trump ally, also pressed her on her decision to identify herself as a “lawyer”.“Why get into this long, drawn-out definition of the difference between a lawyer and an attorney? Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction,” he asked.In a Friday appearance onFox & Friends, host Lawrence Jones continued, telling Zacharia: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary, and you never want to be the story.”Jones then asked: “Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?”“I’m standing here,” Zacharia replied, referring to the fact that she was speaking from the White House north lawn.She said she hoped to “build the trust and confidence of everyone around me” but could not say when her next press briefing would be.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarks | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Alan Feeney, who sat on Solihull and Birmingham councils, said there was ‘no excuse’ for his comments
Author: Sinéad Campbell
Headline: Alan Feeney, who sat on Solihull and Birmingham councils, said there was ‘no excuse’ for his comments
Content: Alan Feeney was revealed to have made racist comments about Asian homeowners in secretly recorded footage.Photograph: ITVView image in fullscreenAlan Feeney was revealed to have made racist comments about Asian homeowners in secretly recorded footage.Photograph: ITVReform UKReform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarksAlan Feeney, who sat on Solihull and Birmingham councils, said there was ‘no excuse’ for his commentsSinéad CampbellFri 16 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlan Feeney has resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after backlash overracist comments that were capturedin an undercover investigation.In aFacebookpost on Friday, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”Earlier this week, anITVinvestigation revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.Feeney has apologised for his comments. “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said,” he wrote in a Facebook post.“The comments do not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report. These are communities I have supported countless times in my personal and professional life over many years, many of whom I have been lucky enough to call friends.”Earlier this year, Feeney won seats in the Shard End ward ofBirminghamcity council and the Castle Bromwich ward of Solihull metropolitan borough council, and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull.Following the ITV investigation, which is part of a longer series onReform UK, Feeney announced on Facebook that he was leaving Reform for “personal reasons”, but kept his seats as an independent councillor before resigning.In a Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “Byelections will be held on a timescale laid out by those councils in the due course. I hope that in time these councils, and the communities they serve can heal and move on.”Secretly filmed footage showed Feeney making racist remarks alongside two other Reform candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, while canvassing during May’s local elections. Both Campbell and Whelan have also resigned after the fallout from the investigation.Nigel Farage has repeatedly pledged to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots”. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.The clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Feeney calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.In a Facebook post Feeney wrote: “I understand that my words have caused hurt and anger, particularly among those from the communities I serve. For that, I am deeply sorry. I will be undertaking intensive personal analysis to understand how these sentiments could have taken root, and ensure they can never do so again.”Alan Feeney and Reform UK have been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsReform UKLocal politicsHate crimeBirminghamLocal governmentITV NewsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand was ‘wild-eyed maniac’ when trying to drag woman into toilets, court told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Woman says she ‘wrenched’ herself free from alleged assault that she says took place when she was working at MTV in 2001
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Woman says she ‘wrenched’ herself free from alleged assault that she says took place when she was working at MTV in 2001
Content: Russell Brand leaving Southwark crown court on Friday. He is facing three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenRussell Brand leaving Southwark crown court on Friday. He is facing three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAUK newsRussell Brand was ‘wild-eyed maniac’ when trying to drag woman into toilets, court toldWoman says she ‘wrenched’ herself free from alleged assault that she says took place when she was working at MTV in 2001Emine SinmazFri 16 Oct 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand transformed into a “wild-eyed maniac” when he tried to drag a woman into a men’s toilets for a sexual encounter before she “wrenched” herself free, a court has heard.The 51-year-old comedian is accused of indecently assaulting the woman, who told Southwark crown court: “I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me.”The woman, who was working for MTV at the time, said she did not report the incident then because she was “scared” as Brand was famous “and a big asset” to the TV channel.Brand is facing three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges.Wearing a dark pinstripe suit, the TV personality sat bolt upright in the dock on Friday as the woman gave evidence from behind a screen.She said she was working at MTV in 2001 when she met Brand and they had “banter” about an I Am Spartacus T-shirt he was wearing. She later offered to show him the way to the toilets, where he allegedly assaulted her.The woman said she felt “bewildered and confused”, telling the court: “This person went from someone jovial and friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet.”Detailing the alleged assault, she added: “His demeanour changed. He grabbed my forearm and he was leaning into the door. It was quite forceful, the grip. It took me unawares, I wasn’t expecting that.”In response to questions from the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, the woman said Brand began pleading with her to come into the toilets as she tried to get away.“I said to him: ‘What are you doing? Are you mad? Let me go.’ Then he started to plead, almost ‘go on, go on, come in’,” she told the court.She said he had a “wild” look in his eyes and she had to use her strength to escape his “hard” grip in an interaction that lasted about 20 seconds.The woman said she told two colleagues what had happened but she did not make a police complaint until she saw a 2023 documentary that accused Brand of sexual misconduct.“It brought everything back,” she said. “I thought I’d managed to get away. It could’ve been very different … I thought it was the right thing to come forward.”In cross-examination, the defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested the woman had reassessed her memory of the incident after the documentary, but she said it had not changed her mind.“I don’t think it’s quite as straightforward as that,” she said. “It would have been my word against his, I had a job to consider, I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me. I managed to get myself out of the situation.”She rejected the barrister’s suggestion that Brand had “invited” her into the toilet for a consensual sexual encounter. She said: “You don’t drag someone by the arm, not in my world anyway. You don’t grip someone to drag them in, that’s not consensual.”She said he had been “grabbing and pulling” her, telling the court: “That’s not inviting someone in. That’s forcing someone to do something against their will.”Winter suggested it was “a short-lived, very, very minor incident” and that after the woman declined, Brand “left it there”. The woman responded: “The intent was there. It could have been very different.”Earlier, the court heard evidence from witnesses relating to the first complainant, who gave evidence on Thursday. She alleges Brand raped her after a fringe cabaret show at the 1999 Labour party conference in Bournemouth.Andrew Dobson, a former flatmate of Brand’s who composed the music for the show, described his impressions of the comedian, saying he was “a very vibrant character, very egotistical … lively, sort of quite demanding and persuading”.Dobson told the court: “I think sex was a huge preoccupation for him. I do recall clearly nights where the pursuit of ultimately getting somebody into bed would have been a preoccupation.”He said there was a “hurried and rushed” tone at their shared guesthouse in Bournemouth on the morning after their final show. “I recall Russell coming in and there suddenly being an urgency to leave,” he said.John Rogers, who wrote the show, described Brand’s reaction to an “encounter” the actor had had with a woman during the week of the conference, saying it was “a bit odd” and he appeared “flustered”.The court also heard statements from two women whom the first complainant had told about the alleged rape after the 2023 documentary.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Met police investigating row over founding of Your Party | UK news | The Guardian
description: Inquiry said to have been launched after force received report ‘relating to alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database’
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Inquiry said to have been launched after force received report ‘relating to alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database’
Content: Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana founded the leftwing Your Party in 2025.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenJeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana founded the leftwing Your Party in 2025.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyUK newsMet police investigating row over founding of Your PartyInquiry said to have been launched after force received report ‘relating to alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database’Alexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice are carrying out a criminal investigation into a row over the founding of Your Party, which split the leftwing party as it was established last year.A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan police said they had launched an investigation after they received a report in September 2025 “relating to the alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database”, the Politico website reported.Your Party was founded in summer 2025 by the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and the former Labour MP Zarah Sultana, both of whom now sit as Your Party MPs in the House of Commons.But relations between the different factions in the party have been strained since its creation in July last year. That September Sultana revealed a new membership portal on X, and encouraged members to become paying members for £55.Corbyn described the site as a “false membership system” and told supporters to ignore an email requesting funds. Sultana said her only aim had been to “safeguard the grassroots involvement that is essential to building this party”, and later accused the party of being run by a“sexist boys’ club”.Officers had now arrested a man on suspicion of an offence under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act, a police spokesperson told Politico. The man was released pending further inquiries and has not been charged.Officers also previously interviewed a woman in her 30s under caution in connection with the same investigation. The spokesperson added: “The investigation continues.” The police spokesperson did not name any political party in their statement, and the spokesperson did not confirm which political party their investigation was related to.Sources told the Guardian that the investigation was linked to the long-running dispute connected to the establishment of Your Party. Neither the man arrested nor the woman interviewed by police are MPs and neither have been charged with an offence. Neither Corbyn nor Sultana were accused of wrongdoing, Politico reported.In January, it emerged that the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) advised the party that while it was taking no further action over the Your Party membership portal launch,it may have involved “serious criminal activity”and should be referred to the police.A Your Party spokesperson said: “It would not be appropriate to comment any further about ongoing police investigations.”They also said: “We can reassure our members and supporters that our systems are secure and that this was an isolated incident.”Your Party has struggled to make a widespread national impact since it was founded, while the Green party of England and Wales, rebranded as an eco-socialist party, has seen its membership quadruple.In February, Corbyn won a comprehensive victory to become thede facto leader of the leftwing startup party. He said Your Party would work with the Green party and others to push for a “coordinated left-flank offensive” against Reform and Labour. Sultana was also voted on to the party’s leadership committee under its collective leadership model.Corbyn-backed candidates took 14 of the 24 available places on the party’s central executive committee (CEC). Sultana-backed candidates took seven of the seats and three went to independents.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK national security adviser under pressure over wife’s comment on supporting Palestine Action | Palestine Action | The Guardian
description: Author Sarah Helm, married to Jonathan Powell, wrote to back novelist Sally Rooney’s support of proscribed direct action group
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Author Sarah Helm, married to Jonathan Powell, wrote to back novelist Sally Rooney’s support of proscribed direct action group
Content: The author Sarah Helm is a former Sunday Times journalist and diplomatic editor at the Independent, and spent many years covering the Middle East.Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe author Sarah Helm is a former Sunday Times journalist and diplomatic editor at the Independent, and spent many years covering the Middle East.Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianPalestine ActionUK national security adviser under pressure over wife’s comment on supporting Palestine ActionAuthor Sarah Helm, married to Jonathan Powell, wrote to back novelist Sally Rooney’s support of proscribed direct action groupRobyn VinterandRachel HallFri 16 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, is under pressure to distance himself from a comment made by his wife, the award-winning writerSarah Helm, in support of Palestine Action.The post was made in defence of the critically acclaimed Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who said she had been forcedto pull her books from shelvesin the UK after pledging proceeds from their sales to Palestine Action.Helm, a former Sunday Times journalist and diplomatic editor at the Independent who spent many years covering the Middle East, wrote on X indicating support for the direct action group, which was proscribed last year.Under terror laws, this could constitute a criminal offence, carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years in prison. The ban has so far resulted in more than 3,700 arrests for backing the group, with more than 2,250 people formally charged as terrorists.In response to comments by the broadcaster Adam Boulton that Rooney’s support for Palestine was “anti-Jewish”, Helm wrote: “God help us authors who support Palestine andPalestine Action. Sounds like Adam would have all our books swept off the shelves in a jiffy.”Police said the post was “in the process of being assessed” to determine whether an investigation was required.Downing Street distanced itself from Helm’s post on Friday, with a spokesperson saying: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”Helm’s works include a bookabout the women imprisoned by the Nazis at the Ravensbrück concentration camp, andLoyalty, a play about the Iraq war, inspired by her husband’s decade as the chief of staff to the then prime minister, Tony Blair.The author, who is writing a book about Gaza, married Powell in 2007. He was appointed in 2024 as a national security adviser under Keir Starmer.View image in fullscreenJonathan Powell.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesAccording to government guidance, being married to a suspected or convicted terrorist would normally result in the revocation of security clearance. Under the vetting framework for a job as national security adviser, being married to someone tied to a proscribed terrorist organisation is viewed as creating an automatic, unmitigated national security risk.Responding to questions about Powell’s position after his wife’s comments, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”A spokesperson for Defend Our Juries, a free speech group which supports the right for people to protest peacefully, thanked Helm for “defying this absurdly authoritarian ban”.“How can Andy Burnham’s government possibly defend this banin the supreme court next monthwhen his own national security adviser’s wife has openly defied it? This unprecedented attack on free speech in our country is plainly unsustainable,” they said. “We know of 36 people who have been arrested and had their homes raided for similarly expressing support for Palestine Action on social media.“We hope Sarah will not face the same treatment for standing up for free speech and Palestinian lives. But her defiance further exposes the absurdity of a ban that cannot be enforced against everyone who challenges it. There are simply too many of us who will continue to defy this unjust law until the government is forced to see sense and abandon it.”However, the Campaign Against Antisemitism called for Helm to “face the full force of the law”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA spokesperson said: “This is gobsmacking. Clearly, the police need to investigate and Sarah Helm must face the full force of the law, just like others who appear to express support for any proscribed terrorist organisation.“But this raises extremely serious questions forJonathan Powelland the government. Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country’s national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post.”A Met Police spokesperson said: “We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action. It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required.View image in fullscreenSally Rooney has been supported in her stance by an open letter signed by hundreds of writers.Photograph: Kalpesh Lathigra/ FaberHundreds of writers have signed an open letter in support of Rooney, whose books includeNormal PeopleandConversations With Friends, warning that “a country that bans its writers for speaking out is not a free country”.The letter has been signed by 419 novelists, poets, editors and illustrators including Ali Smith, Kamila Shamsie, Robert Macfarlane, Daisy Johnson, Eliza Clark, Jeanette Winterson, Alice Oseman, Derek Landy, Louise O’Neill, AM Dassu and Nikesh Shukla.The letter states: “As authors, illustrators, poets, and editors, we stand withSally Rooneyand Faber Books, and condemn a government whose actions, and inactions, have led to her books being pulled from sale in the UK.“Writers already face book bans worldwide and at home. It is unconscionable that a government can now effectively ban a single author for protesting that government’s own conflation of protest with terrorism. What future governments might do with this power should frighten us all.”Rooney said she had made the decision to withdraw from the UK market with her publisher, Faber, after learning that passing earnings on to her for the sale of her books in the UK could constitute a serious criminal offence. In a letter shared with the Guardian, Rooney said she was “wholly prepared to accept the consequences”. Faber will continue to sell Rooney’s books in other countries.Explore more on these topicsPalestine ActionJonathan PowellUK security and counter-terrorismSally RooneyProtestFreedom of speechActivismnewsShareReuse this content

title: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes | China | The Guardian
description: The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies
Author: Danny Vincent
Headline: The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies
Content: China disaster simulator in HangzhouChinaChina’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishesThe concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragediesDanny Vincentin Hong KongFri 16 Oct 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods.“I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-westChina. “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.”She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario.View image in fullscreenParticipants brace for surging water in a flash flood simulator at the Lvxing centre in Hangzhou.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersStanding in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.”Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”.Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments.At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster.“I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.”It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations.View image in fullscreenPeople want to feel ‘what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like’, says general manager Wang Kuanghan.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersThe offering are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake.Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country.In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis.‘A new generation of travellers’“The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction.In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside.View image in fullscreenA classroom inside a destroyed school building lies preserved following the 2008 Sichuan earthquake at Beichuan.Photograph: Wu Hong/EPAIn Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck.“I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.”Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered.In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wanghas seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres. Japan’s official position is that it acknowledges that large numbers of civilians were killed but says the number of victims is “difficult to determine”.View image in fullscreenPeople choose chrysanthemums to dedicate to victims at the Nanjing Massacre memorial hall in September 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesEntry to the hall is free but tourists must book online The local government reserves 25,000 places a day. In August, tickets to attend the museum are frequently sold out in advance, she says.“There are more tragic sites in China, and I see more people interested to know about that. That’s a new trend” says Wang.Inside the memorial hall hang photos of victims. “They [visitors] feel sad when they see those pictures, when they see those kids who were killed … After the visit, they feel relieved, and they feel encouraged that they should work harder to make China stronger,” she says.*Name has been changedAdditional reporting byYu-chen Liin TaipeiExplore more on these topicsChinaExtreme weatherAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Katie Zacharia’s five days as press secretary expose flaws in Trump’s TV-driven hiring | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: The president reportedly chose Zacharia after seeing her on television, but her first press briefing and disastrous interviews sealed her fate
Author: David Smith
Headline: The president reportedly chose Zacharia after seeing her on television, but her first press briefing and disastrous interviews sealed her fate
Content: Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia delivered her first press conference in the White House press briefing room on Tuesday. She was fired on Friday.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenFormer White House press secretary Katie Zacharia delivered her first press conference in the White House press briefing room on Tuesday. She was fired on Friday.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPATrump administrationAnalysisKatie Zacharia’s five days as press secretary expose flaws in Trump’s TV-driven hiringDavid Smithin WashingtonThe president reportedly chose Zacharia after seeing her on television, but her first press briefing and disastrous interviews sealed her fateFri 16 Oct 2026 18.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 20.50 EDTShareAnd so Katie Zacharia joins the mayfly ranks of Liz Truss,Anthony Scaramucci, New Coke, CNN+ and Quibi. To say she burned twice as bright and half as long would be too kind. She went out like a firework on a soggy night.The White House confirmed on Friday that Zacharia wasleaving her roleas press secretary after just five days on the job. No one was surprised after a lacklustre press briefing debut and scrutiny over her legal credentials.But even more importantly, Zacharia lived by the sword and died in the one arena thatDonald Trumptruly cares about: television.She reportedly got the job by closely monitoring the US president’s public schedule and tracked his active hours on Truth Social to predict exactly when he would be watching TV. She then timed her own appearances on air to make sure she caught his eye. The fact that she fitted the glossy blond aesthetic from what Trump calls “central casting” also helped.But TV also proved her undoing. On Thursday, Zachariagave a series of interviewsto Trump-friendly outlets in a desperate bid for redemption. Instead, she sealed her own fate with more hapless performances.She must have expected Fox News hostSean Hannity, who has even spoken at Trump rallies, to give her an easy ride. But even he was sceptical when she admitted she had “stepped up to the plate with very little prep time” for the first briefing. Hannity asked: “Am I hearing that you think the staff should have prepped you better?”Zacharia rejected the notion that she had only taken questions from conservative outlets, incorrectly asserting that the Daily Mail is “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Hannity also quizzed her about her dubious legal credentials, saying: “Why not just say: ‘I went to Pepperdine law school, and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn’t pass?’”Zacharia tried again onFox & Friendsbut ran into host Lawrence Jones, who said: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary and you never want to be the story.”He also asked: “Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?” Zacharia responded: “I’m standing here,” referring to the fact that she was speaking from the White House North Lawn.Her exit hours later was met with widespread ridicule – and a measure of human compassion for someone whom Trump had subjected to a very public humiliation.Scaramucci, who lasted only 11 days as White House communications director during Trump’s first term,tweeted: “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”Joe Lockhart, a former White House press secretary under Bill Clinton, said in a phone interview: “It’s hard to generate sympathy for this woman, but there was no way for her to succeed. It takes years to be ready to do that job. Not days, not hours. I spent 20 years preparing for my first briefing from the very first campaign I did. It was very unfair for her, but very bad judgment on her part to think she could wander out there and smile.”The fiasco was also a reminder of Trump’s woeful judgment as a manager whose chief criteria are looks and loyalty. During his 2015 presidential campaign, he promised that he would only hire “the best people”, comparing his future administration to corporate boardrooms. His first national security adviser,Michael Flynn, resigned after 23 days.His second term has featured incompetents such as Kristi Noem, fired as homeland security secretary after multiple controversies, Robert F Kennedy Jr, a health secretary who spent years promoting anti-scientific claims about vaccine safety, and Pete Hegseth, a defence secretary who bungled the Iran war and announced a livestreamed execution only to be overruled by his boss.Kurt Bardella, a political commentator, said: “It shows the limitations of the president making decisions like this based solely on: ‘Oh, I liked watching this clip of her on this segment in the most friendly environment possible.’ We’ve seen this time and again with this president selecting figures for very meaningful, important and substantive positions solely based on cable news, and just look at how the war in Iran is going to know that ain’t working out too good.”Trump also entrusted tech bro Elon Musk to take a chainsaw to the federal government. His choice of personnel has had damaging consequences for US institutions. The position of White House press secretary is the latest example.Lockhart added: “It one more time shows how Trump cheapens everything he touches. He wants everything to be in his image. He tears down the East Wing. He puts his name onthe Kennedy Center. Now he has tried to put someone in that job who reflects him, not the country and the values and the power of this country.“He has cheapened another institution. I hold that room somewhat dear, and it’s sad to watch each of these things get remade in his image because he is cheap, tawdry, corrupt, and he has managed to make the United States reflect those values around the world rather than the ones we knew about for 250 years before him.”Zacharia will survive and maybe thrive as a “former White House press secretary” in rightwing media, just as Scaramucci still makes the most of his “former” title. Meanwhile, the hunt is on, presumably, for a successor who can at least look reporters in the eye and not get into a tangle about their credentials.Who could replace Katie Zacharia as White House press secretary?Read moreBut the cold truth is that the job of White House press secretary is superfluous when Trump is a word machine who holds two-hour campaign rallies, turns social media into a stream of consciousness andtakes calls from reporterson his mobile phone. Playing the role of Trump’s spokesperson carries the inherent risk of inadvertently factchecking him.“He’s certainly remade the job because all the press secretary does now is repeat what the president says and tell him how brilliant he was in saying it,” Lockhart concluded. “It used to be that credibility was the currency in the room. It’s impossible to be credible when you’re working for someone who lies almost every time he speaks.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationTelevisionUS politicsDonald TrumpTV newsFox NewsanalysisShareReuse this content
