title: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the world
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the world
Content: A scene from NAZA, which interviewed military insiders anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night.Photograph: NAZA/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA, which interviewed military insiders anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night.Photograph: NAZA/The GuardianNAZA‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentaryFilm interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the worldSammy GecsoylerFri 16 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCritics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentaryNAZAas a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, wasreleased in UK cinemas this weekand will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.44:17NAZA: the film Israel does not want you to see - videoThe Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an exposé” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.When the film opened in Italy last month, ittopped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.1:55NAZA - official trailerThe film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.Various organisations, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went onto win the special jury prize.Explore more on these topicsNAZAIsraelGazaIsrael-Gaza warPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: I’ve debated with Israel’s most fervent defenders – NAZA debunks their talking points | Mehdi Hasan | The Guardian
description: The film’s testimonies from Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers expose years of baseless propaganda. Don’t take my word – take theirs
Author: Mehdi Hasan
Headline: The film’s testimonies from Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers expose years of baseless propaganda. Don’t take my word – take theirs
Content: A scene from NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: NAZA/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: NAZA/The GuardianOpinionNAZAI’ve debated with Israel’s most fervent defenders – NAZA debunks their talking pointsMehdi HasanThe film’s testimonies from Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers expose years of baseless propaganda. Don’t take my word – take theirsFri 16 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 09.21 EDTShareIwatched the extraordinary newGuardian-produced documentaryfrom Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor the other night, and I have struggled to stop thinking about it ever since. The film’s title comes from a Hebrew military term for collateral damage, and it consists of eye-opening interviews with two dozen Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers sitting in darkness, often on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, their voices “digitally altered to disguise their identities”.At one point, Abraham asks one of the soldiers a remarkably blunt question.“Do you think it’s a genocide?”“Yes,” the soldier replies. “Completely.”He points to what he describes as the “intentional” killing of Palestinian civilians, including children.“We have to describe things as they really are.” That sentence could serve as the film’s subtitle. Because for the past three years, there have in effect been two wars over Gaza: the war itself, and the war over how we are allowed to describe it.double quotation markHow much Israeli testimony describing the killing of children are we expected to ignore?HasIsraelbeen targeting civilian sites – or is Hamas simply using “human shields”?Were Palestinian children knowingly killed – or is even making that claim anti-Jewish “blood libel”?Were hungry Palestinians shot while seeking food – or was Hamas responsible for those killings?Are many of the Palestinian dead really civilians – or are huge numbers of them “terrorists”?Does the Israeli military’s conduct in Gaza invite comparisons to the Holocaust – or is making such a comparison itself evidence of antisemitism?NAZA matters because, one after another, Israelis who actually participated in the surveillance and killing infrastructure of the Gaza war weigh in on these issues themselves. And what they say is pretty devastating.I have spent the past few years debating some of Israel’s most committed defenders – on the live stages ofOpen to Debatein New York and theMunk Debatesin Toronto, oncable news, and on Piers Morgan’sYouTube show.I wish every one of them would sit down and watch all 80 minutes of NAZA. Not because the film contains another argument from me. Because it contains testimony from precisely the side they think they’re on.The ‘human shields’ defenseIsrael and its supporters have repeatedlyclaimedthat Israel is confronted by the “Hamas human shield strategy” in Gaza, in which “Hamas deliberately embeds its fighters within civilian areas”.How do human beings explain taking part in genocide? NAZA provides a chilling look | Omer BartovRead moreIn NAZA, Israeli military and intelligence sources undermine that defense. Listen, for example, to the Israeli source in NAZA who unpacks theAI-led strategyto track and then bomb Hamas commanders at night, in their homes, alongside their families. “Hamas uses human shields in some cases but the human shield claim about private houses is absurd. It’s just not true. We bomb them in houses because that’s how we find them,” he said. “They just come home to sleep. That’s where we catch them.”The civilians were not shielding the target. The target was followed by Israelto the civilians.The childrenSome have claimed that media coverage of Palestinian children killed in Gazaconstitutes“blood libel” and stirs ancient images of “the child-killing Jew”.“Ask how Israel is able to target innocent children with such deadly accuracy and no one can tell you,” the celebrated British novelist Howard Jacobsonwrote. “Ask why they would want to target innocent children … and no one can tell you that either.”NAZA settles the argument: it is not antisemitic blood libel to point out that Israel knowingly killed children in Gaza. One Israeli intelligence source describes being able to hack the phone of a 12-year-old Palestinian girl in order to figure out when her father – the actual target – might return home. At that point, the house could be bombed.Abraham asks the obvious question. What happens to the 12-year-old girl?“You hack her phone and then kill her,” comes the reply.What is perhaps most chilling is not merely the content of the answer but its delivery: calm, matter-of-fact, almost bureaucratic.Another Israeli interviewee recalls a boy entering a military-controlled zone. “He didn’t do anything,” the soldier says. “They bombed him.”Then comes one of the most horrifying details in an already horrifying film: according to the soldier, corpses are left to be eaten by dogs.So perhaps the question is no longer: why would Israeli forces ever kill children? Perhaps the question instead should be: how much Israeli testimony describing the killing of children are we expected to ignore?The ‘terrorist’ body countSome military experts are still, after all the slaughter,arguingthat Israel achieved a historically low civilian-to-combatant casualty ratio in Gaza, while uncritically parroting Israeli claims that more than 24,000 combatants had been killed.But NAZA raises a rather fundamental question. Who gets counted as a “combatant”?Israeli soldiers and intelligence officials describe “annihilation zones” in northern Gaza in which Palestinian civilians who crossed invisible boundaries could be killed.“Anyone who enters the zone needs to die,” one interviewee says the troops were told.His unit killed 140 unarmed people in such zones. Yet, he says, they were counted as terrorists anyway. “Whoever you decided to kill was considered a terrorist.”The food linesWhen reports emerged of Palestinians being shot around food-distribution sites in 2025, supporters of Israel argued that Hamas did the killing.If they watched NAZA, however, they would hear Israeli soldiers and intelligence officials breezily describe how Israeli military snipers gunned down hungry and desperate Palestinians who had stepped out of line to swarm the food distribution sites like “ants”.One interviewee tells Abraham how “three separate teams of soldiers would massacre the population” as they tried to reach the food. They did not mention Hamas.ComparisonsSupporters of Israel have long balked at comparisons between Israel’s government and the Third Reich. In June 2026, Haviv Rettig Gur, Israeli journalist and Middle East analyst at Bari Weiss’s Free Press, published anessaytitled: “Why the Gaza war cannot be compared to the Holocaust”. Gur called the comparison an “inversion so callous it’s hard to believe” and argued that its purpose was specifically “to make the Jews into the Nazis”.In NAZA, an anguished Israeli soldier tells Abraham that he visited Poland as a school kid, studied the Nazis from a very early age, and wondered how such Germans, the embodiment of “pure evil”, could “live with themselves”.Watching NAZA was like peering through a window – and seeing the machinery of killing in Gaza | Mahmoud MushtahaRead moreNow, as an adult and as a veteran of Gaza, he says, “I understand it,” revealing how he and his fellow soldiers blew up homes in the strip and then returned to their university degrees. In a haunting line, he says: “I still see those Nazis as evil, but what does that mean I am?”Understandably, the comparison triggers particularly sensitive reactions among Israelis, and as Abraham himself emphasized in a recentHaaretz podcast, he isn’t interested in a “simplistic and direct comparison”. Rather, he believes the Holocaust holds universal lessons about how individuals contribute to systems of dehumanization.“He understood something about being a perpetrator,” Abraham said of the soldier. “When we use the words ‘never again’, part of that is about understanding patterns of dehumanization.”Is this Israeli veteran really engaged in a bigoted propaganda campaign? Or does he have something to teach us about what happens when an entire people are dehumanized?The ‘blood libel’NAZA has provoked incendiary responses from officials in Israel.Former Israeli prime minister Naftali Bennettdenouncedthe documentary as a “horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters”. Israel’s military chief, Eyal Zamir,invokedthe language of “blood libel” too.Their rhetoric is beyond parody. We have become numb to Israeli officials smearing and dehumanizing Palestinian eyewitnesses. But are we seriously expected to believe that these Israeli military insiders and eyewitnesses are blood-libeling …themselves?The inconvenient yet undeniable truth for Israel and its apologists is that over the course of less than 90 minutes, 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence officials have, wittingly or unwittingly, fully exposed 36 months of baseless propaganda, lazy talking points and disgusting lies.Don’t take my word for it. Take theirs.Mehdi Hasan is the CEO and editor-in-chief ofZeteoNAZA, which is produced by the Guardian, is currently in cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries, includingacross the UK and the US. It will be available for free on the Guardian’s website from late NovemberExplore more on these topicsNAZAOpinionDocumentary filmsIsraelGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinecommentShareReuse this content

title: Some Woman review – Anne-Marie Duff is wholly believable but this twisty drama is not | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The far-fetched plot turns and some underdeveloped characters undermine the powerful messages about prejudice in Helen Edmundson’s play
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: The far-fetched plot turns and some underdeveloped characters undermine the powerful messages about prejudice in Helen Edmundson’s play
Content: Moving, harrowing … Anne-Marie Duff in Some Woman at Dorfman theatre, London.Photograph: Ellie KurttzView image in fullscreenMoving, harrowing … Anne-Marie Duff in Some Woman at Dorfman theatre, London.Photograph: Ellie KurttzTheatreReviewSome Woman review – Anne-Marie Duff is wholly believable but this twisty drama is notDorfman theatre, LondonThe far-fetched plot turns and some underdeveloped characters undermine the powerful messages about prejudice in Helen Edmundson’s playArifa AkbarFri 16 Oct 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 09.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpposing forces tug against each other in this new drama asAnne-Marie Duffis magnificent amid playwright Helen Edmundson’s implausible plotting. The result is a failed suspension of disbelief yet a convincing central performance.Duff plays Julie, a mother, ex-wife and working woman whose already over-burdened life is turned upside down by an incident at a tube station when an 11-year-old boy randomly and aggressively insults her. She challenges him, reasonably, and in a series of unconvincing plot turns, winds up facing a legal battle and potential prison sentence.As a story of an ordinary middle-aged woman being buffeted by patriarchal forces around her, this play is stuffed full of important issues. We hear stories of casual sexual abuse, laughed off by those around Julie. Now we see her life virtually destroyed by the boy’s allegation.There is mention of CCTV footage and you wonder if an Adolescence-style video reveal is to come. But the plot makes clear that there is no incontrovertible evidence against her, yet she stands to lose everything.View image in fullscreenPotential brilliance … Ioanna Kimbook (left) and Anne-Marie Duff in Some Woman at the National Theatre, London.Photograph: Ellie KurttzThe points about everyday misogyny come through loud and clear, especially that the legal system is rigged to distrust women and believe men (or an 11-year-old boy in this instance). The West End dramaPrima Facie, recently adapted for the screen, showed us just that in relation to sexual violence against women. But this is not a courtroom drama and the alleged crimes on which it turns are simply not believable.Directed byBlanche McIntyreand staged without an interval, there is potential brilliance here, if only the plot were better crafted and so many unfocused issues not thrown at us – from the eating disorder of one daughter (Grace Doherty) to Julie’s difficult relationship with another (Hannah Onslow), both barely explored, as well as Julie’s experience of infidelity and divorce. Each of these issues gets its moment, briefly, with characters around Julie too flimsy to feel true.View image in fullscreenConfrontation … Stephen Wright in Some Woman.Photograph: Ellie KurttzThe structural failings of the script aside, there are many individually moving and harrowing scenes. They culminate in a confrontation between Julie and the boy’s father (Stephen Wight). Again, this plot-turn challenges the bounds of believability but this time you can brush that aside because the forces of threat, anger and fear feel horribly, sadly real.Julie seems pushed towards victimhood yet she refuses this foisted powerlessness in a society where toxic masculinity is chillingly in plain sight: men openly express loathing of women, boys spit obscenities at female strangers. Truth is all Julie has and upholds, whatever the legal repercussions. She is not only the everyday victim of misogyny but an everyday female hero too. This message has its own power, however bad the plotting may be.At theDorfman theatre, National Theatre, London, until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreNational TheatreAnne-Marie DuffBlanche McIntyreViolence against women and girlsWomenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The last thing I did for my mother was illegal | Well actually | The Guardian
description: An urn cost more than my rent. So I scattered my mother’s ashes at Yosemite from a Ziploc bag, without the federal permit I couldn’t afford to wait for
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An urn cost more than my rent. So I scattered my mother’s ashes at Yosemite from a Ziploc bag, without the federal permit I couldn’t afford to wait for
Content: ‘The industry of dying [in the US] wasn’t always so onerous.’Illustration: Ibrahim Rayintakath/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The industry of dying [in the US] wasn’t always so onerous.’Illustration: Ibrahim Rayintakath/The GuardianMemento mori: a series about deathWell actuallyThe last thing I did for my mother was illegalAn urn cost more than my rent. So I scattered my mother’s ashes at Yosemite from a Ziploc bag, without the federal permit I couldn’t afford to wait forJasmine DesireeFri 16 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTShareMy mother is in a Ziploc bag on my lap, wedged between a half-eaten bag of trail mix and my purse.My stomach is queasy from the switchbacks up to Yosemite, where I’ve come to spread her ashes, and I’m having an existential crisis.I had imagined this day as a beautiful send-off that would feel profound. Instead, it was all improvisation: a plastic bag, a last-minute decision, and ginger chews to stop me from being carsick.I thought my 20s would be about kissing the wrong people in Los Angeles bars, not reading paperbacks on a hospital cot while my mom underwent her fifth brain surgery. My friends were off at college, debating sororities and semesters abroad; I was learning an entirely different set of skills.At 21, I learned my mom hadglioblastoma, a deadly brain cancer. Soon I was in the Bakersfield law library, Googling how to become my 16-year-old brother’s legal guardian, and learning that the same charm I used to snag me a table at Nobu could also get my mom a better room at Cedars-Sinai hospital. She ended up in the room Elizabeth Taylor had died in a few weeks earlier, a detail she loved to regale her friends with.double quotation markWhen you can’t afford to pay, you end up grieving illegallyI don’t remember much from that last month of her life. I mostly just remember the goop I wiped from her eyes as she settled into her final nap. The home hospice nurse told my brother and me to give our mother “permission” to let go. Her fragile body was still fighting, and the nurse believed she was holding on for us. So through our snot and tears, we told her to go. But secretly, in every paused breath, I hoped she wouldn’t.She passed away within eight months of her initial diagnosis. She was 44 years old.When the paramedics arrived, I left the room. A white sheet over her body would finalize things in a way I wasn’t ready for yet. Eventually, in the middle of everything else, I had to figure out what to do with her body.Then there was the price tag. A typical funeral with a viewing and burial in the US costs $8,300. Even cremation now costs more than $2,200 – an unthinkable sum for me at the time. I was a senior airman in the US air force, making about $2,200 a month.When you can’t afford to pay, you end up grieving illegally – as I did.My mom had asked to be cremated. Because my family and I were “sharing” her remains, we needed a way to divide her across multiple people: me, my brother and my aunt.The cheapest option the funeral home offered was a maroon plastic box. I bought one, brought her home, and we portioned her into plastic bags.Later, my aunt took me to a boutique and helped me pick out little wooden boxes for each of us. Small carved wooden things, prettier than what the funeral home had offered – and cheaper. It felt like a repair. It also didn’t quite work. The box had seams, and my mother kept slipping out of the cracks, a thin layer of her showing up on shelves and dressers and inside drawers.When it came time to drive to Yosemite, I put her back in a plastic bag.One thing I didn’t know was that scattering human remains in a national park requires a special use permit. That seems obvious now, but when you’re grieving, reading any fine print is a big undertaking.The industry of dying wasn’t always so onerous. Before the civil war, most Americans died at home and were prepared for burial by their own families. Embalming became widespread only after the war, when battlefield deaths created a mass market for preserving bodies long enough to ship them north.What followed was tradition making way for a business model: the funeral home, the professional embalmer, the licensed director, the sealed casket, the manicured lawn cemetery.One factor pushing the industry toward higher prices is consolidation. Over the last two decades, large death-care conglomerates have absorbed independent funeral homes, in some markets amassing enough pricing power to draw federal antitrust action. What used to be a family business is, increasingly, a subsidiary.None of this happened by accident, and it is not, as the industry sometimes claims, a response to what families want. Justin Crowe, the founder ofParting Stone, a Santa Fe company that turns cremated remains into solidified stones, told me that the shift from burial to cremation went from 5% in 1970 to over 63% today.“When the customer said, actually, we want cremation,” he said, “I think the industry kind of made a mistake at that moment. It didn’t really nurture that change. It didn’t provide the value to the experience of cremation, like it had to the experience of burial.”What families were asking for, in other words, was a cheaper, less institutional death – one where the body didn’t disappear into a funeral home and come back as an invoice. But what they got was the same process, marked up, only this time with cremated remains.And a growing number of families, faced with a version of dignity they could not afford, began improvising.My friend Danielle Directo-Meston, a fellow journalist in Los Angeles, grew up in a family where death doesn’t happen offstage.“Filipinos, my family in particular, we go to the cemetery to hang out,” she told me. “We just hang out there for most of the morning and afternoon. And then we’ll go get lunch together.”They go to sit with relatives who have died, to clean the graves, adorn them with flowers, and spend time as a family; it’s a habit with roots in Undas, the Filipino tradition of spending All Saints’ and All Souls’ Day at the family plot.‘We live in grief-phobic societies’: experts on how to get more comfortable with deathRead moreUnlike many Americans, Danielle was raised to be comfortable around the dead. She has also had a lot of practice. In the last several years, she has lost a cousin in a motorcycle accident, an uncle after a series of strokes, and both of her grandmothers. She was still not prepared for how the American death-care industry actually operates.The clearest example came at Rose Hills, a large cemetery in Whittier, California. Rose Hills is owned byService Corporation International, a conglomerate absorbing independent funeral homes across the country. Danielle’s family was there for a gathering, honoring a passed loved one, when a salesperson approached them.“When you’re at the cemetery having a family gathering,” she said, “they have salespeople try to sell you on more plots.”She made it clear this wasn’t one bad day, or one bad salesperson. It was the norm. Anyone attending a service there would encounter it.After watching her family cycle through this multiple times, Danielle made a different choice for herself. She decided to preplan her own funeral with a Washington-based company that offers natural organic reduction, the process of transforming a human body into soil, legal in a growing number of states.“It’s around $5,000, which is doable,” she said. “I can pay that when I’m alive, and no one has to worry about it. Compared to $20,000 just for the plot alone at the cemetery, and that’s on top of the mortuary and all of that stuff.”Danielle will be composted. I scattered my mother by hand in a national park without a permit. Neither of us did what the industry wanted us to do.Somewhere between the seventh and the eighth bend, I pulled over and slid down an escarpment to an opening with shrubbery and trees. There wasn’t anything particularly special about the space, except for how the light passed through the leaves.The year before she died, my mother told me she was taking me and my brother to Hawaii. It would have been our first family trip; the furthest we had ever vacationed was Kern River, 90 minutes from home. She had spent years trying to piece together where she came from. Her father was Hawaiian and had left when she was a baby. Her mother had never known her own father either. So my mother spent her life learning who she was the way you learn a language, alone and slowly.She had already booked the flights for October. But by fall, she was too sick to travel. She died on 26 December after a few months in hospice care, exactly one year after she had told me about the trip.I looked down at the bag in my hands. I wished I had planned her scattering at night under a full moon, where I could dance naked in front of a fire and chant her blessings. Or that I had carried her to the Redwoods, finding a spot at dawn when the rocks are covered in moss and dew, and the air is crisp. Or even better, smuggled her to Hawaii, and released her over the Pacific at sunset - her favorite time of day.Instead, I settled on a sunny spot by a newborn tree. It was about 3ft high and eager to grow taller. It would usher in her remains with enthusiasm, and its new life would overcome her old one; a suitable symbolism for the cycle of life.I opened the bag and shook it around, flinging her into the breeze, watching the particles of a woman who loved me travel toward Half Dome.I walked back to my car and stretched my arm out the window on the drive down, surfing the wind with my hand. Pieces of my mother flew out from under my fingernails. It is the most loving thing I have ever done for her.This article was amended on 16 October 2026 to clarify that the author’s mother died after spending a few months in hospice care.

title: The best retinol and retinal serums for smoother, firmer skin – tested | Skincare | The Guardian
description: Not sure where to start with retinoids? Whether you’ve got sensitive, acne-prone or mature skin, here are our beauty expert’s favourite vitamin A creams for everyone
Author: Sabine Wiesel
Headline: Not sure where to start with retinoids? Whether you’ve got sensitive, acne-prone or mature skin, here are our beauty expert’s favourite vitamin A creams for everyone
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSkincareReviewThe best retinol and retinal serums for smoother, firmer skin – testedNot sure where to start with retinoids? Whether you’ve got sensitive, acne-prone or mature skin, here are our beauty expert’s favourite vitamin A creams for everyoneThe best LED face masksSabine WieselFri 16 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRetinol is the buzziest ingredient in skincare – and for good reason. You’ve almost certainly heard of it, but are you actually using it? Some studies suggest topical retinol can improve theappearance of fine linesandother signs of skin ageing. I’ve been using it to smooth the look of wrinkles and rejuvenate my complexion for years, and here’s why it’s worthy of a place in your routine, too.Let me first point out that when I say retinol, I’m really talking about a wider family of retinoids – vitamin A derivatives that include retinol itself. Retinol is just one member of the family, but it’s become well known thanks to its widespread use in over-the-counter skincare.The benefits of retinoids, fromaccelerating cell turnovertostimulating collagen production, are well evidenced. Tretinoin was first prescribed in the US in the 1970s as an acne treatment, and retinoids soon revealed their potential beyond breakouts, helping tosoften the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles,fade pigmentationandsmooth skin texture.However, any changes don’t happen overnight. It can take time to develop a tolerance to retinoids, as side effects such as redness and irritation are common. Over a short period, though, “you can expect to see early improvements in skin texture and brightness within four to six weeks and more significant results around pigmentation, acne or fine lines closer to eight to 12 weeks with consistent use,” saysDr Ahmed El Muntasar, GP and aesthetics doctor. It’s also even more important than usual to use a broad-spectrumface SPF, as retinoids can make skin more sensitive to sunlight.Why you should trust me​​I’m an experienced beauty editor with 17 years as a journalist, so I’ve witnessed the retinoid revolution first-hand – from the early pioneers to today’s more advanced formulas. Pretty much every skincare brand now has at least one retinoid product in its lineup.Part of my job is to test these products as they launch, so you’d be hard-pressed to find a retinoid I haven’t slathered on my face at some point. And as a fortysomething showing all the natural signs of ageing – fine lines, wrinkles and pigmentation – I’m the ideal test case.How I testedView image in fullscreenFace value: the writer puts the retinoids to the test.Photograph: Sabine Wiesel/The GuardianHaving carefully considered all the retinol (and retinoid) products I’ve tested over the years, I started by putting together a list of my favourite 15 products. To make the cut, the formula had to be one I’d used until the bottle was empty – or bought again afterwards. For a beauty editor who’s sent skincare to test every day, that’s the real test of a product: whether I’d choose to use it again when I have countless others to try.I used each product as part of my evening routine for a minimum of eight weeks. As my skin is already accustomed to retinoid use, I could do this without affecting my skin barrier. If you’re new to retinoid use, introduce them into your regime slowly – I really can’t emphasise this enough.The products were assessed on texture, ease of use, side effects, noticeable skin changes, value and ingredients. Below you’ll find my list of the 10 best performers.The best retinol and retinal serums in 2026View image in fullscreenRetinoid roundup: the serums and creams tested for this guide.Photograph: Sabine Wiesel/The GuardianBest retinal serum overall:Medik8 Crystal retinalMedik8Crystal retinal, 30mlfrom£36From £45 at Medik8From £45 at LookfantasticWhy we love itAdvanced retinal formula; no irritation in testingWhy we don’t love itPrices vary depending on strength of formulaView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sabine Wiesel/The GuardianFrom £36 at LookfantasticFrom £45 at Medik8Retinal (short for retinaldehyde) has been fast and furiously coming for retinol’s popularity crown, with an increasing number of beauty brands turning to this advanced retinoid. Medik8 has been using retinal since 2018, and this serum is now among the bestselling retinal serums worldwide.Why we love itHeavily hyped by experts and consumers alike, I’m here to add to the noise: this vitamin A serum really is excellent. The brand claims it works faster than standard retinol while being gentler on the skin. Medik8 says its crystal encapsulation gradually releases retinal throughout the night, limiting the risk of irritation. And that’s why it’s always my go-to recommendation: I’ve seen such speedy skin rejuvenation and haven’t experienced any of the irritation that can come with integrating retinol into your skincare routine.I’ve seen this formula banish breakouts, fade pigmentation, plump out lines and wrinkles and firm the skin with continued use. By gradually working my way up the ladder to increase the strength, I’ve seen increasingly impressive results. Add to this its light and easy-to-apply texture, and it really is the best over-the-counter retinoid serum I’ve tried.It’s a shame that …if you’re new to retinoids,you may still experience breakouts, flaking or dryness.Product:serumRecyclable packaging:all recyclable except for the pumpSize:30mlPrice per ml:from £1.20Strength and type:0.01 to 0.24% retinalVegan?YesCertified cruelty-free?NoMedik8Crystal retinal, 30mlfrom£36From £45 at Medik8From £45 at LookfantasticWhy we love itAdvanced retinal formula; no irritation in testingWhy we don’t love itPrices vary depending on strength of formulaBest budget retinal serum:Naturium retinaldehyde cream serumNaturiumRetinaldehyde cream serum, 50mlfrom£32£32 at Space NK£32 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value; fragrance-free; two strengthsWhat we don’t loveSome may find it dryingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sabine Wiesel/The Guardian£32 at Space NK£32 at AmazonUS skincare brand Naturium has been gaining serious momentum in the UK beauty space. That’s because it strikes the sweet spot between science-led skincare – including some top-notch body care – and affordable luxury.Why we love itNaturium’s formula may not be at the bottom of the price scale, but it comes in a much larger-than-some 50ml tube, so you get a lot of vitamin A for your buck. There are two strengths to choose from here in the UK (in the US, there’s a third, stronger one).Its lightweight texture absorbs in seconds, making it easy to add into your evening skincare routine. Note that while the serum is bright yellow out of the tube, it massages in clear, so don’t let that put you off.Just like Medik8, it uses a sustained-release retinal, which the brand sayssupports skin comfort. I’ve experienced no irritation at all in use, and saw the same rejuvenating results over time. If you’re new to retinoids, I’d still suggest building it into your routine gradually, though.It’s a shame that …my skin needs a richmoisturiserlayered on top to keep dryness at bay.Product:serumRecyclable packaging:can be recycled at BootsSize:50mlPrice per ml:64pStrength and type:0.05% and 0.10% retinalVegan?YesCertified cruelty-free?YesNaturiumRetinaldehyde cream serum, 50mlfrom£32£32 at Space NK£32 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value; fragrance-free; two strengthsWhat we don’t loveSome may find it dryingBest retinal cream for wrinkles:Murad Resurgence Retinal ReSculpt overnight creamMuradResurgence Retinal ReSculpt overnight cream, 50mlfrom£98£98 at Murad£98 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveCutting-edge skincare; light but creamy texture; hydratingWhat we don’t loveIt’s expensiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sabine Wiesel/The Guardian£98 at Murad£98 at Cult BeautyClinician-developed skincare is everywhere right now, but Dr Howard Murad was one of the first, in 1989. Now simply known as Murad, the brand is still very much ahead of the curve when it comes to clinical skincare, as this retinal cream shows.Why we love itIt’s a powerhouse formula, combining encapsulated retinal with Murad’s NAD+ Lift Complex, which the brand says boosts production of NAD+, a coenzyme involved in cellular repair that declines with age.Together, the duo makes an innovative tag team for targeting fine lines and wrinkles. I’ve found it so effective that after just four weeks, my complexion already looks smoother, plumper and firmer, with deeper lines noticeably softened.But what I love most about this formula is that it feels like a “proper” night cream – its creamy texture is still beautifully lightweight, so you don’t feel like you’re going to bed with a mask on your face. Packed with hydrating ingredients such as squalane, hyaluronic acid and glycerine, to name a few, my dry skin is content, without any need to layer on something else – unlike other retinoid products.It’s a shame that …it has such a high price, but you get what you pay for with this skincare investment.Product:creamRecyclable packaging:yesSize:50mlPrice per ml:£1.96Strength and type:retinal (strength not specified)Vegan?YesCertified cruelty-free?YesMuradResurgence Retinal ReSculpt overnight cream, 50mlfrom£98£98 at Murad£98 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveCutting-edge skincare; light but creamy texture; hydratingWhat we don’t loveIt’s expensiveBest retinol serum for beginners:The Inkey List Starter retinol serumThe Inkey ListStarter retinol serum, 30mlfrom£9.51£10.40 at Lookfantastic£9.51 at AmazonWhat we loveGentle formula for first-timers and sensitive skinWhat we don’t loveThe packaging is a little basicView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sabine Wiesel/The Guardian£10.40 at Lookfantastic£9.51 at AmazonKnown for its hard-working, ingredient-led formulations at wallet-friendly prices, the Inkey List has done it again with two impressive new retinoid products: anadvanced 0.2% retinal serumfor experienced users and a beginner-friendly retinol, the latter of which I put to the test.Why we love itThis gentle formula is ideal for first-time vitamin A users, and the brand claims it’s suitable for sensitive and rosacea-prone complexions. It combines 1% Granactive Pro+ and 0.01% retinal alongside hydrating, skin-barrier-supporting and calming ingredients.In my testing, I experienced no side effects. It’s lightweight, silky and fragrance-free, making it easy to slot into an evening routine, although I did find it could leave my skin feeling dry without a hydrating moisturiser to follow. You may see improvements to skin texture within weeks, but with retinoids, the best results come from playing the long game. Think of this as a stepping stone to a stronger retinoid.It’s a shame that …it’s a trivial point, but the packaging is basic.Type:serumRecyclable packaging:yesSize:30mlPrice per ml:from about 32pStrength and type:1% Granactive Pro+ retinoid and 0.01% retinalVegan?YesCertified cruelty-free?YesThe Inkey ListStarter retinol serum, 30mlfrom£9.51£10.40 at Lookfantastic£9.51 at AmazonWhat we loveGentle formula for first-timers and sensitive skinWhat we don’t loveThe packaging is a little basicBest retinol serum for mature skin:Lancôme Rénergie CRx Triple Serum retinolLancômeRénergie CRx Triple Serum retinol, 50mlfrom£96£96 at Lookfantastic£120 at BootsWhat we lovePowerful with vitamin C, retinol and peptidesWhat we don’t loveIt’s a splurgeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sabine Wiesel/The Guardian£96 at Lookfantastic£120 at BootsLancôme has been around for more than 90 years, but it’s still at the top of its beauty game. From masteringmascarato launching cutting-edge skincare – and this product is no exception.Why we love itIn the Renergie CRx serum, Lancôme combines three actives: retinol, vitamin C and X-peptides, in a formula it says is non-irritating. The serum feels luxuriously silky and is a pleasure to use, giving instant hydration without stickiness.Together, the three actives target the signs of ageing, withvitamin Chelping to brighten and peptides intended to soothe the skin. On paper, the serum ticks all the boxes, and I found it equally impressive in use. Having come to the end of the bottle, my skin is smoother, more even-toned and more radiant, with pores and lines less visible.It’s a shame that …it has such a big price tag. Shop around, though, since it’s sometimes on offer.Product:serumRecyclable packaging:yesSize:50mlPrice per ml:from £1.92Strength and type:0.3% retinolVegan?NoCertified cruelty-free?NoLancômeRénergie CRx Triple Serum retinol, 50mlfrom£96£96 at Lookfantastic£120 at BootsWhat we lovePowerful with vitamin C, retinol and peptidesWhat we don’t loveIt’s a splurgeThe best of the restThe Ordinary retinal 0.2% emulsionThe OrdinaryRetinal 0.2% emulsion, 15mlfrom£15.20£15.20 at the Ordinary£15.20 at Space NKWhy we love itHigh-strength retinal at a lower priceWhy we don’t love itIt’s a tiny bottleView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sabine Wiesel/The Guardian£15.20 at the Ordinary£15.20 at Space NKBest for:experienced usersDisrupting the beauty space with its ingredient-led skincare at affordable prices, the Ordinary has proven that beauty innovation can be made accessible to all. A case in point is this 0.2% retinal. The Ordinary recommends it for experienced retinoid users rather than beginners, but the brand says continued use can leave skin looking smoother, firmer and more even-toned.It’s beautifully lightweight and a little goes a long way, but I have a few niggles. The yellow hue of the retinal can stain clothing – I learned the hard way – so take care when applying. More disappointing is that you get only 15ml for the price, which isn’t quite the excellent value for money I’ve come to expect from the brand.It didn’t make the final cut …because it may be the cheapest, but it’s also the smallest bottle.Product:serum;recyclable packaging:yes, through TerraCycle and at Boots;size:15ml;price per ml:from about £1.01;strength and type:0.2% retinal;vegan?Yes;certified cruelty-free?YesThe OrdinaryRetinal 0.2% emulsion, 15mlfrom£15.20£15.20 at the Ordinary£15.20 at Space NKWhy we love itHigh-strength retinal at a lower priceWhy we don’t love itIt’s a tiny bottleKiehl’s retinol Skin-Renewing Daily Micro-Dose serumKiehl’sRetinol Skin-Renewing Daily Micro-Dose serumfrom£38.50£38.50 at Lookfantastic£55 at Kiehl’sWhy we love itGentle retinol for beginners and sensitive skinWhy we don’t love itThere are cheaper beginner alternativesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sabine Wiesel/The Guardian£38.50 at Lookfantastic£55 at Kiehl’sBest for:dry skinCombine sophisticated formulations, apothecary-style packaging and a heritage dating back to 1851, and it’s easy to see why Kiehl’s has become such a trusted, much-loved brand. And for me, this is one of its standout products: a gentle retinol Kiehl’s says is designed specifically for first-time users and those with sensitive skin.It contains ceramides, which the brand says help strengthen the skin barrier and improve tolerance of retinol. Having worked my way up the retinoid ladder from beginner formulas to more advanced, I’ve used plenty of bottles of this over the years and have never seen any side effects – not even the dryness that’s so common with retinoid use.It didn’t make the final cut because…cheaper gentle (although not as luxe) formulas, such as the Inkey List’s Starter retinol serum above, are available.Type:serum;recyclable packaging:recyclable bottle, non-recyclable pump. While retinol increases skin cell turnover, niacinamide soothes, and liquorice-root extract helps skin appear brighter.And, being CeraVe, it’s packed with the brand’s signature ceramides to strengthen and support the skin barrier. In tests, I found it gentle, easy to use, and hydrating, which makes it a great choice for retinol beginners and those with sensitive skin.It didn’t make the final cut because …it takes time to see results.Product:serum;recyclable packaging:only through theBoots recycling scheme;size:30ml;price per ml: about 78p;strength and type:retinol (percentage not disclosed);vegan?No;certified cruelty-free?NoCeraVeResurfacing retinol serum, 30mlfrom£23.50£23.50 at Boots£23.50 at LookfantasticWhat we loveGreat for blemish-prone skin and post-acne marksWhat we don’t loveNeeds to be used consistently to see resultsRoC Retinol Correxion Line Smoothing night serum capsulesRoCRetinol Correxion Line Smoothing night serum capsules, 10.5mlfrom£35.99£35.99 at Boots£35.99 at LookfantasticWhat we loveEasy to travel with; won’t overuseWhat we don’t loveSmall bottleView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sabine Wiesel/The Guardian£35.99 at Boots£35.99 at LookfantasticBest for:retinol capsulesRoC says it was the first skincare company to offer stabilised retinol with other ingredients over the counter, and it has several high-quality retinol products in its lineup. My favourites are these biodegradable capsules, which limit exposure to light and air, preserving the retinol’s potency. The pre-measured dose also stops you from using too much.The formula combines ceramides with retinol, and I didn’t experience any drying or redness in testing, even when used daily. My skin felt soft, healthy and comfortable, while continued use left my complexion looking smoother and brighter and fine lines softer – which is why I regularly go back to using them.It didn’t make the final cut because …you get only 10.5ml in total, so they can work out quite expensive.Product:serum;recyclable packaging:only through theBoots recycling scheme;size:10.5ml;price per ml:from about £3.43;strength and type:retinol (strength not specified);vegan?No;certified cruelty-free?YesRoCRetinol Correxion Line Smoothing night serum capsules, 10.5mlfrom£35.99£35.99 at Boots£35.99 at LookfantasticWhat we loveEasy to travel with; won’t overuseWhat we don’t loveSmall bottleLa Roche-Posay retinol B3 serumLa Roche-PosayRetinol B3 serum, 30mlfrom£38.40£38.40 at Lookfantastic£48 at BootsWhat we loveTrusted brand for sensitive skin; gentle formulaWhat we don’t lovePriceyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sabine Wiesel/The Guardian£38.40 at Lookfantastic£48 at BootsBest for:sensitive skinFrench pharmaceutical brand La Roche-Posay is known for a problem-solving approach to skincare, so it’s no surprise it’s mastered the art of creating a retinol serum for sensitive skin. It’s particularly well suited to those who may have struggled with retinol dryness and irritation in the past.The reason for this is a gentle formula that includes skin-soothing and skin barrier-strengthening B3 (better known as niacinamide) and glycerine for hydration. I’ve found this cocktail of ingredients ensures it’s well-tolerated by my skin, with none of the irritating side effects of retinol.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s for sensitive skin only – there are better options for other skin types.Product:serum;recyclable packaging:not entirely;size:30ml;price per ml:£1.28;strength and type:0.3% retinol;vegan?No;certified cruelty-free?NoLa Roche-PosayRetinol B3 serum, 30mlfrom£38.40£38.40 at Lookfantastic£48 at BootsWhat we loveTrusted brand for sensitive skin; gentle formulaWhat we don’t lovePriceyWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenEasy does it: starting with a low percentage minimises the risk of dryness, irritation and redness.Photograph: Sabine Wiesel/The GuardianWhat are the benefits of using retinol serums?Retinoids, or vitamin A derivatives such as retinol and retinal, are skincare powerhouses backed by scientific evidence that shows they do two clever things.Firstly, they can speed up the skin’s natural renewal process. “Retinoids help to increase cellular turnover, which naturally slows down as we age,” says El Muntasar. “This means the skin sheds more effectively, revealing newer, fresher skin underneath that looks brighter, more hydrated and even.” They continue to be recommended for those who have acne, as they help unclog pores, reduce inflammation and outbreaks, and fade hyperpigmentation.Retinoids’ second clever trick is their ability to support collagen and elastin production. As these essential proteins decline, lines, wrinkles and a loss of firmness become more apparent. “They’re not just treating one concern; they’re improving the skin’s underlying structure,” says Dr Sheila Li, founder ofMediject Clinic. “Over time, skin becomes smoother, brighter and more resilient.”What percentage of retinol is most effectiveThere is no set answer to this. The most effective percentage is the one your skin can tolerate without disrupting the barrier or needing to stop. All the dermatologists I’ve interviewed advise starting with the “go low and go slow” method.Starting on a low percentage minimises the risk of dryness, irritation, redness and peeling – all common side effects of using retinoids. This gives your skin time to get used to the active and build up tolerance to it.“Build tolerance gradually,” says Li. “Apply two or three nights a week at first, and increase slowly.”How to use retinol serumRetinoids are best used in your evening routine when your skin naturally goes into repair mode, but also because they can increase photosensitivity. This makesa broad-spectrum SPFan even more essential part of your morning routine.“I recommend pairing a retinoid with a simple, barrier-supporting moisturiser and avoiding too many active ingredients alongside it, especially in the early stages,” says El Muntasar. “Ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, ceramides and niacinamide help support the skin and reduce irritation.”I like to layerAestura’s Atobarrier365 creamon top of any retinol product I’m using. It’s a Korean bestseller that’s packed with skin-strengthening ceramides and keeps skin calm and hydrated.Why are some retinoids prescription-only?It all comes down to potency. “Prescription-only retinoids, such as tretinoin and adapalene, work faster and treat more severe skin conditions,” saysDr Leah Totton, medical doctor and cosmetic specialist. “But they also carry a higher risk of irritation, redness and peeling and so require medical supervision for safe use.”For more:The best LED face masks – testedThe best cleansers for every skin typeThe best eye creams to banish bags, puffiness and fine linesThe best face moisturisers for every budgetSabine Wiesel is a freelance beauty editor.
