title: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis | Transport | The Guardian
description: Protest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licences
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Protest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licences
Content: Wayve robotaxis leave the depot on the day the company launched autonomous passenger rides in London via Uber last month.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersView image in fullscreenWayve robotaxis leave the depot on the day the company launched autonomous passenger rides in London via Uber last month.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersTransport‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxisProtest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licencesGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor passengers in Britain who want to try the latest ride, robotaxis are eagerly awaited: more than 100,000 are on Uber’s waitlist inLondonafter the first UK services started in September.Others view them with trepidation. “I think we should all be worried,” said Florentina Ghiuzan, an Uber driver from Essex. “I was shockedTfL approved it so soon. I knew change would come. But I thought it would come with a solution for us.”London’s rollout is facing mounting opposition, from drivers fearing for their future and the capital’s politicians, with a critical report demandingTransportfor London (TfL) is given full powers to permit or suspend operations.Drivers will this weekend protest outside the headquarters and depot of Wayve, which has partnered with Uber to supply London’sfirst autonomous cabs for hire.The direct action marks the latest salvo between unions and the global tech companies, whose driverless cars trials expanded this week to Manchester, with fears that hundreds of thousands of driver jobs could be lost.Although only a handful of driverless cars now ply the streets, Uber has announced plans to deploy 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis worldwide starting next year, and its senior executives have talked about all new cars being autonomous by 2040. In San Francisco, Waymo’s fully autonomous cars already operate more than a quarter of all rides.The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, and bosses atTfLhave expressed unease, and the London assembly’s transport committee has called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services.In a report published this week, the committee said there was “considerable uncertainty around many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers.The chair, Caroline Russell, said they were not convinced that London should welcome robotaxis. “Rather than just accepting the autonomous passenger service model proposed by operators, London should be looking at the transport problems it is trying to solve and then considering what solutions this technology could provide,” she said.TfL is understood to see little benefit in theaddition of robotaxi services to its crowded city streets, even if the numbers turn out to be relatively few in comparison to the wider traffic.For the robotaxi companies, London is a tempting challenge to crack. Commercially, it is one of the biggest private hire markets in the world and a foothold in Europe; logistically, it is a tricky test bed to prove their vehicles are viable anywhere. Compared with the grid system of US cities in particular, it presents narrower, twisting and unruly streets, without the kind of rules on jaywalking that give cars priority on the road.Wayve autonomous vehicles added to Uber app in LondonUnder current rules, TfL licenses passenger services, but the government decides whether autonomous vehicles can operate. TfL has approved the start ofUberand Wayve’s limited robotaxi services, which retain a human safety driver in the front seat.As it stands, when it comes to fully autonomous passenger services, the Department for Transport would issue permits for robotaxis with TfL only able to grant or refuse consent, rather than regulate their usage on London’s streets.That has alarmed TfL, which sees parallels with when Uber first started business in London, creating problems few had considered, and was twicerebuffed in licence renewalsas not a “fit and proper” operator. Quite how driverless cars will affect the capital’s transport ecosystem is unknown – and TfL wants to retain the power to intervene.City hall is also concerned about the social implications of more than 100,000 licensed drivers losing income or a living. Those at the frontline in the App Drivers and Couriers Union (ADCU) are planning protests outside Wayve’s London base from this Saturday.Their members include Ghiuzan, 42, who started working as a driver four years ago after going back to college. She said: “Our earnings are the same or even lower since I started – and with the robotaxis on the market it could get even worse.”Ghiuzan said she was notified of the start of autonomous services as an Uber customer – but received no notification as a driver. She thinks people will switch to robotaxis: “Young people like them, it’s new, and you don’t have to pay the driver … I might have other skills, but for lots of drivers who are older and have done it their whole life, it’s going to be quite a challenge.”View image in fullscreenUber driver Faisal Osman said robotaxis would ‘decimate the livelihoods of many people including me’.Photograph: Faisal OsmanFaisal Osman, 51, from east London, has been an Uber driver for 12 years, after switching from a long commute to an IT engineering job to allow him to work nights when he had children. He knows four other engineers who joined Uber: “We all used to talk about AI taking our jobs in IT. We thought, we’re not earning as much driving but we’ll be safe for a while, support the family, pay the bills. But robocabs are a massive concern.“People might be interested but it will decimate the livelihoods of many people including me – I really wanted some authorities to say no.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenUber driver Abdurzak Hadi said he was thinking about safety as well as the threat to his job.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianAbdurzak Hadi, an Uber driver and theLondon chair of the ADCU, said Saturday’s protests would follow a similar action held at Waymo’s base in Park Royal in August. He said: “For me as a driver, I’m thinking about competing with a machine that’s not going to get tired, and could work 24 hours a day.“But as a Londoner with family, I’m thinking about safety. As licensed drivers we’re taught by TfL about safeguarding, looking out for a vulnerable child, or for abuse. Or looking after passengers who can only read your lips. We’re a safety net. But losing my job – that’s also losing a safety net for my family.”A recent report from the Centre for British Progress thinktank said more than 400,000 UK drivers (121,000 in London) would soon find “much of this work obsolete”, andurged the government to tax autonomous vehiclesto help pay for the social consequences and economic losses.TheGMB unionhas demanded a “just transition” to help drivers reskill and find new work. Speaking at the Labour conference last month, the GMB’s Mark Betteridge said the union was not against change but added: “The people who do these jobs will know the reality far better of what change will look like … Drivers tell us they want some sort of transition plan to get through this.”The roads minister, Justin Madders, told the meeting that autonomous vehicles could bring “opportunities for well-paid and unionised jobs” and the government wanted Britain to be a “world leader” in the technology. But, he added: “Sometimes government hasn’t worked on the impact on workers … We’re absolutely committed to making sure that doesn’t happen that time.”An Uber spokesperson said: “Drivers and AVs [automated vehicles], which we believe will also offer considerable benefits to cities, are both expected to grow side by side for quite some time. That said, we shouldn’t hide that autonomous mobility will impact workers, riders, and the communities they live in.“We are in conversations with the government and local stakeholders to ensure we can realise the promise of AVs while not leaving drivers and communities behind.”Uber said it had not significantly increased its share of fares in London but VAT changes meant drivers were keeping less of the fares customers paid, and it said it was the only private hire operator in the UK recognising its drivers as workers with employment protections.View image in fullscreenWayve said that with Uber it was taking a ‘deliberately phased approach’.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersWayve said that with Uber it was taking a “deliberately phased approach”, and had engaged extensively with political leaders, community organisations and accessibility advocates. A spokesperson said its robotaxis could “make a positive contribution to London’s transport system, helping to improve road safety, expand connectivity and give people more ways to travel.“There is clear excitement in the potential for this technology to support safer, more accessible journeys, provided it is introduced responsibly and in partnership with the city. We have a positive, constructive relationship with TfL and we’re working pragmatically together to ensure any future services meet its expectations.”A spokesperson for Khan said the mayor was committed to ensuring that Londoners benefitted from the opportunities new technologies could bring but shared “concerns about potential impacts on safety, congestion and jobs”, as any changes needed to “work for our world-leading transport system – including taxi and private hire services, and those who drive them”.Explore more on these topicsTransportSelf-driving carsRoad transportWaymoUberTfLLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Britain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t work | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: The current system is unable to quench the public thirst for locking people up – and certainly doesn’t ensure proper care once they are released, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: The current system is unable to quench the public thirst for locking people up – and certainly doesn’t ensure proper care once they are released, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: A former inmate leaves HM Prison Liverpool on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA former inmate leaves HM Prison Liverpool on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionPrisons and probationBritain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t workPolly ToynbeeThe current system is unable to quench the public thirst for locking people up – and certainly doesn’t ensure proper care once they are releasedFri 16 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 08.53 EDTSharePublic services need more investment across the board. Every day, another wretched story. Look at the Institute for Government’s (IFG)Public Services Performance Trackerfor a plain assessment of A&E corridor care, councils struggling to meet the demands of social care and the Send system, the courts backlog, GP caseloads or families lost in temporary accommodation. A chancellor approaching a budget is besieged by need. It’s easy for us journalists to pick out shock stories and claim each one is an absolute priority, but how should a chancellor choose?Today it’s the probation officers, whoseconference in Newcastleis launching a ballot for industrial action. Their caseloads overflowed long ago, but now thousands of prisoners released early –2,000 this month– have been thrust upon them. The responsibility is overwhelming, with officers blamed for crimes their clients commit.The probation story is told in scores of reports: the National Audit Office found the servicerunning on half the staff neededto cover released prisoners. It also reportedfailures in electronic tagging, echoed by the IFG reporting only 55% oftags were fitted in time. Napo, the probation officers’ union, blames the problems on awarding contractsto the lowest biddersat prices that mean the job isn’t done properly.The number of offenders charged withserious further offences while on probationhas increased, with the public accounts committee blaming staff shortages. Vacancies leave probation services25%-30% below target levels. The government is training another 1,300, but that’s not enough, says Napo, considering thehigh dropout rateonce recruits discover the abuse, threats and stress of the work, alongside the fact that the most common cause of staff sickness ismental ill health.The sheer impossibility of their caseloads caused the government to abandon any attempt to say what their caseload should be, so the “workload measurement tool” wasabruptly ditched in Septemberjust before the October raft of new prisoner releases. There is no point in stating an official workload standard that can’t be met.Eleven hostels and seven halfway houses, places that help probation officers supervise released prisoners, havejust closed for repairs and because of a lack of staff. Drug addiction and mental health problems untreated in prisons, coupled with cuts to education, training and rehabilitation, make prisoners even less prepared for release.The probation system was broken by adisastrous privatisationwhen Chris Grayling (whobanned the sending of books to prisoners) split it apart into 21 private companies, with the workforce organisationally divided in two. Private companies only handled offenders judged low to medium risk, while the most serious offenders remained under the control of the state. Companies under-invested, experienced staff left, and none of the innovation promised was delivered. Afterthis ideological privatisation was abandoned in 2021, the probation service never recovered.The lord chancellor is set to address the probation officer’s conference. “But please,” says Napo chair Ben Cockburn, “no bullshit. Don’t tell us how well we do an exceptionally difficult job. We know that.”. Napo rejected a 5% pay offer on the grounds it falls far behind equivalent offers to workers in local government, police and social work. Under planned industrial action, Cockburn says probation officers will work to contract and refuse unpaid overtime. That, he says, will cause collapse.What probation officers need immediately is reduced workloads, pruned to the riskiest cases, leaving less serious cases unallocated. “Put the service into special measures,” Cockburn says. He also wants the courts to stop piling on more cases until there are enough staff to cope. “We are firefighting from one emergency to another,” he says – or called away to someone in a police cell, or to a paedophile found dating a woman with a child, or a domestic violence case.Cutting workloads for probation officers is only a short-term solution, one that avoids the real question. Why is there an ever-rising prison population, despite the sustained, multi-decade fall in crime rates?“We are addicted to prison,” Cockburn says. In his view, probation works when officers have time for long-term working relationships with offenders. “It’s the best job in the world,” he says, recalling the journey of one prisoner who had committed a terrible crime as a young man. “I saw him in prison, knew him for 15 years, with time for therapeutic work.” But, these days, that’s so rare. “Someone now might see eight different officers, retelling their story over and over, creating no trust.”Why build more prison cells? An inspection of a brand new private prison,HMP Millsikein East Yorkshire, found it unsafe due to a lack of experienced staff, as well as chronic staff shortages.Even at its opening, it was “chaotic”, lacking basic processes for important things like locking doors and counting prisoners. Hundreds of cells are still empty because of a lack of officers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPublic pressure to lock up more prisoners and supervise them when released will never be matched by a willingness to pay the taxes needed to cover the cost of attracting people to work in this sector. That’s the truth Cockburn wants politicians to be brave enough to tell. This country is not alone in wrongly believing crime is ever-rising when all across Europe it hasfallen for decades. But no one believes it. A news and drama fixation on horrific crime stirs primal fears that belie these facts. Politicians everywhere score points with a frightened public by clamouring for more punishment.When I last visited a hard-pressed prison, I asked the governor what she most needed, and was astonished when she said she wouldn’t invest here, but “right at the start, before the damage is done, in early years”.Asking where every pound spent does most good is the kind of mega-question budgets don’t answer. But a brave chancellor would cut prison funding down to housing only the most dangerous, and spending better on what works, such as well-funded probation officers.Keep telling this fact: all crime is horrible – sex crime is at last reported more often – but the overall drop in neighbourhood-level crime in England and Waleshas been about 80%since its peak in 1995. Meanwhile,prison numbers have risen significantly. In his upcoming speech at the probation officer’s conference, it would take unprecedented political bravery for the lord chancellor to dare end the pretence that prison works.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionUK criminal justicePublic sector cutsCrimeStaff shortagescommentShareReuse this content

title: We are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently?  | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: The education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculator, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: The education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculator, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: ‘Lucy Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Lucy Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamyOpinionEducationWe are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently?Simon JenkinsThe education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculatorFri 16 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 05.54 EDTShareAt last the fourth R is born. Articulation – speaking – is to join reading, writing and arithmetic in the education canon. What has become the mighty struggle against the dictatorship of the screen can begin in earnest. The spoken word, human-to-human communication, must finally be recognised by the gods of reactionary schooling. The pundits call it oracy.On Thursday, the education secretary, Lucy Powell, called the academics’ bluff. She wants a radical reform of the national curriculum in England to reduce “desktop” working in favour ofverbal fluency and practical skills. This will take courage. For decades, education’s senior leaders have been ramming easily forgotten “subjects”, such as maths and French,into children’s brains so they can be judged and measured in league tables. These tables have grown ever more dominant as ministers seek to climb “global rankings”.After the second world war, an “academic” secondary education was shaped by the increased demand for a university-educated workforce. Higher education was expanded, but Britain’s technical and vocational schools and colleges wererelegated out of sight. Teaching became enslaved to exam quantification and lost contact with the real world.But the act of excluding communication skills from this academic orthodoxy has come home to roost. Artificial intelligence and mobile phones are progressively distancing young people from adults and each other. I notice gatherings of young people who used to chatter, laugh and banter. They now stand gazing at their screens or they just shout at each other. Conversation – sharing, informing, discussing, sympathising – seems on the way out.Speaking itself is going out of fashion. Research suggests that in the past two decades the number of words people say each day has shrunk bynearly a third. They prefer texting. A quarter of young people now say theynever even answer the phoneunless pre-arranged. They fear a phone call means bad news.Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage. It is about conveying what one means clearly; listening, debating and handling disagreement. Speaking well means using eye contact and appropriately adjusting your tone of voice. It means politeness and tolerance. Above all, it enables young people to present themselves to others effectively, whether in work, play, argument or friendship.To the Greeks and Romans, oracy was the towering skill of rhetoric. It was central to citizenship. The New Education movement of Steiner and Montessori in early 20th-century Europe stressed building on the qualities of the individual child rather than imposing rote learning from above. It is significant that the movement has seen a revival in theWaldorf schoolsnow favoured by California’s AI executives in Silicon Valley.That such ideals of progressive education have long been drummed out of the English curriculum is outrageous. The aversion to the spoken word has corresponded with the increasing prominence of maths in the curriculum, its skills beyond foundational arithmeticirrelevant to all but a tiny minorityof adults. Children need to master elementary maths in primary school. But after that they only need to know how to use a calculator. I wonder how many readers remember being able to answer this question fromlast year’s GCSE paper: “The volume of a sphere is 4/3πr³ whereris the radius. Work out the volume of a sphere with diameter 20cm in terms of π.”It is extraordinary that passing this exam isstill required for most apprenticeships. Yet while he was prime minister, Rishi Sunakwanted maths to be compulsoryuntil the age of 18. Small wonder it has long headed the list of“most hated” school subjects.Quite how the teaching profession will react to Powell is not clear. The hyper-centralisation of British government has meant ever more school time spent on exams. This has led to cutting back on individualised learning and creativity, which typically flourishes in teaching of the arts. Teachers are pressed to “teach to the test”, at peril of damnation from Ofsted. These days, only the private sector dares resist.Winchester collegedevotes an hour a day to its form of oracy: “div” and “forum” sessions, when pupils discuss contemporary topics not covered by the examination syllabus: scientific ideas, philosophy, politics, music, critical thinking and the acceptance of others’ opinions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch speech-centred concepts as group learning and peer tutoring are being pursued in some universities, and the cause was taken forward in the 2024oracy commission report. But the catch is always resources. The essence of teaching people how to speak must lie in personal contact. It is in the human relationship of tutor and pupil, which was once the essence of teaching as a profession, not a mechanical skill.One key might lie in killing maths. Leave it to its enthusiasts. For the rest, school should be about the world outside, a world of other human beings. It is about how to go about handling them that young people have most to learn.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEducationOpinionLucy PowellGCSEsExamsSchoolsEnglandMathematicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: No Nobel again for Trump but he looks a cert to retain Fifa peace prize | John Crace | The Guardian
description: With his war in Iran and siding with Russia, it’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place
Author: John Crace
Headline: With his war in Iran and siding with Russia, it’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place
Content: The US president is put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe US president is put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersDigested weekDonald TrumpDigested week: No Nobel again for Trump but he looks a cert to retain Fifa peace prizeJohn CraceWith his war in Iran and siding with Russia, it’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer placeFri 16 Oct 2026 06.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.40 EDTShareMondayIt might have been more, shall we say, diplomatic if Donald Trump had taken some deep breaths after finding out he had been overlooked for the Nobel peace prize for the second year running before virtually declaring war on Norway. But maybe we should just be grateful he refrained from rubbishing the South African human rights activist Navi Pillay,who picked up the award, and shelved his plans to livestream the execution of the Norwegian prize committee. There again, you can understand his frustration. It’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place. Where would we be had not The Donald started a war with Iran which he shows no sign of knowing how to finish and which has forced up the price of global energy? And it was so good to see him intervening so positively in Russia’s war with Ukraine by appearing to side with the aggressor. These are just the things everyone is looking for in a Nobel peace laureate. The president is also put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts; though it would be helpful if he could let us know which ones. Are they ones he has personally started – Trump appears disappointed that Argentina hasn’t invaded the Falklands again – or ones that only he knows about. During a press conference at Chequers in 2025, he claimed to have brought about a lasting peace between Albania and Azerbaijan. Maybe there are other wars going on we just don’t know about. Perhaps Australia and New Zealand have been bombing each other for years with neither side noticing. And perhaps the border between France and Italy has been a no-go zone ever since the fight between Zinedine Zidane and Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final. Still, Trump looks a cert to retain Gianni Infantino’s Fifa peace prize –if only because it seems likely to be scrapped, making him the only winner.TuesdayWe may be facing higher levels of global threat and energy costs, but the political outlook isn’t all bleak. You’d need to have a major sense of humour failure not to be enjoying Reform sliding in the polls and falling out with one another. Things seemed to start going wrong when the Guardian exposed Nigel Farage’s £5m bung fromthe Thai-based crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne. Nige has still not come up with a convincing explanation of how the money would be spent. Other than maintaining an expensive lifestyle. Then there was the Channel 4 sting when two of Farage’s closest political allieswere caught allegedly trying to take an illegal overseas donation. Nige’s excuse? He wasn’t listening to his conversation with the donor. Who hasn’t dozed off when there’s £500,000 at stake? Since then everyone in Reform appears hell-bent on being the worst versions of themselves as the party loses support by tacking ever further to the right. On Monday, Robert Jenrickdeclaredhe would personally be happy to give the order for the Royal Navy to blow every small boat crossing the Channel out of the water. This was too much for Zia Yusuf. Zia is widely loathed within the Reform elite but no one has found a way of saying no to his money, so he gets to call himself the bogus title of shadow home secretary. His main objection to Honest Bob’s plan is that he wasn’t the one to think of it first. Meanwhile, Nige just sits back and pockets the money. Seemingly unable to stop his party collapsing around him.View image in fullscreenMeghan: ‘I hope I’m not upstaging the – what’s she called? – the Princess of Welsh.’Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersWednesdayAfter several years of consultation,the Bank of England has announced the four animals, insects and birds that will appear on the new banknotes. What goes on what denomination has yet to be decided, but the ones chosen are the European hedgehog, the barn owl, the buff-tailed bumblebee and the Atlantic puffin. And while I’d have quite liked to have seen my much-missed dog Herbie, who died last year, on one of the notes, they all seem reasonable choices to me. I guess the last thing the Bank wanted was to start a war between cat and dog lovers. But not everyone is happy. Partly because they are mad but mostly because they don’t apparently understand how the selection process worked. It was the public who got to choose both the theme of the banknotes and the actual creatures. Needless to say, leading the charge against the new notes are Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, who see the hedgehog and the puffin as some kind of woke symbols. A country going to the barn owls and the bumblebees. They have moaned, what was wrong with having Winston Churchill? Are we now ashamed of our past? No, you halfwits. You don’t have to plaster Churchill’s face on everything to prove you are British. Most of us are secure enough in our identity not to need countless flags and symbols as a reminder. It’s just nice to have a change from time to time. And how many people used to see Churchill’s face on a £5 note and feel a well of pride every time you wanted to buy a sandwich? For that matter, how many people even use cash these days? Mind you, once AI has mined all our data from our emails and bank accounts we could be back to a cash and letter-writing society.ThursdayIn one of his last conversations with a close friend,Jeffrey Archerwas asked if he had any regrets. While he admitted to having some flaws, Archer went on to say that there was nothing he would change. I find that remarkable. I’m not expecting him to apologise for having invented so much of his life – a fantasist is going to fantasise – and he had every right to be proud of his book sales. But not to feel a tiny bit of regret about having lied on oath and being sent to prison. Or feel guilty for the lives he ruined as a result of his lies. That feels borderline sociopathic. Isn’t it human to wish you had done some things differently? I’ve been thinking about this now I’ve turned 70. There’s a lot about my life that I love – family, friends, job – but I have a lasting sadness and guilt about my 20s that I find hard to forgive. The waste, the self-destruction, the damage I did to myself and others. Many of those who knew me had doubts I would even live to 30. I had those doubts, too. And sometimes didn’t much care either way. So yes, I have a whole decade I would love to have done differently. The repair job has been a lifetime’s work and it’s still ongoing. It will probably always be thus.View image in fullscreenBurnham to Zelenskyy: ‘Oh. I was hoping you might have some money for our armed forces.’Photograph: Alastair Grant/APFridayThe Celebrity Traitors continues to be addictive television. A class above the civilian version, partly because we all know something about the celebs, but mainly because the game is different. The civilians are playing for money, the celebs are playing for screen time. That’s why Amol Rajan was gutted to be banished inside 24 hours. The one exception was Richard E Grant, who didn’t care one way or the other. Since his wife died he’s become more disinhibited. The worst has already happened to him. Halfway in, Maya Jama and James Acaster are making great traitors. Maya because she’s so hard to read as her face doesn’t move, James because he genuinely believes he’s too nice to be a traitor while stabbing his friends in the back. I’m amazed Jerry Hall is still in. Not because she’s particularly suspicious but more because she’s incredibly annoying. And why has no one asked her what it was like being married to Rupert Murdoch? The faithful who is playing a blinder is Sharon Rooney. So far she has said and done nothing to attract the film crew, which means she’s likely to be around for a while yet. Being boring is not a bad strategy. I’d like to see a version ofThe Traitorsfor politicians, and in my forthcoming shows (Birmingham MAC on 31 October, Huntingdon theatre in Worcester on 26 November) I will be inviting the audience to offer suggestions for possible contestants. So please come along and let’s see if we can make it happen.View image in fullscreenPrince William: ‘Couldn’t Harry have done this one?’Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAOn Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. title: The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win | Frances Ryan | The Guardian
description: The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Content: People rallying against disability benefit cuts in Parliament Square last year.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople rallying against disability benefit cuts in Parliament Square last year.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianOpinionWelfareThe right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and winFrances RyanThe prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the momentFri 16 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.02 EDTShareBack in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: alandmark reportpromising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”.The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them. They’ve even providedan interactive map(in the yellow and black colours of a road hazard sign, no less) so members of the public can type in their postcode to see if their neighbourhood is “a welfare hotspot”.This is not just another ugly social policy report from a politically sidelined former minister – it is a gauntlet being thrown down ahead of Britain’s big benefits debate.Next month, the government is expected to release two major reports into the social safety net:the Timms reviewon personal independence payments (Pip), which pays for some of the extra costs of disability in England and Wales, and theMilburn reviewinto young people who are out of work.It wouldn’t be overstating the importance of Westminster reviews to say their recommendations could shape the future of our welfare state for decades to come. With almost1 millionyoung people not in education, employment or training (Neet) and the disability benefits bill rising in cash terms, Andy Burnham will face immense pressure to use the proposals to launch a once-in-a-generation overhaul of the social security system.An overhaul in itself is no bad thing. Disabled people applying for benefits face a debilitating mess of bureaucracy and barriers, while too many young people have been abandoned, facing greater obstacles and fewer services. The question is, will the overhaul actually improve conditions for the people who rely on it, or buckle to the anti-benefit sentiment that’s been bubbling up for months?That the right is not currently in power won’t stop it from wielding significant influence on what’s to come, in large part thanks to its dominance of Britain’s media ecosystem. Legacy media are not even hiding their attempts to shape November’s reforms before they are announced, with the Times this week launching a “welfare inquiry” to investigate the impact of the benefits “crisis” on public finances.Some of this is made up of concrete policy proposals, such as the Daily Mail’s pitch toradically means-test Pip. But increasingly much of it is just vibes, a vague sense that this disability problem is getting out of control (or having one isbecoming “cool”, as the Telegraph recently put it), and that disabled people – particularly the young – are somehow grifting “perks” while everyone else struggles with rising bills.The changes in how people consume media since the last major benefits reforms in the early 2010s mean the risks of misinformation and outright bigotry are even greater. Last week, Nigel Farage announced plans for a new video studio in Westminster for thelaunch of Reform TV on YouTube, with the party’sproposed £50bn benefits cutspresumably being lined up as viral content.Keep an eye out too for a revival of the striver v scrounger rhetoric asenergy and housing costsare set to lead to the worst living standards in modern times by 2029-30. There are few easier ways to convince workers that the unemployed should go hungry than when they’re cutting back on their own food shop. It is telling that the CSJ study includes a section directly comparing “economically inactive claimants” with workers: someone on minimum wage would have to work six days a week to match “the security, cash and ease” a disabled person gets from a package of state benefits, it proclaims. About 1.4 million foreign nationals receive working-age benefits, it ominously adds. Divide and conquer never gets old.A Labour government is no guarantee these divisions – worker v claimants, old v young, migrant v citizen – won’t be espoused from the cabinet table. No recommendations by Timms or Milburn have been confirmed yet, butWhitehall sources saythere are potential plans to scrap a key part of universal credit for under-25s and replace it with a multi-billion pound package to get people back into work.Sure, it’s depressing if ministers are tempted to bow to the prevailing political winds by pulling cash from young people, but it’s not exactly surprising. For decades, the right has set the boundaries for what Britain’s safety net can be, resulting in little more than subsistence-level benefit rates, an ever crueller culture of testing and a sicker population.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe conventional wisdom has always been that change can only go one way: the benefits system can repeatedly become more punitive and error-strewn, but never more compassionate or accurate. For a leader who has defined himself as someone unafraid of large-scale change, Burnham is well placed to challenge that orthodoxy – if he wants. The opportunity to transform the benefits system does not come up often, and it is rarer still for a Conservative prime minister not to be at the helm.It’s unfashionable to say it out loud but the truth is that Labour has the power to radically improve the disability benefits system: introduce moreevidence-based assessmentsand reduce the need for mass appeals against incorrect decisions; stop using public money to line the pockets of private companies; and endunnecessary reassessments for lifelong disabilities. Similarly, ministers can address why more people need disability benefits in the first place: by investing in threadbare mental health support; addressing NHS waiting times and poor preventive health services;fixing Access to Work; and tackling employer attitudes to disabled candidates.The right has long believed it has a monopoly on Britain’s benefits system, as if it were still paternalistic Victorians punishing and pitying the lower orders. But check the calendar and it is 2026. There is aLabourgovernment in office and two big wads of research coming that can at last lay the groundwork for remaking our safety net. The millions who rely on it must hold their breath to see whether that chance will be grabbed or thrown away.Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsWelfareOpinionBenefitsDisabilityLabourAndy BurnhamUniversal creditcommentShareReuse this content

title: Since my daughter moved out of home, my household has shrunk. A yearly tradition brings us together | Nova Weetman | The Guardian
description: Since my mother died, I have tried other jams – Seville orange, apricot, rich plum – but there are no memories to the taste
Author: Nova Weetman
Headline: Since my mother died, I have tried other jams – Seville orange, apricot, rich plum – but there are no memories to the taste
Content: ‘Making cumquat jam is a tradition I inherited from my mum. Along with her recipes for plum pudding, broad bean falafels and tomato relish.’Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Making cumquat jam is a tradition I inherited from my mum. Along with her recipes for plum pudding, broad bean falafels and tomato relish.’Photograph: Getty ImagesOpinionJams, preserves and spreadsSince my daughter moved out of home, my household has shrunk. A yearly tradition brings us togetherNova WeetmanI wait each year for my cumquat tree to fruit. Then I make Mum’s jamFri 16 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTShareIt’s citrus season, and the trees of my streets are heavy with the bright balls of fruit. My son sometimes picks me a lemon or two on his way home from school, and I help myself to the basket of limes that hang from the fence of a nearby house. The potted plant on my balcony fruited early this season, and for weeks I watched as the hundreds of small green cumquats slowly ripened. I finally picked them when they were fattened with juice and seeds and colour, the cat squatting on the ground to watch. When I dropped a cumquat she sniffed at the skin and turned away, as if sensing the sharpness of its flesh.When life gives you cumquats or kumquats make a marmalade and mezcal cocktail – recipeRead moreSince my daughter moved out several years ago, my household has shrunk. It is now only my son and me. And the cat. A scratchy, sullen creature who delights in ignoring us both unless we are sitting in the seat she believes is hers. My son has begun cooking for himself, and so I find my services in the kitchen required less often. Except for the yearly making of cumquat jam.The jam is a tradition I inherited from my mum. Along with her recipes for plum pudding, broad bean falafels and tomato relish. When I was a kid, Mum would scavenge each year in her friends’ gardens for cumquats and then spend close to two days chopping, deseeding, soaking, boiling and jarring the fruit to fill our cupboards with the stained glass orange jam. Years later, when I had children, Mum introduced them to the tart taste, and they were hooked too. When she died, 15 years ago, winter came and went without our usual jars to see us through. We tried eating jam made from other fruits. Seville orange, apricot, rich plum, but there were no memories to the taste, and the jars would sit unfinished in the fridge for months.Witnessing my grief at losing my mum, some friends bought me a baby cumquat tree in a large yellow ceramic pot that proved itself hardy enough to survive my limited gardening skills. The first year that it flowered with delicate white buds, we watched, delighting in the growth of the cumquats, waiting until they were large enough to pick. My kids helped strip the tree of fruit. It was nothing like the haul Mum used to make jam with, but it filled a bowl. I hacked up the cumquats, not neatly like Mum did, but fast and furious, not bothering to remove the pips because I’d read somewhere they would float up during boiling and you could scoop them from the top with the scum. Impatiently, I didn’t follow the ratio of sugar or simmer for the correct amount of time, and that first batch was overcooked. The jam was too dark in colour, and the texture was all wrong, but we ate it anyway, the taste taking me immediately back to my childhood home, where I’d perch up at the bench each morning before school and work my way through rye toast smeared with jam.View image in fullscreen‘Witnessing my grief at losing my mum, some friends bought me a baby cumquat tree in a large yellow ceramic pot.’Photograph: Nova WeetmanThe following year, I channelled Mum’s patience and made two large jars of jam. They were the perfect amber-colour, rich and bright, with chunks of rind and the occasional pip. It wasn’t enough to squirrel away in the cupboard like a true survivalist, but it saw us through a month or two of breakfasts. This year, I managed six jars, enough to spare for giving one to a friend, and another to my daughter when she came for dinner one night. She took half our loaf of fresh sourdough bread with her too so she could replicate the favourite breakfast of her childhood.My son and I are now down to our last jar of jam, and we have started rationing it without discussion, eating it on toast weekly instead of daily, to make it last as long as we can. I do sometimes buy cumquat jam if I see it at a market, but it never quite tastes the same. There is something treasured in waiting each year for the tree to grow the fruit to make the jam. It is ritual that connects us to the jam that Mum once made.My cumquat tree still lives in the same yellow pot. It has moved house twice with us, requiring four people to lift it on to a trolley, and it now grows in the strip of sun on our apartment balcony. It is not much to look at it until the flowers come and the fruit arrives, but then it brings with it all the promise of the taste of my childhood.Nova Weetman is an award-winning author of books for children and young adultsExplore more on these topicsJams, preserves and spreadsOpinionFruitFamilyAustralian food and drinkcommentShareReuse this content

title: AI threatens democracy. But we are not powerless: here’s how to fight back | Carine Fouteau | The Guardian
description: Tech platforms pillage public-interest journalism for profit. But we have leverage, as they sow the seeds of their own downfall, says Carine Fouteau, head of Mediapart
Author: Carine Fouteau
Headline: Tech platforms pillage public-interest journalism for profit. But we have leverage, as they sow the seeds of their own downfall, says Carine Fouteau, head of Mediapart
Content: ‘Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance. AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator.’Photograph: Marcela Barsse/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance. AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator.’Photograph: Marcela Barsse/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI threatens democracy. But we are not powerless: here’s how to fight backCarine FouteauTech platforms pillage public-interest journalism for profit. But we have leverage as they sow the seeds of their own downfallCarine Fouteau is president and publishing director of the French investigative news outlet MediapartFri 16 Oct 2026 03.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 04.43 EDTShareBig tech companies pose an immeasurable threat: socially, politically, militarily and ecologically. They are also causing a profound crisis of information. The tools they design now serve as weapons of mass destruction against democracy. There is so much at stake that an urgent and broad mobilisation is required.From theharvesting of personal dataand the weaponisation of public opinion, to the destruction of jobs, the infringement of civil liberties and environmental damage, ordinary citizens are the main victims of this predatory economy – an economy with an agenda that aligns with the interests of the planet’s most authoritarian and reactionary states.The threats facing the information landscape affect us all. Journalists of my generation have witnessed four major digital revolutions: the internet, social media, smartphones, and now, artificial intelligence. What fundamentally changes with AI is our relationship with the truth. For big tech companies, the boundary between truth and falsehood has vanished. This makes it essential to reaffirm the role of public-interest journalism. Our mission is to publish information that is in the public interest by seeking the factual truth, standing against “fake news” and propaganda. Our mission is to help create a democratic public sphere that serves citizens.Yet AI companies are completely reshaping this space to their own advantage; their mission is not the public interest, but generating profits. Their methods include plundering news outlets without authorisation or compensation. By disseminatingso-called summaries of our reporting, they siphon off our audiences and revenue, serving the private interests of a select few at the expense of the common good.The difference between AI-generated content and a real news article is journalism. AI-generated responses are not information. They are merely a logical assembly of words that all too often produces falsehoods, distorts facts and misinterprets information. A real news article is something else entirely. Quality journalism is the product of expertise guided by ethical standards: persuading sources to speak, painstakingly gathering eye-witness testimonies, cross-referencing, verifying and establishing facts. This process relies on reporting or investigative work – in other words, human effort in the field.Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance; AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator and breeds confusion. Journalism uncovers facts that certain parties – particularly economic and political powers – would prefer to see hidden, ignored, or suppressed. Generative AI uncovers nothing, it merely regurgitates and condenses existing material.Quality journalism comes at a high price. Some of the costs can’t even be quantified. Journalists who report from war zones for example, risk their lives. Mediapart’s recentinvestigationinto Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party, has resulted in anonymous cyber-harassment and death threats against our editorial team.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators protest outside an Anthropic office in New York, 14 October 2026.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAUltimately, media outlets are accountable for the information they publish. They answer to the courts and to their readers. AI companies appear answerable only to their shareholders. They refuse to vouch for the reliability of their conversational agents to evade legal liability. If nothing is done to stop it, this pillaging will result in the destruction of journalism. This is dangerous not just for news publishers, but for all of us, because it signifies the demise of a public sphere defined by free, pluralistic and democratic discourse.Do we want a public sphere that guarantees access to reliable, independent information, or one governed by algorithms that amplify fake news, deepfakes and propaganda – fuelling fear, anger and division?Fortunately, the tech companies have sown the seeds of their own downfall. Since they are bleeding dry the very sources of information from which they derive their profits, they are courting their own failure; without quality information, they will produce nothing but AI slop.This is precisely where we find leverage.OpenAI has admittedthat it would be impossible to train today’s leading AI models without using copyrighted material. AMicrosoft vice-president acknowledged thattraining models on quality contentsignificantly improves the quality of output.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe priority is to act collectively, pressuring these platforms by every available means – including legal action – to uphold the rights of the press and the public. Some newspapers, such as the New York Times, havetaken legal action. Its publisher, AG Sulzberger, recently cited a figure of $20m spent on litigation. Legal proceedings are also under wayin France– notably through the organisation responsible for collecting press-relatedneighbouring rights.Beyond pressuring lawmakers at national and European level, we must broaden our fightback to include the entire research and knowledge community – stakeholders who, like us, are committed to the public interest and factual truth.It falls to us, as journalists, to convince the public that our work is an essential part of democracy. We have to demonstrate that our reporting – aimed at holding power to account – has real impact and drives change; that it makes sense of a rapidly shifting world and serves as a powerful catalyst for civic action.Carine Fouteau is president and publishing director of the French investigative news outlet MediapartMediapart is hosting Hacking Big Tech, a public event about technology, AI and democracy in partnership with the Guardian, in Paris on Saturday 17 October 2026. The conference will be live-streamed free on Mediapart’s website, app and YouTube channel and can be accessedherefrom 1pm CEST on 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionEuropeInvestigative journalismDigital mediaPublic service reportingOpenAIcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Financiers owe their windfalls and bonuses to higher interest rates. Britain should reclaim more for the public and resist City lobbying
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Financiers owe their windfalls and bonuses to higher interest rates. Britain should reclaim more for the public and resist City lobbying
Content: ‘Banks need to be both public utilities and good corporate citizens.’Photograph: Ian West/PAView image in fullscreen‘Banks need to be both public utilities and good corporate citizens.’Photograph: Ian West/PAOpinionBudgetThe Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to taxEditorialFinanciers owe their windfalls and bonuses to higher interest rates. Britain should reclaim more for the public and resist City lobbyingFri 16 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 17.41 EDTShareJohn Healey is planning to tax British banks, the Guardianrevealed, in the forthcoming budget. It’sabout timefor the chancellor to act. Banks have been raking it in. The campaign groupPositive Moneyreported this summer that Britain’s four biggest banks made £29bn in the first half of this year, up a fifth on 2025. These windfalls owe more to higher interest rates than better products or services. Households and businesses pay more to borrow. Meanwhile, the Bank of England pays the banks tens of billions in interest on their reserves, with theTreasuryfooting the bill.The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around£2bn a year. This would recover a very modest share of the sector’s bonanza. Louis XIV’s finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, said that “the art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing”. Britain’s banks have plenty of feathers. That hasn’t stopped themhissing. The banks say that they already facehighertaxes than other companies, that they won’t be able to lend as much, and that their profits won’t last.View image in fullscreenJohn Healey.Photograph: ReutersBut banks aren’t taxed on their windfall gains, and what levies they face are less than those paid byoil and gas companies. The Bank of England said banks spent£7.7bnon dividends and buying back shares in the first quarter of 2026 withoutaffectinglending. Higher taxes might mean trimming shareholder payouts. There’s nothing to suggest productive lending must take the hit. Over the past five years Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest – which control the majority of UK personal and business accounts – madeprofits of £200bn. Positive Money says that households lost out on£44bnin deposit interest in 2025. Some of this paid for banking services. But that does not explain why the sum is five times the equivalent average figure for 2009-21.The chancellor could be more radical. The precedent here is not a socialist one. Margaret Thatcher taxed banks’windfallsin 1981. A comparable 2.5% levy on today’s interest-free deposits would, a paper by the New Economics Foundation and Positive Money suggests, raise more than£11bn. In August, Positive Money suggested looking at Spain’s success in levying a windfall tax on banks’ net income above €800m. It says that such a windfall tax – levied at the same rate as that paid by fossil fuel companies on a comparable tax base – would bring in£19bnfrom the UK arms of the big four banks. That would pay for a universal and comprehensive adultsocial caresystem.Banks need to be both public utilities and good corporate citizens. Yet the sector is paying thehighestbankers’ bonuses since the 2008 global financial crisis. “Most financial sector activity,” concluded a paperpublishedin The Manchester School journal this month, “is simply negative for overall economic performance.” Politicians should stop mistaking finance lobbyists’ demands for a growth strategy. Their job is to curb a finance sector so large that it risks crises and weaker growth. Taxpayers rescued the banks after they helped crash the economy 18 years ago. Public protection carries public obligations. As Sir Philip Augar, the author and former banker, told the BBC: “Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Winnie-the-Pooh: now we are 100 | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: He may have been eclipsed by the more progressive Paddington of late, but AA Milne’s creation is not just a Silly Old Bear
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: He may have been eclipsed by the more progressive Paddington of late, but AA Milne’s creation is not just a Silly Old Bear
Content: The new set of stamps issued by Royal Mail to celebrate Winnie-the-Pooh’s 100th birthday.Photograph: Royal Mail/PAView image in fullscreenThe new set of stamps issued by Royal Mail to celebrate Winnie-the-Pooh’s 100th birthday.Photograph: Royal Mail/PAOpinionAA MilneThe Guardian view on Winnie-the-Pooh: now we are 100EditorialHe may have been eclipsed by the more progressive Paddington of late, but AA Milne’s creation is not just a Silly Old BearFri 16 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 17.33 EDTShare“Pooh, promise you won’t forget about me, ever. Not even when I’m a hundred,” Christopher Robin implores his bear in the final chapter of AA Milne’s The House at Pooh Corner. This week Winnie-the-Pooh himself turned 100, and he certainly hasn’t been forgotten. Birthday celebrations have includeda week of special programmes, introduced by the queen, on Radio 4; a collection ofRoyal Mail stamps; and aGoogle doodle.Not bad for “a bear of very little brain” who appeared in four slim books. Winnie-the-Pooh, illustrated by EH Shepard, was published on 14 October 1926 and had sold 150,000 copies in the US by the end of the year.Despite his success, the honey-loving bear was resented by both Milne and his son Christopher Robin Milne, the first for eclipsing his work as a playwright and comic writer, the latter for stealing his childhood. And he was too sugary for some. “It is that word ‘hummy,’” Dorothy Parkerwrotewaspishly under her pseudonym Constant Reader, “that makes the first place … at which Tonstant Weader fwowed up”. PG Wodehouse and Evelyn Waugh were equally sniffy. But generations of children disagreed. Winnie-the-Pooh was voted No 7 in theBBC Big Read pollin 2003.Pooh’s position as Britain’s favourite bear is under threat from a younger ursine model. Separated by 32 years and one day, Michael Bond’s A Bear Called Paddington was published on 13 October 1958. These two polite and accident-prone bears differ in more than a taste for honey or marmalade.Both stories were created in the aftermath of war: Winnie-the-Pooh was Milne’s escape from the horrors of the Somme; Paddington was inspired by evacuees in the second world war. Pooh was based on a toy from Harrods, Paddington on a solitary teddy that Bond found in a toyshop on Christmas Eve. The Hundred Acre Wood is a sheltered rural idyll; Paddington arrives at a bustling postwar London station. Both are beloved at Buckingham Palace, but it was the bear from Peru who was invited to tea forthe platinum jublee of Queen Elizabeth II.Thanks to three hit films and nowan award-winning musical, Paddington has shaken off his slightly fusty image to become an emblem of modern Britain. Where Paddington is progressive, Pooh seems stuck in a posher past.Aside from being one of the world’s biggest merchandising franchises, Winnie-the-Pooh’s cultural afterlife has been bumpier. Screen adaptations have been mixed, from Disney’s 1966 animation, which EH Shepard declared“a complete travesty”, to the indie slasher horrorWinnie the Pooh: Blood and Honey, made after Milne’s US copyright expired in 2022. Pooh has become an unlikely symbol ofpolitical dissent in Chinaafter President Xi was visually likened to him in 2013, with protesters in Hong Kongpicking up the comparisonin 2019.According to aCanadian medical journal, each character represents a form of neurodivergence or mental health disorder: Tigger stands for ADHD, Piglet for anxiety, Eeyore for depression and so on. The article may not have been entirely serious, but the author Matt Haig has described Winnie-the-Pooh as“the ultimate self-help book”. Pooh is not just a “silly old bear”. In our speeded-up age, where children spend more time on screens than outdoors, Milne’s world of freedom and innocence remains deeply comforting, for “in that enchanted place on the top of the forest a little boy and his Bear will always be playing”.Explore more on these topicsAA MilneOpinionChildren's books: 7 and underChildrenWalt Disney CompanyeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Kitchen utensils with family stories to tell | Family | The Guardian
description: Letters: Guardian readers reflect and reminisce about the cooking equipment that has been significant in their families
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Guardian readers reflect and reminisce about the cooking equipment that has been significant in their families
Content: A 1950s kitchen.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenA 1950s kitchen.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyFamilyLettersKitchen utensils with family stories to tellGuardian readers reflect and reminisce about the cooking equipment that has been significant in their familiesFri 16 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTShareAmong the wedding presents from 1963 that I still use (Letters, 9 October) are Denby ovenware, a complete set of Prestige kitchen utensils, a Victorinox paring knife we bought with money given to us for bedsheets, and smoked-glass wine and sherry glasses from a friend of my parents. When a grandchild noticed that we had rather a lot of flower vases, we had to confess that when asked what we would like as a present, we were so embarrassed that we always said “a flower vase”, knowing that it could come in at any price. It was a vintage year, 1963.Prue BakerBrightonI inherited my mother’s potato masher, bought just after the war. As a newly married housewife setting up home with everything in short supply and rationing continuing, she told me that she was delighted to see the masher for sale and bought two – one for her sister. It was flimsy – a thin circular metal holed base with three wires attached, which were twisted to form the stem, and a wooden handle painted blue. History and memories in a utensil.Sue RawsonScarborough,North YorkshireFor Christmas 1944, I gave my mother a breadboard fashioned from a slab of elm – probably an offcut from a coffin board. In spite of decades of mockery about its imperfection – I have to confess that it is a far-from-regular octagon – she used it for many years before passing it back to me. It is still in daily use.Martin KnightHovingham, North YorkshireMy elder daughter has insisted I leave her my bag of clothes pegs – they largely consist of very worn spring-loaded ones which belonged to my mother. I suspect that many of them date from late 1930s.Joy StephensonHigh Peak, DerbyshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The appeal of eating a loved one’s ashes | Bereavement | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Rachael Stirling
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Rachael Stirling
Content: Rachael Stirling with her mother, Diana Rigg.Photograph: Chris Barham/ANL/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRachael Stirling with her mother, Diana Rigg.Photograph: Chris Barham/ANL/ShutterstockBereavementLettersThe appeal of eating a loved one’s ashesReaders respond to an article by Rachael StirlingFri 16 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTShareI would like to reassure Rachael Stirling (‘I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a cannibal’: Rachael Stirling on eating her mother Diana Rigg’s ashes, 11 October) that, far from grimacing or feeling disgust over her admission of eating a few grains of her mother’s ashes, I was deeply moved. My best friend’s beloved mother died last year and I immediately sent the quote to her, as I knew it would resonate with her.Asyour reviewof Stirling’s book entitled All About My Mother states, she eats a grain of her mother’s ashes so that she is “cloaked in her, shielded and shrouded by her. I am her. My mother is my superpower. She always was.”These words perfectly encapsulate how my friend feels about her own mother, and how so many of us feel about the person from whose body we came.Emily HallLlanbadarn Fawr, CeredigionI was interested to read Rachael Stirling’s article as I have long been familiar with the practice of drinking the ashes of the deceased. Kenneth Good’s book Into the Heart: An Amazonian Love Story describes his anthropological study of the Yanomami people in the Amazon, where, after cremation, all the ashes are mixed into a drink made of sweet, ripe plantain and consumed – with an accompanying feast – by the close family, friends and others who wish to show their respect. I find that the practice has a certain appeal and can fully sympathise with Rachael’s use of her mother’s ashes.Pauline LoweBryn Y Maen, Colwyn BayI don’t expect to be the only one writing to reassure Rachael Stirling – I did it too! A tiny bit of my mum’s ashes in 1990, and of my partner’s in 2020. It’s a way of keeping them part of you. And I don’t see how it counts as cannibalism, whichis definedas eating human flesh.Fiona CollinsCorwen, DenbighshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Bringing more women out of the shadows and into the Wiki world | Books | The Guardian
description: Letters: We need to work together to build a more inclusive history, writes Mags L Halliday. Plus a letter from Shane Ritchie
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: We need to work together to build a more inclusive history, writes Mags L Halliday. Plus a letter from Shane Ritchie
Content: Books in the window of Waterstones on Princes Street, Edinburgh, 2018. ‘Earlier historians and archivists did not record the lives of women, making it harder to retrieve them from the shadows.’Photograph: Alan Wilson/AlamyView image in fullscreenBooks in the window of Waterstones on Princes Street, Edinburgh, 2018. ‘Earlier historians and archivists did not record the lives of women, making it harder to retrieve them from the shadows.’Photograph: Alan Wilson/AlamyBooksLettersBringing more women out of the shadows and into the Wiki worldWe need to work together to build a more inclusive history, writesMags L Halliday. Plus a letter fromShane RitchieFri 16 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTShareSandi Toksvig is right to highlight the systemic bias in information about women’s lives in history (Pass notes: Is Wikipedia ‘deeply biased’? Sandi Toksvig says it is – so she’s backing a rival, 12 October). Her comment about Wikipedia, however, implies that no one is working to correct this bias on the site itself. I belong to several projects whose goals are to reduce the gender gap on Wikipedia.One,Womenin Red, started in October 2014. At that point, only 15.53% of biographies on the encyclopedia were of women. As of October 2026, that has risen to 20.42%, in part thanks to the many volunteers who spend their spare time searching for reliable sources to draw on. The Women in Red project currently publishes an average of 1,500 new biographies every month.Whenever volunteers are creating a biography, we are hampered by far wider system biases than Wikipedia’s alone. There is the well-established difficulty that earlier historians and archivists did not record the lives of women, making it harder to retrieve them from the shadows.A quick look in a bookshop shows that this bias towards the Great Man view of history still holds sway, with far more biographies of individual men than of individual women being published. As Wikipedia does not accept primary research by the volunteer editors, there is an urgent need for more secondary sources such as Toksvig’s proposed Mappa Mundi and well-sourced biographies. This is not an either/or situation, but one where people need to work together to build a more inclusive history of the world.Mags L HallidayExeterYour article repeats Sandi Toksvig’s claim that the site is edited by “mostly white, middle-aged, European men”, as if it were a closed club. It isn’t. Anyone can edit Wikipedia, with or without an account, from a phone, today. If women’s biographies are missing, the remedy is free and open to Toksvig, to Cambridge and to every reader of this paper. A rival project needs fundraising only if the obstacle were access, and it isn’t.Most of the gap has a simpler cause. Wikipedia only covers people who have already been written about elsewhere. If newspapers and historians ignored women, Wikipedia has little to work with. That is the record’s fault, not the editors’.Wikipedia is one of the best things that the internet has produced: free, open, sourced, and fixable by anyone. Its gaps deserve a serious debate. Jokes that hint at an argument without making it are not that.Shane RitchieBangor, County DownHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: British students, like their French peers, have been known to challenge authority | Education | The Guardian
description: Letters: Pete Crockett says the history of British education is not simply one of children dutifully accepting adult instruction, while Simon Dawson says Kitty Sayers misses the mark when describing English attitudes. Plus a letter from Kevin Donnelly
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Pete Crockett says the history of British education is not simply one of children dutifully accepting adult instruction, while Simon Dawson says Kitty Sayers misses the mark when describing English attitudes. Plus a letter from Kevin Donnelly
Content: Pupils demonstrating in Parliament Square, London, demanding urgent action to tackle climate change in 2019.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/AlamyView image in fullscreenPupils demonstrating in Parliament Square, London, demanding urgent action to tackle climate change in 2019.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/AlamyEducationLettersBritish students, like their French peers, have been known to challenge authorityPete Crockettsays the history of British education is not simply one of children dutifully accepting adult instruction, whileSimon DawsonsaysKitty Sayersmisses the mark when describing English attitudes. Plus a letter fromKevin DonnellyFri 16 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTShareReading Kitty Sayers’ interesting article, I was reminded of the rich, and perhaps too easily forgotten, history of direct action by British schoolchildren (Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why, 10 October). Far from being historically meek or unquestioningly compliant, they have demonstrated a remarkable capacity for challenging authority.At Marlborough college, troops were once summoned to dislodge rebellious pupils occupying an island in the school grounds.In the late 1700s, Winchester college experienced several rebellions.Nor was such defiance confined to the more privileged.In 1889, strikes by schoolchildren in the Scottish lowlands spread across Tyneside, London, Bristol and Cardiff.In 1911, a strike beginning at Bigyn school in Llanelli developed into a remarkable wave of protest, reaching some 60 towns across England and Wales.Schoolchildren and their families also played their part in the extraordinary 1914Burston school strike, which endured for 25 years and became the longest‑running strike in British history.Those of us of a certain generation may also recall the National Union of School Students in the 1970s, whose challenges to established educational authority infuriated traditionalists such as the headmasterRhodes Boyson, who later became a Conservative minister.The history of British education is not simply one of children dutifully accepting adult instruction. It also has a rich tradition of collective action and resistance to perceived injustice. Schoolchildren challenging the established order is hardly a peculiarly French phenomenon. There is a substantial, if sometimes overlooked, British history of such action too.Pete CrockettRoyal Wootton Bassett, WiltshireKitty Sayers is illuminating on French attitudes to protest, but she misses the mark when describing English attitudes. She says that Britons are subjects rather than citizens; that word deserves more analysis.InThis Land is Our Land, Marion Shoard argues that England is in effect a colonised country, but conquered so long ago that we no longer notice how much it shapes us. Within a generation of 1066, the English landowning class had been almost entirely replaced, and many free peasants were pressed into serfdom. Shoard argues that when, centuries later, the English poor did protest, “as a defeated class, they looked only to improve the terms of their subjection, and … they failed even in that.”France, by contrast, eventually overturned its feudal order. Edward Carpenter wrote (in Towards Industrial Freedom) that victory at Waterloo had been a misfortune for England, denying us the upheaval that swept such structures away elsewhere. Perhaps that is why a French teenager reaches for the barricade and an English one reaches for a petition.The British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition is rightly presented as a marvel. As we queue to admire it, we should ask whether we still see the conquest it depicts, and its long shadow over our country, with necessary clarity.Simon DawsonWinterbourne Gunner, WiltshireKitty Sayers identifies the differences between the French and British education systems as a major contributory factor in why French students protest and British students don’t. Another may be in how protests are framed by the mass media in the UK.Often, the default position is what is known as the “protest paradigm”, which leads journalists to emphasise the methods used by protesters over the message; and in which even legitimate protests then receive delegitimising coverage.Changing the optics could bring more people out on to the streets, particularly if they feel they have a legitimate reason for doing so, and the media have a major role to play in creating and maintaining that environment for legitimate protest.Kevin DonnellySanremo, ItalyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: ‘It’s really not a drama’: Carrick sticks to the script after Martínez storm | Michael Carrick | The Guardian
description: The Manchester United head coach produced a masterclass in dialling down emotion before a tricky trip to Leeds on Sunday
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The Manchester United head coach produced a masterclass in dialling down emotion before a tricky trip to Leeds on Sunday
