By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.‘They have total impunity’: West Bank settler violence surges after Gaza ceasefireRead moreThe rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited, for the purpose of preventing settler violence, from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026.The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers razed trees.Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well-documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop it.Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelWashington PostJournalist safetyMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms | Amazon rainforest | The Guardian
description: Forest clearance at smallest total since records began in 1988 in success for Lula ahead of presidential run-off
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Forest clearance at smallest total since records began in 1988 in success for Lula ahead of presidential run-off
Content: A deforested area of the Amazon rainforest in Amazonas state.Photograph: Edmar Barros/APView image in fullscreenA deforested area of the Amazon rainforest in Amazonas state.Photograph: Edmar Barros/APAmazon rainforestBrazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote loomsForest clearance at smallest total since records began in 1988 in success for Lula ahead of presidential run-offJonathan WattsFri 16 Oct 2026 15.37 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDeforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since records began, new government data shows.But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed ison a knife edgeahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump.The incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988.This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro.Since 2022, the year before the start of the Lula administration, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies.The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%).However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold.Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savannah – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soya and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%.View image in fullscreenDeforestation near a forest on the border between the Amazon and the Cerrado in Mato Grosso state.Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/ReutersThese spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5%increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses.The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.The former environment ministerMarina Silva, who has arguably done more than anyone to defend the rainforest,has warnedthat Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon.The stark contrast between the two candidates is evident in the electoral results map in the Amazon, where Bolsonaro secured the most votes near areas of degraded forest, mines, ranches and soya monocultures, while Lula’s support was higher in big cities or areas of forest where the vegetation was relatively intact.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is also evident in their very different relations to the US. Lula has warned that Trump is trying tocolonise the countryand capture its resources. He defends the Amazon as a sovereign asset for Brazil, an important home for Indigenous peoples and an essential element in global efforts to stabilise the climate.The Bolsonaro family, by contrast, has close ties to the US. Flavio’s brother Eduardo haslived in Texassince last year and called upon the Trump administration to impose punitive tariffs on his own country.Jair hassaluted the US flagand led chants of “USA, USA”. If the family secure power, they areexpected to shift Brazil’s trade priorities, particularly when it comes to critical minerals, from China and Europe to the US.The biggest difference, however, is likely to be the far right’s willingness to exploit natural resources in the Amazon and elsewhere in Brazil and then sell them to the highest bidder, regardless of environmental and social concerns.Conservation groups said the new deforestation data showed how much was at stake in the presidential run-off.Marcio Astrini, the executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, said: “The figure makes it clear that putting an end to forest destruction in Brazil is entirely possible.“However, everything depends on the election result. The country will decide whether we move toward the end of deforestation or toward the end of the forest.”Explore more on these topicsAmazon rainforestDeforestationBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroAmericasConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Extreme heatwaves in Europe not changing Britons’ holiday plans, say travel bosses | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Hot summer getaways are still popular – but tourism industry fears impact of rising jet fuel costs and squeezed household incomes
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Hot summer getaways are still popular – but tourism industry fears impact of rising jet fuel costs and squeezed household incomes
Content: People pack La Concha beach in the Spanish Basque city of San Sebastián, 21 June 2026, during the first heatwave in the summer.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople pack La Concha beach in the Spanish Basque city of San Sebastián, 21 June 2026, during the first heatwave in the summer.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesTravel & leisureExtreme heatwaves in Europe not changing Britons’ holiday plans, say travel bossesHot summer getaways are still popular – but tourism industry fears impact of rising jet fuel costs and squeezed household incomesGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a year marked by extreme heat and war sending fuel prices skywards, British travel executives hoped for solace in Madeira’s benign subtropical climate, separated by hundreds of miles of blue sea from the overtourism protests and six-hour EU-entry queues seen on the Portuguese mainland.As bosses admitted, holidays will be ever less affordable, AI is coming for their jobs, and the visitable world is shrinking – not least those parts where tourists remain welcome.Some of the biggeranxieties in spring, such as widespread border chaos and planes running out of fuel, have not come to pass; others now appear chronic issues. Newsupplies of jet fuel, a major concernafter the US first attacked Iran in February, have been established – but the cost is staying far higher for longer than most expected.“Fuel is a huge part of any holiday and people are going to have to reckon with the cost,” said Neil Swanson, Tui UK & Ireland managing director, among the attendees at the Abta convention.Tui and airlines such aseasyJetand Ryanair escaped the worst immediate impact by having secured much of their 2026 fuel supply at a fixed price. But the latter airlines are now slashing capacity for winter.“It’s not great for consumers, who are going to have to pay a lot more for their holidays. But airlines are going to be less and less hedged and prices are going to go up,” Swanson added.The oil price impact goes beyond jet fuel, said Mark Tanzer, the chief executive of Abta: “The bigger worry is the squeeze on household incomes that’s going to come through their domestic costs. It will be a much tighter market.”View image in fullscreenPlumes of smoke caused by a wildfire in Málaga, seen from Playa el Bajondillo beach in Torremolinos in 2022.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersPerhaps surprisingly,numbers have held up– but customers have been leaving it ever later to book, he said, whether in search of a deal or because of uncertainty from disruption, war or weather.Despite the intense heat, mass travel firms are clear that the template has not changed: most customers still want a hot holiday, in summer, on the beach.Garry Wilson, the chief executive of easyJet Holidays, said: “Will there be long-term effects on demand? Perhaps. But in the short-term, no, we don’t see it.”Growing “shoulder season” travel outside the school holidays for those who can, including city breaks, are driven by price more than climate, several people suggest. And talk of “coolcations” or people turning towards northern climes cuts little ice here. “We’re not seeing any of that,” said Swanson. “Nothing’s changed, the destinations are the same.”When Tunisia was forecast a 10-day stretch of 45C temperatures this summer, Tui offered customers the chance to switch their holiday elsewhere. Swanson said: “We didn’t get the interest and take-up. People were expecting it to be hot and were happy to go there, and we’re not seeing any change in demand. Brits like a warm holiday – if it’s got a pool and air-conditioning, that works for them.”Neither does Wilson see many heading north. Citing easyJet destinations such as Tromsø in Norway or Malmö in Sweden, he said: “They’re all very nice to launch, but we send more customers to Majorca in a week than those in a year.”Outbound holidays prospered in the heatwave, he suggested. “People thought: ‘You know what, we maybe don’t need to go away.’ But it became apparent that the UK doesn’t have the infrastructure to cope … people actually were going abroad to escape the heat in the UK.”For now, the big firms see little change in destinations, Swanson said, but added: “We’ll keep it under review. Who knows where the temperature’s going to go in the next few years?”More people could get priced out. At last year’s convention, the Spanish tourist board started pushing its cooler northern destinations; but, said Tanzer, “I’m not sure the north has 100m beds” to accommodate the visitors who predominantly go to Spain’s south, east and islands.He added: “Certain types of holiday could become more expensive just because there’s limited availability. If the snow is higher up the mountain, there’s going to be fewer skiing holidays and the price is going to go up – there’s little room at the top.”Tui has not been immune. Its river cruises in Europe were marooned when the Danube’s water levels dipped last month to the point where some passengers spent most of their return Austro-Hungarian cruise on a boat-replacement bus.View image in fullscreenUsually submerged areas of the Danube lie exposed in Romania amid exceptionally low water levelsPhotograph: Vadim Ghirdă/APKaty Berzins, the head of river cruises at Tui, said: “Every year has highs and lows and it’s part of river cruising, rivers are changeable.” But 2026, she said, was “unprecedented”.The division is expanding nonetheless. Two new ships are joining its fleet – initially destined for the Seine and the Douro – that are built with lower draught levels (the vessel’s vertical depth below the surface), meaning they are able to keep sailing in shallower rivers.Others are seeing faster change. James Thornton, the chief executive of Intrepid Travel, said the firm no longer sold active travel group tours in southern Europe in the summer; few had wanted to trek or cycle in that level of heat.Last year, Thornton said, there were 185 different extreme weather-related incidents that affected Intrepid holidaymakers around the world. “When we first started, there would be a handful.”Intrepid has long wrestled with its own impact on climate: for years, before offsetting fell into disrepute, it paid millions to offset its emissions. That did not cover the biggest factor, the flights taken by its customers to reach Intrepid tours – not entirely dissimilar from how an airport might declare itself net zero. Instead now the firm has a decarbonisation fund for local projects: “Ultimately you can’t have sustainable travel, you can only limit the impact,” Thornton said.Having grown from backpacking to a A$1bn annual business, its own footprint is becoming significant. This year the firm is launching Timor-Leste, or East Timor. Thornton said: “Some customers have done 30 to 40 trips, so they’re often looking for places that they haven’t been able to travel to.”Asked about overtourism, Thornton said: “We’re definitely worried about it.” Intrepid tries to advertise the less visited destinations, he added. “We call it the not-hot list – drawing out the places where the infrastructure is available and the locals are willing to welcome travellers.”View image in fullscreenPeople hold a placard that reads ‘tourism yes, but not like this’ during a protest against overtourism and housing prices in Mallorca in 2024.Photograph: Jaime Reina/AFP/Getty ImagesRising tourist taxes around the world underline that many places feel they have more than enough visitors. For Wilson, it is “grossly unfair”; destinations such as Mallorca, he said, “built enormous economic positions on the back of mass tourism, and then pull up the bridge and put on an extra tax. All that does is go back to the days of travel being only for the rich.”How many of the UK outbound travel industry remain in sufficient paid work to afford it may also be in question.Shaun Morton, the chief executive of On the Beach, laid off 20% of the Manchester-based online agency’s staff this summer to “automate and streamline” processes. He told delegates: “You’ve got the technology, people, processes and you hold them all dear … We just started to ask not how do we get 10% more out of that, but how do we get 10 times that, you know?”He added that “very bright people with a sharp head with technology” probably would keep their jobs longest, but acknowledged: “They’re worried, because they can see a little bit further ahead than everyone else.”The Guardian’s travel to the convention in Madeira was provided by AbtaExplore more on these topicsTravel & leisureAirline emissionsTui TravelAirline industryeasyJetEuropean Union holidaysUK cost of living crisisShareReuse this content

title: Sod’s law: what can two turf swaps 40 years apart tell us about Britain’s biodiversity crisis? | Art and design | The Guardian
description: In 1983, David Nash dug up a section of Kensington Gardens and swapped it with Welsh grassland. Four decades later, Mike Perry’s reverse swap revealed a striking reversal in the fortunes of urban and rural nature
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: In 1983, David Nash dug up a section of Kensington Gardens and swapped it with Welsh grassland. Four decades later, Mike Perry’s reverse swap revealed a striking reversal in the fortunes of urban and rural nature
Content: ‘When you make work outside, things happen’ … the results of Reverse Sod Swap in Springfield Park, London, in 2025.Photograph: Mike PerryView image in fullscreen‘When you make work outside, things happen’ … the results of Reverse Sod Swap in Springfield Park, London, in 2025.Photograph: Mike PerryArt and designSod’s law: what can two turf swaps 40 years apart tell us about Britain’s biodiversity crisis?In 1983, David Nash dug up a section of Kensington Gardens and swapped it with Welsh grassland. Four decades later, Mike Perry’s reverse swap revealed a striking reversal in the fortunes of urban and rural naturePatrick BarkhamFri 16 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1983, an open-topped truck unloaded an unusual cargo in Kensington Gardens: 83 hunks of turf cut from Cae’n y Coed, a wooded hillside in the Ffestiniog valley. The ring of turf measuring eight metres in diameter that was removed from the park beside the Serpentine Gallery in west London to make space for the Welsh sods was then trucked from London to north Wales.So began Sod Swap, a piece of sculptural defiance byDavid Nash, which has had an unexpected and epic afterlife. More than 40 years later, photographic artist Mike Perry restaged the work asReverse Sod Swap, exchanging exactly the same amount of turf between Springfield Park in Hackney, east London, and pastureland in Pembrokeshire, with strikingly different results. With twin works acquiring new relevance in a time of extinction and climate crises, the sod swapping is now the subject of a new book.It all began, says Nash, who is 80 and still working with wood and trees, with his own “bloody-mindedness”. He was invited to contribute to a new Serpentine gallery show of British sculpture. He submitted an idea of some wood sculptures for an indoor gallery because he felt too many outdoor sculptures were “like UFOs, they came and they went”, as he puts it. “But the gallery said: ‘Oh, David, you’re an outside artist, so we’d like you to participate in the outdoor space.”Nash, who made his very outdoorsyAsh DomeandWooden Bouldera few years before, bristled. He’d actually created an outdoor piece for a Serpentine show when he was a postgrad student at Chelsea Art School in 1970. When he tried to secure it in the ground he was told he couldn’t touch the Kensington Gardens turf because it belonged to the queen.View image in fullscreenMaking the cut … David Nash’s original Sod Swap being installed at the Serpentine gallery in west London in 1983.Photograph: © David NashSo this time, he plotted to rough up the manicured London park’s immaculate lawns by installing a ring of wild grassland from north Wales while also challenging definitions of “sculpture”. There was a lot of “bright red metal” around in the early 80s, says Nash wryly. “I wanted to create something that didn’t need to be cleaned.”Sod Swap, he says, was a declaration of his identity. “I was very keen that what I put in had a sense of where it came from, which was where I was, which was north Wales.” When he realised he would have to dig up a load of Kensington turf, he decided to take that back to Wales. “That became the swap, and I liked the connotation of being a sod. It was nothing to do with the environment, really, but it turned out to be.”Nash was anticipating a reaction and he got one. After several worried meetings about the dig, and head-scratching from council officials about the risk of “invasive” Welsh plants contaminating Kensington Gardens, Sod Swap went ahead. “He’s very subversive, David,” saysPerry. “He doesn’t look it, but he is. The Serpentine expected him to bring in a big wooden sculpture. And he said: ‘No, I’m going to cut up your lawn.’ He wanted to show who he is as a person but also what sculpture could be – it doesn’t have to be a solid object on a plinth. It can be an ephemeral piece of organic material.”In 2023, when Perry started a rewilding and art project on 4.9 hectares (12 acres) of farmland in west Wales, he wondered if he might revisit Nash’s concept, four decades on. Slightly nervously, he contacted Nash, and was relieved when the sculptor gave an enthusiastic “yes”. A week later, Perry drove over to north Wales, where Nash took him to see the site of the Kensington Garden sods. Amazingly, 40 years on, they could still detect a faint circle in mossy grass now punctuated by mature trees.View image in fullscreenThe grass is always greener … Reverse Sod Swap, Ffynnonofi, West Wales, 2024Photograph: Mike PerryThe Welsh turf hadn’t lasted so long in London. After the show ended, the gallery planned to simply to remove the turf but, thankfully for Nash, the “archangels of art outside”, Sue Clifford and Angela King, stepped in. The two co-founders of environmental arts charityCommon Groundhurriedly found another unlikely London home for Nash’s Welsh sods: in the lawns of Kenwood House on Hampstead Heath.Clifford and King also had the bright idea of convening ecologists to count the species in each turf circle. The Welsh sods held 28 different species, including grasses, wildflowers, brambles and even nettles, while the manicured sods cut from Kensington Gardens were made up of a meagre three different species of grass. Suddenly, Nash’s little challenge to the art world held an ecological message, highlighting the biodiversity to be found in rural meadowlands and the sterile quality of urban parks.While Nash’s little piece of Wales acclimatised to Hampstead Heath, the artist conscientiously watered the London turf at Cae’ny Coed, even buying a secondhand mower so he could keep it in the condition to which it was accustomed. The original plan was to return it to Kensington Gardens, but Nash says the Arts Council told him they had run out of project money and couldn’t afford to transport it back. Sod Swap became permanent.Eventually, after 10 years at Kenwood House, English Heritage removed the Welsh sods. “The London turf stayed in Wales,” remembers Nash. “Chestnut trees I planted grew and grew and shaded the turf, and moss came in. There were daisies from London which came up for about five years but then disappeared. I kept up mowing it as if it was in London for 20 years until it was virtually all moss and then I thought I would let it go.” Over the years, artists, curators and students made a pilgrimage to visit it.View image in fullscreenGrass-roots movement … David Nash with Mike Perry in one of Nash’s shelters in Cae’n y Coed, north Wales, in 2023.Photograph: Cornelia ParkerReverse Sod Swap was “a kind of biographical piece for me,” says Perry. He lived in London for 20 years before moving to an old farm by the sea in north Pembrokeshire. “My parents retired down here so I’ve always been going between east London and west Wales,” he says. The landscape and seascape of the Pembrokeshire Coast national park still looks gorgeous but “it’s a very melancholy thing walking down to the sea because there’s nothing in the hedges. They’re stripped right back and the grass is just mown 24/7 by so many sheep. The chair of the RSPB [Royal Society for the Protection of Birds] said national parks are where wildlife goes to die.”Perry had hoped Reverse Sod Swap would be an ecological statement, but he couldn’t have anticipated just how much of a statement it would make. In Wales, he took the turf from pasture still heavily grazed by sheep belonging to a tenant farmer. At the London end, he was given “a really poor” plot in Springfield Park with “bad bits of soil from everywhere and a little bit of grass out of all sorts of rough material. But I quite liked it because there were giant burdocks and ‘weeds’ and thistles. I liked that mix.”Perry’s first challenge was to replicate the dimensions. Nash couldn’t remember the exact size of his 1983 turf circles but Perry dug out the old catalogue statement, which noted that there were 83 sods measuring 90x30cm (35x12in) in size. He then followed Nash’s idea of making little wooden “stretchers” to carry each sod from the ground to the waiting lorry. On the journey to Wales, they twice stopped at motorway services to water the precious sods.In the two-and-a-half years since Reverse Sod Swap, Perry has been surprised by how the project has continued to transfix him. “David put his hand on my shoulder and looked me in the eye and said: ‘Mike, when you make work outside, things happen.’ I didn’t really know what he meant. But what’s amazing is that the work is living and changing all the time – it keeps giving me new images and new findings.”View image in fullscreenNatural exchange … Mike Perry marking out Reverse Sod Swap, Ffynnonofi Farm, West Wales, 2024.Photograph: Mike PerryAfter the reverse transplant, botanists surveyed the transplanted turfs and, strikingly, found the reverse of Nash’s 1983 swap. The turf taken from Springfield Park contained 39 species in total, whereas the Welsh sheep-grazed turf contained just four species. And so, across four decades, the two works starkly illustrate the loss of rural biodiversity – a loss often disguised by the superficially unchanging character of the British landscape, with its patchwork of hedges, fields and woods. But Reverse Sod Swap also reveals a more hopeful trend in London, where species have been revived by urban rewilding efforts, from creating wildflower areas in parks to building new sustainable urban drainage areas.Perry is encouraged by what he sees when he returns to London and walks down the Grand Union canal. “It feels like there’s butterflies, there’s rough stuff. It’s not scientific because there are obviously areas in Wales that can’t be farmed and there’s amazing biodiversity, but I was just really trying to make a point through art.”Nash is touched by the longevity of his Sod Swap, and the ecological message it has taken on. “What Mike has done is an amazing bonus,” he says. “My Sod Swap highlighted the paucity of plant species in London, not that that was my main intention. Reverse Sod Swap is much more pertinent environmentally because it’s highlighting the paucity of rural land. We artists put work out there and hope people will see it and make something of it – be stimulated or take it on as part of their awareness.”Reverse Sod Swap by Mike Perry and David Nashis published by Little Toller on 16 October (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsArt and designArtSculpturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Clean air is not a favour’: Indonesia’s neighbours fed up with acrid haze as Singapore threatens to prosecute  | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Millions affected by smoke from wildfires as schools close, respiratory illnesses soar and diplomatic tensions rise
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Millions affected by smoke from wildfires as schools close, respiratory illnesses soar and diplomatic tensions rise
Content: Motorcyclists in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, ride through thick orange haze caused by fires in the region.Photograph: REINA/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMotorcyclists in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, ride through thick orange haze caused by fires in the region.Photograph: REINA/AFP/Getty ImagesIndonesia‘Clean air is not a favour’: Indonesia’s neighbours fed up with acrid haze as Singapore threatens to prosecuteMillions affected by smoke from wildfires as schools close, respiratory illnesses soar and diplomatic tensions riseOliver HolmesSouth-east Asia correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 06.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 04.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSingapore is threatening to prosecute companies responsible for some of the worst fires in years in neighbouring Indonesia, as the region grows increasingly frustrated with a persistent, acrid haze that could result in diplomatic relations fraying.Lawrence Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, said his government was distributing masks to vulnerable citizens and working with countries in the region to deal with the smoke. “At the same time, we are looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires,” he said ina Facebook poston Thursday, adding that he was exploring the idea of “joint action with other countries”.‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guideRead moreSingapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions inIndonesiaare reportedly based in the city-state.Haze is a persistent problem in Indonesia, but drier-than-usual conditions mean the thick smoke has been drifting into nearby Singapore,Malaysia, Brunei and Timor-Leste, and as far afield as the Philippines and Vietnam. Millions are affected, with school closures, respiratory illness spiking and air pollution indexes reaching unhealthy levels.View image in fullscreenA boat passes Singapore’s Marina Bay Sands, shrouded in haze.Photograph: Feline Lim/AFP/Getty ImagesMalaysians and Singaporeans have been sharing images online of their cities, with skyscrapers disappearing into the smog, and frustration with the region’s most populous country is boiling over.“Year after year, the haze comes back. It affects our health, closes schools, hurts businesses, and costs us billions,” a veteran Malaysian social activist and former politicianwrote in a public letterthis week. Lee Lam Thye said that real enforcement and “not just polite words” were needed. “Those responsible must be named, investigated, and punished. Clean air is not a favour. It is a basic right.”While Indonesia regularly battles wildfires in the dry season, these blazes are the most intense in more than a decade and exacerbated by slash-and-burn practices to clear land for agriculture, including palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.Regional diplomats have offered to help Indonesia, but their offershave not always been immediately accepted. On Monday, an Indonesian official said the country was “still capable of handling it”. By the end of the week, Jakarta said it would accept assistance.Such delicate diplomacy is routine among the region’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), which is built on ​quiet engagement and non-interference. A meeting of regional foreign ministers in the Philippines is due next month, but that might be too late.View image in fullscreenPutra Mosque and the Prime Minister’s Office in Putrajaya, Malaysia, covered in haze.Photograph: Mohd Rasfan/AFP/Getty ImagesNerves are fraying. In remarks that went viral on social media, Syahganda Nainggolan, the head of Indonesia’s government communication agency, hit back at the criticism on Saturday. “We don’t only send haze,” he said, “the oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia comes from our forests.”Rare strong words came earlier this month from Anwar Ibrahim, the Malaysian prime minister. He said he had been in contact with Indonesia’s president,Prabowo Subianto, “who agreed to take the necessary steps, and this commitment must be followed by immediate and effective action from the Indonesian side to tackle the root causes of the haze”.At the same time, pressure is growing on Jakarta to declare a national disaster, first from civil society groups but now also from Indonesian politicians and neighbours.According to the Jakarta Post, Indonesian students have been holding protests across Kalimantan and Sumatra, demanding accountability and government action. Inone video posted online, a child in a mask stands outside under a dark orange sky and calls on the local and national government to help. He holds a sign that says: “Save our little lungs”.View image in fullscreenThick smoke and haze from forest and land fires in the region in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe country has dispatched firefighters and announced a crackdown on arsonists, but declaring a disaster would unlock funds and help thousands with medical expenses.On Friday, the Indonesian forestry ministry said four firefighters were killed in a national park in Java.Longtime onlookers say the issue is not just firefighting, but targeting the companies involved. In recent years, several attempts to take legal action against the companies exacerbating “transboundary haze” have failed, both locally and internationally, and posed a diplomatic minefield.Haze is complex for Singapore and Malaysia, as they host companies working in Indonesia. A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia that it claimed were linked to burning land in Indonesia.Ultimately, Indonesians bear the brunt of the blazes. The health ministry has reported nearly 280,000 people in the country with respiratory infections linked to the fires, with children under five accounting for more than 60,000.Michelle Dyonisius, a campaigner at Amnesty International Indonesia, said rights groups and civil society organisations were ramping up pressure on the government to declare a national disaster emergency. “It has been going on for months, affecting millions and millions of people, including abroad,” she said.“I think there is a refusal to acknowledge the gravity of the issue at hand and also the belief that it is under control. But considering the gravity of the issue and all of the people affected, it seems quite naive to remain in that position.”Explore more on these topicsIndonesiaSingaporeMalaysiaPrabowo SubiantoAsia PacificAir pollutionPollutionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands | Mining | The Guardian
description: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia
Author: Stefano Valentino
Headline: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia
Content: Deforestation in Indonesia linked to nickel mining.Photograph: Didi Hardiana, NGO PuspahamView image in fullscreenDeforestation in Indonesia linked to nickel mining.Photograph: Didi Hardiana, NGO PuspahamMiningRevealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous landsMines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in IndonesiaStefano Valentinoin Sulawesi andAjit NiranjanFri 16 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolkswagen, Ford andTeslaare among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot inIndonesiathat houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”View image in fullscreenWadimula: ‘Destroying [the forest] means destroying our own life.’Photograph: Stefano ValentinoElectric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.View image in fullscreenMorowali industrial park on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary.Photograph: Stefano ValentinoPublic filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a reportfoundlithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communicationsfoundlast year.The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests.View image in fullscreenA track cut through forest in the Hengjaya concession.Photograph: Stefano ValentinoSulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo,Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits.Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain.Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.”Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.”Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.”Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.”Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.”General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.”Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.”Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.”CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment.This investigation was supported byJournalismfund EuropeandThe Pulitzer Center. Lorenzo Di Stasi and James Jackson contributed reporting.Explore more on these topicsMiningDeforestationElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsAutomotive industryTravel and transportTrees and forestsIndonesianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Well-known individual’ tries to secure permanent injunction against Guardian and ITN | The Guardian | The Guardian
description: Lawyers tell high court that client could harm himself if serious allegations against him are made public
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Lawyers tell high court that client could harm himself if serious allegations against him are made public
Content: The Guardian’s investigation concerned serious allegations about an individual’s conduct over a period of years, a judge said.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s investigation concerned serious allegations about an individual’s conduct over a period of years, a judge said.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe Guardian‘Well-known individual’ tries to secure permanent injunction against Guardian and ITNLawyers tell high court that client could harm himself if serious allegations against him are made publicMichael SavageMedia editorFri 16 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA “well-known individual” is trying to secure a permanent injunction against the Guardian andITNto prevent them from publishing details of serious allegations made against him.At a high court hearing on Friday, the claimant’s legal team said there was a serious risk that he could harm himself should the allegations be made public.They have told the court publishing the claims would breach articles two and three of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), the former of which relates to the right to life.A trial is due to take place later this month to examine whether an injunction preventing reporting of the allegations should be made.An earlier ruling by the judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said the case included two media organisations that had “conducted a journalistic investigation into allegations concerning the claimant’s conduct towards a number of individuals”.“The proposed publications concern serious allegations about the claimant’s conduct over a period of years,” it stated.“The matters alleged are said to have arisen in a variety of professional and personal contexts.”The judge explained that the claimant had given a broad denial of the allegations which the defendants propose to publish.In a submission to the court, the claimant’s legal team, led by Sara Mansoori KC, said he was “a well-known individual who suffers from very serious mental health problems”.The submission stated he had attempted to take his own life on two occasions and remained seriously ill.ITN and the Guardian are opposing the injunction sought.In their own written submission to the court, their legal team set out their position on the questions that fall to be decided at trial.In a skeleton argument, they said the relevant duties under the ECHR were not triggered and should not prevent publication, and in any event, mitigations could be put in place to protect the claimant.Nicklin said on Friday that it was important to have the proceedings as open as possible, adding: “This case is going to be controversial either way it is decided.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsThe GuardianNational newspapersNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesITNnewsShareReuse this content

title: Six-figure payout for senior civil servant sacked over Peter Mandelson vetting | Politics | The Guardian
description: Former head of Foreign Office Olly Robbins applied for judicial review after Keir Starmer dismissed him in April
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Former head of Foreign Office Olly Robbins applied for judicial review after Keir Starmer dismissed him in April
Content: Olly Robbins was removed from his post following the Guardian’s disclosure that he had overturned a recommendation to deny clearance for Mandelson.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/AlamyView image in fullscreenOlly Robbins was removed from his post following the Guardian’s disclosure that he had overturned a recommendation to deny clearance for Mandelson.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/AlamyPoliticsSix-figure payout for senior civil servant sacked over Peter Mandelson vettingFormer head of Foreign Office Olly Robbins applied for judicial review after Keir Starmer dismissed him in AprilRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 16 Oct 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 13.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlly Robbins, the former head of the Foreign Office sacked by Keir Starmer over his role in vettingPeter Mandelson, has received a six-figure payout from the government over his dismissal.Robbins had applied to the high court for a judicial review of the prime minister’s decision to remove him as the top civil servant at the Foreign Office after he was dismissed in April.He was removed from his post by Starmer after the Guardian’s disclosure that he hadoverturned a recommendationfrom UK Security Vetting (UKSV) to deny clearance for Mandelson.In a statement on Friday, Robbins said he was “grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time”.He added: “I want to thank the FDA [union] for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life.”Dave Penman, general secretary of the FDA, which represents senior civil servants, said: “This settlement may bring an end to the judicial review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.“The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgment of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations – which is quite the feat.“We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process.”The government will ultimately have to publish how much it has given Robbins in a settlement, which is believed to be six figures but not as much as the record £860,000 given to former cabinet secretary Chris Wormald after he was forced out by Starmer after just a year in post.At the time of his dismissal, Downing Street said Robbins had lost the confidence of Starmer and Yvette Cooper, then foreign secretary, due to his handling of the vetting of Mandelson, who wassackedover the extent of his links to the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.The Guardian later revealed thatMandelson’s associations with senior figuresin China, Russia and Israel had been among the concerns raised by UKSV when it concluded he should be denied clearance. His relationship with Epstein was not among the reasons.Robbins’ legal submission had made the case that Starmer had no statutory authority to dismiss him as the head of the diplomatic service, and that there had been “no fair procedure” and “no process at all” in the dismissal. It also said Robbins had been given “irrational” reasons for being fired.There had beenstrong supportfor Robbins within Whitehall, with senior civil servants said to believe he had in effect been sacked for doing what No 10 wanted by swiftly passing Mandelson through vetting, and that the focus should instead have been on the prime minister’s initial decision.The Commons foreign affairs select committee has previously said that Robbins believed he was “delivering the outcome that was wanted” and concluded that his dismissal “seems to have been taken without full due process and the establishment of the facts”.Questions remainabout the defence Robbins mounted, both of his own actions and the system through which the national security establishment vets people, and the lack of mitigation put in place to get around the security concerns.The Foreign Officerefused to hand overa summary of Mandelson’s security vetting to the official tasked with compiling documents detailing his appointment as ambassador to the US, in response to a Commons motion forcing the release of documents linked to the process.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsKeir StarmerPeter MandelsonCivil servicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Norwegian teenage hitman hired for UK murder by Iran-backed crime gang jailed for 20 years | Crime | The Guardian
description: Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was arrested in Huddersfield with two guns and live ammunition
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was arrested in Huddersfield with two guns and live ammunition
Content: Natland was found guilty of conspiracy to murder after agreeing to shoot an unknown target for €25,000.Photograph: Metropolitan police/ReutersView image in fullscreenNatland was found guilty of conspiracy to murder after agreeing to shoot an unknown target for €25,000.Photograph: Metropolitan police/ReutersCrimeNorwegian teenage hitman hired for UK murder by Iran-backed crime gang jailed for 20 yearsJohannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was arrested in Huddersfield with two guns and live ammunitionHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 08.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA teenage hitman who travelled fromNorwayto the UK with the intention of carrying out a murder on behalf of an Iran-backed international crime gang has been jailed for 20 years.Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, a talented footballer, had agreed to shoot an unknown target in return for €25,000 (£21,500).He travelled to the UK in March last year from his home in Stavanger, and two days later – before he could carry out the hit – armed police arrested him at a hotel in Huddersfield,West Yorkshire.Officers found him in possession of a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver, 12 rounds of live ammunition and gloves.Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition and said he had intended to shoot himself in the foot to get out of the “pickle” he was in. However, he was found guilty of conspiracy to murder and on Friday was sentenced to 20 years in detention.The court heard that Natland had been recruited by another teenager, referred to as Generalen, who was working for the proscribed Swedish Foxtrot gang, which is backed by the Iranian regime and known for recruiting children as young as 13 to become involved in drug smuggling and violent crimes.Natland had been controlled by an English-speaking boss called Agent 47, an apparent reference to the Hitman gaming and film franchise. The identity and whereabouts of Agent 47 remain unknown.Natland flew into Manchester on a temporary passport and was stopped by Border Force officials, who bailed him to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.Instead, he travelled by taxi toHuddersfieldwhere he booked into the Briar Court hotel and picked up the guns and ammunition, as well as £2,000 in cash. He was directed to a stolen Nissan with false number plates, which was to be used in the murder.While in the hotel, Natland took selfies with the guns and cash spread out on his bed, and bragged to his girlfriend that he had the “bangs in the bag”. Armed police arrived to arrest him at 5.15am the next day.Paul Hynes KC, defending, pointed to Natland’s age at the time of the offending and said he had been a “young, popular, successful student and sportsman” before he went “off the rails” after he became addicted to drugs.Giving evidence, Natland told jurors: “I wasn’t an international assassin. I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn’t.”However, in a televised sentencing at Woolwich crown court in south-east London, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb said messages he had sent showed “not only participation but at points excitement” about what he had been planning to do.“You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself,” she said. “Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to.”Explore more on these topicsCrimeHuddersfieldWest YorkshireYorkshireEnglandNorwayEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Judi Dench joins calls by The Archers cast to keep show in Birmingham | The Archers | The Guardian
description: The actor, who made a cameo in the Radio 4 drama in 1989, has signed a letter urging BBC not to move studio elsewhere
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: The actor, who made a cameo in the Radio 4 drama in 1989, has signed a letter urging BBC not to move studio elsewhere
Content: Judi Dench made a cameo as Pru Forrest in The Archers’ 10,000th episode.Photograph: Lia Toby/Getty Images for BFIView image in fullscreenJudi Dench made a cameo as Pru Forrest in The Archers’ 10,000th episode.Photograph: Lia Toby/Getty Images for BFIThe ArchersJudi Dench joins calls by The Archers cast to keep show in BirminghamThe actor, who made a cameo in the Radio 4 drama in 1989, has signed a letter urging BBC not to move studio elsewhereJamie GriersonFri 16 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cast and crew behindThe Archers, including the one-time guest star Judi Dench, have written to the BBC director general urging him to keep the recording of the Radio 4 drama in Birmingham.It emerged this week that the corporation was planning to stop recording the rural community soap opera in the city for the first time in the show’s 75-year history, after it scrapped plans for a radio drama studio.Staff were informed last week that the BBC, as part of its £500m cost-cutting drive, hadditched plans to build a bespoke studioat the Tea Factory in Digbeth, the corporation’s new Birmingham headquarters.Production staff will still move to the Tea Factory, but the broadcaster is looking for an existing studio where the show could be recorded. TheWest Midlandsis included in the search, but there is no guarantee The Archers will be recorded in the region.View image in fullscreenActors rehearse an episode of The Archers in the BBC studios in Birmingham.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesA letter to Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, signed by more than 100 current and previous cast members, says: “The Archers leaving the Midlands is akin to Corrie leaving the north-west, or EastEnders the south-east. It is born of the very fabric of the place, and deserves to stay at home.”It adds: “Removing the recording of The Archers from the Midlands and divorcing the production team from the cast will have a tangible impact on the quality of the programme and represents an existential threat to its future.”The letter, which is also signed by current and former editors, scriptwriters, sound effects workers, programme advisers and the trade unions Equity and WGGB, highlights the history and heritage of the show, which is set in the fictional village of Ambridge in the West Midlands.View image in fullscreenThe Archers’ recording studio.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“A flagship show deserves flagship facilities, from which both the BBC and the city ofBirminghamwould benefit for decades,” the letter says.It ends by saying: “[We] stand in solidarity with our colleagues and the region, and to safeguard this beloved programme for generations of listeners and artists to come.”Dench played the character Pru Forrest in a cameo for the 10,000th episode of The Archers in May 1989, meeting guest star Terry Wogan, who played himself.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe studio’s semi-anechoic room, known as the dead room, because of the extensive soundproofing.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIn an email to staff last week, a BBC executive said: “After careful consideration and as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, the decision has been made … to not build a new radio drama studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory in Digbeth.“Consequently, options are being explored to identify suitable studio facilities where The Archers will be recorded. That currently includes looking into potential opportunities in the West Midlands, as well as across other parts of the UK.“To be clear, no decision has yet been reached. The priority is to find the most cost-effective solution which will maintain The Archers’ high production standards in addition to delivering significant savings.“The Archers is a jewel in the BBC’s crown. It’s been going for an incomparable 75 years – as has its connection with the West Midlands. It remains a hugely vital part of our future.”A BBC spokesperson said: “We recognise and value The Archers’ longstanding relationship with the West Midlands, which remains an important part of the programme’s future and The Archers production team will remain in their current home in the Mailbox and move, as planned, to the Tea Factory in Digbeth in early 2028.“However, after careful consideration, as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, we are no longer building a new recording studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory. We’re currently assessing the BBC’s existing studio facilities around the UK as well as other external studio options in the West Midlands to find a more cost-effective solution, which will deliver significant savings while also maintaining The Archers’ high production standards.”Explore more on these topicsThe ArchersBirminghamRadio dramaRadioRadio 4West MidlandsBBCnewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s Cockroach Janta party leader detained amid crackdown on protests | India | The Guardian
description: Abhijeet Dipke was arrested before planned anti-government demonstrations in Delhi
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Abhijeet Dipke was arrested before planned anti-government demonstrations in Delhi
Content: Abhijit Dipke called on supporters to protest after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow Cockroach Janta party leaders.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersView image in fullscreenAbhijit Dipke called on supporters to protest after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow Cockroach Janta party leaders.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersIndiaIndia’s Cockroach Janta party leader detained amid crackdown on protestsAbhijeet Dipke was arrested before planned anti-government demonstrations in DelhiHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiFri 16 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in centralDelhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of themost substantial challengesto the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused ofoverseeing a revisionof India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.11:32India’s Cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown - The LatestThe authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They weresentenced to five daysin jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and showNarendra Modi“that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streetsRead moreDespite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.Explore more on these topicsIndiaNarendra ModiSouth and central AsiaProtestDelhiActivismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Family of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventable | Georgia | The Guardian
description: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after reportedly ‘passing out’ and falling off Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia while beside niece
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after reportedly ‘passing out’ and falling off Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia while beside niece
Content: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem in an undated photo. Kariem died after he was thrown from his seat while riding a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday.Photograph: Kelvin Johnson/APView image in fullscreenHassan Jihad Ibn Kariem in an undated photo. Kariem died after he was thrown from his seat while riding a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday.Photograph: Kelvin Johnson/APGeorgiaFamily of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventableHassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after reportedly ‘passing out’ and falling off Goliath rollercoaster in GeorgiaMarina DunbarFri 16 Oct 2026 18.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe family of a man who was ejected from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park inGeorgiaanddiedhas publicly questioned whether the death could have been prevented.Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was riding the Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia nearAtlantaalongside his niece during a family trip to celebrate her birthday when he was thrown from the ride. His niece witnessed her uncle’s death, a relative told the Atlanta ABC News affiliateWSB-TV.“A large part of me does believe, you know, it was a freak accident, but the other part of me questions … could this have been prevented?” Joshua Nelson, Kariem’s brother-in-law, told the outlet.Nelson, whose daughter was seated beside Kariem, shared her account of the terrifying moments leading up to her uncle’s death.Man who died in Six Flags rollercoaster fall in Georgia was a father and educatorRead more“She said he fainted, or passed – her words were ‘he passed out,’” Nelson said. “And then they went up and down, up and down, up and down – and she said it went up again and his latch, I guess, snapped or came loose and he fell,” Nelson remarked.During the celebratory family outing, Kariem had expressed his excitement about riding the Goliath, which was one of his favorite attractions, according to Nelson.Nelson said that he hoped Kariem did not experience pain during his final moments.Kariem was an educator and a father to a 10-year-old daughter. According toAtlantapublic schools, Kariem started his career at Wesley International Academy as a technology teacher before being promoted to an information technology manager.Georgia authorities as of Friday werestill investigatingthe circumstances of Kariem’s death at Six Flags Over Georgia, which opened its gates Friday evening for the first time since the incident. Cobb county police department’s major crimes unit haslaunchedan investigation.Since Kariem’s death, Six Flagstemporarily closednine rollercoasters across six amusement parks around the US.Deaths such as Kariem’s are rare. But his death has prompted some to call for federal oversight of amusement parks, which in the US has been left to individual states, asthe New York Times reported.Explore more on these topicsGeorgiaAtlantaTheme parksnewsShareReuse this content

title: British man fined €3,000 for causing two-year-old son’s death in Cyprus  | Cyprus | The Guardian
description: Joshua Foster pleaded guilty over death of toddler who fell from fourth-floor window of hotel during family holiday
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Joshua Foster pleaded guilty over death of toddler who fell from fourth-floor window of hotel during family holiday
Content: Joshua Foster (right) arriving at Paphos district court in Cyprus for the sentencing hearing, with his lawyer.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenJoshua Foster (right) arriving at Paphos district court in Cyprus for the sentencing hearing, with his lawyer.Photograph: James Manning/PACyprusBritish man fined €3,000 for causing two-year-old son’s death in CyprusJoshua Foster pleaded guilty over death of toddler who fell from fourth-floor window of hotel during family holidayHelena Smithin AthensFri 16 Oct 2026 10.05 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British man has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) after his two-year-old son fell 10 metres (33ft) to his death from the fourth-floor window of a hotel in Cyprus.Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he approached it with the boy to show him the view of a waterpark and “lost control” of him, the court previously heard.The 37-year-old appeared at Paphos district court on Friday for sentencing having pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.In emotional scenes at the court, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident on 12 July, the first day of the family’s holiday in Cyprus, as a “tragic event”.“Jail is not appropriate,” the judge said, telling the courtroom that as there was “clearly no intent to kill” she had decided against a custodial sentence and would instead order Foster to pay the fine.The Essex-born auditor, who had previously appeared in court visibly distraught, struggled to hold back tears as the sentence was handed down. As it dawned that the case was finally over, he hugged his lawyer before telling reporters: “Thank you for your support. I’m looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter.”The light sentence – the minimum for the charge – meant Foster could retrieve his passport and other documents he had been forced to surrender. More usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents, the charge carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison.Speaking outside the district court in Paphos, the defendant’s lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said Foster, who works for one of the UK’s big four accounting firms, would finally be able to grieve.View image in fullscreenThe family were on holiday at the King Evelthon Beach hotel and resort in Chlorakas, Cyprus, when the incident happened.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA“He’s been through a lot and it’s been very emotional but he’s relieved it’s over,” he said of his client, who posted €30,000 in bail to return to the UK to attend the toddler’s funeral in August before being forced under threat of extradition to return to Cyprus for the proceedings.“This case should not have gone to court. We asked for the charges to be suspended. Unfortunately this was not accepted.”Alexandrou had appealed to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds, arguing that prosecution “does not serve the public interest”. The request was denied.The boy fell to his death from the window of the King Evelthon hotel within hours of the family arriving in Paphos.In mitigation on 5 October, Alexandrou recounted how Foster was making his way to a lift along the corridor when he stopped at the window and the “inconceivable” occurred. The Briton, he said, had not realised the window was ajar when, lifting the child, who was excitedly pointing to the hotel’s waterpark outside, he “lost control” and he slipped through his hands. The boy was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after suffering severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.Summing up, Christodoulidou said while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.View image in fullscreenLawyer Alexandros Alexandrou (right) speaks to journalists outside the court.Photograph: James Manning/PA“It is no exaggeration to say that for the rest of his life he will have guilt for losing his child in such a tragic way,” she added. Mitigating factors presented by the defence, including the Briton’s lack of criminal record, as well as his guilty plea, had also played a role in her decision, she explained. In a country so dependent on tourism, criticism had mounted as Cypriot human rights defenders, media pundits and foreign diplomats all questioned the perceived lack of compassion with which officials approached the case.A former British colony, the eastern Mediterranean island attracts roughly 4 million visitors and is particularly popular with tourists from the UK.Alexandrou, the lawyer, said he had advised his client to admit the negligence charge to avoid a potentially drawn-out and disturbing trial when he and his family were still processing the grief of their “unimaginable loss”.Conceding the case had been “emotional” for the entire defence team, the lawyer added: “He can finally grieve. Now that the court proceedings are over, the explosion of his emotions at the loss of his child will be immediate.”In a statement issued after the sentencing, the Foster family said: “Today marks the end of the legal proceedings in Cyprus, and we are grateful to the court and Judge Christodoulidou for her decision to apply the maximum mitigation afforded to her.“We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end. Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day.“Our focus now is on supporting one another and finding a way forward as a family. We ask that our privacy is respected as we do so.”Explore more on these topicsCyprusEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Barack Obama pays tribute to Manchester cotton workers and cites them as an inspiration  | Barack Obama | The Guardian
description: Speaking at live UK event, former US president expresses hope rooted in the past and discusses the modern challenges to democracy
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Speaking at live UK event, former US president expresses hope rooted in the past and discusses the modern challenges to democracy
