Content: Barack Obama was interviewed by the writer and broadcaster Afua Hirsch.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenBarack Obama was interviewed by the writer and broadcaster Afua Hirsch.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PACotton Capital: ongoing seriesBarack ObamaBarack Obama pays tribute to Manchester cotton workers and cites them as an inspirationSpeaking at live UK event, former US president expresses hope rooted in the past and discusses the modern challenges to democracyChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTShareBarack Obama cited the “wonderful” story of how Manchester cotton workersstood in solidaritywith enslaved African Americans as an inspiration for our times in a live appearance in the city.Tens of thousands of people packed Co-op Live in the city on Thursday for An Evening WithBarack Obama, where the former US president was interviewed by the writer and broadcaster Afua Hirsch.Obama closed the 90-minute event, punctuated by cheers, whoops, laughter and applause from the audience, by discussing the work of the Obama Presidential Center, a museum, library and education project in Chicago, and that of his foundation – committed to challenging economic inequality, the climate crisis, education and health, with programmes for women and girls, global emerging leaders, and journalists in oppressive regimes.He spoke of the hope he took from the younger people he worked with, and from the Lancashire cotton famine, in which workers fromManchesterand surrounding towns supported Abraham Lincoln’s blockade of cotton from enslaving Confederate states.Obama said the centre was about reminding people what was possible. “I was reminded being here at Manchester of just this wonderful story of the cotton workers here at Manchester. During the American civil war in 1862 at a time when their livelihoods depended on cotton and the union had set up a barricade and prevented cotton from leaving the South as part of the civil war effort.“And yeah, the business people and manufacturers, and I think even the Guardian editorialised ‘don’t mess with that, you know, this is our lifeblood’ and over at the Free Trade Hall, a bunch of British working workers who are hungry and not sure whether they’re gonna be able to hold things together, sit there and they meet, and they collectively say, we are going to stand with those who are fighting for freedom, even if it’s going to cost us.“And so you hear a story like that. And they write a letter to Lincoln and he writes back. And commends them for a historic expression of Christian humility and charity, and grace. And so you then say to yourself, if they could do it, why can’t we?View image in fullscreenObama in Manchester.Photograph: Chris Osuh/The Guardian“There was no guarantee that they were gonna benefit in any way from it, but somehow, their life was better for that. Even in the midst of hardship. And I think if we could tell each other those stories, and pass those to our children and are our grandchildren. We’ll get through these times too.”The Guardian’s Cotton Capital series launched in 2023 to explore its founders’ links to the cotton trade and transatlantic enslavement, including how thenewspaper covered the subjectat the time.Hirsch spoke of the huge impact Obama’s 2008 A More Perfect Union speech had had, including for her as a “a black British person of mixed heritage”.Asked to share the ways his identity is reflected in his politics and leadership, Obama said it did so in ways “particular to the United States”, and ways that were “more universal”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe added: “Race is this faultline of so much of American history … our union made a series of compromises, including, essentially, tacitly ratifying slavery, and a civil war was fought and enormous struggle to secure a more inclusive notion who we the people are.“And for whatever variety of reasons, I became, I think, a symbol of that journey that our country took. Not to get to a post-racial America, that was never possible, but I do think it marks the point in time in which the idea that ‘we the people’ means all people and not just some, seemed to have been validated for at least a moment.“It marked a promise, and I was mindful of that. It did not erase the institutional, structural legacies of slavery and Jim Crow. But it did signify that the country changed, that the change was possible. Namely, through efforts of sacrifice of countless people, many of them nameless.”Obama described democracy as a “journey”, that required “continual replenishment” to avoid falling back into “old ways”, amid great economic, social and technological disruptions, saying “we tend to forget how recently democracy has taken hold and how fragile it is … For most of human history for millennia, societies were organised around caste and hierarchy, violence and force.”The statesman said it was a “good thing” for the prime minister and formerGreater Manchestermayor, Andy Burnham, to “have [the Ukrainian president] Zelenskyy here and remind people what’s at stake”.Explore more on these topicsBarack ObamaCotton Capital: ongoing seriesManchesterGreater ManchesterRaceColonialismSlaveryEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: British food and drink exports to EU collapse by more than a third since Brexit  | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: NFU analysis of official data shows falls in exports to UK’s largest trading partner since 2019 include 70% for sugar and 74% for egg products
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: NFU analysis of official data shows falls in exports to UK’s largest trading partner since 2019 include 70% for sugar and 74% for egg products
Content: A chicken-egg farm in Suffolk. Food exporters have long complained about the extra paperwork that Brexit has entailed.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA chicken-egg farm in Suffolk. Food exporters have long complained about the extra paperwork that Brexit has entailed.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianFood & drink industryBritish food and drink exports to EU collapse by more than a third since BrexitNFU analysis of official data shows falls in exports to UK’s largest trading partner since 2019 include 70% for sugar and 74% for egg productsLisa O’CarrollFri 16 Oct 2026 08.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 09.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third sinceBrexitwith eggs, chicken and potato producers badly hit, new figures show.Analysis by the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) of HMRC data shows a sharp fall in exports in the year to July compared with the same period in 2019, with sugar dropping the most, down 70%.Data for the first seven months also shows poultry exports fell 53%, with eggs and egg products sold for confectionary and baking industries down 65% for the same period.Changes in UK exports to the EUFull-year data from 2019 to 2025 showed an even deeper impact since Brexit with exports of eggs and egg products down 74%.The NFU president, Tom Bradshaw, said: “The EU is our largest trading partner for agri-food products, accounting for 68% of agri-food exports last year, but trade volumes have fallen over a third since 2019.”Boris Johnson’s governmentsigned a dealon the UK’s future trading and security relationship with the EU in late 2020, after the UK’sformal exitearlier that year.Andy Burnham is reconsidering Labour’s red lines on EU membership under pressure torepair the economic damageof Brexit. Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far.Food exporters have longcomplainedover the added paperwork that Britain’s exit has brought. Since Brexit all food exports are required to have customs paperwork with different codes for every single product. This includes, for example, every variation of an egg product, whether it is fresh, dried, steamed, shelled, or contains added water or sugar. The paper pulp used in egg cartons as well as the eggs also need health certification to show they are free of disease.Also hit hard by Brexit is the horticultural sectorwith seed potatoes from Britain,mainly Scotland, banned from the EU after trade negotiators failed to agree on equivalent standards in the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement in 2020. Horticultural exports fell more than 50%.Pre-Brexit, Scotland exported around 20,000 tonnes of seed potatoes, worth almost £11m, to Europe each year.Speaking in parliament earlier this week Andy Burnham said that Brexit trade barriers meant “entire truckloads of plants or fresh product can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or minor paperwork delay”.He hoped to “land a positive outcome” in the upcoming UK-EU reset talks with a new agreement removing many of the sanitary and phytosanitary checks on fresh farm produce exports that came in after Brexit.Burnham told MPs: “Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100m in lost exports.“British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU. Seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned. This is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage.”A deal to ease sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) checkswas largely agreed in Maygiving food producers time to prepare for changes expected to come in next summer, but key details remain to be finalised.The NFU is calling for “transition arrangements” for some UK crops that have been grown with fungicides or breeding techniques not yet approved in the EU.This is to allow those harvesting this autumn and winter to make use of the new export freedoms when they come in next year.Bradshaw said: “British farmers and growers must retain access to precision breeding technologies that will help to strengthen food resilience to extreme weather and to science-based plant protection products that help protect food being grown for 29m households from pests and diseases.“Any changes must also provide an appropriate transition period to minimise disruption for farm businesses and we will continue to make this case to government while we await the final agreement.”Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryRural affairsFarmingBrexitEuropean UnionTrade policynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK risks losing key role in European space industry over satellite contract, says Airbus boss | Airbus | The Guardian
description: Guillaume Faury writes to Andy Burnham warning him against choosing US firm Lockheed Martin to build Skynet satellites
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Guillaume Faury writes to Andy Burnham warning him against choosing US firm Lockheed Martin to build Skynet satellites
Content: Airbus, Thales and Leonardo areworking on a long-awaited mergerin an effort to build a single European space subsidiary to rival leading US companies.Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAirbus, Thales and Leonardo areworking on a long-awaited mergerin an effort to build a single European space subsidiary to rival leading US companies.Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty ImagesAirbusUK risks losing key role in European space industry over satellite contract, says Airbus bossGuillaume Faury writes to Andy Burnham warning him against choosing US firm Lockheed Martin to build Skynet satellitesJasper JollyFri 16 Oct 2026 10.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss ofAirbushas told Andy Burnham that choosing its US rival Lockheed Martin to manufacture military satellites could cost the UK a key role in the European space industry, intensifying a last-minute lobbying effort for the £2.4bn contract.It is understood that Guillaume Faury, the chief executive of France-headquartered Airbus, has written to the prime minister suggesting that the choice of provider of the Skynet system could have effects for decades to come on the UK’s strength in military satellites in Europe, in an effort to tip the contract away from its US rival.Yet politicians in north-east England have lobbied in favour of the Lockheed Martin bid, which would include a new factory in Durham.The military satellites under the Skynet 6 contract will carry the British armed forces’ most sensitive communications up to 2042,replacing the Skynet 5 system operated by Airbus.The delayed decision on which company will manufacture the UK’s sovereign satellites comes at a sensitive moment, after Ukraine complained that its access to Elon Musk’sStarlink satellite network was restricted, apparently at the behest of the US government.Several sources said they believed no final decision on the contract had been made. However, some said they believed that Lockheed Martin’s bid was preferred by theMinistry of Defence. The final decision will rest with Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey.It is thought that Faury’s letter warned of longer-term consequences for the UK’s role in the European space sector if Airbus were to lose out. Senior industry figures have previously claimed that Airbus’s UK satellite operations would not be viable without the next Skynet contract, meaning the company might close its sites at Stevenage and Portsmouth, which employ 3,000 people, including 600 working on Skynet.The manufacturers Airbus, Thales and Leonardo areworking on a long-awaited mergerbetween their space subsidiaries, known as Project Bromo, in an effort to build a single European champion with the scale to rival the leading US companies.Faury is understood to have warned that if its British operation were no longer viable it could mean the UK missing out on the chance to be the European hub for military satellite communications once the merger was complete.Lockheed Martin is one of the US’s largest defence “prime” contractors, but it says its UK subsidiary will have full control over the satellites eventually built in the UK. People close to Lockheed Martin have strongly denied that the US government would have control over the satellites.A Lockheed Martin spokesperson said the company was “unable to comment on the ongoing procurement process”, but added: “Lockheed Martin UK, a British company, will establish facilities to develop an ecosystem alongside our regional partners in the north-east of England to provide the UK with a sovereign space capability. It will create jobs, supply chain opportunities and the potential for exports. It will have a UK design authority and a UK chief engineer.”Luke Akehurst, the Labour MP for North Durham, said Lockheed’s bid would mean a “state-of-the-art new manufacturing facility” in the region. “This represents a massive investment in the reindustrialisation of the north-east of England, building on our region’s proud heritage of advanced manufacturing.”The personal intervention from Faury, one of the most powerful executives in Europe, is a sign of the importance of the contract to Airbus, which is headquartered in Toulouse.A decision had been expected in the summer but it has been delayed in part by the arrival of Burnham in office.Unite, one of the Labour party’s biggest union backers, had warned against “handing the British space industry over to the Americans” at a time when there are increased questions over whether the UK can rely on the US government.Burnham will also have to consider the two bids on their financial terms and the capabilities the two companies can offer.A government document for a related system said satellites had to deal with the “proliferation of counterspace capabilities to disrupt, deny, degrade or destroy space-based enablers”. It highlighted radio jamming, hacking and direct physical attacks on the satellites as possible concerns.The first Skynet satellite was launched in 1969, well before the use of the name for ahostile artificial intelligence in the 1984 film The Terminator.Kim McGuinness, the mayor for north-east England, said: “Bringing satellite manufacturing to the north-east is a huge opportunity to build on what we have already achieved, including the close ties we have forged between our world-class universities and industry. If secured, this investment would be a gamechanger for the space and security sector, bringing £100m of investment and creating 500 high-skilled jobs as well as a much greater impact through the supply chain.”An MoD spokesperson said: “This is an ongoing procurement process, and no final decisions have been made. Both of the UK-based bidders are subject to full evaluation of their proposals and must offer satellites that are assembled, integrated and tested in the UK.”Airbus declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsAirbusAerospace industryMinistry of DefenceDefence policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals
Content: Meta says its new open-weight AI model rivals and in some cases outperforms Chinese equivalents.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta says its new open-weight AI model rivals and in some cases outperforms Chinese equivalents.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI modelMeta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivalsAgence France-PresseThu 15 Oct 2026 20.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them.‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cutenessRead moreChinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.“Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.Muse Spark Open is also “optimized” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signaling an unusual partnership between the two tech companies.Muse Spark Open requires significant computing power. Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said.The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model, which it said rivalled the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude.Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)MetaChinaComputingShareReuse this content

title: Ofgem could force energy suppliers to pay rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals | Ofgem | The Guardian
description: Regulator for Great Britain weighs up reintroducing market stabilisation charge to prevent firms going bust
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Regulator for Great Britain weighs up reintroducing market stabilisation charge to prevent firms going bust
Content: Ofgem says it is ‘preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households’.Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyView image in fullscreenOfgem says it is ‘preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households’.Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyOfgemOfgem could force energy suppliers to pay rivals if they lure customers with cheaper dealsRegulator for Great Britain weighs up reintroducing market stabilisation charge to prevent firms going bustMark SweneyFri 16 Oct 2026 04.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 04.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnergy suppliers could be forced to pay a charge to rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals, as the industry regulator for Great Britain attempts to prevent suppliers going bust this winter.Ofgem has published a consultation on a proposal to reintroduce the market stabilisation charge (MSC), which aims to prevent suppliers failing if there is customer exodus, as it frets over the impact of sharp swings in energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.The charge was last activated between April 2022 and March 2024, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sparked soaring wholesale prices thatcaused more than 30 energy companies to go bust.“We’re preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households,” said Neil Kenward, the interim director general of markets at Ofgem. “While the energy market is stronger than it was during the energy crisis, volatility remains and the market stabilisation charge helps to protect consumers from that volatility.“In volatile market conditions, it’s important that suppliers can continue to secure the energy their customers need without taking unsustainable risks.”Under the mechanism, the MSC would be triggered if wholesale prices fall more than 10%. At that point, suppliers who win customers by being able to then offer cheap deals would have to compensate rivals 85% of the drop in wholesale rates.“When wholesale prices fall sharply, suppliers that have bought energy in advance for customers on default tariffs can face losses if large numbers of customers switch to cheaper fixed deals,” Ofgem said.When Ofgem last activated the MSC in 2022 Martin Lewis, the founder of the consumer advice site MoneySavingExpert, swore at the regulator on a press call and said the mechanism sold consumers “down the river” because it would deter competition. He laterposted an apology for his “emotional rant”on the social media platform X.Reacting to Ofgem’s consultation, Lewis said on Friday that consumers’ will not get as good deals if wholesale prices drop because the mechanism acts as a“switching penalty”.He added: “The new supplier can’t pass a chunk of the saving from lower wholesale rates on to you, because it has to hand much of it to your old supplier. The cheap fixes and switcher deals offered will be a lot more expensive, in order to protect energy firms’ profits. It ain’t good for consumers.”He questioned the need to reintroduce the mechanism, pointing out that many energy companies have made significant profits since last time it was triggered.“The supplier market is pretty stable, and I doubt we are at the domino risk of suppliers going bust in the way they did in the early 20s,” he said. “Protecting them over winter by effectively dampening competition … feels raw. I don’t like it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOfgem said that reactivating the MSC would not “automatically create charges or increase customer bills”.The consultation is seeking views on how the mechanism should operate, including trigger levels, notice periods and deactivation arrangements.“The MSC supports responsible energy purchasing and helps reduce the risk of instability in the market during periods of significant price volatility,” Kenward said. “By acting now, we can help maintain a stable and resilient energy market and protect consumers from the costs and disruption that can arise when markets become unstable.”Households are facing the highest energy charges in three years this winter after rising market wholesale prices pushed up the government’s price cap from this month.About 22m homes are paying the equivalent of £1,723 a year for typical gas and electricity usage between October and December, up from £1,663 for the July to September period.Ofgem’s quarterly energy price cap is forecast to climb by the equivalent of a further £149 a year in January, according to energy consultants at Cornwall Insight, which would put the average annual bill at £1,872.The chancellor, John Healey, isplanning a major interventionto cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget.Explore more on these topicsOfgemEnergy industryEnergy billsUK cost of living crisisUS-Israel war on IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screen | Jamaica | The Guardian
description: As violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: As violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’
Content: Gugu Mbatha-Raw stars in Sky’s supernatural series Possession set in Jamaica.Photograph: Des WillieView image in fullscreenGugu Mbatha-Raw stars in Sky’s supernatural series Possession set in Jamaica.Photograph: Des WillieCotton Capital: ongoing seriesJamaica‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screenAs violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’Natricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 15.05 EDTShareAwoman opens a 300‑year‑old box, unleashing a violent spirit – it is the spirit of colonialism and oppression roaring back to life. It is a pivotal scene in Sky’s supernatural series Possession and symbolises a wider shift in Jamaica’s film industry, where directors are increasingly using the landscape to tell Jamaican stories – including those that confront enslavement, trauma and historical memory.The series is about a biracial British lawyer who travels to Jamaica to investigate a multimillion-pound inheritance dispute, only to uncover a dark, vengeful spirit tied to the plantation’s brutal colonial past.For the Jamaican director, Storm Saulter, ensuring that the trauma and enduring legacy of enslavement and colonisation were powerfully represented was critical. Caribbean countries are increasingly arguing that centuries of enslavementhave left the region at a lasting disadvantage– fuelling renewed calls for reparations.Dr Lisa Tomlinson, a lecturer in film studies at the University of the West Indies, says the themes in Jamaican films are changing. “They’re now very much connected and reflective of Jamaican stories – stories that were previously taboo or avoided.”View image in fullscreenMbatha-Raw plays a lawyer who travels from Bristol to Jamaica to handle an inheritance claim over a former slave plantation.Photograph: Des WillieWhile Jamaican films are not always explicitly about reparations, she argues that many are engaging with the legacies of enslavement through cultural memory. “Reparation is not just a political act,” she says. “It’s also culture. These African‑derived spiritualities, the historical knowledge – when they come through creative expression, what they do is give us authority to tell our own stories.”This, she says, is a form of “cultural reparation”, a reclaiming of narratives devalued or suppressed under colonialism, and a way of educating audiences about the past in ways that academics or politicians struggle to do. “The arts play a critical role in how we are educated in public awareness around reparation,” she says.Jackie Jackson, Jamaica’s film commissioner, sees the shift too. She says productions such as Possession andDelroy Lindo’s Jabari’s People– shot entirely in Jamaica – reflect growing confidence and ambition among Jamaican creatives. “We are well established as a destination for international productions,” she says. “But what we want to see more of is local production and international collaboration that enables us to tell our own stories.”View image in fullscreenDelroy Lindo’s directorial debut Jabari’s People (he is pictured here in Spike Lee’s Da 5 Bloods) is shot entirely in Jamaica.Photograph: NetflixBoth productions, she notes, worked closely with Jamaican talent to ensure authenticity and demonstrate what is possible when international financing and distribution unite with Jamaican creativity. “They show the growing interest in Jamaican stories and their potential for global audiences,” she says.Tomlinson believes diaspora film-makers are playing a particularly important role in this shift. Unlike foreign productions that often use Jamaica as an exotic backdrop, diaspora directors are “moving away from the tourist‑gaze depictions” and are “capturing Jamaican everyday life”.Saulter sees his series as part of a broader political awakening. “The mask has slipped … We’ve been told it’s one thing, and that thing is proven to be false. So there’s a seeking of what is true,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStorm Saulter, Possession’s director, aims to ‘open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret’.Photograph: Bertie WatsonHe says the box‑opening scene is not simply a plot device, but a metaphor for something larger: the resurfacing of long‑suppressed histories and the growing willingness amongCaribbeancreatives to confront the legacies of enslavement, inherited trauma and colonial violence through film.“Literally, we’re going to open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret,” Saulter said. “It’s the spirit of colonial enslavement and oppression coming roaring back.”That “spirit”, he explains, is embodied in a character who has lived through centuries of brutality – “a witness to history” – whose presence forces the protagonists to reckon with the past they have inherited.Saulter’s interest in the subject is rooted in his upbringing. “I grew up in the countryside,” he says. “The Obia man, the church …nine nights… I’ve lived through all of those things.”His experiences inspired him to tell stories that educate and have “real societal political impact”, while remaining thrilling, intriguing and entertaining. That approach, he argues, allows film-makers to tackle difficult histories. “As opposed to doing something that was like talking heads … we’re bringing you on a journey,” he says.For Dr L’Antoinette Stines, a Yoruba priestess and cultural expert who advised on Possession, the series’ engagement with Afro‑spiritualist traditions is part of a longer history of resistance.View image in fullscreenSheldon East plays Cudjoe East, the son of a British man who grew up at the Hope Hill plantation in Jamaica.Photograph: Des Willie/©Sky UK Ltd“Black people have been fighting and using the arts for a very long time. It’s just that there is greater attention on it today,” she says. For decades she has choreographed similar work, she says, and stresses the importance of honouring the academics, poets and creatives who paved the way for today’s boom in authentic Jamaican storytelling.She praises Saulter’s insistence on authenticity and creating a series that feels both contemporary and deeply rooted, exploring inherited trauma, ancestral memory and the unfinished business of colonialism.Possession is on Sky Atlantic and NowExplore more on these topicsJamaicaCotton Capital: ongoing seriesWorld cinemaSlaveryReparations and reparative justiceCaribbeanAmericasColonialismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘She asked me to lie on her feet while she did sit-ups’: your memories of Esther Rantzen | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: From inspiring careers to treating people to unforgettable curries, the late presenter and campaigner had quite the impact on Guardian readers. Colleagues, admirers and TV show guests share their stories
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From inspiring careers to treating people to unforgettable curries, the late presenter and campaigner had quite the impact on Guardian readers. Colleagues, admirers and TV show guests share their stories
Content: Esther Rantzen was one of the most recognisable figures on British television.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen was one of the most recognisable figures on British television.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyEsther Rantzen‘She asked me to lie on her feet while she did sit-ups’: your memories of Esther RantzenFrom inspiring careers to treating people to unforgettable curries, the late presenter and campaigner had quite the impact on Guardian readers. Colleagues, admirers and TV show guests share their storiesGuardian readersandAlfie PackhamFri 16 Oct 2026 04.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 04.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Esther visited our home, causing much teenage excitement’The summer of 1976 held a particularly fond memory for my family. In one episode of her programme The Big Time, my father took part in conducting the Royal Philharmonic in Croydon and met several of his musical idols. Esther and her team visited our home, causing much teenage excitement, took us for lunch at a local Indian restaurant (the height of sophistication) and after lunch asked me to sit on her feet in our back garden while she did sit-ups. We were kids, probably in the way of filming, but were included and treated warmly and impressed by her down-to-earth manner. We fondly remember the visit and as Dad said at the end of the film: “lovely Esther”. I’m glad she went on to make so many important contributions to the lives of so many.Rosalind Cresswell, Maine, USA‘I applaud her for this little defiance of the expected norm’Around 1980, I worked for the National Consumer Council, a quango that has now been absorbed into something else. I took the minutes of a meeting of the council whenEsther Rantzenwas an elected member. She had a new baby and fed him during the meeting. Nobody did this, she was a trailblazer, and I applaud her for this little defiance of the expected norm. I am sad to hear that she no longer in our lives, but I thank her for her work and her legacy.Lesley Foote, 70, retired health manager, London‘I was struck by her professionalism’Some time before Esther Rantzen became a household name, I edited two documentaries which she presented – Until Armageddon (about Jehovah Witnesses) and Come Come Ye Saints (about Mormons). Esther would often visit the cutting room and I was struck by her professionalism and desire to learn the TV trade. Esther would have acknowledged her debt to the director, Peter Chafer, whose guidance certainly helped mould her later career.Paul O’Dell, 83, France‘She was a pioneer’I was a second year student nurse in 1983 when I watched a programme called The Lost Babies, which Esther presented. I was so moved that I wrote to her saying that I would be training as a midwife when I finished my nursing training. She replied with a lovely letter of encouragement, which I still have. I went on to become a midwife and then a sister in a neonatal intensive care unit. I remembered what I had heard and learned from the women in the programme every day of my clinical career.Having a baby is usually a joyous occasion, but for some women and their families it is a time of great sorrow whether their baby dies before or after birth. The way that healthcare staff care for and support women has changed greatly over the years, and I feel that this programme was a huge step forward in learning from those brave women who never forgot their lost babies. Many people are afraid of the idea of death and Esther shone a light on the reality of it. She was a pioneer in 1983 discussing what was a taboo subject, and she remained a pioneer in advocating for dignity in death, even as she was facing the reality the end of her own life.Breedagh Hughes, 68, retired midwife, Spain‘She told me about her passion for justice’Social workers are notoriously sniffy about celebrities coming to tell them how to do their job, particularly those in children’s services. But Esther came to talk to a conference I attended and she was great. She talked about why she set up Childline. She was fun and entirely respectful. I ended up sitting next to her at lunch; she didn’t run off or seek to sit with the organisers. She told me about her passion for justice and how that drove her forward in journalism. Her sister was a social worker who kept her informed and right. She was not jumping on a bandwagon to help her own career, she was using whatever celebrity she had to push a message and did so powerfully. I left thinking what a nice person she was and how we could all do with just a little of her drive to correct injustice.Linda Devlin, retired social worker, Glasgow‘Esther transformed the lives of so many people’This is such a sad loss. Esther Rantzen has been a strong and positive influence on my career. When I was a postgraduate media student I was sent to interview Esther. She kindly invited me to spend a week of work experience on That’s Life! From the morning news meetingto the editing suites, she shared the whole process of programme making with me. She drove me round London in her car, giving me the benefit of her wisdom and advice as we chatted.View image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen filming an episode of That’s Life! in 1976.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyEsther’s advice and experience helped launch my own career and I have been ever grateful to her for taking such trouble with a mere work experience student. This is typical of her openness, kindness, enduring positivity and drive. Esther Rantzen has transformed the lives of so many children and lonely elderly people.Rene Wyndham, Lyme Regis‘An amazing ambassador for women and the world’Every Sunday evening I watched That’s Life! religiously as a young teen and it was the most informative, investigative and funny show. I will always remember the guar gum slimming pills that blocked a ladies toilet, and the dog who could say “sausages”. Rest in peace you beautiful, amazing ambassador for women and the world.Janet Rochford, 48, Cork, Ireland‘Charming and great fun’I had the joy and challenges of working with Esther at Childline from 2000 to 2006 when it joined with the NSPCC. We travelled together on numerous fundraising and awareness campaign trails around the UK organising media interviews and photo opportunities. She was always a stickler for the details and if you made a mistake she could be fierce, but she was also charming and great fun. Working on the BT Childline Awards I saw how much she loved meeting people from all walks of life who had done amazing volunteering work. Esther was invested in shining a light on these unsung heroes.View image in fullscreenRantzen collecting money for Childline in London in 2008.Photograph: Andrew Parsons/PAAlthough it was work, she remembered things you’d shared about family or friends and would ask how they were. She liked that my wife was also from Berkhamsted and enjoyed remembering her childhood growing up there, asking what had changed since. I last saw her in 2017, and I’m glad my lasting memories are of Esther being the force of nature she was, campaigning for children and adults who would not otherwise have had a voice. I am so happy to have known her. It feels like the end of an era with her passing.Adrian Brown, 55, LondonExplore more on these topicsEsther RantzenTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Look Back review – Kore-eda’s ode to friendship, manga and artistic success | Movies | The Guardian
description: Two obsessive artists team up to achieve their dreams, but then their aspirations diverge
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Two obsessive artists team up to achieve their dreams, but then their aspirations diverge
Content: An ideal team … Natsuki Deguchi and Aju Makita in Look Back.Photograph: Courtesy: London Film FestivalView image in fullscreenAn ideal team … Natsuki Deguchi and Aju Makita in Look Back.Photograph: Courtesy: London Film FestivalMoviesReviewLook Back review – Kore-eda’s ode to friendship, manga and artistic successTwo obsessive artists team up to achieve their dreams, but then their aspirations divergePeter BradshawFri 16 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHirokazu Kore-eda’s sad and beautiful film is about friendship, about the ecstasy and burden of success and about what it means to have an artistic vocation, especially when that vocation is pursued collaboratively, with your best friend. It is adapted by Kore-eda from the standalone, or “one-shot”,online manga story of the same titleby Tatsuki Fujimoto, which has in fact already had an anime movie adaptation.Fujino, played by Furi Nanase as a 13-year-old and later by Natsuki Deguchi, is a dedicated would-be manga artist who dreams of being published and adapted for the movies. It is her personal and artistic destiny to come into contact, in her early teens, with fellow manga obsessive Kyomoto, who is played first by Rokka Okada and then as an adult by Aju Makita. Theirs is a kind of platonic but passionate love story.Fujino begins the story as someone who is very pleased with herself. In school, she has became a virtual celebrity for her simple four-frameyonkomamanga strips in the class magazine. But then her homeroom teacher tells her that he is giving space to a regular manga from another girl, Kyomoto, who suffers from anxiety and never comes into school. Kyomoto’s work stuns Fujino. It seems to her (and all her classmates) to be patently better than hers. Her own work had been simplistically about the faces and the dialogue and the story; Kyomoto’s is more subtly about background ambience – the still life-type landscapes and scenes are far more accomplished.Fujino feels like a Mozart who suddenly turned into a Salieri. She more or less abandons manga in that moment, morosely pursuing sports, in particular karate. When, at the end of term, her teacher asks her to drop off Kyomoto’s graduation certificate at her house – Kore-era playfully allows us to see that the teacher is trying to engineer a friendship between these two young people – Fujino is resentful and reluctant. She goes there intending brusquely to leave the item and go, but a chaotic mishap means they meet face to face and Kyomoto emotionally calls her “sensei” and says she is her biggest fan. Fujino joyfully resumes drawing and they become soulmates and partners, fusing into one manga creator, an ideal team, winning prizes and commissions. Fujino devises the foregrounded story and characters while Kyomoto’s considered artistry creates the deep emotional mood and context.But just when they are on a roll, their careers at a staggering momentum that other, older, artists can only dream of … Kyomoto says she wants to quit and go to art college, to be a better artist, while she still has enough time, enough humility to learn. Fujino is furious and the break between them is more painful, more important, than any sundered love affair.Kore-eda shows us the heartbreak that this leads to, and to an agonising “sliding doors” type reverie about how things could have been different, how Fujino could have redeemed herself as the lesser artist. Fujino wants to reach into the past and change things: and in a sense that is what artists do, especially those whose work is strongly personal or autobiographical. They look back, they retrace their steps to the wellspring of their inspiration, the source of their life’s meaning; they see the form and substance of experiences whose meaning they could not grasp at the time.Or perhaps it is that they create the form and substance and impose it retrospectively. Looking back is an authentic, vital gesture, but outside the realm of art it is poignant and futile. You can change nothing by looking back; it is simply a forum for sadness and regret. Such is the emotional dynamic of this engrossing, affecting film from Kore-eda, a film of great clarity, intimacy and high seriousness.Look Back screened at theLondon film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsMangaJapanLondon film festivalAsia PacificComics and graphic novelsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Face of Horror review – a future cult classic delights with playful spin on Hammer horror | Movies | The Guardian
description: Anna Biller’s intricate tribute to the British 1960s genre plays melodrama for laughs and pulls it off wonderfully in a medieval tale based on a Japanese ghost story
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Anna Biller’s intricate tribute to the British 1960s genre plays melodrama for laughs and pulls it off wonderfully in a medieval tale based on a Japanese ghost story
Content: Homage to Hammer horror … Jonah Hauer-King and Kristine Froseth in The Face of Horror.Photograph: Courtesy: London Film FestivalView image in fullscreenHomage to Hammer horror … Jonah Hauer-King and Kristine Froseth in The Face of Horror.Photograph: Courtesy: London Film FestivalMoviesReviewThe Face of Horror review – a future cult classic delights with playful spin on Hammer horrorLondon film festivalAnna Biller’s intricate tribute to the British 1960s genre plays melodrama for laughs and pulls it off wonderfully in a medieval tale based on a Japanese ghost storyPeter BradshawFri 16 Oct 2026 01.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 01.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s over-the-top … and there’s this playfully bizarre new film from US indie film-maker and genre connoisseur Anna Biller, whoseprevious film The Love Witchfirst alerted me to her ecstatic love of style, surface and the A-pleasures of the B-movie. The Face of Horror is a deadpan homage to the garish Technicolor horror pictures of Britain’s Hammer Films in the Peter Cushing 1960s, with an extraordinary visual emphasis on red velvet, whose Freudian significance can only be guessed at. Perhaps it’s not accurate to call it pastiche – in any event, the advent of AI has arguably undermined the value of skilled pastiche in movies and literature. It is more an attempt simply to make another film in the same vein as Hammer, to continue in the same rackety tradition of melodrama, eroticism and black comedy – and to create a film that can be laughed at as well as laughed with, just as they were at the time.The setting is a cod-medieval England, a land of courtly nobles, smudgy-faced peasants and ladies wearing floor-length gowns with rope-style belts – although Biller has taken as her starting point the classic Japanese ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan,which is also an inspiration to, among others, Takashi Miike and Hideo Nakata. Edward (Jonah Hauer-King) is a handsome, unscrupulous knight, suspected of robbing his former master, seen here in the opening scene riding through a sun-dappled forest with his similarly shifty squire Richard (Leo Suter). Edward wishes to marry the blond, beauteous Eleanor (Kristine Froseth), who appears in a separate scene demurely preparing a preposterously lavish meal with her equally blond sister Beatrice (Ellie Bamber) in one of the vast, oppressive wood-panelled halls that Hammer horror was known for.Edward and Richard brutally murder the women’s father and brother, who disapprove of them – blaming their death on “brigands” – and then marry Eleanor and Beatrice. But it isn’t long before the caddish Edward has designs on another evilly smiling noblewoman, Lady Isabel (Bella Heathcote), whose court of lute-strumming, recorder-blowing ladies-in-waiting is pictured in the vivid colour of a Ladybird book illustration from the same era as Hammer. They plot murderously against poor Eleanor, who has become the sickly, exhausted mother to Edward’s infant son. (The child is rather forgotten about here, but Biller may want to bring him back in adult form for a sequel.) It is to lead to the horror of supernatural revenge.The most uproarious part of the film is the memento mori Danse Macabre scene at Lady Isabel’s decadent court, something that Ken Russell might have enjoyed – or Roger Corman, whoseversion of Poe’s The Masque of the Red Deathmay be an influence on Biller. The stamina and consistency of tone is what makes the film amusing and fascinating – a cult midnight movie of the future.The Face of Horror screened at the London film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsFilm adaptationsPeriod and historical filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dogmatic Nordic liberals v eastern family values: culture-clash drama Fjord touches nerves in Norway and Romania | Movies | The Guardian
description: Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner echoes the news story of a Romanian couple whose children were taken by the Norwegian government. As it heads to London film festival, two writers explain how the film exposes real hypocrisies
Author: Magnus Nome
Headline: Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner echoes the news story of a Romanian couple whose children were taken by the Norwegian government. As it heads to London film festival, two writers explain how the film exposes real hypocrisies
Content: Problematic … Fjord, written and directed by Cristian Mungiu.Photograph: ©Tudor PanduruView image in fullscreenProblematic … Fjord, written and directed by Cristian Mungiu.Photograph: ©Tudor PanduruMoviesDogmatic Nordic liberals v eastern family values: culture-clash drama Fjord touches nerves in Norway and RomaniaCristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner echoes the news story of a Romanian couple whose children were taken by the Norwegian government. As it heads to London film festival, two writers explain how the film exposes real hypocrisiesAndrei PopoviciuandMagnus NomeFri 16 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘On paper, both countries agree that smacking your child is illegal’: Romanian journalist Andrei PopoviciuWhen Cristian Mungiu’sFjordwas shown in Romania as a one-day preview this June, the reception was extraordinary. Across 53 towns and 96 cinemas, the film reportedly pulled in over 40,000 viewers in a single night, a number arthouse cinema rarely sees in Romania. But the response here had little to do with cinema. It felt instead like a reopening of a familiar fault line about the clash of values within the EU itself.Fjord review - Cristian Mungiu at sea with strange child abuse drama starring Renate Reinsve and Sebastian StanRead moreThe film echoes events from 2015, when the five children of Marius and Ruth Bodnariu, a Pentecostal couple fromRomanialiving in Norway – part of a Neo-Protestant minority long viewed with suspicion in Orthodox Romania – were removed from their home by Barnevernet, Norway’s child welfare authority, amid concerns over possible corporal punishment and religious indoctrination.The fallout in Romania stretched on for months, with diplomatic friction, public demonstrations and constant media coverage. The children were eventually returned, and the Bodnarius later resettled in Romania. Mungiu doesn’t retell the story beat for beat, but Romanian viewers had no trouble recognising where it came from.What divided viewers here was what the film did with a well-known story. Some have called it “dangerously confusing”, raising questions about abuse, integration and belief without taking a clear position. Others counter that its stance is embedded in form, in how sympathy is distributed, which characters get interiority and which are reduced to function.To some, it’s a brave critique of dogmatic liberalism, while to others, it dilutes a clear moral boundary on corporal punishment while extending undue warmth to religious conservatism. At its most charged, the debate spills into a broader anxiety about whether the EU can sustain its own contradictions.That tension surfaced again weeks later, when a viral video of a Romanian mother mistreating her daughter in public reignited the same split online (many defended her as exercising necessary discipline, others condemned her outright) suggesting attitudes here may be shifting, but unevenly.It’s worth pausing on how narrow the legal gap between the two countries actually is, because the film’s reception treats it as a chasm. Romania criminalised corporal punishment in 2004,Norwayin 1987. On paper, both already agree smacking your child is illegal, but the real distance is between law and belief.A UN human rights body recentlynotedthat despite the ban, Romania still needs to shift the mindset of parents who believe corporal punishment works better than the alternative. The Orthodox church, meanwhile, has never fully shed a folk theology in which strict discipline raises a righteous child, even as doctrine and law increasingly say otherwise.What’s notable is how little agreement there is about what the film actually endorses. Some say the supporting characters – social workers, lawyers, neighbours – are too thin to carry the moral weight asked of them. Others accuse Mungiu of stacking the deck, giving the Christian-conservative family warmth while leaving Norwegian institutions cold and procedural.Mungiu has spoken of challenging “leftwing fundamentalism”, a phrase conservatives have seized on as vindication, though he has equally condemned its rightwing counterpart. Defenders counter that a director sympathetic to victims must be willing to defend a conservative minority in a progressive society just as he’d defend a progressive one surrounded by conservatives, since majorities of any stripe tend to need an “other” to demonise.Some critics have said that intent stops mattering once a film reaches an audience, so whatever Mungiu meant by refusing to pick a side, the dramatic architecture produces sympathy for the family almost by default.My own sense is that Fjord is a film about whether a system convinced of its own good intentions can imagine being wrong. It’s the same reflex found in churches, homes and government offices from Oslo to Bucharest and across the polarised world we live in – the certainty that one’s side only ever needs vindication, never correction.‘Norway sees itself as a country that takes the rights of children more seriously than others’: Norwegian writer Magnus NomeThe flipside of Norway’s often lauded “trust society” can manifest as a naive belief in the wisdom of its institutions, but there have long been discussions about Barnevernet, the child protection service: an imperfect system consisting of fallible humans, wielding the power to reach into the inner sanctum of the family.Systemic mistakes have been made: the European court of human rights ruled against Norway in multiple cases between 2018 and 2021. In a key case, the ECHR found the system in violation by not prioritising family reunification, treating an initial foster home placement as permanent from the start instead of working towards reunification with the biological mother. In another ruling against Barnevernet, the court criticised placing the son of a Muslim mother in an Evangelical Christian family, despite the mother’s request for her child to grow up in an environment reflecting his cultural and religious background.The former case resulted in a series of Norwegian supreme court rulings that made a reunification goal mandatory, ensured a higher level of minimum contact for parents and raised the threshold for forced adoption. The latter resulted in a revision in the country’s Child Welfare Act, mandating active steps to preserve a child’s cultural, religious and linguistic identity during foster placements. Fjord is a portrait of the system prior to these changes.A serious public debate about these issues has often been hard to accomplish, partly because discussion of specific cases is inevitably based on one-sided information, as Barnevernet adheres to strict confidentiality for the sake of the children involved. We only get the parents’ version, allowing them to form the public narrative, flipping the power dynamic. At the same time it relieves Barnevernet of having to counter concrete allegations of wrongdoing.There has long been a deep vein of harsh criticism directed at Barnevernet, reaching wide and far; social media groups numbering tens of thousands of furious members, more or less full-time activists (often with personal experience) and street protests in more than a dozen countries. It’s a surprising amount of international commotion around the social services of a small nation.View image in fullscreenProtests against Barnevernet in 2016.Photograph: CTK/AlamyWithin the activist circles, the critiques frequently cross from principled concern into radical conspiracy theories: there are claims of adoptions for profit, organ harvesting and organised sex trade of minors, and accusations of being an ultraliberal indoctrination project, or a state-sanctioned eugenics programme. As a result, social workers have experienced harassment and threats.While the wild conspiracy theories have been debunked, most recently by the major newspaper VG, the reach of dramatic tales far surpasses that of well-documented refutations – not least when amplified by both foreign media with little local insight, and propaganda outlets such as the Russian RT, always happy to present “evidence” of the degeneracy of the liberal west.Such rampant misinformation (not limited to Norway) can at times hinder necessary debate, with criticism automatically assumed to originate from cranks. But most agree, including within Barnevernet itself, that an ongoing debate about the system is necessary and healthy.One can see Fjord, and the issue it portrays, as conservatism against liberal leftism, powerless individuals against an arrogant system, or a conflict between prioritising parents’ rights over those of the children.Most parents, myself among them, will insist they know what’s best for their own children better than any arm of the state – but some of those parents will also know of families with dangerously unfit parents that hold exactly the same opinion. Norway sees itself as a country that takes the rights of children more seriously than others, aware that while taking action carries the risk of harm, passive inaction and automatic acquiescence to parents can be equally damaging.Fjord may not be entirely objective or tell the complete story, but it’s a more nuanced work than the previous cinematic depiction of Barnevernet, Mrs Chatterjee vs Norway– a sensationalist Bollywood drama based on a mother’s account. To balance the film with a sympathetic portrayal of the dilemmas faced by social workers, the award-winning dramedy TV series Pernille, whose eponymous main character works in Barnevernet, is available on Netflix.Fjord is showing at the BFILondon film festivalon 17 October and in cinemas across the US from 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmCannes film festivalRomaniaEuropeFilm criticismNorwayLondon film festivalShareReuse this content

title: The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable review – Netflix doc on ‘secret album’ is strictly for super fans | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: The lore of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, once bought by Martin Shkreli, is explored in a rambling film produced by RZA
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The lore of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, once bought by Martin Shkreli, is explored in a rambling film produced by RZA
Content: Tarik Azzougarh and RZA in The Disciple.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenTarik Azzougarh and RZA in The Disciple.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixDocumentary filmsReviewThe Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable review – Netflix doc on ‘secret album’ is strictly for super fansThe lore of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, once bought by Martin Shkreli, is explored in a rambling film produced by RZAAdrian HortonFri 16 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor every reason except one, Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, the seventh album by theWu-Tang Clan, should’ve been a commercial hit. The 31-track double album, recorded in secret between 2007 and 2013, reunited all of the remaining members of the hallowed Staten Island rap crew and featured eye-catching collaborators from the standard (Redman, offshoot group Wu-Tang Killa Bees) to the unexpected (Cher, Game of Thrones actor Carice van Houten). The sound, at least according to those involved, harkened back to the glory days of the group’s beginnings in the 90s.Nuthing ta F’ wit: Wu-Tang Clan’s greatest albums – ranked!Read moreBut for years, almost no one heard it. The group only issued a single copy of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin – on CD, ensconced within layers of filigreed silver – with the stipulation, in legalese, that it could not be used for any commercial purposes for 88 years. The decree, either a stunt or a bold artistic statement on streaming’s devaluation of music, depending on your generosity and perhaps your net worth, succeeded in drumming up plenty of hype. And if you were anywhere around the blogosphere or cable news in 2015, you may recall that the beneficiary of that hype – the purchaser and thus single intended listener of this$2m musical treasure– was oneMartin Shkreli, the “pharma bro” widely despised for gleefully hiking the costs of prescription drugs for profit.A baseline level of fluency in these occasionally arcane events is assumed, if not required, for The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable, a new documentary which retraces the long saga of the buzzy single album, which still holds the record for the most valuable album ever sold, and its controversial producer. The film, directed by Joanna Natasegara (who won the best documentary short Oscar in 2016 forThe White Helmets) and executive produced by de facto Wu-Tang leader RZA, in fact goes much farther back than those covert recording sessions in the late 2000s; The Disciple, casual fans and Shkreli rubberneckers may be surprised to learn, is less a rehashing of the album’s infamy than a subjective, meandering examination of its controversial producer, Tarik Azzougarh, the Dutch Moroccan rapper and Wu-Tang associate also known as Cilvaringz.Azzougarh, who narrates much of the film built around his personal archive (the Disciple doubles as an evolution of digital self-recording, from camcorders to selfies), can be a compelling lead: an unnervingly even-keeled presence, at once well-connected and under-the-radar, who came to the Clan via unrelenting ambition, having connected to their music with fellow immigrant friends, as outsiders in largely white Holland. But centering the bulk of a 105-minute film around one somewhat reticent lead can also prove repetitive and dead-ending, extraneous digressions on the Clan’s Hong Kong film references or tours around Staten Island notwithstanding.Martin Shkreli ordered to turn over all copies of unreleased Wu-Tang Clan albumRead moreNatasegara banks on, and draws out, Azzougarh’s fervent yet vaguely described obsession with Wu-Tang, particularly RZA, his eventual infiltration of their scene by phone and by simply showing up, his later entrenchment in RZA’s inner circle. There’s certainly something fascinating, at once hopeful and maybe sinister, in the ascendance of the self-described “fanboy” to the right-hand man. (See: last year’s underrated filmLurker.) But with minimal input from other Wu-Tang members beyond vague recollections and niceties, there’s little grist in what amounts to a slightly complicated and one-sided love letter to a genuinely formative, culture-shifting group. Though blessed by RZA, the leader only appears in archival footage or in ponderous grayscale interludes before a chess board, as if the relationship between mentor and subject were tricky and adversarial, not largely symbiotic.View image in fullscreenRZA and Tarik Azzougarh in The Disciple.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixThings pick up, at least, once the secret project gets going, bringing up artistic questions – why is a Warhol painting valued in the millions but not music? Why do people feel entitled to music for free? – and the practical matter of making one’s money back. Azzougarh’s idea to release but one CD, as the Mona Lisa of albums, was radical, but a multidimensional chess game this was not. As Cyrus Bozorgmehr, a seemingly bon vivant adviser to the album, recalls in the film, “buyers wanted to know what was hype, what was just a headline, what happened when you got to the nitty-gritty. And the answer was, we had no idea.”I just listened to Wu-Tang Clan’s Once Upon a Time in Shaolin. As music, it’s good. As art, it’s truly greatRead moreShkreli, for those wondering, doesn’t enter the story until the final third – the “poorest” of the potential buyers, one subject recalls, with a reported net worth of just $200m. There’s probably some intriguing nugget here for those locked into the story – that Shkreli planned to film a video threatening Wu-Tang members with mock guns, for one – but The Disciple is not trying to generate clickbait or conflict.It does not, however, generate much interest, either. The film gestures at many potentially fruitful deep dives – on the passage of time and the curdling of one’s ambition, on the relationship between artist and fan, or just more simply the disputes over how to handle a true rogue like Shkreli – but largely does not wander, keeping viewers instead on the glossy surface or stranded in long-winded stories about parties. It’s unclear, for instance, where Azzougarh and RZA stand now, though one can probably assume that both endorse the exhibitions now being held by PleasrDao, an NFT collective, who bought the album for $4.75m in 2021. For true fans – the ones who’d, say,fly to Tasmaniato hear the album or be thrilled by a 30-second snippet in a documentary – there’s plenty here to keep one’s attention. For everyone else, it remains a crazy headline.The Disciple is out now in select US and UK cinemas and is streaming on NetflixExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsWu-Tang ClanMartin ShkreliRapBlack US cultureFilm criticismNetflixreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums? | Fontaines DC | The Guardian
description: Once scrappy post-punk poets, they’re now one of the biggest bands in the world. As they release new album Dopamine Chamber, fans including Kneecap and Shame explain their sensational rise
Author: Kate Solomon
Headline: Once scrappy post-punk poets, they’re now one of the biggest bands in the world. As they release new album Dopamine Chamber, fans including Kneecap and Shame explain their sensational rise
Content: Fontaines DC, with frontman Grian Chatten, centre.Photograph: Ewen SpencerView image in fullscreenFontaines DC, with frontman Grian Chatten, centre.Photograph: Ewen SpencerFontaines DC‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums?Once scrappy post-punk poets, they’re now one of the biggest bands in the world. As they release new album Dopamine Chamber, fans including Kneecap and Shame explain their sensational riseKate SolomonFri 16 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Irish rockers Fontaines DC emerged in 2019, they were a bunch of post-punk poets making abrasive guitar music at a time whenDance Monkey,Drakeand The Greatest Showman reigned supreme. But today, as their fifth album Dopamine Chamber is released, the quintet are looking towards a 2027 filled with gigs in UK stadiums, US arenas and headline slots at big European festivals – plus rumours of topping Glastonbury’s Pyramid stage. It’s quite a trajectory.Their rise has been strangely traditional for a time when social media has culture in a chokehold. Ever more ambitious albums, the support of radio and institutions such as the BBC, and a lot of touring have all played parts. Beyond that, “fact is, they’re one of the best bands in the world,” says fellow countryman Mo Chara, one third ofKneecap.Fontaines DC formed at the BIMM Music Institute in Dublin in 2014. The school’s dean, Alan Cullivan, describes them as having had “an absolute focus. It was all about writing a better song after a better song after a better song.” They’d apparently play to 30 people in a dive bar one week, then come back three weeks later and half the songs would be new.That caught the attention of Trevor Dietz, who became their manager and was described by Fontaines as “the sixth member of the band” when he died earlier this year. “He brought this unwavering sense of self-belief, and that was very contagious,” says Jeff Bell, who’d end up signing the band to Partisan Records.Dietz’s connections brought Fontaines into orbits outside the Dublin gig circuit. By 2017 the band had released the single Liberty Belle and Dietz introduced them to south London bandShame, who were playing their first headline Dublin shows. “We went on this tour together for our first album,” remembers Shame singer Charlie Steen. “It felt like they had their own crowd even with just a few songs out – it’s one thing to have that in Dublin, but it’s another thing to have it in Leicester.” He adds that Fontaines’ frontman Grian Chatten “gave me aYeatsbook to read on that tour”: typical of the singer’s unashamed poetic leanings.BBC Radio 6 Music’s Steve Lamacq was an early champion of the band around the same time. “They sent us the self-released seven-inch of Hurricane Laughter, and we played that a couple of times – it had a power and an atmosphere that a lot of records around at the time didn’t really have,” he recalls.In March 2018 the band played the Victoria in Dalston, east London, a tiny pub backroom. In the crowd was Lamacq, enthralled by Chatten’s stage presence, and Bell, who flew to Dublin the next week to sign them. “As soon as I met them, it was clear that they were the biggest band in the world,” Bell says. “It just hadn’t happened yet.”The label developed a clear gameplan with the band. “There were two guiding principles: authenticity and urgency,” Bell says. “If the mixes weren’t right, start again. If an edit didn’t feel right, it didn’t go to radio. If a writer didn’t get it, don’t do the interview. We also made a point of showcasing the lyrics wherever we could; that was a real point of access for a lot of people.” After their 2019 debut album Dogrel went Top 10 in the UK and Ireland, the Covid lockdown could have scuppered them, like it did so many small acts on the rise. But instead of cancelling releases as others did, they pressed ahead with the release of their second album, A Hero’s Death, which was nominated for a Grammy.View image in fullscreenFontaines DC pictured in 2026.Photograph: Elizaveta PorodinaThe enormous crowds that Fontaines DC now command are not a result of pandering to the TikTok algorithm, though, even mid-lockdown. The band has a presence on social media, but they haven’t done viral video series such as Hot Ones,Chicken Shop DateorSubway Takes. “They are one of those artists that has very quickly become contrarian to the rule, where they’ve taken a less-is-more approach,” says Liam Ward, founder of music-focused social media marketing agency Something Something.That doesn’t stop Fontaines having hardcore fans who film entire shows for social media and, in Ward’s opinion, this fan activity online is organic (as opposed to manufactured by legions of fake accounts,as deployedby some of their indie peers). “I have not even heard rumours or whispers [of that],” he says. “They put out what they put out, and all of that craziness and noise happens around them.”Their previous album, 2024’s Romance, which came with DayGlo artwork and rave-adjacent new looks for the members, was derided by some early fans as too pop but became their first platinum seller in the UK and Ireland and earned another couple of Grammy noms. Dopamine Chamber,raved about in a five-star review in the Guardian, is just as strange and arresting. “Arctic Monkeys, in a way, have done a brilliant job setting up a space for Fontaines by being a really interesting rock band who have evolved a lot since the early days,” Lamacq says. “There’s a new, younger audience who are perhaps more lyrically led. They like the vocabulary as well as the music.”Kneecap’s Mo Chara says Fontaines’ political leanings, citing a homelessness benefit show the band curated, and their stance against the genocide in Palestine, further endeared the group to him and many others. He adds: “If you’re making music as good as they are, the mainstream can’t ignore it, but it feels like they were making music their own way and not to appeal to the masses. The mainstream has come to them rather than the other way round.”Fontaines DC: Dopamine Chamber review – gloomy, gorgeous and a gargantuan triumphRead moreThere are plenty of bands making amazing music who don’t reach the upper echelons of commercial success, though. For Abel González, who is on the booking team for Barcelona’s Primavera festival, “it’s all about feelings”. Fontaines first played the festival on a small stage in 2018, but next year they’re among the big-name headliners. “Every time they’ve come back to the festival, they’ve had new things to say, and we’ve wanted to hear them.”The true reason for Fontaines DC’s dizzying rise likely lies somewhere in the middle of a complex Venn diagram: a once-a-generation confluence of talent, commitment, good people and luck. The consensus seems to be that there’s no limit to how massive they could become. Bell agrees, still rabidly enthusiastic about the band even after they’ve moved from Partisan to current label XL Recordings. “They still haven’t reached the top of their mountain. I’m excited to see where it keeps going.”Dopamine Chamber is out now on XL RecordingsExplore more on these topicsFontaines DCPop and rockIndiePunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the top | Music | The Guardian
description: Adored by Madonna and Charli xcx and buoyed by finding true love, the Londoner is branching out into rock and breaking the mainstream. She explains how her working class upbringing made her so fearless
Author: Simran Hans
Headline: Adored by Madonna and Charli xcx and buoyed by finding true love, the Londoner is branching out into rock and breaking the mainstream. She explains how her working class upbringing made her so fearless
Content: ‘I work hard, but I really prioritise chilling’ … Shygirl in 2026.Photograph: Jessica MadavoView image in fullscreen‘I work hard, but I really prioritise chilling’ … Shygirl in 2026.Photograph: Jessica MadavoMusicInterview‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the topSimran HansAdored by Madonna and Charli xcx and buoyed by finding true love, the Londoner is branching out into rock and breaking the mainstream. She explains how her working class upbringing made her so fearlessFri 16 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaving the important stuff to chance isn’t Shygirl’s style. First aid kit, wind-up radio, batteries: earlier this morning, the singer filled her online shopping basket in preparation for impending disaster. She had read a news article advising households to put together an emergency kit. “I’m that kind of person,” she says, grinning. She woke her boyfriend, who was asleep in bed next to her. “I was like: babe, we’re sorted! I’ve got the water purifying tablets, everything!”It’s a sticky September afternoon in east London, and the singer, whose real name is Blane Muise, introduces herself as “Shy” and slides into the booth opposite me at an Italian trattoria. She first burst on to the club scene with the naughty, pulsating Want More in 2016, and in the decade since, the singer, rapper and DJ has applied the same rigour to her career as she has to her emergency prepping, going from cult underground artist to rising pop star, opening arenas for Beyoncé and Charli xcx, winning a Mobo award in 2024, and appearing in Madonna’s recent Confessions II – The Film, in which she shared a toilet stall with Arca and Richard E Grant.She has also grafted hard at falling in love and entering a long-term relationship, which is the subject of her forthcoming second album, Swallow!. An epic, soaring rock record, with more than a touch ofWilliam Orbit-era Madonna, it is an ode to intimacy, vulnerability and mutual devotion. Love, she says, is “scary, exciting and big”. The 33-year-old’s particular mix of hard and soft, of brash swagger, blunt humour and slippery feminine desire has found an exhilarating new form of expression.View image in fullscreenBrash swagger and blunt humour … Shygirl.Photograph: Jessica MadavoIn December 2022, Shygirl was preparing to go on tour. Her debut album Nymph had received rave reviews and she was finally earning enough money from music to rent her own place. “I felt good about the reception, but there’s always that anticlimactic feeling when you get what you wanted. You’re like: OK, now I have it. Now what?” she says, tossing her tangerine corkscrew curls. “Then I met George.”Go on, I say, tell me the story. “It was on Raya,” she says conspiratorially. She was hungover from a night out while browsing the members-only dating app. When they matched, she asked him to send a voice note: “I don’t like meeting up with people unless I can hear what they sound like and their cadence.” Satisfied, she invited him over to watch one of her favourite films, Alien. “Then we got Thai takeout and hooked up,” she says matter-of-factly.She was leaving for Australia later that week, but they kept talking for almost two months. When she decided to extend her trip and add a visit to Japan, “I was like: fuck it. Do you wanna come to Tokyo?” She flew him out – “in economy”, she says, laughing – and she and actor George Smale have been together ever since. “We had 10 days there and one other date in London when I got back before saying, ‘I love you.’” By the summer, they’d moved in together. Unlike previous relationships, she says, “I didn’t feel like I was all of a sudden so enamoured with someone that I didn’t know where my footing was.”View image in fullscreen‘Love is scary and exciting’ … Shygirl and George Smale at British Vogue’s Forces For Change at The Maine Mayfair, London, 23 November 2023.Photograph: Mike Marsland/WireImageThat contentment and calm was a source of inspiration. “When I made Lucky, I sat in the room with the mic.
