I didn’t write anything down, I just said how I felt,” she says of the album’s lead single. “It’s me saying: I am an active participant because of the choices that brought me here.” Like many of the tracks on Swallow!, Lucky[Hymn] is an indie song. “It had more of a classic tone to it because I felt like I was in a classic part of my life,” she says.With its dreamy, moody guitars and anthemic, crashing drums, Swallow! is a different sound for an artist whose previous records have flirted with hyperpop, UK garage and electronica. As a millennial, Shygirl came of age when guitar-driven pop music was dominating the charts. “It was very prevalent in all the pop I grew up listening to: Keane, Madonna, random shit like the Rasmus,” she says. In the 2010s, when she was a teenager, musical discovery was serendipitous: “We had HMV, where you could just walk in and put the headphones on.” Her curiosity, she says, was encouraged by her parents. “I’m not from a family where they would just give you answers.”Shygirl is the eldest of three children born to young parents in south-east London, and spent her early years bouncing between Downham, Catford and Lee Green. “My life has shown me that you are never entitled to anything,” she says. “You can be deserving but not receive.” When has she felt like that? “I grew up with that experience. My parents worked really hard. They didn’t have everything.”Her dad, who is of Grenadian origin, worked for the UK government’s Welsh office and later as a club promoter in Notting Hill. She didn’t see him much when he was working nights. Meanwhile, “my mum used to work as a cleaner, a toilet attendant, a receptionist, a dinner lady,” she says. “She’s always had a job.” So has Shygirl, who as a teenager worked at a restaurant her mum managed.Her parents are no longer together, though she is quick to clarify that hers was a happy childhood. “I wanted for nothing,” she says. “But I’m of the mindset that if you want something, you have to go get it. I’m only the one to blame if I don’t.” That determination runs through new songs such as Live the Life You Like, a stomping, Prodigy-esque anthem. “And then I’m pushing / It’s not enough,” she purrs.In Amsterdam, in 2018, she booked her first show before her debut EP, Cruel Practice, had even been released. “I was like: I don’t even have any music out and someone’s taken a chance on me,” she remembers. Soon afterwards she handed in her notice as a booker at a modelling agency. “I’m about to quit a day job that had holiday pay, sick pay, and I’m gonna go be a musician? But because I used to do contracts with the model agency, I knew how to push a rate up.” She negotiated requests from brands who wanted to use her music in their adverts, until one came in from Rihanna, for Fenty Beauty, and she got overexcited – “not as sharky as I usually am” with making the deal. She got a manager, the money came in and Shygirl paid off her credit card. She likens herself to a gambler: “My money was up from being, like, two grand in debt. I’d owed my housemate money for rent.”She signed a record deal in 2020; this year, she bought a house. She hadn’t even entertained owning one, “because I was so busy thinking I need to pay my rent and bills. My dad still doesn’t own a house. My mum just got one.” Her drive to make music, she says, “has always been to make my life better than my origins, and to prove to my family that their sacrifice is worth something”. But “living an experience they have never lived” has been accompanied by a dose of “mad guilt”.She played New York’s Madison Square Garden with Charli xcx and Troye Sivan as2024’s Brat summerraged on into Brat autumn. Seeing how Charli, a peer and friend, was able to maintain her sense of self even as everything became “as big and stressful as it gets” made pop domination feel more achievable. Although, “we definitely have different intentions for our day to day”. Charli, she stresses, works incredibly hard. “I work hard, but I really prioritise chilling,” she laughs.View image in fullscreen‘All of us are trying to open doors for each other’ … Charli xcx and Shygirl at Madison Square Garden, New York, 2024.Photograph: Rich Fury/MSG/Getty Images for MSG Entertainment HoldingsSpending an afternoon hanging out with Shygirl, as she radiates self-possession, grace and plenty of gossipy wisdom, one gets the sense that she is something of a girl’s girl. “All of us are trying to open doors for each other – all the female artists that I’ve worked with.” Being a woman, she says, is her biggest barrier as an artist. “In my experience, that is the most prevalent block at the moment.” She gives the example ofBeyoncé’s Grammy win for best country albumwith Cowboy Carter, which prompted the Recording Academy to create two separate categories for best country album: traditional and contemporary. “The rules shift, and the doors’ locations change,” she says.Realising there might be a ceiling for her ambition, one imposed on her by others, has meant she is now “only interested in working with people who want different-ness. Who are not comfortable with the status quo, because I can’t relate to that. It’s not an experience I’ve had in any avenue of my life.” And, she adds, “it’s usually men” upholding that status quo. “Not to be a man hater: I love my boyfriend!”Shygirl and Smale have been collaborating creatively, too. He provided background vocals on album opener Alyse and they have worked together on the interconnected videos for the new album, which she co-directed and which form an elliptical thriller narrative based around a kidnapping. “You’re dropped into a situation the same as The Bourne Ultimatum or Tell No One. You may have been an ordinary person; you’re now in extraordinary circumstances: what do you do?” she says. Her character ends up tied to a chair. She seldom even thinks of not acting in any situation, she says, so it was a challenge to play someone barely able to move.But her character screams, shouts, cries and thrashes as she’s held captive, giving Shygirl an outlet for emotions she didn’t realise she needed to express. “I never raise my voice,” she says. “To shout at someone who has made you angry? To show that you’re affected by them in that way? I would never do that.” An eldest daughter, she describes herself as a protector who feels responsible for everyone else in her life.“I feel like every child gets to a point where they see their parents as human beings, not just as their caregivers. That happened for me when I was very young.” How young? “Ten, 12.” It meant she never had idols. “I don’t really look up to anyone in that way,” she says. “I see everyone with faults.”‘I lost a $3m brand deal. I was like: OK, losers!’ Swedish pop provocateur Zara Larsson on fame, fun and fighting the powerRead moreIn the video’s final shot, Shygirl looks directly into the lens, “accepting that this is a contrived environment”. She wanted to break the fourth wall, even if that movie trope is a bit of a cliche: “Sometimes cliches are cliches for a reason, you know?”Of course, falling in love is the biggest cliche of all, I add. “Exactly!” Once you’ve said “I love you” a million times to your partner, she says, “you’re looking for other ways to express it”. Her smile is beatific thinking about it all. Playing the new album to her boyfriend made her cry; the delicate, intensely vulnerable ballad Real allowed her “to revisit the memory of when we were in Japan, and recognise that now as falling in love”. It has an incredulous, awestruck quality, as though she can’t believe her own good fortune. “We’re always choosing each other,” she says. “I’m always choosing what’s happening in my life.”Swallow! is released on 6 November via Because Music. Shygirl’s 2027 world tour begins 13 March at Columbiahalle, BerlinExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockDance musicIndieElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Worldpeace DMT: Stick Around for Tea review – ‘laptop twee’ duo keep things goofy but strengthen songs | Indie | The Guardian
description: Bringing back the hyperliterate sound design of their acclaimed 2025 debut, the London duo explore childhood with whimsical humour and terrific musicality
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Bringing back the hyperliterate sound design of their acclaimed 2025 debut, the London duo explore childhood with whimsical humour and terrific musicality
Content: Devastatingly contemporary … Leo Fincham and Rowan Miles, AKA Worldpeace DMT.Photograph: Thomas ConnollyView image in fullscreenDevastatingly contemporary … Leo Fincham and Rowan Miles, AKA Worldpeace DMT.Photograph: Thomas ConnollyIndieReviewWorldpeace DMT: Stick Around for Tea review – ‘laptop twee’ duo keep things goofy but strengthen songs(WPDMT)Bringing back the hyperliterate sound design of their acclaimed 2025 debut, the London duo explore childhood with whimsical humour and terrific musicalityShaad D'SouzaFri 16 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of last year’s surprise highlights was The Velvet Underground & Rowan, the debut album by the wacky, hyperliterate London duo Worldpeace DMT. That irreverent album title summed up their approach to their references: Leo Fincham and Rowan Miles – also of theFemcels– buttressed nods to Fleetwood Mac and the Beach Boys with a palette straight out of NME circa 2011. If it isn’t a coup to make the sound of Grouplove and Darwin Deez sound cool and urbane in 2025, I don’t know what is.View image in fullscreenStick Around for Tea album artwork.Photograph: PRThis year, Worldpeace DMT have changed tack, perhaps in response to suggestions that they’re at the forefront of an emergent genre called “laptop twee”. The duo’s August mixtape Flowers Powers mostly eschewed plunderphonics and heavy sampling in favour of live instrumentation that ran the gamut from Spiritualized to outlaw country; Stick Around for Tea, their second album, brings back a shade of the goofy,Sung Tongs-esque sound design that made their debut such a joy, while pulling Fincham and Miles’ songwriting to the fore.Stick Around for Tea seems, loosely, to be a concept album about childhood. The inherent whimsy of the Worldpeace DMT project suits these songs, which wring dry humour from lyrics about spiders, tigers and anthropomorphised guitars. Fincham and Miles sing in a self-consciously childish way that belies their taut musicality: a lush, almost Van Dyke Parks jauntiness on Munich Gyaru, for example, or a knack for bulletproof pop structure on the title track. The result is the kind of devastatingly contemporary record that even arch classicists couldn’t possibly turn up their noses at.Explore more on these topicsIndiePop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: PatKop & Say album review – playfulness and beguiling delicacy in mix of new and old  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Compositions by both musicians themselves frame works by Szymanowski and Prokofiev
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Compositions by both musicians themselves frame works by Szymanowski and Prokofiev
Content: Complementary … Patricia Kopatchinskaja and Fazıl Say.Photograph: borggreve/Courtesy of Marco BorggreveView image in fullscreenComplementary … Patricia Kopatchinskaja and Fazıl Say.Photograph: borggreve/Courtesy of Marco BorggreveClassical musicReviewPatKop & Say album review – playfulness and beguiling delicacy in mix of new and oldPatricia Kopatchinskaja and Fazil Say(Alpha)Compositions by both musicians themselves frame works by Szymanowski and ProkofievErica JealFri 16 Oct 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatricia KopatchinskajaandFazil Sayhave recorded Say’s music together before, but this is their first recording to feature Kopatchinskaja as a composer as well, but this is no vanity project: Say’s and Kopatchinskaja’s pieces make good complements to Szymanowski’s three Mythes and Prokofiev’s Violin Sonata No 1.View image in fullscreenAlbum artwork for Patkop & Say.Photograph: Courtesy of Marco Borggreve for Alpha ClassicsSay’s Lost Screams Sonata is driven by repeated piano rhythms, its fierceness tempered by an episode in which Kopatchinskaja plays low, ghostly harmonics and Say gently plucks the strings of the piano so it almost sounds like a second violin. Kopatchinskaja’s three-movement piece UniSolo is an impish work with a searching, thoughtful playfulness that comes from the parallel world to the Kurtág miniatures she plays so well.These two frame a haunting performance of Mythes that embraces the strange sumptuousness of these pieces, with playing of beguiling delicacy from both musicians. With an even bigger scope, Prokofiev’s wartime Sonata No 1 has moments in which Kopatchinskaja turns her tone almost ugly, even in places where other violinists might choose to soar heroically. Each of these works pushes at the edges of what the violin can do, and casts the instrument in a kind of narrative role: Kopatchinskaja, who always looks to play the storyteller, seizes upon these qualities with relish.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup | Crime fiction | The Guardian
description: The Heights by Ian Rankin; The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier; Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings; The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West; Inheritance by Gillian Slovo
Author: Laura Wilson
Headline: The Heights by Ian Rankin; The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier; Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings; The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West; Inheritance by Gillian Slovo
Content: Ian Rankin … The Heights is his first standalone thriller in almost two decades.Photograph: Robert Ormerod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIan Rankin … The Heights is his first standalone thriller in almost two decades.Photograph: Robert Ormerod/The GuardianCrime and thrillers roundupCrime fictionReviewThe best recent crime and thrillers – review roundupThe Heights by Ian Rankin; The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier; Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings; The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West; Inheritance by Gillian SlovoLaura WilsonFri 16 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenThe Heightsby Ian Rankin (Orion, £25)Luxury tower blocks, those potent symbols of hyper-gentrification, the increasing wealth gap and the displacement of existing communities, are a gift to novelists. Rankin’s first standalone thriller in almost two decades centres on The Heights, 18 storeys high and facing London’s Hyde Park, where DS Gillian Gish is investigating the suspicious death of night-shift security guard Dwayne Hogarth. The high-net-worth individuals who live there, including a young singer, a gangster’s wife, a man who “made a mint in post-glasnost Russia” and the daughter of a very well-connected Zimbabwean, are either uncontactable or tight-lipped, and it soon becomes clear that the developer, despite his bravado, is in financial trouble. Everyone, it appears, has something to hide – and then a second corpse is discovered. Rankin is a superb storyteller, and this is well up to his usual high standard, while DS Gish – less complex, but considerably more relatable than John Rebus – is worthy of her own series.View image in fullscreenThe Mortonsby Scott Westerfeld & Justine Larbalestier(Viking, £18.99)There are shades of both The Sopranos and Wednesday Addams in this tale of a powerful old American family whose trade is murder, blackmail and financial fraud. As the Mortons’ great hope, Jessica, puts it, “Give your child a strong hand, a sharp knife, and a big family, then teach them loyalty without care.” The children are given pet rabbits on which to prove their lack of compassion; the family are as ruthless with their own as with everyone else, their graveyard being full of youngsters who failed to make the grade. Jessica, who achieved her first kill aged 20, looks set to take on the murderous mantle, but a summer internship leads to a train of events that culminate in the discovery of a conscience. The Mortons is vivid and exciting, with a nice vein of mordant humour, but there’s a lot of world-building to get through, some of it lacking in internal logic; it’s hard to keep track of the many characters, and the violence towards innocent people and animals may leave some readers feeling queasy.View image in fullscreenMurder Most Crypticby Alys Cummings (Michael Joseph, £16.99)Cummings’s entertaining debut begins with a man walking into a meeting of people in recovery, announcing that his name is Laurence and he’s an alcoholic, then dropping dead. The group, who spot a handwritten cryptic crossword clue that’s fallen out of Laurence’s pocket – answer: Murder – are quicker to suspect foul play than the police, and when the same clue appears in the following day’s newspaper, they decide to figure out what’s going on. Told from the points of view of people trying, with varying degrees of success, to remain sober, this book involves a fair amount of unreliable narration – not least because of the memory gaps of the blackout drunk. The emergence of pertinent backstories lends rather more emotional depth than is found in the average cosy, while the discovery of further cryptic crossword clues provides an ingenious puzzle element (answers given at the end for non-cruciverbalists).View image in fullscreenThe Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonaldby AJ West (Orenda, £20)West’s latest historical mystery is a re-imagining of real events: actor William Terris was stabbed to death outside London’s Adelphi theatre in 1897 by deranged and destitute fellow performer Richard Archer Prince, who was subsequently found “criminally insane” and sent to Broadmoor. The action here takes place in 1917, against the backdrop of the first world war, as Everest Macdonald’s father, brother of William, hands her a packet of papers and charges her with finding out the truth about her uncle’s death. What follows is a fascinating journey that takes us back to the Indian sepoy rebellion of 1857 and encompasses “blackmail in all directions, secret love affairs, loyalties, vendettas, even phantoms and tribal curses”, as well as a plethora of hysterical thespians including real-life stars of the turn-of-the-century British stage such as Herbert Beerbohm Tree and Seymour Hicks. Well-researched, atmospheric and suitably melodramatic, this is a rip-roaring read-at-one-sitting historical mystery.Inheritanceby Gillian Slovo (Peepal Tree, £12.99)The eponymous inheritance of Slovo’s latest novel involves political and financial corruption in a South Africa still emerging from the long shadows cast by apartheid. Novelist Deborah Harrison’s younger sister Gail killed herself after denouncing Deborah’s latest book – a re-imagining of the family tragedy that blighted their childhood – as a misrepresentation. Deborah has always accepted the official version of events, that her mother killed her father in 1984 and went to prison for it, but Gail, whose adulthood was blighted by addiction issues and escalating paranoia, maintained that this was not the case. Now she has left a will tasking her sister with finding their now-released mother, with whom they have had no contact for over 40 years, and Deborah discovers that the truth is far more complicated than she has been led to believe. This is a suspenseful and moving tale about generational trauma, the complex nature of memory, making peace and letting go.Explore more on these topicsCrime fictionCrime and thrillers roundupThrillersFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Make Me Well by Xand van Tulleken – an eye-opening takedown of wellness myths | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: The engaging TV doctor dismantles the spurious science behind modern day snake oils, from collagen to turmeric
Author: Simon Usborne
Headline: The engaging TV doctor dismantles the spurious science behind modern day snake oils, from collagen to turmeric
Content: Are supplements really benficial to our health?Photograph: Viktoriya Skorikova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAre supplements really benficial to our health?Photograph: Viktoriya Skorikova/Getty ImagesBook of the dayScience and nature booksReviewMake Me Well by Xand van Tulleken – an eye-opening takedown of wellness mythsThe engaging TV doctor dismantles the spurious science behind modern day snake oils, from collagen to turmericSimon UsborneFri 16 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Xand van Tulleken set off on a journey into the wild west of wellness, he didn’t expect to discover anything new about vitamin D. Of all the supplements that line our shelves and social media feeds, it ought to be the least controversial; even the NHS website, which is hardly a wellspring of quackery, advises that everyone should consider taking a daily dose during autumn and winter, when we risk becoming deficient (D is the vitamin we get mostly from sunlight, and which helps keep our bones strong).The tiggerish TV doctor and twin brother to Chris (he’s the one who wroteUltra-Processed Peopleabout the food industry) qualified at a time of high excitement in vitamin D circles; in the early 2000s, big studies were linking it not just to bone health but cancer, heart disease and dementia. “The range of potential problems to be solved was dizzying,” Van Tulleken writes in Make Me Well.But – spoiler alert – it turns out evidence even of the benefits of the most medically endorsed supplement shrivels under scrutiny. After immersing himself in decades of trials and speaking to a professor who had devoted his career to what he now views as the false promise of vitamin D, Van Tulleken finds no justification for its routine consumption for all but a tiny proportion of the population who are genuinely deficient.View image in fullscreenXand van Tulleken.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverThe vitamin D chapter follows what becomes a familiar and compelling pattern in Van Tulleken’s first proper solo book, in which he combines the rigour of an investigative journalist with medical expertise and the bouncy bedside manner that makes him such a natural broadcaster. He’s also the best kind of science writer, leaning into complexity while making it as easy to digest as a fish oil gummy (another thing you might want to stop forking out for).As well as vitamin D, he goes deep on collagen, testosterone, multivitamins, turmeric and krill oil supplements, as well as the burgeoning markets for personalised nutrition, glucose monitoring, wearable tech and private blood screening. In each case, he finds a troubling blurring of the lines between wellness and healthcare – and yawning gaps between hype and the evidence. He also uncovers the harm that wellness fads can do to our bodies, our relationship with food and the environment.In a chapter devoted to collagen, Van Tulleken travels to China to learn how a messy byproduct of the meat industry has been marketed as a modern elixir with a mark-up of as much as 1,000%. Ejiao, a premium kind of donkey-derived collagen, has become such a coveted source of “ingestible beauty” that manufacturers have exhausted Chinese supplies of donkey hides; soon rural communities in countries across Africa were finding that their animals were being slaughtered for export so that their skins could be boiled up and turned into expensive gummies and powders.He also explores the history and booming business of supplements, from the literal snake oil of the late 19th century to an unwholesome contemporary market driven by podcasts, influencers and a scientific publishing industry that appears to have striking deficiencies of its own: “The more research I do, the more I see the same patterns repeatedly: conflicts of interest, industry-funded trials, industry-­owned journals and an entire system designed to exploit people.”He concludes that, for the generally healthy person, wellness requires things that it’s hard to package and sell to supermarkets or via a subscription: a diet rich in whole foods and fruit and vegetables, for example, and a hobby that involves the achievable yet challenging mastery of some kind of rewarding skill. (The scientific evidence for the health benefits of, say, becoming a potter or learning the piano is far more robust than that for knocking back testosterone or vitamin D.)“The right people to make you well won’t be health gurus,” Van Tulleken says at the end of a book that deserves to prompt some kind of industry reckoning. “They might be dance instructors or librarians or martial arts teachers or the person who runs your local choir.” While I consider resuming reacquainting myself with my own piano, I have no plans to dust off my bottle of vitamin D pills as the nights draw in.Make Me Well: A Quest to Understand the Confusing World of Wellness by Xand van Tulleken is published by Cornerstone (£22). To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: John Green: ‘I devoured the Sweet Valley High books in the 1980s’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The American author on being inspired by Kurt Vonnegut, coming late to Jane Austen, and the brilliance of Robert Penn Warren
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The American author on being inspired by Kurt Vonnegut, coming late to Jane Austen, and the brilliance of Robert Penn Warren
Content: John Green.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenJohn Green.Photograph: PRThe books of my lifeBooksJohn Green: ‘I devoured the Sweet Valley High books in the 1980s’The American author on being inspired by Kurt Vonnegut, coming late to Jane Austen, and the brilliance of Robert Penn WarrenJohn GreenFri 16 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryI remember learning to read with dull stories about Jane going up a hill, but my earliest thrilling reading memories are of series like The Baby-Sitters Club and Sweet Valley High. In the highly gendered reading days of the 1980s, I knew those books were for girls, but I  devoured them.My favourite book growing upBesides the girls of The Baby-Sitters Club, I loved books about survival and perseverance, especially Gary Paulsen’s The Island, in which a boy discovers a secluded island and ventures there to learn about the natural world.The book that changed me as a teenagerWhen I was 16, I read Toni Morrison for the first time: The Bluest Eye and Sula and Song of Solomonin quick succession. Literature had always felt a little distant (and maybe even slightly dead) to me, but Morrison helped me see that books were vital and present. I’d always known that they could transport me, but Morrison showed me that books could also transform me.The writer who changed my mindAs a young person, the novelist Kurt Vonnegut had an outsize role in developing my values and beliefs. His fundamental humanism – his belief that humans might not yet be good news but stillmightbe good news – inspired me then and inspires me still.The book that made me want to be a writerReading Michael Chabon’s The Mysteries of Pittsburgh made me want to write books. I’d never encountered a novel before with queer main characters or such a vibrant sense of contemporary youth, and this one made me want to tell similar stories.The bookI came back toWhen I was in high school, I found Holden Caulfield in JD Salinger’s The Catcher in the Rye annoying and whiny. I enjoyed the book but thought Holden just needed to snap out of it and realise how lucky he was to be a rich kid in New York City. Revisiting the story years later, it shattered me. The sadness of that novel, and the vulnerability of Holden, only became clear to me in adulthood.The book I rereadI’ve just reread Lily King’s Heart the Lover and enjoyed it even more the second time around. I reread quite a lot, because I am fascinated by how different a great book is each time you return to it. The text hasn’t changed, of course, but I have.The book I could never read againI don’t feel an urgent need to return to the works of Ayn Rand, whose flimsy plots only serve to reinforce flawed ideas about how humans organise themselves and cooperate.The book I discovered later in lifeI didn’t read Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice until I was an adult! How I wish I could have met Lizzy Bennet when I was younger, but even so, I love that book and return to it often.The book I am currently readingIt’s about astrophysics, called How to Build a Universe, by Dr Katie Mack. I’m anxious for anything that can help me zoom out – in this case way, way out – to understand that mine is not the only life (and, indeed, my galaxy is not the only galaxy).My comfort readWhen I need to be reminded of why I love reading and what it is about language that lights me up, I go back to All the King’s Men by Robert Penn Warren, a brilliant novel about US politics and the south but most of all about the inexorable march of time.Hollywood, Ending by John Green is published by Penguin. title: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors | Games | The Guardian
description: This odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appears
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: This odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appears
Content: One of 2026’s boldest, most original games … Penguin Colony by Origame Digital.Photograph: Origame Digital/Fellow TravellerView image in fullscreenOne of 2026’s boldest, most original games … Penguin Colony by Origame Digital.Photograph: Origame Digital/Fellow TravellerGamesReviewPenguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrorsPC; Origame DigitalThis odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appearsLewis GordonFri 16 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleANazi kneels down on frozen snow, staring at an endless Antarctic horizon. Another holds a gun to his head, ready to end his own life. I direct a small waddling penguin up to them, trying to imagine what it could be thinking. Dismay, perhaps. Likely bewilderment. But then a faint smile seems to break out across its beaky face, as if amused by these silly humans and their misguided belief that they could ever best this howling, harsh landscape.For most games, the idea of playing as a penguin observing Nazis losing the plot near the south pole would be weird enough. But Penguin Colony, developed by Origame Digital, pushes further. This is an audacious, frequently brilliant retelling of HP Lovecraft’s 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness, in which eldritch horrors are just as common as Nazis. Further weirdness abounds: the many collectibles scattered about this place are not shiny gold objects à la Super Mario or Sonic. Rather, they are words. So tottering about as a semiaquatic bird, you have a unique mission: collect human language.View image in fullscreenUnnerving, discordant … Penguin Colony.Photograph: Fellow TravellerBut let’s zoom out for a moment because playing Penguin Colony is more straightforward than this description suggests. First and foremost, it is a semiopen world exploration game in which you direct a penguin to the same unearthly entity that the Nazis are chasing. You hop, swim and glide about tummy-first, chewing up miles of frozen wasteland like an indefatigable snowboarder. Tapping a button next to another penguin lets you swap into its body. Some of these, like the rockhopper penguin, are nimble movers, capable of jumping especially high. Fluffy penguin chicks, meanwhile, can squeeze through tiny gaps.At first, the game’s polar levels are straightforward: snow drifts and ice floes peppered with the remnants of human habitation such as fishing huts. But your surroundings quickly grow stranger: supersized stone labyrinths whose architectural splendour evokesDark Souls, alien-looking obelisks and abyssal crevasses. Everything in the world is rendered in jagged, low-poly graphics, looming from the screen like a hallucinated PlayStation 2 game.View image in fullscreenLow-poly nightmares … Penguin Colony by Origame Digital.Photograph: Origame Digital/Fellow TravellerAs you navigate these spaces, a deep-voiced narrator relays the expedition of a scientist from decades before. It’s clear he is driven by the same hubris and racism as his Nazi successors.The layering of space, time and narrative is terrifically unsettling. At one point, having just hopped my way through a challenging platform section, I came across a Nazi cannibal feasting on his fellow soldier as a researcher delivered yet another verbose pontification on his God-given right to plunder Earth’s southernmost tip. At times, jarring cuts to archive footage and what seem to be Indigenous art interrupt the low-poly action. My head was often spinning, trying to reconcile all these conflicting, contrapuntal elements. Better, I found, to let go and soak up the unnerving, discordant whole.Penguin Colony is a little uneven technically: I experienced a small number of audio glitches and, at times, bugs with the controls. Yet this does not overly detract from an experience that builds to an incendiary conclusion: a takedown of Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism while also, intriguingly, inviting the player to see the world in newly reenchanted terms.This latter point is made with aplomb at the game’s end: a spectacular cosmological map that details everything you discovered on that playthrough. More tantalisingly, it shows you all the things you missed. This reveal is liable to induce a feeling of vertigo and wonder: Penguin Colony, one of 2026’s boldest, most original games, is far bigger than it first lets on. To access all of its secrets and excavate all of its meaning, one must think and act less like a human mainlining towards their objective. On the contrary, you must embrace the spirit of a renegade penguin, waddling carefree towards whatever piques your interest: atrocity, beauty and all.Penguin Colony is available now onPC, with PS5 and Nintendo Switch versions planned for 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesAdventure gamesIndie gamesPCGame playPlatform gamesHP LovecraftreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sweet nothings, urinal cakes and headless dogs: 10 artworks worth seeing at Frieze | Frieze art fair | The Guardian
description: There’s plenty that stands out at Regent’s Park this year, from antidepressant pens and an ibuprofen-dolling robotic arm to Miriam Cahn’s 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture and a 150m-year-old dinosaur skull – still with embedded tooth
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: There’s plenty that stands out at Regent’s Park this year, from antidepressant pens and an ibuprofen-dolling robotic arm to Miriam Cahn’s 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture and a 150m-year-old dinosaur skull – still with embedded tooth
Content: Take note … Carolyn Lazard, Portrait IV.Photograph: courtesy the artist/Trautwein HerlethView image in fullscreenTake note … Carolyn Lazard, Portrait IV.Photograph: courtesy the artist/Trautwein HerlethFrieze art fairSweet nothings, urinal cakes and headless dogs: 10 artworks worth seeing at FriezeThere’s plenty that stands out at Regent’s Park this year, from antidepressant pens and an ibuprofen-dolling robotic arm to Miriam Cahn’s 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture and a 150m-year-old dinosaur skull – still with embedded toothFrieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tentEddy FrankelFri 16 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElla Fleckat Ehrlich SteinbergThe raised platform in the middle of British artist Ella Fleck’s installation vibrates under your feet to the sound of a male voice. He’s whispering sweet nothings, intoning sexual fantasies. It’s all based on third-party agencies that manage OnlyFans accounts, interacting with users, creating fictional relationships that horny guys spend thousands on. It’s a greasy, gross, uncomfortable exploration of sex work on an industrial scale.Yuli Serfatyat Xxijra HiiYuli Serfaty’s headless metallic dog sculptures guard this booth, their claws sharp, their heavy teats dragging on the floor. It’s a surreal symbol of femininity pushed to an extreme, a body devalued and exploited. A video shows the creature trying to escape the booth, and succeeding. The whole installation looks like HR Giger meets Wolfenstein 3D, but with a nasty, satirical edge.Rirkrit Tiravanijaat David ZwirnerView image in fullscreenRepetitive, meaningless … Rirkrit Tiravanija, untitled 2026 (a bitter pill).Photograph: Jack Hems/courtesy the artist/David ZwirnerFinally, something to help you get through Frieze. Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija’s sculpture here is a robotic arm that carefully hands visitors a little red-and-white ibuprofen pill. If you don’t reach out, it just drops it on the floor. The robot does its job, over and over, regardless of if you’re there to receive it. It feels futile, obscene, repetitive, meaningless. Quite the comment on modern life.Carolyn Lazardat Trautwein HerlethIt might look like a display of pens, and that’s because it is. But each one is a promotional item from a pharmaceutical company, given out as gifts to American medical professionals. Lazzard bought them in estate sales from real doctors. They become a portrait of selling out, of how healthcare in the US can be bought by corporations. There are pens with branding for antidepressants, ADHD meds, Viagra: corporations are keeping you going, keeping you productive. When it clicks, it’s an incredibly grim conceptual vision of how our bodies are treated as commodities.Gray Wielebinskiin the toiletsThe urinal cakes in the Frieze bogs this year aren’t just there to keep whiffs at bay – they’re art. This is urinal cake as sculptural intervention, thanks to artist Gray Wielebinski, who has designed each one with a custom scent and encased them in metal cages. They sort of look like little chastity devices, glistening lumps of odorous chemicals for you to wee on. They’re weird, almost erotic sculptures. You can hear the anguished cry of thousands of artists wishing they’d thought of it first.Miriam Cahnat Galerie Jocelyn WolffView image in fullscreenStanding out … Miriam Cahn.Photograph: courtesy Galerie Jocelyn WolffThere is such an overwhelming amount of (usually very bland) painting at Frieze that it really takes a special painter to stand out. But Swiss artist Miriam Cahn’s installation is a proper diamond among the swill. It’s a whole booth filled with 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture. Each one plumbs new depths of anxious, monstrous introspection. She grins and screams, stands and falls, all in blurred, messy washes of colour. Psychologically intense, overwrought, emotional stuff.William-Adolphe Bouguereauat Stair SaintyMy love for 19th-century French academic painter William-Adolphe Bouguereau verges on a sickness. I mean, I have a Bouguereau tattoo. So finding this little gem among the Dutch flower paintings and Egyptian busts of Frieze Masters was a genuine thrill. It’s a weird, yellowed little thing – based on a Tintoretto – of a man lying prostrate on the ground. The ropes that bind him have been snapped, wood is splintered. Here is the aftermath of violence, the shocking silence after a traumatic event. This is one of the great things about Masters: getting to spot art historical gold hidden away on the back wall of some booth. This gallery also had a gorgeous James Tissot portrait. It’s 19th-century art nerd heaven.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLuce Turnierat Harlesden High StreetView image in fullscreenLuce Turnier, Nude Woman in Chair (1977).Photograph: Courtesy the artist/ Harlesden High StreetThere are some amazing narratives to discover in the Frieze Masters spotlight section, especially the work of Haitian modernist Luce Turnier, who lived between Paris and Haiti but has largely been forgotten by art history. This small display of stark portraits – like a more sombre Alice Neel – and vitrines is a little glimpse into a lost period of international modernism from an artist who feels ripe for a museum show.View image in fullscreenCamarasaurus supremus skull with embedded allosaurus tooth, 145-155 million years old.Photograph: David Brunetti/courtesy David AaronCamarasaurus supremus skull at David AaronYou eventually go antiquities and Flemish art blind walking around Frieze Masters, so finding the fossilised dino skulls that David Aaron Gallery has lugged to the tent is always a bit of Jurassic relief. This year they’ve brought an enormous triceratops skull and an awesome camarasaurus supremus with the tooth of an allosaurus embedded in it. Absolutely brutal, and possibly the only thing my four-year-old would like in either fair.Sohrab Huraat ExperimenterThere’s death and fear written into all of Sohrab Hura’s paintings here. They’re grotesque expressionist scenes of everyday violence: a man kicked to the ground, a crow pecking at a bleeding carcass above a figure staring aghast at a newspaper. It’s like Edvard Munch but with way more blood and guts. The painting of the woman in the dust storm isn’t good, but the rest are great, angry things.Explore more on these topicsFrieze art fairLondonArtExhibitionsPaintingInstallationMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content
