title: Lena Martell obituary | Music | The Guardian
description: Singer and TV presenter who had a UK No 1 hit in 1979 with One Day at a Time
Author: Anthony Hayward
Headline: Singer and TV presenter who had a UK No 1 hit in 1979 with One Day at a Time
Content: Lena Martell’s ‘light on the ear’ TV shows were perfect for Saturday night programming in the 1970sPhotograph: Dezo Hoffman/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLena Martell’s ‘light on the ear’ TV shows were perfect for Saturday night programming in the 1970sPhotograph: Dezo Hoffman/ShutterstockMusicObituaryLena Martell obituarySinger and TV presenter who had a UK No 1 hit in 1979 with One Day at a TimeAnthony HaywardFri 16 Oct 2026 05.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe singer Lena Martell, who has died aged 86, enjoyed a career that took her from dance halls in her nativeScotlandto cabaret in London and stages in Las Vegas and Australia. She performed on the same bill as Sammy Davis Jr and had her own shows on BBC television.On record, she was a one-hit wonder in Britain withOne Day at a Time, a song written byMarijohn WilkinandKris Kristoffersonthat mixed country and gospel. “Lord, for my sake, teach me to take one day at a time,” she sang.It stayed at No 1 for three weeks in 1979, ahead of Michael Jackson and Abba, making Martell Scotland’s first solo female singer to top the singles chart. The song, which sold 2.5m copies worldwide, had been released two years earlier without making ripples. When it was re-promoted and captured the public’s imagination, Martell said: “I’m happy about the record because its philosophy is cheering people.”Although she failed to follow it up, she did have half a dozen albums in the Top 40 between 1974 and 1980, featuring her rich contralto voice and easy-listening style, and boosted by her television appearances.Her own programmes began with Presenting Lena Martell (1971-73), featuring singers such asVince HillandRoger Whittaker, and other entertainers, which attracted audiences of more than 12 million and was a perfect fit for the Saturday-night TV of the time. Then came Music with Martell (1974), Make the Music Speak (1977) and Lena’s Music (1979). She described her shows as “informal, light on the eye – and light on the ear as well”.Her career continued in fits and starts, with bouts of ill health, but she performed into her 70s.Born Helena Thomson in the Hamiltonhill area of Glasgow, she was the second of three children. Her mother, Helen, supported the family with cleaning and shop work after her father, a trombone-playing shipyard engineer who called his daughter Lena, moved to Canada. Later, a club owner coined the professional name Martell when a member of the audience held up a bottle of brandy.Aged 11, she started singing with her elder brother Allan, a saxophone and clarinet player, in a Dixie band and learned to play drums. On leaving school, she won a bursary to study at art college, but soon left to work in a printing firm by day while continuing to perform with the band. Then, she became a singer with Billy McGregor and the Gay Birds at the city’s Barrowland ballroom – until it burned down in 1958.She headed straight for London, took a job in another print works and recorded a single, Tender and True (1959, as Helen Thomson), after coming fourth in the ITV talent show Find the Singer and performing at the Soho venue Jack of Clubs.Taken on as a singer at the New Bagatelle nightclub in Mayfair in 1960, she gained experience as a compere, then became a star of the cabaret. Jack Fox, the owner, came up with her new name, and the Stage lauded Martell for her “freshness, charm and natural singing”.In 1961, she appeared on The Friday Show, a BBC television showcase for singers and entertainers, and recorded her first single as Lena Martell, Love Can Be.Then she starred with Dickie Henderson in the revue Five Past Eight at the Alhambra theatre, Glasgow (1962). Returning to London clubs, she continued her cabaret act at the Colony (1962), starred in the revue Tropical Paradise at the Pigalle (1963) and was acclaimed for her impressions of Louis Armstrong,Lena Horne,Eartha Kittand Shirley Bassey.In 1963, she was the support act on Sammy Davis Jr’s British tour. A billing alongside Morecambe and Wise in a Blackpool summer season followed, when one critic observed that she “makes her impact by sheer force of personality”.She headed for New York in 1964 to understudy Barbra Streisand as Fanny Brice in the original Broadway production of the musical Funny Girl. But, when Streisand took a break, a growth on Martell’s vocal cords left her unable to step in and her career was on hold for two years.At the same time, she was grieving the deaths of both her brother Allan, in a road accident, and her boyfriend Gordon Cameron, from a brain haemorrhage.Cabaret and revues then kept her busy in London and Scotland, and as far and wide as Las Vegas, Sydney, Johannesburg and Hong Kong. When she sold out the London Palladium in 1978, the London Evening News wrote that Martell and her songs “evoke visions of the days whenVera Lynnwas a superstar”.Over her career, she recorded more than 30 albums featuring cover songs alongside original material.Another break in her career came when she was diagnosed with breast cancer while caring for her mother, who suffered from Alzheimer’s disease. Later, in 2008, Martell underwent a triple heart bypass operation.In 1992, she was made bankrupt after losing money in a property company that went bust.She lived with her partner, David, until moving into a care home. He predeceased her.Lena Martell (Helena Thomson), singer, born 15 May 1940; death announced 5 October 2026Explore more on these topicsMusicTelevisionScotlandobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Game, set and tache: Carlos Alcaraz joins growing trend for a stylish top lip | Men's hair | The Guardian
description: Tennis superstar is latest celebrity to sport a ‘refined’ moustache which owes little to bushy Tom Selleck look
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: Tennis superstar is latest celebrity to sport a ‘refined’ moustache which owes little to bushy Tom Selleck look
Content: Carlos Alcaraz at the Shanghai Masters: ‘I always wanted to step on the court at least once with the moustache.’Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPAView image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz at the Shanghai Masters: ‘I always wanted to step on the court at least once with the moustache.’Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPAMen's hairGame, set and tache: Carlos Alcaraz joins growing trend for a stylish top lipTennis superstar is latest celebrity to sport a ‘refined’ moustache which owes little to bushy Tom Selleck lookEllie Violet BramleyFri 16 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe tennis superstarCarlos Alcarazmight have been knocked out of the Shanghai Masters in straight sets earlier this week, but he did so sporting a moustache that became almost as remarked upon as his aptitude for a sneaky drop shot.“I always wanted to step on the court at least once with the moustache,” Alcaraz said. The Spaniard and his team had all agreed to take the facial-hair plunge if he won the Japan Open, which he did for a second straight year.“¡Bigotes para todos!”or “moustaches for everyone”, they apparently cheered at the end of the match.At Milan fashion week last month, the Wuthering Heights starJacob Elordisported a thin strip of hair on his top lip as he watched his girlfriend, Kendall Jenner, model for the Bottega Veneta show.A moustachioed Harry Styles is roughly halfway through his record-breaking 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York. The actorTimothée Chalamet, who kept his Marty Supreme ’tache on throughout awards season, has been playing around with his facial hair again, adding a goatee.View image in fullscreenNcuti Gatwa poses for photographers at the Albie awards in London.Photograph: Scott A Garfitt/APOn TikTok, gen Z men with moustaches are plentiful, as are tutorials for how to grow and style them – alongside almost as many videos from older generations questioning them.High street barber shops are seeing evidence of it, too. AtCitadel in Sheffield, more young men are asking for moustaches, and a large number are asking specifically for thin ones, which the owner, Marie Williams, describes as “[a] low maintenance, easygoing moustache that’s attainable to most”.According to Jay Byrne, a barber atDog House barbers in Birminghamand a formerBritish barber of the year: “The moustache is certainly making a comeback, particularly among younger men.”The moustaches appearing on young men’s faces are a long way from the bushier ones seen in the 1970s and 80s, epitomised by Tom Selleck in Magnum PI.They seem more to hark back to the Hollywood stars of the 40s and 50s such as David Niven and Clark Gable. “We’re seeing a move away from the heavier, traditional moustaches … towards a much more refined, deliberately styled look,” says Byrne.“Achieving the look is all about precision, proportion and understanding what suits the individual’s facial structure. It’s not simply a case of growing a moustache and leaving it alone. The shape, thickness and detailing are what make the difference.”View image in fullscreenJacob Elordi sporting a moustache at Milan fashion week.Photograph: Luca Bruno/APAccording to Dr Ashley Morgan, a masculinities scholar at Cardiff Metropolitan University: “Skinny moustaches are a sign of difference, especially from men who keep beards.”Given the rise of the manosphere and the complicated state of masculinity at the moment, Morgan thinks these skinnier moustaches could be intended to steer clear of signalling alpha masculinity. “Young men want to demonstrate a carefully curated form of ‘manliness’,” she says.For these young male celebrities in particular, Morgan thinks it could be “an expression of ageing”.“Timothée Chamalet is 30, Jacob Elordi is 29 … it could well be a sign that they want to show that they are mature, they have entered a new phase of life, and want to be seen as more ‘manly’ while remaining youthful.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor 34-year-oldNcuti Gatwa, who starred in the most recent series of Doctor Who, it has certainly been a way to lean into his age after making his name while playing a schoolboy in the hit TV drama Sex Education.‘You look like an Agatha Christie villain!’ The moustache is back – but should it go away again?Read moreGatwa told theRadio Times: “I’d spent the last four years playing a child [in Sex Education], at the age of 30, so I said: ‘Let me have my moustache back.’”The fashion historian Tony Glenville once had a curly moustache but, he says, “like many men, [I] got rid of facial hair during the mask-wearing times of Covid”. He says it is a trend “among young men who’ve not really seen it around so much recently”. Facial hair, as with all things, “has huge fashion phases for men”.Movember, which launched in 2003 and has grown into a global movement, sees men grow moustaches for the month of November to raise money for charity and has arguably made facial hair more popular again.For such a small slither of hair, the moustache is historically and culturally freighted. It can symbolise freedom and has long held a central position in gay culture.While the moustache might be a “trend” in western culture, in other cultures it is much more of a constant. From romance to war, religion to masculinity and sexuality, moustaches connote different things in different contexts.Luckily for anyone wanting to give a thin moustache a whirl, according to barber Williams, it is a style that “requires minimal upkeep; just a few snips with the scissors to maintain”.Explore more on these topicsMen's hairMen's fashionCarlos AlcarazTimothée ChalametJacob ElordiNcuti GatwaBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best travel mugs and reusable coffee cups in the UK for taking hot drinks on the go, tested | Ethical and green living | The Guardian
description: Looking to ditch disposable cups for good? Our reviewer bounced on trampolines and braved boiling brews to find the best
Author: Pete Wise
Headline: Looking to ditch disposable cups for good? Our reviewer bounced on trampolines and braved boiling brews to find the best
Content: Spilling the beans on the leakproof capabilities of reusable coffee cups.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSpilling the beans on the leakproof capabilities of reusable coffee cups.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterEthical and green livingReviewThe best travel mugs and reusable coffee cups in the UK for taking hot drinks on the go, testedLooking to ditch disposable cups for good? Our reviewer bounced on trampolines and braved boiling brews to find the bestThe best lunch boxes – testedPete WiseFri 16 Oct 2026 06.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSingle-use takeaway cups belong with throwaway supermarket carrier bags in the landfill of history. Usually made from plastic-coated paper, the billions used each year burn through copious amounts of energy and water, while also contributingsignificantly to landfill.The solution is simple: switch to a reusable coffee cup. These take various forms, such as cups, bottles and mugs, and are more eco-friendly options when used multiple times. There are leakproof travel mugs that can sit in a rucksack pocket; small ones ideally suited to car cup holders; and ones made from recycled post-consumer materials.Two different terms are used for this type of product: travel mugs and reusable coffee cups. Travel mugs are usually better suited for transporting coffee from place to place, whereas reusable coffee cups are often just something to sip from wherever you get a coffee. The terms are sometimes used interchangeably, and you should always check the product specifications to ensure you’re getting the right mug for your purposes. Some coffee chains incentivise the use of these cups through discounts and reward schemes, too.It may seem obvious, but one of the best things about these travel mugs is that you can fill them at home before going out, so thecoffee machinecollecting dust on your counter might finally get more use, too. To help you find your sip-friendly sidekick, I tested 15 cups from brands including KeepCup, Yeti, Ocean Bottle and Chilly’s, and I’ve featured the 11 best options below.A note of caution from a guy with a singed tongue: some of the cups and bottles featured are excellent at keeping your coffee or tea hot. That’s mostly beneficial, but you should check whether your drink has cooled before taking a hearty sip, which may require leaving the lid off for a few minutes.At a glanceBest travel mug overallKeepCupCommuter£30 at AmazonBest budget travel mugYetiThe Rambler£25 at Go OutdoorsBest leakproof travel mugStanleyAeroLight transit mug£23 at Nevis SportBest travel mug for iced coffeeZwillingThermo Plus Thermo Straw tumbler£39.95 at ZwillingWhy you should trust meAs a regular reviewer for the Filter, I’m well versed in testing products. You may have spotted my guide tothe best suitcases, which culminated in me throwing the unfortunate baggage off a stepladder, or my feature onsunrise alarm clocks, where I played the role of sleep-testing guinea pig. I’ve been writing about consumer products for the past decade, and I still take joy in getting to grips with interesting, useful things.I’m also into my coffee, and I care about how the material and form of a vessel affect a drink. I always carry a reusable cup on days out or while working on the go, so my thoughts on these products are rooted in the daily grind.How I testedA man in white overalls jumps on a mini trampoline. He’s holding a series of reusable coffee cups, and coffee is spraying from the top of themJumping beans: each cup was filled with coffee and subjected to a session on the mini trampoline to test how leakproof they really are. Video: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianI used each model several times while travelling and working. I filled them with coffee at home for my first caffeine hit of the day, before having them refilled at various coffee shops, where I asked baristas for their feedback. Throughout testing, I considered how securely the cups held liquid, how pleasant they were to handle and drink from, and how well they maintained the temperature of hot and cold drinks.On the first point, for more rigorous assessment, I held the cups upside down and shook them over kitchen paper to see how much they dripped; I also bounced on a trampette with them (first with the lid closed, then with it open) to test the degree to which they were leakproof. Finally, I filled them with boiling water and measured the temperature over eight hours to gauge the effectiveness of the insulation.Not all reusable cups are intended to provide the same qualities (eg leakproofing or insulation), and I kept this in mind while writing the reviews. During the process, I drank dozens of hot drinks, preventing the use of a stack of disposable cups and ensuring a pleasantly caffeinated state throughout.Mugs that were not requested back by the manufacturer were donated for fundraising tothe Leeds branch of Cat Action Trust 1977, a small national charity dedicated to the welfare of feral cats.My favourite travel mugs and reusable coffee cupsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianBest travel mug overall:KeepCup CommuterKeepCupCommuterfrom£30£32 at KeepCup£30 at AmazonWhat we loveResists leaks and retains heatWhat we don’t loveToo wide for certain pocketsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£32 at KeepCupFrom £30 at AmazonWidely credited as the originator of the reusable coffee cup, KeepCup remains the best in the business. This Commuter model is advertised as “barista standard”, and it certainly proved a cut above during my tests.Why we love itI was impressed by its temperature regulation. It kept hot drinks hot for several hours, and cold water refreshingly cool while out and about. Removing the broad lid will quickly bring down the temperature of the cup’s contents, though, so your coffee will be sippable before you know it.The flip lid is a well-known KeepCup feature, providing a secure closure that couldn’t be simpler to suss out. Do take care to screw it on properly, though.“This mug will fit under the group head on an espresso machine, so saves us from using another vessel to prepare the coffee before pouring it into the reusable cup,” said Scarlet, barista at Holding Patterns listening bar in Leeds.Hand-washing is recommended to preserve the mug’s finish. Thankfully, reaching inside with a soapy sponge didn’t prove a chore. The Commuter claims to offer “leakproof coffee on the go”, and this rang true. It performed very well during my bounce and drip test.It’s a shame that …this mug may be too wide for some cup holders andbackpackpockets.Capacity:340mlMaterial:silicone, electropolished steel, polypropyleneDimensions:8.6 x 12.7cmTemperature after one hour:74.4CTemperature after eight hours:34.1CWeight:218gDishwasher safe?Hand-washing recommended to preserve finishWarranty/guarantee:12 months, withthree yearsfor stainless steel partsKeepCupCommuterfrom£30£32 at KeepCup£30 at AmazonWhat we loveResists leaks and retains heatWhat we don’t loveToo wide for certain pocketsBest budget travel mug:Yeti the RamblerYetiThe Ramblerfrom£25£25 at Go Outdoors£25 at AmazonWhat we loveBeautifully designed and well madeWhat we don’t loveLacks the capacity for long drinksView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£25 at Go Outdoors£25 at AmazonIsn’t this a fine little thing? I found the Rambler ideal for small drinks such as espressos, short blacks and cordials on the go – and it proved effective at keeping drinks suitably hot or cold.Why we love itPerhaps the best trait of this cup is its portability. It’s small and narrows towards the base, which makes it handy for rucksack pockets or car cup holders. Thanks to the ridge about halfway up, it’s convenient to carry by hand, too.I was impressed with the Rambler’s chunky Magslider closure, which makes it easy to open or seal the aperture on the splashproof (note: notleakproof) lid. In my bounce test, it didn’t leak whatsoever when the lid was closed, but it did spray out coffee with the lid open. Just remember to close it before running to catch a bus. This mug’s vibrant colourways are just my cup of tea, too – especially the Rescue Red.“It’s a convenient size, but it would’ve been helpful to have a mark inside the cup to show the right fill level,” said Saeed Hussain, owner of Cravings By Sid in Calverley. “You might be best off handing it to the barista with the lid, so they can see how high to fill it.”It’s a shame that …it’s not big enough to hold a high-street-style americano or latte.Capacity:236mlMaterial:stainless steel, ceramic and plasticDimensions:7.2 x 10.5cmTemperature after one hour:74.1CTemperature after eight hours:34.9CWeight:200gDishwasher safe?YesWarranty/guarantee:five yearsYetiThe Ramblerfrom£25£25 at Go Outdoors£25 at AmazonWhat we loveBeautifully designed and well madeWhat we don’t loveLacks the capacity for long drinksBest leakproof travel mug:Stanley AeroLight transit mugStanleyAeroLight transit mugfrom£23£23 at Nevis Sport£29 at MilletsWhat we loveExceptionally leakproofWhat we don’t loveIf anything, it keeps drinks too hotView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£23 at Nevis Sport£29 at MilletsThe aptly named AeroLight feels dainty. The lid seal is secure, barely allowing any steam through, even when opened for drinking. In normal use and temperature testing, it proved effective at keeping things hot. On opening, this bottle sometimes greeted me with a tiny spray of coffee, but that’s a small price to pay for its tight closure.Why we love itThis was the model I trusted most to stay sealed inside my bag – and, as expected, it didn’t leak. I bounced on the trampette with it, shook it upside down, threw it over my head – and not a drop was spilled. Note that Stanley advises that users fill the AeroLight no higher than 7mm from the threads of the lid.The narrow, fairly tall profile of the AeroLight is ideal for backpack side pockets and slimline cup holders, although it also means its capacity may be lower than you expect. The barista who served me at an excellent King’s Cross coffee kiosk was utterly bemused when I asked her what she thought of the bottle. I’ll take this as a sign that it’s easy to fill up.The AeroLight is dishwasher safe and comes with a lifetime guarantee.It’s a shame that …the insulation of this bottle may be too great, if anything. I had to leave the lid off for quite some time to bring coffee down to a drinkable temperature.Capacity:350mlMaterial:stainless steel and plasticDimensions:6.9 x 16.3cmTemperature after one hour:83.8CTemperature after eight hours:49.3CWeight:180gDishwasher safe?YesWarranty/guarantee:lifetimeStanleyAeroLight transit mugfrom£23£23 at Nevis Sport£29 at MilletsWhat we loveExceptionally leakproofWhat we don’t loveIf anything, it keeps drinks too hotBest travel mug for iced coffee:Zwilling Thermo Plus Thermo Straw tumblerZwillingThermo Plus Thermo Straw tumbler£39.95£39.95 at ZwillingWhat we lovePerfect for iced drinksWhat we don’t loveDoesn’t fit all drink holders and pocketsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£39.95 at ZwillingZwilling’s high standards are showcased in this double-wall insulated travel tumbler, with its robust lid and smooth stainless steel interior. The grooved texture on the handle makes it tactile and pleasant to hold.Why we love itAs well as ensuring hot drinks stay hot, which it does effectively, this tumbler is designed to keep cold drinks cold. I was impressed when using it with iced coffee, as the ice cubes were still barely melted by the time I finished sipping, about an hour after the drink was made.Another plus point for cold coffees is the straw accessory, which comes with a cleaning tool to scrub inside it. The collapsible section at the bottom of the straw means you can reduce its length for storage inside the tumbler after sipping your drink. The cleaning tool also turned out to be useful for scrubbing towards the bottom of the tumbler, as this area proved impossible for me to reach with a scourer.It’s a shame that …this tumbler proved cumbersome. I struggled to fit it into a car cup holder, and only certain backpacks proved capable of carrying it in their side pockets. On the plus side, it never leaked during testing.Capacity:900mlMaterial:stainless steel, BPA-free Tritan plastic (lid), silicone sealsDimensions:8.5 x 11.8 x 25.6cmTemperature after one hour:85.3CTemperature after eight hours:49.3CWeight:550gDishwasher safe?YesWarranty/guarantee:lifetimeZwillingThermo Plus Thermo Straw tumbler£39.95£39.95 at ZwillingWhat we lovePerfect for iced drinksWhat we don’t loveDoesn’t fit all drink holders and pocketsThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘One of the easiest reusable cups to clean’: the Klean Kanteen Rise mug.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianBru ceramic travel mugBruCeramic travel mug£23.95£23.95 at BruWhat we loveTight seal and neutral tasteWhat we don’t loveLid retains water from washingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£23.95 at BruBest for:tasteThis travel-friendly option from Bru has a nice outer texture that I found both smooth and grippy, while the ceramic surface on the inside ensures a neutral taste.For me, the level of insulation was just right – coffee bought on the go was nice and hot, but drinkable, after about an hour stored in the cup. The lid feels secure and is intuitive to open or close with a press.The maximum fill-level line on the inside seemed to help baristas avoid overfilling the cup, allowing for the lid to be replaced without any spurting. It proved perfectly leakproof, even when I turned it upside down and shook it.It didn’t make the final cut because…while the lid works well at preventing leaks, it tends to retain water after cleaning, so you’ll need to give it a good shake and dry before taking it out.Capacity:340ml;material:stainless steel body, ceramic-lined interior, polypropylene lid with silicone seals, and a silicone base;dimensions:6.5 x 17.5cm;temperature after one hour:84.2C;temperature after eight hours:50.4C;weight:320g;dishwasher safe?No;warranty/guarantee:two yearsBruCeramic travel mug£23.95£23.95 at BruWhat we loveTight seal and neutral tasteWhat we don’t loveLid retains water from washingGrind reusable coffee cupGrindReusable coffee cup£18.72£18.72 at GrindWhat we loveLovely designWhat we don’t loveNot the easiest to gripView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianFrom £18.72 at GrindBest for:cute designI felt compelled to test this cute, chic reusable cup from Grind, which sports a line drawing of the Pokémon Eevee that sings the song of my millennial soul. If you’re not a Pokémon lover, though, you can also buy the cup in Grind’s signaturepinkorblackfrom £24.95.As well as looking lovely, it’s great at controlling temperature, keeping drinks like americanos and long blacks hot while barely transferring any heat to the outside of the vessel. It also comes with a stainless steel straw for sipping iced or cold drinks.“It’s beautiful,” said Scarlet, from Holding Patterns. “This has one of the better form factors of the reusable coffee cups we get handed over the counter, and it’s great that it means we save on disposable takeaway cups.”It didn’t make the final cut because…I think the flat, smooth outer of this cup could make it easy to drop when filled, and it isn’t leakproof. So, this model is perhaps best suited to home use.Capacity:360ml;material:stainless steel, plastic (on part of lid);dimensions:11 x 9cm;temperature after one hour:75.6C;temperature after eight hours:34.9C;weight:200g;dishwasher safe?No;warranty/guarantee:noneGrindReusable coffee cup£18.72£18.72 at GrindWhat we loveLovely designWhat we don’t loveNot the easiest to gripChilly’s Big MouthChilly’sBig Mouthfrom£60£60 at Chilly’s£60 at ParasolWhat we loveA family-size optionWhat we don’t loveBest when used with cupsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianFrom £60 at Chilly’s£60 at ParasolBest for:a family-size reusable bottleFamily-size flask meets trendy reusable bottle in the Chilly’s Big Mouth. It has plenty of space for everyone’s tea, coffee or water on a group trip, and it serves equally well as a daylong sipping solution for the chronically hydrated.The rim of the bottle is pretty deep, and I found I had to drink from it carefully to avoid a drenching. Personally, I’m OK with that, but dainty sippers might prefer to decant their drink into a cup.This bottle’s lid felt very secure, and I was confident enough to carry it, filled, in my bag. But given how good the Big Mouth looks, vibrant and pleasantly textured, proud owners might prefer to tote it by the handle instead. It performed exceptionally well in my bounce, drip and temperature tests.It didn’t make the final cut because …most people will need something smaller for on-the-go coffees.Capacity:2l;material:90% post-consumer certified recycled stainless steel, plastic, rubber base;dimensions:13.5 x 26.5cm;temperature after one hour:88.8C;temperature after eight hours:65.4C;weight:862g;dishwasher safe?No;warranty/guarantee:two yearsChilly’sBig Mouthfrom£60£60 at Chilly’s£60 at ParasolWhat we loveA family-size optionWhat we don’t loveBest when used with cupsNinja Sip Perfect travel mugNinjaSip Perfect travel mugfrom£34.99£34.99 at Ninja£35 at VeryWhat we loveMaintains a good drinking temperatureWhat we don’t loveLow capacity relative to sizeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£34.99 at Ninja£35 at VeryBest for:daylong useNinja’s mug was one of the top performers in my drip, bounce and temperature tests. If you’re looking for a large, leakproof option to fill at home and drink from throughout the day, this would be a fine choice. Interestingly, it’s supposed to cool hot drinks down initially, then keep them at a pleasant sipping temperature. This is exactly how the mug worked in my temperature testing.Drinking through the lid is very simple – you pop down the seal and then sip through the opening, which allows just the right flow for my taste. I often find Ninja’s products intuitive and well designed, and that’s certainly true of this bottle.I wouldn’t recommend drinking without the lid while on transport (especially with a driver who tends to slam on the brakes) as the metal is thin and could cause harm if jolted towards your mouth.Baristas Ivy and Theo at Flamingos Coffee House in Leeds were happy to use the Sip Perfect, but they had some reservations. “It’s too tall for our machine, so I had to pour the coffee into a mug first,” said Ivy.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s not quite a match for our top picks in terms of portability. However, you may feel that the higher capacity justifies the added heft.Capacity:400ml;material:stainless steel, BPA-free plastic;dimensions:7.7 x 22.7cm;temperature after one hour:62.2C;temperature after eight hours:47.4C;weight:573g;dishwasher safe?Yes, but hand-washing is recommended to preserve the finish;warranty/guarantee:five years if registeredNinjaSip Perfect travel mugfrom£34.99£34.99 at Ninja£35 at VeryWhat we loveMaintains a good drinking temperatureWhat we don’t loveLow capacity relative to sizeOcean Bottle Brew flaskOcean BottleBrew flaskfrom£35£35 at Ocean Bottle£39.99 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent eco credentialsWhat we don’t loveReleases water quite slowlyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianFrom £35 at Ocean Bottle£39.99 at AmazonBest for:an eco-friendly bottleThis is a useful little bottle to have in your collection. It’s perfectly leakproof (even when you take it on a trampoline), insulates hot or cold liquids very well, and slots neatly into a backpack pocket or cup holder.Perhaps its most important role is its environmental impact: maker Ocean Bottle funds the collection of the equivalent of 1,000 ocean-bound plastic bottles with each one bought.It didn’t make the final cut because …the lid doesn’t allow enough liquid through at once for a really satisfying sip. I also needed a few tries to learn when the lid is properly sealed. Make sure you figure this out before taking the flask on your travels.Capacity:350ml;material:recycled stainless steel, BPA-free plastic, silicone;dimensions:6.8 x 16.8cm;temperature after one hour:81.8C;temperature after eight hours:47.1C;weight:226g;dishwasher safe?Yes;warranty/guarantee:10 yearsOcean BottleBrew flaskfrom£35£35 at Ocean Bottle£39.99 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent eco credentialsWhat we don’t loveReleases water quite slowlyKlean Kanteen Rise Mug 399mlKlean KanteenRise mug£29.95£29.95 at AmazonWhat we loveBig enough for generous poursWhat we don’t loveLacks portabilityView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianFrom £29.95 at AmazonBest for:campingThe Rise mug has a lovely brushed steel, canteen-like interior, while its double-wall vacuum insulation helps keep drinks hot.I found it one of the easiest reusable cups to clean. It’s wide enough to reach inside effortlessly with a sponge, and the lid has a simple design that should minimise grime buildup.Whereas most reusable cups probably won’t get used much at home, this one’s so pleasant to drink from with or without the lid that you might reach for it when in need of a homely cuppa.Pete Wise holds a red Klean Kanteen coffee cup over a small black iron table with a piece of kitchen paper on it to check if any drips come from the cup. The kitchen paper is soakedThe Rise mug may not be leakproof, but it was still lovely to drink from. Video: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianIt’s worth noting that the Rise mug is not leakproof – as I discovered when I tipped it upside down for a drip test. However, the lid seal holds up well when you’re using the cup sensibly.Cravings By Sid’s Hussain only had good things to say about this mug. “I loved it – I’m tempted to get one for myself,” he said, after filling the mug with a large iced coffee.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s too wide to fit conveniently inside most rucksack pockets. The handle is ideal for looping on to the strap of ahiking backpackor bikepackingpannier bag, however.Capacity:399ml;material:90% post-consumer recycled steel, BPA-free plastic;dimensions:9.7 x 9.9cm;temperature after one hour:76.5C;temperature after eight hours:32.5C;weight:309g;dishwasher safe?Yes;warranty/guarantee:lifetime limited warrantyKlean KanteenRise mug£29.95£29.95 at AmazonWhat we loveBig enough for generous poursWhat we don’t loveLacks portabilityEcoffee cupEcoffeeReusable cupfrom£13.95£13.96 at Fruugo£13.95 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat for short coffee drinksWhat we don’t loveGets hot in the handView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£13.96 at Fruugo£13.95 at AmazonBest for:affordabilityIts stubby form makes this a convenient cup to squeeze into a tight backpack pocket or cup holder. I really appreciated its ease of cleaning, its lightness and most of all its natural feel: the cup itself is made from a plant-based material derived from sugar beet.There are limitations to this style of cup. It leaked a little during my trampette testing, and released coffee liberally when upended. For quickly drinking a short coffee drink bought from a cafe, it works very well, but I wouldn’t recommend it for transporting liquids.It didn’t make the final cut because …heat transfer through the cup’s material is considerable. You wouldn’t want to keep a tight hold of it when it’s freshly filled with black coffee.Capacity:240ml;material:PLA (plant-based), silicone;dimensions:8.2x 10.1cm;temperature after one hour:48.3C;temperature after eight hours:24.8C;weight:150g;dishwasher safe?Yes;warranty/guarantee:three yearsEcoffeeReusable cupfrom£13.95£13.96 at Fruugo£13.95 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat for short coffee drinksWhat we don’t loveGets hot in the handWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenLeak-free drinks on the go and coffee shop discounts are among the reusable cup perks.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianWhich brands have perks for bringing your own cup?The eco-friendly decision to carry your coffee in a reusable cup or bottle is well rewarded by various coffee chains and independent cafes.Ideally, you’ll keep taking your reusable cup to your favourite local independent when you can. You won’t always get a discount, but savings of about 10% are not uncommon.Several of the big chains offer incentives to use a reusable cup, including:Starbucks: 25p discountPret a Manger: 50p discountCaffè Nero: double loyalty stamps via its app (so the sixth coffee is free)Costa: double loyalty card stamps (so the sixth coffee is free)Greggs: 25p discountSupermarkets are also getting in on the trend.Waitrose provides free hot drinks to its members who bring a reusable cup; Marks & Spencer cafes offer a 50p discount.Are travel mugs actually eco-friendly?A travel mug comes with environmental costs. Manufacturing and selling one requires energy and materials, and it will be cleaned with soap and water by the eventual owner.Thankfully, the environmental toll of a reusable cup tends to be lower than that of habitually drinking from single-use cups, which are typically made from paper modified with plastic. A study by Ciraig (a sustainability research organisation based in Canada) found that a reusable cup becomes less harmful than using single-use cups after 20 to 100 drinks, in terms of greenhouse gas emissions generated. This varies depending on the material of the reusable cup.You would hope to use your cup or bottle at least that many times – and perhaps even for a lifetime. Some models are built to last with decades-long guarantees.Reusable cups are sometimes made largely from recycled materials, which reduces their embodied carbon (the sum of emissions created by making the cup and getting it into the customer’s hands). The maker’s business model might also seek to offset or outweigh environmental costs. For example, Ocean Bottle funds the collection of plastic waste through the sale of each product.In short, reusable coffee cups are the most eco-friendly solution we’ve come up with for carrying hot drinks on the go. To minimise the environmental downsides, use yours for as long as you can, apply minimal (eco-friendly) washing-up liquid and hot water during routine washes, and choose a sustainability-focused brand.For more, readthe best reusable water bottlesand thebest backpacks for work, travel and wild adventurePete Wise is ajournalist with more than a decade’s experience covering everything from global development and social causes to technology and music. He’s writtenvarious articles about coffee, including reviews of coffee machines and coffee grinders, and features on the health effects of caffeine. title: Cocktail of the week: Àclèaf’s PX martini – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: Like a classic espresso martini, but with the addition of vanilla vodka
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Like a classic espresso martini, but with the addition of vanilla vodka
Content: Àclèaf’s PX martini.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenÀclèaf’s PX martini.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Àclèaf’s PX martini – recipeLike a classic espresso martini, but with the addition of vanilla vodkaAndréa NuningerFri 16 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is our twist on the much-loved classic. It takes inspiration from a classic espresso martini, with the addition of vanilla vodka bringing with it an oaked edge that cuts the sweetness of the sherry.PX martiniServes150ml vanilla vodka– we useAbsolut Vanilia35ml pedro ximénez35ml freshly brewed espresso– we useJamaican BlueFill a cocktail shaker with ice, then add the vodka, PX and espresso – for the best texture, measure in the espresso last, so the ice doesn’t melt too quickly and over-dilute the cocktail. Shake vigorously for at least 20 seconds, so the mix emulsifies and produces that classic, creamy, frothy, off-white layer on top. Fine strain into a chilled martini glass or coupe and serve.Andréa Nuninger, restaurant manager,Àclèaf, Plympton, DevonExplore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodWineCoffeerecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for baked oats with morello cherries and almond  | Breakfast | The Guardian
description: This moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfast
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: This moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfast
Content: Helen Goh’s baked oats with morello cherries and almond.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s baked oats with morello cherries and almond.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotBreakfastHelen Goh’s recipe for baked oats with morello cherries and almondThis moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfastHelen GohFri 16 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been making versions of these baked oats ever since discovering Heidi Swanson’s recipe inSuper Natural Every Day. This is my favourite store-cupboard version, for when stone fruit and berries have slipped out of season. Morello cherries are a dark, tart variety of sour cherry, with an intensity of flavour and bright acidity that stand up particularly well to baking. I love them here paired with almonds and coconut drinking milk (the light kind sold in cartons, not the rich tinned variety). The cherries I use are whole fruit in syrup, which I drain and dot over the oats – they remain distinct while becoming deliciously jammy as they bake. Almost any fruit compote or jam will work here, though, so choose your favourite.Baked oats with morello cherries and almondJarred cherries come in many forms, so if yours is more like a compote or jam, simply add it in small teaspoonfuls instead.Prep10 minCook45 min, plus coolingServes4-630g unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly, plus extra for greasing210g jumbo rolled oats1 tsp baking powder1 tsp ground cinnamon½ tsp fine sea salt1 large egg60ml maple syrup, plus extra to serve500ml coconut drinking milk1 tsp vanilla extract100-120g morello cherries in syrup, drained, or cherry compote or jam30g flaked almondsIcing sugar,for dusting (optional)Yoghurt or cream,to serveHeat the oven to 195C (175C fan)/385F/gas 5½ and lightly grease a 26cm ovenproof dish that’s about 5-6cm deep – the oat mixture will form a fairly shallow layer.Put the oats, baking powder, cinnamon and salt in a medium bowl, mix well, then tip into the greased dish. In a large jug, whisk the egg, maple syrup and melted butter, then add the coconut drinking milk and vanilla, and whisk again to combine. Pour this evenly over the oats, then gently press down any oats that remain dry.Dot the drained cherries evenly over the oats. If using a thicker compote or jam, drop small teaspoonfuls over the surface, then use the tip of the spoon to drag each one out slightly, creating ripples rather than deep pools. Scatter over the flaked almonds.Bake for about 30 minutes, until golden on top and just set in the centre. Leave to stand for five to 10 minutes before serving, dusted with icing sugar if you like, and with yoghurt or cream and a little extra maple syrup alongside.Explore more on these topicsBreakfastThe sweet spotFoodDessertBakingFruitAutumn food and drinkCereals and grainsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: How to dress a tech oligarch: The Social Reckoning’s costume designer on Zuckerberg’s style evolution | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters
Content: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning (2026), directed by Aaron Sorkin.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenJeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning (2026), directed by Aaron Sorkin.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyFashionHow to dress a tech oligarch: The Social Reckoning’s costume designer on Zuckerberg’s style evolutionSusan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweatersHannah MarriottFri 16 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first Aaron Sorkin Facebook movie, 2010’s The Social Network, helped cement the early aughts image ofMark Zuckerbergrebelling against corporate norms in rumpled hoodies and T-shirts.The follow-up, The Social Reckoning, is carbon-dated from 2019 to 2021. This is “post-hoodie”, as the movie’s costume designer, Susan Lyall, describes it, “post-thumbing his nose” to formality. It is also peak robot. Zuckerberg’s reserved wardrobe of suits or interchangeable long-sleeved shirts echo his chilling composure throughout, even as fury simmers under the surface.The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet ZuckerbergRead moreThe costume was based on deep research by Lyall and also by actor Jeremy Strong who, she says, is “very into costume”. Having worked together before, on the Sorkin movies Molly’s Game and The Trial of the Chicago 7, they would text a lot during the preparation process.“He reaches out before I even get to reach out to him. It’s my third movie with him, so I’m pretty used to it. He’s very proactive. He’s one of my favourite actors because of that. He would know exactly where [Zuckerberg] wore what. He wanted the exact Nike shoe – the footwear was very important to him – and the exact Brunello Cucinelli T-shirt and sweater, and so on,” she says.Strong has become notorious for method acting, and method dressing, too, seems to be part of his process. “It’s sort of the first step in the performance. That and the haircut,” says Lyall.The conversations went deep. “It’s actually kind of nerdy, you know, to sit there and talk about the color of the shoelaces. There aren’t that many people who want to talk about that. I always joke with him, if the acting thing doesn’t work out, you can have a position in my department!” she says.Lyall found those Nikes – to be specific, the 2018 Nike Flyknit trainer in black anthracite – on Grailed. For the sweaters, it was Strong, she says, who worked out how to reach the eye-wateringly expensive Italian luxury brand Brunello Cucinelli, in order to buy specific pieces, “because we don’t want the latest. We want stuff from five or six years ago, and they were very helpful at procuring it. And that was because of him. He was really proactive.”Lyall has spent a lot of hours thinking about how tech oligarchs dress. Not only Zuckerberg but Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and others too, who were partial inspiration for another of her recent credits, the 2025 Jesse Armstrong movie Mountainhead about four devilish plutocrats.View image in fullscreenA still from Mountainhead (2025), directed by Jesse Armstrong.Photograph: HBO/2025 Home Box Office Inc. All Rights ReservedThey, too, wore a lot of Brunello Cucinelli. That brand sells cashmere cardigans for $16,500 and ribbed sweaters for $4,600. Amusingly, it currently has the Immanuel Kant quote “beauty is the symbol of the morally good” in prime place on its website homepage.In Lyall’s view, Brunello Cucinelli is a “safety net for people like Mark Zuckerberg. If they’re not sure about what they’re wearing, if they pay a lot for it, they feel a little better about it. You know, if this little sweater is $2,000, it must be good. It’s kind of a security blanket, or just an affirmation of your own success. You’re going to be OK if you’re wearing this tasteful thing.”double quotation markI think [tech billionaires] have discovered a new way to flexSusan LyallThe Zuckerberg of The Social Reckoning had moved on from the earlier antifashion stance that prompted him to declare, in 2014, that he was “not a cool person”, and only wore grey T-shirts because he wanted to make “as few decisions as possible … I feel like I’m not doing my job if I spend any of my energy on things that are silly or frivolous.”By the period captured in the movie, says Lyall, “I believe Zuckerberg was trying to be relatable, but also starting to understand Silicon Valley’s obsession with taste and the cost of things.” He was also more buff than he had been. In her interpretation, he seemed to be thinking: “My fit physique looks very nice in this clingy but expensive sweater. And ‘if you know, you know’ – I think there’s a bit of that. But I also think, he’s nouveau riche without being gaudy. It’s not without taste.”Since then, Zuckerberg’s outward presentation has graduated to outright peacocking.For the tech billionaires, in general, says Lyall: “I think something happened. I think they have discovered a new way to flex. And it’s not quiet luxury. It’s loud.”For Zuckerberg specifically – whose makeover came suddenly with ostentatious gold chains, Loewe shorts and Alexander McQueen suits embellished with dragonflies in around 2024 – it could not feel much more strategic.View image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect conference on 25 September 2024 in Menlo Park, California.Photograph: Godofredo A Vásquez/APDabbling with fashion allows Zuckerberg to look like a different guy from the one we have seen so many times sweating in a suit in front of Congress. It also provides a distraction from the reality of his products and work, giving him something soft and harmless to talk about.Zuckerberg has even used the classic fiction writer’s trick of embedding backstory within his jewellery. In 2024, when he started wearing a large, gold pendant necklace over his T-shirt, he claimed it wasn’t just because he wanted to look like a hip-hop star, as the internet understandably concluded.When finally asked about his pendant in an interview (“oh this?” he said, with an approximation of spontaneity) he explained that it was embossed with a Jewish prayer he sings to his kids every night at bedtime, thus reminding the public of his humanity – his faith, and the importance he places on being there for his children.This year, asMetahas recruited fashion stars such as Kylie Jenner to market its smart glasses, he has spent yet more time courting fashion, attending Prada shows and the Met Gala.Last month, he gave the New York Times an interview purely about clothing, claiming that he buys almost all of his wardrobe on Instagram himself – which sounds extremely decision-requiring and time-consuming for a person of his workload.Many of the labels he mentioned were more contemporary, less oligarch-coded, among them Mike Amiri, a purveyor of $400-ish T-shirts, with whom he has worked on bespoke items including the “Building is my love language” he wore to present Muse at a Facebook conference. Online, too, when he buys something of the $200-ish, rather than $2000-ish price tag, he may even pop into the comments, when complimented on that item, to draw users’ attention towards it (“It’s@johnelliottco– I’m loving their stuff recently”).Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?Read moreJust as the new personal AI assistant Muse has been fashioned to look utterly adorable – surely such a cute fluffy Labubu-like creature could never spark an apocalypse! – Zuckerberg’s own continuing makeover appears conceived to make him a more friendly and, ideally, more human.In fashion, though, it’s not as simple as ticking the box to confirm you are not a robot. When he explained his interest in style tothe New York Times, for example, he said, “I think the company is an instantiation of my values” and claimed he wanted to “be intentional about how I program that”.A turn of phrase that suggests that, under his vibrant new clothing, the cashmere-clad machine depicted in Sorkin’s movie may not have been properly deactivated.Explore more on these topicsFashionMark ZuckerbergMetafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Victoria Beckham, ‘duck face’ and onesies: nine things Zoolander predicted about fashion | Fashion | The Guardian
description: It’s been 25 years since the release of Ben Stiller film that skewers an industry that famously takes itself very seriously. It might have been comedy gold, but it also predicted our fashion-saturated 21st century
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: It’s been 25 years since the release of Ben Stiller film that skewers an industry that famously takes itself very seriously. It might have been comedy gold, but it also predicted our fashion-saturated 21st century
Content: Still got it … Ben Stiller in Zoolander.Photograph: Paramount/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenStill got it … Ben Stiller in Zoolander.Photograph: Paramount/Sportsphoto/AllstarFashion Statement newsletterFashionVictoria Beckham, ‘duck face’ and onesies: nine things Zoolander predicted about fashionIt’s been 25 years since the release of this film skewering an industry that famously takes itself very seriously. It might have been comedy gold but it was also, in its own way, propheticDon’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up herePriya ElanFri 16 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCritics were divided, the US release date couldn’t have been worse (a few days after 9/11) and the sequel was a flop. Yet few films have predicted fashion’s own present like 2001’s Zoolander. The memeable absurdist comedy about the “three-times male model of the year” was a cinematic Cassandra: correctly predicting themes, styles and sensibilities of the industry that still ring true today.Pucker up… Blue Steel became a way of lifeThe joke around Derek Zoolander’s trademark look, the Blue Steel, was how ridiculous it was. Still, the shocked but vacant stare with the exaggerated pout later becamethefacial pose on social media. Officially defined as “duck face” (after the Japanese term “ahiru-guchi”, duck mouth), the look gained traction on Instagram in the early 2010s, when people finally took a break from smizing. But tweakments such as lip-filler and forehead botox mean that faces have begun artificially morphing into the pose. So now everyone can be really, really, really Zoolander, without even trying.Donald Trumpkept telling talesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump with Melania Trump in Zoolander.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyThere is a popular theory that Trump crept into the hearts and minds of the American public through his appearances on his reality TV show The Apprentice. But he also made fleeting cameos in films such as Two Weeks Notice, Little Rascals and Home Alone 2. His one line in Zoolander? “Without Derek Zoolander, male modelling wouldn’t be what it is today.” A fabulous little fib that he imparts very believably.Shocking to hear in 2026, I know.Theonesie became a winter stapleThe morning after the VH1 Fashion Awards, Derek and his model flatmates Brint, Rufus and Meekus (played by Alexander Skarsgård) are all hanging out, when Zoolander’s nightwear of choice is revealed to be a onesie covered in penguins. A decade later the onesie would become ubiquitous, with high-street sales skyrocketing after One Direction brought them intopeople’s living rooms. File next to man-buns – and never forget Zoolander did them first.Sweat shop abuse continuedAt the start of the film, a shady fashion cartel are intent on keeping sweat shop labour going, despite the prime minister of Malaysia’s plan to ban it. One fiendish fashionista complains: “50% of my inventory is manufactured in sweat shops in Malaysia!” Zoolander satirised fashion’s cognitive dissonance about sweat shop labour deftly. 25 years on, it’s still, tragically,very much an issue.Very nichedrinks ordersbecamethe normDonatella Versace likes her espresso servedin apink-and-gold china cup, Anna Wintour’s order is reportedly a grande, extra-hotwhole-milk latte from Starbucks, while Calvin Klein infamously got his staff to compare the hue of his milky coffeeto a Pantone colour swatchto get it “just right”.In the film, Derek, Meekus, Brint and Rufus share a love of the orange mocha frappuccino, while freaky designer Mugatu (Will Ferrell) loses it when his latte is too foamy. Fashion’s niche drinks orders have arguably only become more extreme – as any fashion intern with a long list of hyper-specific morning matcha and iced coffee orders will tell you.It’s Posh’s world, and we’re just living in itskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionZoolander has more guest stars than an episode of Friends. Hi David Bowie, Tommy Hilfiger, Paris Hilton, Gwen Stefani, Tom Ford, Winona Ryder, Mark Ronson, Donatella Versace, Lil Kim and Sandra Bernhard. Groaning under the weight of its own star power, there is one cameo that feels slightly more significant than the others. Victoria Beckham delivers the line “he’s a fashion icon!” about Derek. Givenher move from non-smiling Spice Girl to non-smiling creative director in the last 25 years, she could have been talking about herself.Gasp! Fashion retirementsremain shockingView image in fullscreenStiller as Zoolander, who made a shock return from retirement in Zoolander 2, with Owen Wilson as Hansel.Photograph: Photo credit: Philippe Antonello/© 2015 Paramount Pictures. All Rights Reserved.When Derek announces his early retirement from modelling at the triple funeral of his flatmates (“I’m sure there’s a lot more to life than being really, really good looking,”) the assembled mourners are shocked. But the surprise catwalk curtain call has become familiar: Jean Paul Gaultier stood down in 2020after 50 fantastique years, Dries Van Noten said goodbye in 2024, while stylist Law Roach “retired” on Instagram in 2023 before sneaking back two years later. Cheeky. Even Derek himself came out of retirement for Zoolander 2.Top magazineswent the way of thedodo“Not many people read your Time magazine, or whatever it’s called,” Derek tells journalist Matilda. At the time of release this was a joke at the expense of our model hero. Time magazine’s paid circulation was 4m copies per week. Now, not only is Time’s paid digital circulation at about 370,000 but many of the fashion magazines featured in the film have long ceased production: Look, Marie Claire and InStyle to name but a few. Hearing that line in 2026, it hits differently. Earth to Matilda, Derek was right, not many peoplearereading your magazine (although maybe they are reading your Substack).‘Derelicte’became the distressed trendMugatu’s Derelicte collection, crassly inspired by unhoused people, was a stinging comment on how far-removed fashion can be from reality. While John Galliano had already produced a collection inspired by those living along the Seine and purses resembling bin bagsdidappear on the catwalk (Lanvin), the Derelicte collection, which included a battered cardboard box worn as a dress, a feather boa of inflated condoms and a cape made of rubbish, picked at a concept which the likes of Demna later focused in on at Vetements and Balenciaga, elevating wear-and-tear as the distressed look.To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletterZoolander 2newslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘A haven of soft light, warm sunshine and sandy beaches’: readers’ favourite autumn escapes | Winter sun | The Guardian
description: In search of autumn festivals, good food and islands where it still feels like summer? We asked you to recommend your best off-season breaks
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: In search of autumn festivals, good food and islands where it still feels like summer? We asked you to recommend your best off-season breaks
Content: ‘Sunkissed seaside sensuality’ … Collioure in France, near the Spanish border.Photograph: Patrick Donovan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Sunkissed seaside sensuality’ … Collioure in France, near the Spanish border.Photograph: Patrick Donovan/Getty ImagesReaders' travel tipsWinter sun‘A haven of soft light, warm sunshine and sandy beaches’: readers’ favourite autumn escapesIn search of autumn festivals, good food and islands where it still feels like summer? We asked you to recommend your best off-season breaksTell us about a spooky spot in the UK– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 16 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCollioure is a Mediterranean dreamLast October, while I was cycling around south-west France, near the Spanish border, a tip from a local waiter led me toCollioure, near Perpignan. The town was like a Mediterranean dream, where the summer crowds had faded, leaving behind a peaceful, artistic haven of soft light, warm sunshine, cobbled streets, sandy beaches – and the Pyrenees as a backdrop. In the early evening, the still balmy autumn air was perfect for wandering through the quiet, pastel-coloured alleyways of the Le Mouré district to enjoy €5 off-season happy hour wine with fish tapas. I had planned to stay a weekend but ended up staying a week, seduced by Collioure’s perfect autumn cocktail of chilled Catalan culture and sunkissed seaside sensuality.AprilPeaceful Portuguese sunsetsView image in fullscreenTagus River in Lisbon.Photograph: Mauricio Abreu/AlamySitting outside in T-shirt and shorts on the deck of a boat gliding along the Tagus River in Lisbon, sipping a glass of crisp Portuguese wine as the setting autumn sun illuminated the pastel-coloured hills, is a lasting travel memory for me. October temperatures were still in the mid-20s, perfect for exploring fascinating areas on foot, or hanging out of trams as they rattled up and down the cobbled streets. In the evenings, I joined local people basking in the remaining warmth of the year at outdoor cafes or waterside tavernas likePonto Final,enjoying coffee and pastries, or anchovies and beer, while watching magnificent sunsets without the summer masses.NicolettaWild times in St Davids, PembrokeshireView image in fullscreenWhitesands bay, near St Davids.Photograph: Drew Buckley/AlamyMy autumn escape isSt Davidson the Pembrokeshire coast. Once the summer crowds disappear, it feels wonderfully wild and tranquil. We walk the coast path towardsWhitesands, stopping to watch for seals below the cliffs, before heading back into tiny St Davids for something warm to eat. The beaches are often almost empty and, even when the weather turns, the dramatic sea and windswept coastline are part of the charm. My tip is to visit in early autumn; pack proper walking boots and layers, and embrace the weather – you get one of Britain’s loveliest coastlines almost to yourself.TessBaroque beauty in eastern GermanyView image in fullscreenRakotzbrücke (Devil’s Bridge) in Kromlau park, Gablenz, in Saxony.Photograph: Andrew Mayovskyy/AlamyGörlitz makes for a fascinating autumnal base, with its location on the German-Polish border to the east of Dresden. The highlights were day excursions to Bad Muskau, where there is a wonderful baroque palace, and the Rakotzbrücke (Devil’s Bridge), reached by a narrow-gauge forest railway (waldeisenbahn.de). It’s a part of Germany rarely visited, but those who go there will be rewarded with amazing photographs.MartinBliss on a lesser-visited Canary islandView image in fullscreenCharco Azul swimming hole on El Hierro.Photograph: Henner Damke/AlamyThe Canary Islands are well-trodden choices for autumn sun, but the island of El Hierro remains a wilder alternative to Tenerife or Lanzarote. The scenery is beautiful and bizarrely varied: from pine forests to black volcanic lava flows – most of which you’ll have to yourself. You can pass hours exploring the rugged coastlines, where volcanic swimming holes such asCharco Azulcan be found. We spent a blissful few hours there, relaxing on the rocks and looking out at the Atlantic. There are no big resorts but plenty of guest houses and smaller hotels, and sunshine is almost guaranteed into November.Leo MarkProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Dramatic Devon walksView image in fullscreenEndless sand … at Woolacombe beach, north Devon.Photograph: James Cassap/Getty ImagesWe stayed inWoolacombe, north Devon, with our three-year-old in October 2023 and the off-season suited us well. The three-mile beach gave us room for proper sandcastle engineering, and the Atlantic offered drama rather than deckchair weather. We watched the sunset turn the sea orange and purple from the hill above the bay. We could walk into the village, then use Woolacombe as a base for Mortehoe and theSouth West Coast Path. Pack waterproofs as well as sunglasses: north Devon makes no promises. But on a bright autumn day, those enormous sands feel almost privately hired.Katharina Parsonsskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCoast, culture and cable cars on MadeiraView image in fullscreenFunchal, Madeira.Photograph: Aleh Varanishcha/Getty ImagesFunchal on Madeira is my pick for an autumn escape because it still feels properly alive after summer. The seafront is made for slow walks in the sunshine, with cafes and gardens open year-round. You can browse the colourfulMercado dos Lavradores, ride the cable car for views over the terracotta rooftops and Atlantic, then cool off at one of the city’s lidos. The weather is pleasantly warm rather than overpowering, while the mountains andlevada(aqueduct) walks are within easy reach. It combines coast, culture and dramatic scenery without feeling like a resort that closes down for winter.BerniceClifftops and crab rolls in the Scottish BordersView image in fullscreenRugged charm … St Abbs.Photograph: Jason Baxter/AlamyIf you’re looking for a cracking wee coastal escape, head straight toSt Abbsin the Scottish Borders. My wife and I absolutely fell in love with its rugged charm and bonny views. First off, Marvel fans will know it as New Asgard from Avengers: Endgame, and taking a selfie by the official sign set the right tone. Beyond the film fame, the dramatic clifftop walk up toSt Abb’s Headis brilliant, packed with seabirds and proper fresh sea air. Afterwards, grab a fresh crab roll down at the harbour cafe – nae hassle, just proper good cheer.CraigNonstop sun in a Cretan havenView image in fullscreen‘A year-round magic place’ … Palaiochora on Crete.Photograph: Witold Skrypczak/AlamyAutumn came brutal and early to Crete this month. But the ferocious northerly that drenched the northern coast got stuck on the White Mountains. And on just one tiny south-west speck of the island, the sun shone all and every day. Palaiochora is a year-round magic place anyway. No big hotels. Still proudly Greek. A place where the town’s rhythms are set by the comings and goings of the Loutro ferry. But this past week, while thunder stalked the mountains, we swam and walked every day. “We’re unique,” said the man at the cafe. “Please don’t tell anyone.” What have I done?Kay JonesWinning tip: Fiestas and feasts in Zaragoza, SpainView image in fullscreenMaking a floral tribute to the Virgin Mary is a key part of the Fiestas del Pilar, held in October in Zaragoza.Photograph: Visual and Written/AlamyFor an autumn city break, Zaragoza comes alive during theFiestas del Pilarin October. We spent a week there, wandering bustling streets lined with people, many in traditional dress, queueing to lay flowers at the vast floral tribute to the Virgin Mary in Plaza del Pilar. Along the river, food stalls served Aragonese specialities, fromchistorra(sausage) and stews to roast chestnuts and sweet wine. Between festivities, we explored the stunningAljafería Palaceand discovered tiny tapas bars tucked down side streets. The city felt wonderfully local, lively and full of surprises.CarrieView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsWinter sunReaders' travel tipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I rate benches | Life and style | The Guardian
description: My Instagram page started as something to amuse my friends, but it took off – and led to me meeting Sophie, who is now my wife
Author: Heather Main
Headline: My Instagram page started as something to amuse my friends, but it took off – and led to me meeting Sophie, who is now my wife
Content: ‘We’ve spent hours sitting here’: Sam Wilmot with his wife, Sophie, on their favourite bench. Photographs: Gareth Iwan Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘We’ve spent hours sitting here’: Sam Wilmot with his wife, Sophie, on their favourite bench. Photographs: Gareth Iwan Jones/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I rate benchesMy Instagram page started as something to amuse my friends, but it took off – and led to me meeting Sophie, who is now my wifeSam WilmotFri 16 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe idea came to me in summer 2019, when I finished studying at Swansea University. One day I went walking with friends around the beautiful Penllergare Valley woods. As they played Poohsticks, I sat on a bench and took in the view.I noticed that someone had left flowers on the bench. I wondered who had put them there, who they were for, and why they’d chosen this location. By the time we reached the next bench along the route, I was deep in thought about all the people who had sat there before me.Both benches had beautiful views, and my friends and I started comparing them. I joked that someone should start rating benches of the world. In the following days, I set up an Instagram account calledRateThisBenchand then posted a handful of reviews of benches near my family home in Bristol, mostly to amuse my friends.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueAt the end of the summer, I planned to close the account. But my dad, Chris, had become quite invested in it. It became our joint project; after dinner we’d go out for a walk and assess a bench.I wasn’t interested in growing the account, but the page took off. I suddenly had hundreds of followers – I’m currently at about 27,500.I decided to devise a proper rating system. I usually post a picture of me sitting on the bench, a brief description of the site, and a mark out of 10. Its mark depends on the location, whether there is an arm and backrest, and the quality of its base. I give extra marks to wooden benches, because I think they’re the nicest, and also for interesting plaques or dedications. My lowest-rated are always ugly metal ones in city centres, with armrests mid-bench. Some are unusual – one had an inbuilt USB charging port – but most are unremarkable. My favourites have a wooden back and a lovely view.double quotation markI’ve only awarded one a 10/10 – it’s the one I sat on with my new brideView image in fullscreenBefore long, people started messaging me, asking me to review their favourite benches. I feel a bit bad if I don’t give them a high mark, but it’s just my opinion. One woman asked me to visit one that’s dedicated to her brother, who was also called Sam, and she thought I looked like him. She was thrilled when I posted a picture of me on his bench, even though I don’t think I awarded it a high mark.My favourite message, however, was from a girl named Sophie. She contacted me when the page was taking off, and reviewed me as a reviewer. She gave me top marks, and it made me laugh. We started chatting; she lived near me and I asked her to dinner. We were three dates in when I saw a great bench and asked her to photograph me on it. She’s been photographing me on benches ever since.I’ve now reviewed more than 300 benches. Most of them are in the south-west, but I also do reviews whenever I travel. Some people might think it’s a boring hobby, but there’s nothing boring about spending time outdoors and sitting with your own thoughts.I think that’s why so many people want to have a bench dedicated to their memory when they die – they’re a place to take a moment out of our busy lives, appreciate what’s around us and think for a while.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExperience: I’m allergic to the coldRead moreWhile I’ve sat on a lot of nice benches, I’d never awarded a perfect 10, because there’s always room for improvement. However, in June this year, I gave 10/10 to the bench I sat on after marrying Sophie. I’d previously rated it a 9/10. It’s in a churchyard a short walk from our home in Gloucestershire. We wanted to get married at that church, in part because of the bench – we’ve spent hours sitting there, talking about our dreams for the future. Sitting on the bench alongside my wife for the first time was an amazing moment that merited upgrading the score. Since posting our wedding photos, the vicar has told us they’ve had a surge in wedding bookings.I briefly contemplated stopping the page after we got married – in a way, it felt as though it had reached a natural conclusion. However, I ended up reviewing a bench on our honeymoon in Mexico and decided to carry on. It’s probably something that will be with me for ever now. Life may be busy, but I don’t ever want to be too busy to enjoy five minutes sitting on a bench.As told to Heather MainDo you have an experience to share?
