title: Container gardens are pots of fun – and autumn is the ideal time to give them a makeover | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: Here is everything I’ve learned from my container gardener days – from the best plants to choose for low-maintenance gardening to why it pays to go big
Author: Alice Vincent
Headline: Here is everything I’ve learned from my container gardener days – from the best plants to choose for low-maintenance gardening to why it pays to go big
Content: ‘Think about your planting in layers.’Photograph: Andrew Kearton/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Think about your planting in layers.’Photograph: Andrew Kearton/AlamyGardening adviceContainer gardens are pots of fun – and autumn is the ideal time to give them a makeoverHere is everything I’ve learned from my container gardener days – from the best plants to choose for low-maintenance gardening to why it pays to go bigAlice VincentFri 16 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was a container gardener, this was the time of year I’d start to think about sprucing up my pots. It’s similar to a seasonal wardrobe switcheroo: putting shorts and summer dresses away until next year; getting jumpers out from under the bed and inspecting for moth holes. The pots, which usually had some late summer goodies in them, would be looking a bit worse for wear and I’d heave them all up, replace the compost and put in new things to perk up the balcony for the cooler months.The more I gardened, the more I left the pots alone. They became their own annual microgardens, with bulbs and perennials that rose and died back like little symphonies. Far less hard work, aside from a heavy mulch now and another in the spring, occasionally removing a bit of dead foliage and watering in the summer.This year, though, I’m thinking about pots again. They are holding the most precious cargo in the building site that used to be my garden, namely the plants that I want to get into the ground once the builders have left. Others are filled with homemade compost, including one that’s managed to grow a squash plant. This is as close to vegetable-growing as I get, and I still find the leaves and tendrils more intriguing and beautiful than whatever fruit it might bear.double quotation markI urge you to do your planting in the largest container possible – ideally, one with at least a 40cm diameterNow’s a good time to overhaul a pot garden – or the pots in your garden – as you can get hardy 9cm plants started off nicely before next spring, plant whips, or tiny trees, to get established with the cooler weather, and put in some bulbs, all in one fell swoop.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile I dream of garden greenhouses, a coldframe will do me just fineRead moreNot to be a bore, but if you’re reading this and feeling inspired (imagine!), I must urge you to do your planting in the largest container possible. I like to work with at least a 40cm diameter. Yes, they can be painfully expensive, but pick one you love and that will last. Neighbourhood groups and Facebook Marketplace can be plentiful sources.Once you have your nice big pot, think about planting in layers. Ideally you’ll want something with height: a grass, a rose, a cardoon, fennel, climbing hydrangea or – arguably better – something that will stand stoically against the winter: bare-root hedging such as spindle. Against this foundation you can fold in your future flowers: spring bulbs, especially true perennials (tulips aren’t, technically). I have some white ipheions that are still flowering in the same pots a decade on. Then you can top and fill with either seasonal annuals such as violas or, as I prefer, perennials that don’t need replacing. Small-leaved ivy orMuehlenbeckia complexa, which can be voracious but is easy to contain in a pot, are among my go-tos.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: A three-day perambulation around my own parish | Environment | The Guardian
description: Golden Valley, Herefordshire: Even vicars can get stuck too much behind a desk, and the 800th anniversary of St Francis of Assisi’s death is a good excuse to strike out, and speak to local people
Author: Rev Simon Lockett
Headline: Golden Valley, Herefordshire: Even vicars can get stuck too much behind a desk, and the 800th anniversary of St Francis of Assisi’s death is a good excuse to strike out, and speak to local people
Content: The view of St Peter’s, Peterchurch, in the Golden Valley with the Black Mountains in the background.Photograph: Simon LockettView image in fullscreenThe view of St Peter’s, Peterchurch, in the Golden Valley with the Black Mountains in the background.Photograph: Simon LockettCountry diaryEnvironmentCountry diary: A three-day perambulation around my own parishGolden Valley, Herefordshire:Even vicars can get stuck too much behind a desk, and the 800th anniversary of St Francis of Assisi’s death is a good excuse to strike out, and speak to local peopleRev Simon LockettFri 16 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 00.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwas sitting at my desk again, with the dull hum and the blue glow of the screen. It seems that every occupation traps people at their desk, and being a vicar is no different. But I wanted to resist, and it happened to be the 800th anniversary ofSaint Francis of Assisi’s death. With Jesus of Galilee as inspiration, Saint Francis was known for his vow of simplicity, his love of the Earth and his critique of the wealth accumulated by the religious elite at the expense of the poor. He was also horrified by the Fifth Crusade, so he travelled to Egypt, hoping to make peace.Francis also walked the walk, as it were, sleeping in caves in the Umbrian hills, taking nothing with him. No sitting at the desk for Francis. So I decided to do the same, spending three days walking the bridleways, holloways, footpaths and country lanes of the Golden Valley, speaking to people along the way. My sanctuary for the night was one of my parish churches –Madley, Tyberton, then Peterchurch, with its very welcome underfloor heating.The conversations were rich. People love Saint Francis because of his love of animals. Some found his actions, such as disrobing before a bishop – a sign of his rejection of church corruption – “extreme”. Thomas, a young farmer, challenged me when I said Francis’s rejection of wealth inspired me. Thomas spoke of the importance of “the posture of the heart” towards wealth – that riches can be used for good. The children in the primary school loved the story of Francistaming a wolf.Country diary: It’s hard being a vicar in a long, hot summer | Simon LockettRead moreBut the conversation that stayed with me most took place looking over the valley, with Bill, a businessman out walking his dog. We chatted about Saint Francis, and he bemoaned the culture that was taking hold in his business. His wish was for a Franciscan simplicity. Instead of a company that cherished belonging, community and purpose, one that was relational and people-oriented, it had become full of policies, programmes and technique. Simplicity had given way to complexity.I walked on through an oak wood, buzzards mewing overhead, a complexity of relationships that had led to simplicity. Ecology and Saint Francis have much to teach us.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentCountry diaryRural affairsChristianityWalkingCommunitiesReligionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms | Amazon rainforest | The Guardian
description: Forest clearance at smallest total since records began in 1988 in success for Lula ahead of presidential run-off
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Forest clearance at smallest total since records began in 1988 in success for Lula ahead of presidential run-off
Content: A deforested area of the Amazon rainforest in Amazonas state.Photograph: Edmar Barros/APView image in fullscreenA deforested area of the Amazon rainforest in Amazonas state.Photograph: Edmar Barros/APAmazon rainforestBrazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote loomsForest clearance at smallest total since records began in 1988 in success for Lula ahead of presidential run-offJonathan WattsFri 16 Oct 2026 15.37 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDeforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since records began, new government data shows.But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed ison a knife edgeahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump.The incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988.This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro.Since 2022, the year before the start of the Lula administration, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies.The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%).However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold.Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savannah – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soya and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%.View image in fullscreenDeforestation near a forest on the border between the Amazon and the Cerrado in Mato Grosso state.Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/ReutersThese spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5%increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses.The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.The former environment ministerMarina Silva, who has arguably done more than anyone to defend the rainforest,has warnedthat Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon.The stark contrast between the two candidates is evident in the electoral results map in the Amazon, where Bolsonaro secured the most votes near areas of degraded forest, mines, ranches and soya monocultures, while Lula’s support was higher in big cities or areas of forest where the vegetation was relatively intact.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is also evident in their very different relations to the US. Lula has warned that Trump is trying tocolonise the countryand capture its resources. He defends the Amazon as a sovereign asset for Brazil, an important home for Indigenous peoples and an essential element in global efforts to stabilise the climate.The Bolsonaro family, by contrast, has close ties to the US. Flavio’s brother Eduardo haslived in Texassince last year and called upon the Trump administration to impose punitive tariffs on his own country.Jair hassaluted the US flagand led chants of “USA, USA”. If the family secure power, they areexpected to shift Brazil’s trade priorities, particularly when it comes to critical minerals, from China and Europe to the US.The biggest difference, however, is likely to be the far right’s willingness to exploit natural resources in the Amazon and elsewhere in Brazil and then sell them to the highest bidder, regardless of environmental and social concerns.Conservation groups said the new deforestation data showed how much was at stake in the presidential run-off.Marcio Astrini, the executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, said: “The figure makes it clear that putting an end to forest destruction in Brazil is entirely possible.“However, everything depends on the election result. The country will decide whether we move toward the end of deforestation or toward the end of the forest.”Explore more on these topicsAmazon rainforestDeforestationBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroAmericasConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s Lula says he now backs lowering age of criminal responsibility to 16 | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Lula reverses position on age of responsibility for ‘heinous’ crimes in what many see as a desperate electoral gambit
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Lula reverses position on age of responsibility for ‘heinous’ crimes in what many see as a desperate electoral gambit
Content: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, speaks during Brazil's constitution law amendment ceremony at the Brazilian federal senate in Brasilia on Friday.Photograph: Ton Molina/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, speaks during Brazil's constitution law amendment ceremony at the Brazilian federal senate in Brasilia on Friday.Photograph: Ton Molina/Getty ImagesBrazilBrazil’s Lula says he now backs lowering age of criminal responsibility to 16Lula reverses position on age of responsibility for ‘heinous’ crimes in what many see as a desperate electoral gambitTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroFri 16 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazil’s president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit.The U-turn, which Lulaannouncedduring a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls.Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change.After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.”He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16.The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated.Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”.The columnist Josias de Souzawrotein his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.”The incumbent has doubled down in recent days in an effort to overturn Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead by appealing to independents and undecided voters. He has secured congressional approval for ashorter working week– a proposal on which Bolsonaro himself U-turned and decided to support at the last minute, when it appeared ready to pass – and debt relief for microentrepreneurs, as well as promising free public transport on weekends.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasFlávio BolsonaronewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screen | Jamaica | The Guardian
description: As violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: As violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’
Content: Gugu Mbatha-Raw stars in Sky’s supernatural series Possession set in Jamaica.Photograph: Des WillieView image in fullscreenGugu Mbatha-Raw stars in Sky’s supernatural series Possession set in Jamaica.Photograph: Des WillieCotton Capital: ongoing seriesJamaica‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screenAs violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’Natricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 15.05 EDTShareAwoman opens a 300‑year‑old box, unleashing a violent spirit – it is the spirit of colonialism and oppression roaring back to life. It is a pivotal scene in Sky’s supernatural series Possession and symbolises a wider shift in Jamaica’s film industry, where directors are increasingly using the landscape to tell Jamaican stories – including those that confront enslavement, trauma and historical memory.The series is about a biracial British lawyer who travels to Jamaica to investigate a multimillion-pound inheritance dispute, only to uncover a dark, vengeful spirit tied to the plantation’s brutal colonial past.For the Jamaican director, Storm Saulter, ensuring that the trauma and enduring legacy of enslavement and colonisation were powerfully represented was critical. Caribbean countries are increasingly arguing that centuries of enslavementhave left the region at a lasting disadvantage– fuelling renewed calls for reparations.Dr Lisa Tomlinson, a lecturer in film studies at the University of the West Indies, says the themes in Jamaican films are changing. “They’re now very much connected and reflective of Jamaican stories – stories that were previously taboo or avoided.”View image in fullscreenMbatha-Raw plays a lawyer who travels from Bristol to Jamaica to handle an inheritance claim over a former slave plantation.Photograph: Des WillieWhile Jamaican films are not always explicitly about reparations, she argues that many are engaging with the legacies of enslavement through cultural memory. “Reparation is not just a political act,” she says. “It’s also culture. These African‑derived spiritualities, the historical knowledge – when they come through creative expression, what they do is give us authority to tell our own stories.”This, she says, is a form of “cultural reparation”, a reclaiming of narratives devalued or suppressed under colonialism, and a way of educating audiences about the past in ways that academics or politicians struggle to do. “The arts play a critical role in how we are educated in public awareness around reparation,” she says.Jackie Jackson, Jamaica’s film commissioner, sees the shift too. She says productions such as Possession andDelroy Lindo’s Jabari’s People– shot entirely in Jamaica – reflect growing confidence and ambition among Jamaican creatives. “We are well established as a destination for international productions,” she says. “But what we want to see more of is local production and international collaboration that enables us to tell our own stories.”View image in fullscreenDelroy Lindo’s directorial debut Jabari’s People (he is pictured here in Spike Lee’s Da 5 Bloods) is shot entirely in Jamaica.Photograph: NetflixBoth productions, she notes, worked closely with Jamaican talent to ensure authenticity and demonstrate what is possible when international financing and distribution unite with Jamaican creativity. “They show the growing interest in Jamaican stories and their potential for global audiences,” she says.Tomlinson believes diaspora film-makers are playing a particularly important role in this shift. Unlike foreign productions that often use Jamaica as an exotic backdrop, diaspora directors are “moving away from the tourist‑gaze depictions” and are “capturing Jamaican everyday life”.Saulter sees his series as part of a broader political awakening. “The mask has slipped … We’ve been told it’s one thing, and that thing is proven to be false. So there’s a seeking of what is true,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStorm Saulter, Possession’s director, aims to ‘open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret’.Photograph: Bertie WatsonHe says the box‑opening scene is not simply a plot device, but a metaphor for something larger: the resurfacing of long‑suppressed histories and the growing willingness amongCaribbeancreatives to confront the legacies of enslavement, inherited trauma and colonial violence through film.“Literally, we’re going to open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret,” Saulter said. “It’s the spirit of colonial enslavement and oppression coming roaring back.”That “spirit”, he explains, is embodied in a character who has lived through centuries of brutality – “a witness to history” – whose presence forces the protagonists to reckon with the past they have inherited.Saulter’s interest in the subject is rooted in his upbringing. “I grew up in the countryside,” he says. “The Obia man, the church …nine nights… I’ve lived through all of those things.”His experiences inspired him to tell stories that educate and have “real societal political impact”, while remaining thrilling, intriguing and entertaining. That approach, he argues, allows film-makers to tackle difficult histories. “As opposed to doing something that was like talking heads … we’re bringing you on a journey,” he says.For Dr L’Antoinette Stines, a Yoruba priestess and cultural expert who advised on Possession, the series’ engagement with Afro‑spiritualist traditions is part of a longer history of resistance.View image in fullscreenSheldon East plays Cudjoe East, the son of a British man who grew up at the Hope Hill plantation in Jamaica.Photograph: Des Willie/©Sky UK Ltd“Black people have been fighting and using the arts for a very long time. It’s just that there is greater attention on it today,” she says. For decades she has choreographed similar work, she says, and stresses the importance of honouring the academics, poets and creatives who paved the way for today’s boom in authentic Jamaican storytelling.She praises Saulter’s insistence on authenticity and creating a series that feels both contemporary and deeply rooted, exploring inherited trauma, ancestral memory and the unfinished business of colonialism.Possession is on Sky Atlantic and NowExplore more on these topicsJamaicaCotton Capital: ongoing seriesWorld cinemaSlaveryReparations and reparative justiceCaribbeanAmericasColonialismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme | Trade policy | The Guardian
description: Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
Content: An electric vehicle production line in Ningbo, China.Photograph: Nick Carey/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn electric vehicle production line in Ningbo, China.Photograph: Nick Carey/ReutersTrade policyNo 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU schemeBeijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe packageRowena Mason,Lisa O’CarrollandJasper JollyFri 16 Oct 2026 14.09 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 15.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made inEuropepackage, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after Francedropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”.“We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned thatlocking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leadersto “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan toimpose quotason Chinese hybrid cars.While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.Liam Byrne, theLabourchair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.Explore more on these topicsTrade policyElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsInternational tradeLabourChinaChinese economyTariffsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed  | Amelia Earhart | The Guardian
description: Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance
Content: Aerial view from a plane wing of Nikumaroro’s lagoon and forested coastline taken during a 1938 aerial survey, when it was known as Gardner Island.Photograph: RNZAFView image in fullscreenAerial view from a plane wing of Nikumaroro’s lagoon and forested coastline taken during a 1938 aerial survey, when it was known as Gardner Island.Photograph: RNZAFAmelia EarhartMuseum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashedImages from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearanceOliver HolmesFri 16 Oct 2026 06.09 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island whereAmelia Earhartis believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a USexpedition to the Pacific atollof Nikumaroro in search of new clues.While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and hadreleased the full set of 47 imagesin digital high-resolution format on its website.The negatives were found more than a decade ago by Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.View image in fullscreenOne of 47 images released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand of Gardner Island, now Nikumaroro.Photograph: RNZAF/RNZAF OfficialEarhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” inhis blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, filled with false leads.A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.View image in fullscreenAmelia Earhart standing in front of the Lockheed Electra in which she disappeared in July 1937.Photograph: AlamyThis week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, aresearching a part of the islandfor the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll has been visited dozens of times.In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said severe weather had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience. This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”TheNew Zealandmilitary images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.Explore more on these topicsAmelia EarhartNew ZealandPacific islandsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands | Mining | The Guardian
description: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia
Author: Stefano Valentino
Headline: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia
Content: Deforestation in Indonesia linked to nickel mining.Photograph: Didi Hardiana, NGO PuspahamView image in fullscreenDeforestation in Indonesia linked to nickel mining.Photograph: Didi Hardiana, NGO PuspahamMiningRevealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous landsMines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in IndonesiaStefano Valentinoin Sulawesi andAjit NiranjanFri 16 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolkswagen, Ford andTeslaare among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot inIndonesiathat houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”View image in fullscreenWadimula: ‘Destroying [the forest] means destroying our own life.’Photograph: Stefano ValentinoElectric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.View image in fullscreenMorowali industrial park on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary.Photograph: Stefano ValentinoPublic filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a reportfoundlithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communicationsfoundlast year.The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests.View image in fullscreenA track cut through forest in the Hengjaya concession.Photograph: Stefano ValentinoSulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo,Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits.Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain.Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.”Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.”Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.”Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.”Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.”General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.”Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.”Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.”CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment.This investigation was supported byJournalismfund EuropeandThe Pulitzer Center. Lorenzo Di Stasi and James Jackson contributed reporting.Explore more on these topicsMiningDeforestationElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsAutomotive industryTravel and transportTrees and forestsIndonesianewsShareReuse this content

title: Gone to the dogs: racing fans mourn closure of ‘Wenty’, Sydney’s historic greyhound track | Sydney | The Guardian
description: Thousands pack Wentworth Park for the final time before the stadium is demolished and returned to parkland
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Thousands pack Wentworth Park for the final time before the stadium is demolished and returned to parkland
Content: Fans watch greyhound racing for the final time at Wentworth Park in Sydney on Friday night.Photograph: Jeremy Ng/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFans watch greyhound racing for the final time at Wentworth Park in Sydney on Friday night.Photograph: Jeremy Ng/Getty ImagesSydneyGone to the dogs: racing fans mourn closure of ‘Wenty’, Sydney’s historic greyhound trackThousands pack Wentworth Park for the final time before the stadium is demolished and returned to parklandGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressFri 16 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 19.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe end of an era has fallen upon an Australian sporting landmark as the greyhound races at an inner-city track kicked off for the very last time.Thousands packed into Wentworth Park in centralSydneyon Friday night, where greyhound races have been held since 1932, for the last race meeting before the track’s planned demolition.The final race of the night was the richest in the world – the Million Dollar Chase – and was won by Magical Ang.View image in fullscreenMagical Ang, winner of the Million Dollar Chase at Wentworth Park, with her handler.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAPFor Geoff Rose, the closure was a sign of the times – the land in the inner-west suburb of Glebe is worth a fortune in a city where growth will not slow down.But the NSW Greyhound Breeders, Owners and Trainers Association chair remained sad to see the park go.“It is quite heartbreaking to a lot of people,” he said.Another spectator mourning the closure was Jeff Collerson, a veteran greyhound writer who first set foot on the track at Wentworth Park in December 1962 as a 17-year-old cadet journalist.Now 81, he was trackside as the dogs raced around the circuit, nestled against the Sydney city skyline, for the final time and reminisced about his career.View image in fullscreenJeff Collerson not longer wants his ashes scattered at Wentworth Park. He is pictured at the track on Friday night.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAPHe said the closure of what locals refer to affectionately as “Wenty” was tragic.“I remember saying to my wife years ago, I want you to cast my ashes in front of the winning post at Wentworth Park, but I told her not to do that now,” Collerson said.“Wentworth Park’s got a special aura about it that the other tracks won’t have … it’s got a special buzz to it.“That will be lost forever because having a city track is just fantastic.”All buildings are slated for demolition after October 2027, and the site is planned to be returned to parkland under the auspices of Sydney’s council.Wentworth Park was created between 1876 and 1880 using silt dredged from Sydney’s harbour.Greyhound racingbegan in the park in 1932, and by the 1970s, the sport was attracting large crowds.View image in fullscreenSpectators at Wentworth Park on Friday.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAPGreyhound Racing NSW, the state’s regulator for the sport, announced this week it had chosen the existing Richmond race club, about an hour north-west of central Sydney, as the replacement site for the industry.Rose said his association was also exploring another option, which could see it establishing race meetings at a site near Appin, south-west of Sydney.Either way, the state’s racing minister, David Harris, has previously promised $10m in government funding to help the industry find a new home – a move criticised by those calling for the industry to be shut down altogether.View image in fullscreenAnti-greyhound racing protesters outside the stadium.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAPSome have welcomed the track’s closure as a move towards the whole industry’s end.A crowd of protesters stood outside the park as punters filed in, chanting that the sport kills dogs, and calling for an end to taxpayer dollars propping up the industry.Aleisha Kernan and Kirsten Lambros work for Greyhounds as Pets, which helps facilitate the adoption of retired racing dogs.Kernan said the sport’s potential new facilities would “open new avenues”.“I think people should look at the future as well,” she said.But for one young punter, Harry Dunlop, nothing would replace what he described as a “prominent piece of Australia”.“It’s very unlikely that we’ll be going out to Richmond,” he said.Explore more on these topicsSydneyAustralia sportGreyhound racingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mortgage repayments are now cheaper than rent in some Australian suburbs. Is yours among them? | Housing | The Guardian
description: As house prices plateau, the gap between the cost of buying and renting is narrowing in dozens of suburbs
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: As house prices plateau, the gap between the cost of buying and renting is narrowing in dozens of suburbs
Content: Australia’s median rent prices rose 5.5% over the year to September, while the median property price across houses and units remained flat over the year.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia’s median rent prices rose 5.5% over the year to September, while the median property price across houses and units remained flat over the year.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesHousingMortgage repayments are now cheaper than rent in some Australian suburbs. Is yours among them?As house prices plateau, the gap between the cost of buying and renting is narrowing in dozens of suburbsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniFri 16 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 21.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHigh rents and falling property prices have opened a rare window for Australian tenants to become homeowners, with mortgage repayments cheaper than rent in dozens of suburbs.Guardian Australia’s analysis of Cotality data shows that median rents in inner-cityMelbourne, suburban Canberra and Darwin are now nearly matching weekly home loan repayments.‘Are they going to fall enough?’ The renters waiting for the house price downturn to change their fortunesRead moreIn one in 10 suburbs and towns across the country, repayments are less than $200 a week higher than rent, for the typical property. In some suburbs, they are actually cheaper.Australia’s median rent prices rose 5.5% over the year to September to reach $713 per week, Cotality data shows. The median property price across houses and units was flat over the year, after six months of steady falls.Is it cheaper to buy or rent in your suburb?Is it cheaper to buy or rent in your suburb?The typical rent for a Melbourne apartment was $628 a week after rising 4.8% over the last year.The typical repayments for a Melbourne flat were $211 more, or $839 a week, based on a median value of $624,740 in September, down nearly $25,000 from a year earlier.The analysis assumes a new 30-year loan of 95% of the value, at a 6.2% interest rate. It does not account for any additional costs. Smaller loans made with bigger deposits would make repayments even more affordable compared with rents.Owner-occupiers purchasing with a 5% deposit would typically do so through the government’s low deposit scheme, which is designed to help first home buyers.Repayments were cheaper than rent for the typical property in Carlton, Melbourne CBD, Notting Hill, Travancore and Southbank.Repayments on new loans had risen overall in the last year for most suburbs, as lower values were offset by interest rates rising 1 percentage point. Where values had fallen more than 10%, though, repayments were likely lower.Clint Waters, a Melbourne mortgage broker, said home buying interest had dropped but renters were inquiring in strong numbers as they weighed lower house prices against higher rents.“They’re certainly doing the maths … [and] the equation at the moment is starting to narrow,” Waters said.Australia’s housing market is definitely in a downturn – but let’s put that in perspective | Hal PawsonRead moreWaters, director at Axton Finance, said a stable or growing number were looking to buy direct from their landlord, making the switch without moving.“Landlords are getting slammed left, right and centre, and going ‘screw this, I’m going to offload,’” Waters said. “Tenants will ring us up and say, ‘I need to work out if I’ve got the capacity to buy this thing.’”New apartments pushing down pricesInSydney, repayments were just $100 a week more than rents in inner-city Ultimo and western suburbs Warwick Farm, Rosehill, Liverpool and Granville.In theCanberrasuburbs of Belconnen and Phillip, repayments were less than $75 a week more than rents. If only apartments are included, Braddon, Lyons, Gungahlin and Harrison join the list.Gerard Burg, a Cotality researcher, said areas with significant apartment development tended to be cheaper to buy than rent, especially where flats were being sold direct to owner-occupiers and not rented out.“That just [shows] this influx of supply pushing down the value of the purchase, while comparatively tight rental availability had led to this increase in rents,” Burg said.But such areas were “anomalies”, he said. Houses remain generally more expensive to buy than rent.“If it was a sustained thing that you could buy a property more cheaply than renting it, then everyone would buy and everyone would exit the rental market,” Burg said.It was cheaper to buy in a quarter of suburbs inDarwin, where rents have risen 11.6% in the year. Most areas where buying was cheaper than renting were mining or resource project areas in which fly-in fly-out workers temporarily rent rather than buy, Burg said.Burg said mortgage repayments would likely fall if the Reserve Bank held rates steady and values kept falling, as expected by financial markets, potentially narrowing the gap with rents.“[With] rents continuing to increase or … go sideways, that could occur.”Explore more on these topicsHousingBusinessRentingVictoriaMelbourneInterest ratesSydneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Greens leader denies knowledge of ‘secret dossier’ on how to handle Jordon Steele-John misconduct allegations | Australian Greens | The Guardian
description: David Shoebridge says 47-page document not ‘made by, used by, or seen by’ his office as matter referred to parliamentary standards commission
Author: Sarah Basford Canales
Headline: David Shoebridge says 47-page document not ‘made by, used by, or seen by’ his office as matter referred to parliamentary standards commission
Content: The Greens leader has denied knowledge of a secret dossier containing allegations against senator Jordon Steele-John, pictured.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenThe Greens leader has denied knowledge of a secret dossier containing allegations against senator Jordon Steele-John, pictured.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian GreensGreens leader denies knowledge of ‘secret dossier’ on how to handle Jordon Steele-John misconduct allegationsDavid Shoebridge says 47-page document not ‘made by, used by, or seen by’ his office as matter referred to parliamentary standards commissionGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastSarah Basford CanalesFri 16 Oct 2026 04.55 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 03.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreens leaderDavid Shoebridgehas denied knowledge of the existence of an alleged crisis management document on how to deal with allegations against Jordon Steele-John being made public.The Nine newspapersreported on Friday afternoonthe existence of a “secret dossier”, first drafted in 2016, which contained misconduct allegations against the Western Australian Greens senator and how to suppress their media coverage.Guardian Australia has not independently confirmed the document’s contents.In a statement responding to claims that the federal leader’s office had access to the 47-page document, Shoebridge said it was not “made by, used by, or seen by the leader’s office”.“The office is committed to having the matters comprehensively investigated with a fair, independent and timely process,” he said.“Everyone deserves a safe workplace, and all complaints should be considered in a fair and robust process.”Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe WA Greens confirmed the existence of the document and said it was created in response to allegations first made against the senator in 2016.“The Greens WA responded to allegations about Jordon Steele-John in 2016. The allegations were not substantiated and the named persons have never lodged a formal complaint,” the statement said.“Reference has been made to an internal document that has been provided to the media. This document outlines the management of communications about this matter.”Greens senator Jordon Steele-John takes leave amid investigation into complaintsRead moreSteele-John confirmed he would leave the party room on Thursday after some details of historical complaints about inappropriate comments made to women ranging between 2017 and 2025 were publicly aired in the media.The 32-year-old senator rejected the claims and said he had referred them to the WesternAustralian Greensfor a “fair, independent process” that “upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved”.“I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not,” Steele-John said in a statement.Shoebridge told ABC on Friday morning he referred the complaints outlined in a letter to the parliamentary workplace support service (PWSS), which he said was “unable to deal with it because of the circumstances and nature of the allegation”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe PWSS’s chief executive, Leonie McGregor, said the office had not been given the letter but had provided Shoebridge’s office with options, including referring the complaints to the independent parliamentary standards commission (IPSC).Guardian Australia understands Shoebridge has now referred the matter to the IPSC.The WA Greens confirmed on Thursday they would “seek legal advice on how best to establish an independent inquiry” into the matters raised.A statement from the co-conveners, Giz Watson and Simone Collins, and state director, Dean Smith, said: “Our party is built on the contributions of members, volunteers, staff and supporters, and every one of them deserves to feel safe and respected when they take part in our work. Maintaining that safety is a responsibility we hold seriously.”Shoebridge confirmed Steele-John would not return to parliament until the independent investigations had been completed.“It’s my understanding that leave means leave,” he told ABC.“I have responsibility for the party room and the Greens’ functions, and I have some capacity to direct in relation to the party room. But Senator Steele-John has indicated to me that he’s on leave, and that leave means leave.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian GreensAustralian politicsWestern AustraliaDavid ShoebridgenewsShareReuse this content

title: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case not ‘prioritised’ due to high workload, inquest hears | Queensland | The Guardian
description: Eight-year-old Queensland girl died in 2022 after being denied insulin by her religious parents
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Eight-year-old Queensland girl died in 2022 after being denied insulin by her religious parents
Content: All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of eight-year-old Elizabeth Struhs’ manslaughter last year, including her parents, Kerrie and Jason, and the group leader, Brendan Stevens.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenAll 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of eight-year-old Elizabeth Struhs’ manslaughter last year, including her parents, Kerrie and Jason, and the group leader, Brendan Stevens.Photograph: BBCQueenslandElizabeth Struhs’ child protection case not ‘prioritised’ due to high workload, inquest hearsEight-year-old Queensland girl died in 2022 after being denied insulin by her religious parentsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAndrew MessengerFri 16 Oct 2026 03.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 03.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElizabeth Struhs’ child protection case was not “prioritised” or worked intensively because the staff member assigned to her case was “very busy”, a coroner has heard.TheQueenslandcoroner’s court also heard the case worker may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of Struhs’ “upper class home”, putting cases believed to involve a more immediate risk ahead of Elizabeth’s.The eight-year-old died on 7 January 2022 of diabetic ketoacidosis, after her father, Jason Struhs, stopped providing insulin to treat her type 1 diabetes at their home in Toowoomba, Queensland. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailCoroner Ainslie Kirkegaard is holding an inquest into Elizabeth’s death. She has previously heard the eight-year-old came to the attention of child safety after a 2019 incident where she presented to hospital in a coma.Child safety ended its involvement with the family after just 17 weeks of what was supposed to be an intensive intervention, assessing her as “safe”.But the single child safety officer assigned to Elizabeth’s case told the court on Friday her approach wasn’t intensive and she didn’t make weekly check-ins during that period, despite departmental guidelines.Doctors treating Elizabeth Struhs recommended involuntary mental health assessment of her mother, coroner hearsRead moreThe department chose to release her back into Jason’s sole careover the objections of specialist doctorswho treated Elizabeth in Brisbane, subject to a voluntary intervention with parental agreement (IPA).The coroner heard just a single child safety officer was assigned to the case, and would often conduct home visits alone.The officer gave evidence on Friday.“Ideally I wanted to visit with the family at least once a week, in accordance with our IPAT (intervention with parental agreement team) guidelines,” according to her statement, presented to the court.“During my management of the IPA for the Struhs family, I recall that I was not always available to conduct home visits with the family. I recall this being a very busy time for the CSSC (child safety service centre) and I also recall being regularly out of the office travelling to visit other families.“I note that one of the home visits to the Struhs family was conducted by a student who was working in the team at the time.”She said Elizabeth’s case wasn’t treated as a complex case, which it should have been due to the intervention.But at the time, she had a “big caseload” – approximately 25-28 children in 15 families on the same intervention– she said. The coroner has previously heard that the Toowoomba region was among the busiest in the state for child safety.Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris said most of them were experiencing significant domestic violence, drug use, sexual abuse and it was not often that she was required to work with “upper class families” like the Struhs.The case worker agreed that she may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of the Struhs home.“I believe that we may have prioritised other cases at the time for children who were presenting at more immediate risk,” she told the court.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe also told the court that she may have had a bias because her own child had nearly died of type 1 diabetes at age 6. She had asked not to be assigned to the case, she said.Several witnesses have previously told the coroner they expected the intervention to last months or a year, but the case worker said they were supposed to not last longer than three months, because they were an intensive approach.On Friday, Kirkegaard asked another child safety witness whether they felt “organisational pressure to get a matter like this finalised quickly”.“Absolutely,” the witness said, adding an IPA could be intrusive and potentially harmful to a child if dragged out.“I don’t believe it impacted our decision making,” she said.On 13 November 2019, a more senior child safety officer assessed Elizabeth as “safe” and the intervention was ended.The case worker told the coroner on Friday that she hadn’t appreciated the danger of Elizabeth’s mother’s church group, which was considered a source of support for the family.All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including Elizabeth’s parents, Kerrie and Jason, and the group leader, Brendan Stevens.In her statement she said Jason had agreed to continue to treat his daughter against his wife’s beliefs and that she had “faith” that should Kerrie stand in the way he would leave her.None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.The inquest continues.Explore more on these topicsQueenslandChild protectionnewsShareReuse this content

title: One Nation proposes $2,000 baby subsidy in Victoria but says it won’t touch state abortion laws | One Nation | The Guardian
description: Announcement comes a day after Liberal and Labor parties say they will cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: Announcement comes a day after Liberal and Labor parties say they will cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care
Content: Deputy leader of One Nation in Victoria, Colleen Harkin, announced a plan to remove out-of-pocket costs for pregnant women in the public health system and a $2,000 subsidy for those accessing private maternity care.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenDeputy leader of One Nation in Victoria, Colleen Harkin, announced a plan to remove out-of-pocket costs for pregnant women in the public health system and a $2,000 subsidy for those accessing private maternity care.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPOne NationOne Nation proposes $2,000 baby subsidy in Victoria but says it won’t touch state abortion lawsAnnouncement comes a day after Liberal and Labor parties say they will cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion careGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastBenita KolovosVictorian state correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 03.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 03.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne Nation has proposed a $2,000 baby bonus for new parents in Victoria – a day after the Labor and Liberal parties both agreed to cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care.The deputy leader of One Nation inVictoria, Colleen Harkin, announced the plan on Friday to remove out-of-pocket costs for pregnant women in the public healthcare system and a $2,000 subsidy for those accessing private maternity care.She said it would cost $136m over four years but admitted it was a “ballpark” figure that would depend on how many babies were born each year.“We don’t go hard on figures, because we actually don’t have access to the detail of this stuff,” Harkin told reporters.She said One Nation “will not touch the abortion laws” in Victoria despite the federal party’s national platform pledging to “seek every opportunity to roll back brutal and extreme abortion law”.As One Nation rises, Victoria’s Labor and Liberal parties promise to make abortions free. Is the timing pure politics?Read more“We have no state abortion policy because it is not our focus whatsoever,” Harkin said, accusing the Labor party of “lying” and “engaging with really cheap American-style scaremongering”.On Thursday, Labor announced that, if re-elected in November, it wouldeliminate out-of-pocket costs for abortion care, costing $30m over four years, and claimed One Nation could use abortion as anegotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailUnder Labor’s plan, private providers would be paid to deliver medical and surgical abortions up to 16 weeks’ gestation. Women would no longer have to pay for GP and specialist consultations, scans, tests or medication, which can cost up to $1,000. Those in regional Victoria who must travel long distances for care would also be eligible for a subsidy.The government would extend access to medical abortion from nine to 10 weeks’ gestation, while commissioning a clinical review into whether it could safely be offered at up to 12 weeks’ gestation.Within hours the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said the Coalitionwould match the plan to cover out-of-pocket costsand the travel subsidy. In a statement she said “the Liberals and Nationals will not allow Labor to play politics on this issue”.On Friday, Fiona Carroll, the wife of the premier, Ben Carroll, defended her husband for raising abortion in the leadup to the election.“It does build on the Labor legacy, and I don’t think I’m politicising this because it is fundamental to the women in this state,” she said.Fiona said it was “even better” the Coalition had matched the commitment, as it would “take some of that fear” out of the election for women.Neither the Liberal party nor Labor responded to a request for comment on One Nation’s policy.Anti-abortion activist Joanna Howe criticised Wilson, describing the Liberals as being in “lock step with Labor on every vile and evil policy” and directing her followers in Victoria to back One Nation. The Australian Christian Lobby’s Victorian director, Jasmine Yeun, said it was “getting more difficult to vote for a major party”.But the chief executive of Women’s Health Victoria, Sally Hasler, welcomed the bipartisanship on the issue. It means no matter who is elected, Victoria will become the first state to provide abortion free.“We are very reassured to know that it won’t be an election issue because we have support from both the ALP and the Coalition to not just protect rights but to expand rights,” Hasler said.She described One Nation’s announcement as a deliberate attempt to frame reproductive healthcare as a choice between abortion and maternity care.“Responding to an abortion care announcement with a maternity care announcement is a false trade-off, and it’s a deliberate one,” she said.“It is a well-played move from the international anti-rights agenda to wind back women’s rights – one which narrowly defines women’s reproductive health.”Explore more on these topicsOne NationVictoriaAbortionAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House
Content: A Ukrainian soldier sets up Starlink satellite internet system near the frontline in DonetskPhotograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenA Ukrainian soldier sets up Starlink satellite internet system near the frontline in DonetskPhotograph: ReutersUkraineStarlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says ZelenskyyUkrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White HouseJennifer Rankinin Brussels andAndrew Rothin KyivFri 16 Oct 2026 14.01 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president,Donald Trump.Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’Read moreHours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having thebiggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant.Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttlingStarshield, the military versionof the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.View image in fullscreenFirefighters working at the scene of a Russian drone strike in a residential area in Kyiv on Thursday.Photograph: Vincenzo Circosta/Anadolu/Getty ImagesSpeaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that theSpaceXStarshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.Trump said on Friday he did not think either ⁠he or ⁠Elon ​Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starshield access and that any limits were not imposed by the US.Starshield is produced by Musk’s SpaceX butcontrolled by the US government.Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 ⁠across Ukraine on Friday, hitting two shopping centres and temporarily power to more than 1 million people, ⁠officials said.When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.View image in fullscreenZelenskyy with the presidents of the European Council, António Costa (left), and the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen (right), on Friday.Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty ImagesAccording to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with Zelenskyy that “it is clear that we have a gap of €70bn that has to be covered” for 2027, although she expected Ukraine’s other partners – which she did not name – to cover part of the sum.The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments froma €90bn funding plan agreed last Decemberthat was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong.
