But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyDonald TrumpSpaceXEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: EU’s support to Ukraine matters more than ever, von der Leyen says, as US relationship sours – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: European commission president says ‘no one wants more peace than the people of Ukraine, and it is our duty to support them’
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: European commission president says ‘no one wants more peace than the people of Ukraine, and it is our duty to support them’
Content: 13.14 EDTEU's support to Ukraine matters more than ever, von der Leyen saysVon der Leyenthen turns toUkraine.She says the EU’s support “matters more than ever.”She says the bloc “is doing a long, butthe reality is simple: as long as this war continues, Ukraine’s financing needs will keep growing.”“Right now, the European Union and its member states account for 80% of external aid to Ukraine, and we will continue to lead. But we urgently need also other partners to step in.”She ends:“As throughout these five years of war,no one wants more peace than the people of Ukraine, and it is our duty to support them, to be in the position to find a just and sustainable peace for Ukraine.”ShareUpdated at13.33 EDT

title: Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Kremlin turning to punishment of Ukraine’s population in major cities as frontlines remain frozen
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Kremlin turning to punishment of Ukraine’s population in major cities as frontlines remain frozen
Content: Kyiv and Kharkiv have experienced rolling blackouts and water outages this week.Photograph: Gleb Garanich/ReutersView image in fullscreenKyiv and Kharkiv have experienced rolling blackouts and water outages this week.Photograph: Gleb Garanich/ReutersUkraineAnalysisPower plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivableAndrew Rothin KyivKremlin turning to punishment of Ukraine’s population in major cities as frontlines remain frozenFri 16 Oct 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 19.46 EDTShareAs Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian.Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapsesRead moreThe potential goals of the Russian campaign, according to an assessment seen by the Guardian that Ukrainian intelligence said it intercepted from Russia last month, range from “degrading the quality of life” of Ukrainians through power outages to fully shutting off the water supply, which the document cooly predicts would cause the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.”The document does not specify which Russian agency developed the assessment, which is titled Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy, Housing and Utilities Sectors, includes vulnerable Ukrainian energy grid targets and even contemplates strikes against high-risk sites, including the switchyards at several nuclear power plants. But several European officials familiar with the document have said it is likely to have been produced by analytical departments linked to the Russian military or intelligence agencies, and that copies have circulated in Ukraine in previous years.This year, however, Russia appears to be putting those plans into practice. On Tuesday night, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region – Combined Heat and Power Plants 4 and 5, and the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region – as well as a major electrical substation that transfers electricity from two of the country’s main nuclear power plants to the capital. Those, along with other substations that make up the “Kyiv energy ring” that helps bring electricity from across the country to the capital, have all been targets of a Russian barrage that, if it succeeds, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in a city of 3 million people.Ukraine’s energy minister first briefed European allies last month about the plan, a copy of which was first reported on by the New York Times. Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian power grid precisely as Washington and Kyiv are embroiled in a major political quarrel. The Guardian is withholding some specifics of the military assessment at the request of Ukraine’s energy ministry, which said it could aid in further strikes against the country.“There are two large documents, written very coldly and very clearly, with tables showing the number of weapons needed for each facility to destroy it,” Ukrainian energy minister Denys Shmyhal said last month. “The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones. We understand how they are going to act.”The leaked documents identify bottlenecks and prescribe the number of ballistic and hypersonic cruise missiles and jet-powered drones needed to knock out power plants and substations with brutal efficiency. If that was done, it could destroy more than 90% of the power that Kyiv is budgeted for each winter, the document predicts, plunging the city into the dark and cold. A worst-case scenario could lead to blackouts lasting up to 20 hours a day until damaged equipment is repaired, according to expert projections.The strikes on Ukraine’s energy system have become the country’s new frontlines – and the country is badly outgunned, as its stocks of US-provided PAC-3 missiles have dwindled. Zelenskyy this week castigated city authorities for poor planning for the winter and for failing to protect the city’s energy infrastructure. Protests over heat and electricity blackouts are also planned for Saturday, highlighting how the difficult conditions in winter could provoke a political crisis for the wartime government.Economic Pravda, a leading Ukrainian news site that covers business, reported on Thursday that the three major power plants in Kyiv no longer have the ability to generate electricity, leaving the city more reliant on electricity brought from elsewhere in the country (the government generally does not confirm specific damage to critical infrastructure). The outlets’ experts predicted that, given a moderate winter and quick repairs of damaged substations, Kyiv residents could face up to eight hours of blackouts a day. Its worst case scenario of frigid temperatures and frequent attacks would leave Kyiv in the dark for up to 20 hours a day.This is no accident for the Kremlin, which has increasingly turned to punishing Ukraine’s population in major cities as the frontlines of the conflict have frozen. “Last year, we were really on the brink,” said Volodymyr Fesenko, a Ukrainian political analyst. “But the risk this year will be even worse, so the plan [to attack Ukrainian infrastructure] does seem realistic. There’s a very high chance that Russia tries to break us this winter.” If the Kremlin believed in the chance of a clean military victory before now, he added, it may now believe that not to be possible, and focus on destroying Ukraine’s remaining infrastructure rather than trying to capture it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe secret plan, which officials here say was intercepted by Ukrainian intelligence and then briefed to senior European diplomats by Shmyhal last month, sets itself several goals: to destroy electricity generation, heating, water and sewage systems in such a way as to to make life in Ukrainian cities unliveable. Destroying electrical generation alone, it says, would lead to a “significant decrease in the quality of life of the population.”Graph showing rise in Russian attacks on Ukrainian heating infrastructureTo do so, it specifies the number of weapons that should be allocated – Geran 4/5 jet-powered drones and hypersonic or cruise missiles – in order to destroy key infrastructure such as thermal power plants, substations, water pumping stations and more.Considering strikes against the basis of Ukraine’s water, sewage and heating systems, the document says it would create a “large-scale municipal infrastructure crisis.”When contacted by the Guardian, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said that the document contained information that could aid in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. It did not reply to questions on how the current Russian bombing strategy matched with the proposals made in the document, or which Russian agency had developed the plans.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: British man fined €3,000 for causing two-year-old son’s death in Cyprus  | Cyprus | The Guardian
description: Joshua Foster pleaded guilty over death of toddler who fell from fourth-floor window of hotel during family holiday
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Joshua Foster pleaded guilty over death of toddler who fell from fourth-floor window of hotel during family holiday
Content: Joshua Foster (right) arriving at Paphos district court in Cyprus for the sentencing hearing, with his lawyer.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenJoshua Foster (right) arriving at Paphos district court in Cyprus for the sentencing hearing, with his lawyer.Photograph: James Manning/PACyprusBritish man fined €3,000 for causing two-year-old son’s death in CyprusJoshua Foster pleaded guilty over death of toddler who fell from fourth-floor window of hotel during family holidayHelena Smithin AthensFri 16 Oct 2026 10.05 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British man has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) after his two-year-old son fell 10 metres (33ft) to his death from the fourth-floor window of a hotel in Cyprus.Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he approached it with the boy to show him the view of a waterpark and “lost control” of him, the court previously heard.The 37-year-old appeared at Paphos district court on Friday for sentencing having pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.In emotional scenes at the court, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident on 12 July, the first day of the family’s holiday in Cyprus, as a “tragic event”.“Jail is not appropriate,” the judge said, telling the courtroom that as there was “clearly no intent to kill” she had decided against a custodial sentence and would instead order Foster to pay the fine.The Essex-born auditor, who had previously appeared in court visibly distraught, struggled to hold back tears as the sentence was handed down. As it dawned that the case was finally over, he hugged his lawyer before telling reporters: “Thank you for your support. I’m looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter.”The light sentence – the minimum for the charge – meant Foster could retrieve his passport and other documents he had been forced to surrender. More usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents, the charge carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison.Speaking outside the district court in Paphos, the defendant’s lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said Foster, who works for one of the UK’s big four accounting firms, would finally be able to grieve.View image in fullscreenThe family were on holiday at the King Evelthon Beach hotel and resort in Chlorakas, Cyprus, when the incident happened.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA“He’s been through a lot and it’s been very emotional but he’s relieved it’s over,” he said of his client, who posted €30,000 in bail to return to the UK to attend the toddler’s funeral in August before being forced under threat of extradition to return to Cyprus for the proceedings.“This case should not have gone to court. We asked for the charges to be suspended. Unfortunately this was not accepted.”Alexandrou had appealed to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds, arguing that prosecution “does not serve the public interest”. The request was denied.The boy fell to his death from the window of the King Evelthon hotel within hours of the family arriving in Paphos.In mitigation on 5 October, Alexandrou recounted how Foster was making his way to a lift along the corridor when he stopped at the window and the “inconceivable” occurred. The Briton, he said, had not realised the window was ajar when, lifting the child, who was excitedly pointing to the hotel’s waterpark outside, he “lost control” and he slipped through his hands. The boy was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after suffering severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.Summing up, Christodoulidou said while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.View image in fullscreenLawyer Alexandros Alexandrou (right) speaks to journalists outside the court.Photograph: James Manning/PA“It is no exaggeration to say that for the rest of his life he will have guilt for losing his child in such a tragic way,” she added. Mitigating factors presented by the defence, including the Briton’s lack of criminal record, as well as his guilty plea, had also played a role in her decision, she explained. In a country so dependent on tourism, criticism had mounted as Cypriot human rights defenders, media pundits and foreign diplomats all questioned the perceived lack of compassion with which officials approached the case.A former British colony, the eastern Mediterranean island attracts roughly 4 million visitors and is particularly popular with tourists from the UK.Alexandrou, the lawyer, said he had advised his client to admit the negligence charge to avoid a potentially drawn-out and disturbing trial when he and his family were still processing the grief of their “unimaginable loss”.Conceding the case had been “emotional” for the entire defence team, the lawyer added: “He can finally grieve. Now that the court proceedings are over, the explosion of his emotions at the loss of his child will be immediate.”In a statement issued after the sentencing, the Foster family said: “Today marks the end of the legal proceedings in Cyprus, and we are grateful to the court and Judge Christodoulidou for her decision to apply the maximum mitigation afforded to her.“We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end. Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day.“Our focus now is on supporting one another and finding a way forward as a family. We ask that our privacy is respected as we do so.”Explore more on these topicsCyprusEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Norwegian teenage hitman hired for UK murder by Iran-backed crime gang jailed for 20 years | Crime | The Guardian
description: Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was arrested in Huddersfield with two guns and live ammunition
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was arrested in Huddersfield with two guns and live ammunition
Content: Natland was found guilty of conspiracy to murder after agreeing to shoot an unknown target for €25,000.Photograph: Metropolitan police/ReutersView image in fullscreenNatland was found guilty of conspiracy to murder after agreeing to shoot an unknown target for €25,000.Photograph: Metropolitan police/ReutersCrimeNorwegian teenage hitman hired for UK murder by Iran-backed crime gang jailed for 20 yearsJohannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was arrested in Huddersfield with two guns and live ammunitionHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 08.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA teenage hitman who travelled fromNorwayto the UK with the intention of carrying out a murder on behalf of an Iran-backed international crime gang has been jailed for 20 years.Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, a talented footballer, had agreed to shoot an unknown target in return for €25,000 (£21,500).He travelled to the UK in March last year from his home in Stavanger, and two days later – before he could carry out the hit – armed police arrested him at a hotel in Huddersfield,West Yorkshire.Officers found him in possession of a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver, 12 rounds of live ammunition and gloves.Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition and said he had intended to shoot himself in the foot to get out of the “pickle” he was in. However, he was found guilty of conspiracy to murder and on Friday was sentenced to 20 years in detention.The court heard that Natland had been recruited by another teenager, referred to as Generalen, who was working for the proscribed Swedish Foxtrot gang, which is backed by the Iranian regime and known for recruiting children as young as 13 to become involved in drug smuggling and violent crimes.Natland had been controlled by an English-speaking boss called Agent 47, an apparent reference to the Hitman gaming and film franchise. The identity and whereabouts of Agent 47 remain unknown.Natland flew into Manchester on a temporary passport and was stopped by Border Force officials, who bailed him to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.Instead, he travelled by taxi toHuddersfieldwhere he booked into the Briar Court hotel and picked up the guns and ammunition, as well as £2,000 in cash. He was directed to a stolen Nissan with false number plates, which was to be used in the murder.While in the hotel, Natland took selfies with the guns and cash spread out on his bed, and bragged to his girlfriend that he had the “bangs in the bag”. Armed police arrived to arrest him at 5.15am the next day.Paul Hynes KC, defending, pointed to Natland’s age at the time of the offending and said he had been a “young, popular, successful student and sportsman” before he went “off the rails” after he became addicted to drugs.Giving evidence, Natland told jurors: “I wasn’t an international assassin. I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn’t.”However, in a televised sentencing at Woolwich crown court in south-east London, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb said messages he had sent showed “not only participation but at points excitement” about what he had been planning to do.“You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself,” she said. “Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to.”Explore more on these topicsCrimeHuddersfieldWest YorkshireYorkshireEnglandNorwayEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Settlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and beat photographer Heidi Levine as part of yearly attacks to disrupt harvest
Author: William Christou
Headline: Settlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and beat photographer Heidi Levine as part of yearly attacks to disrupt harvest
Content: Firefighters dousing a burnt car with water after Israeli settlers attacked a group of Palestinians harvesting olives near Turmus Ayya.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersView image in fullscreenFirefighters dousing a burnt car with water after Israeli settlers attacked a group of Palestinians harvesting olives near Turmus Ayya.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersWest BankIsraeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West BankSettlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and beat photographer Heidi Levine as part of yearly attacks to disrupt harvestWilliam ChristouFri 16 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and aWashington Postphotographer.Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives inWest Banktowns on Friday. Palestinian authorities said they recorded attacks in eight villages, and injuries among at least 20 people.1:57American photojournalist recounts Israeli settler attack in the occupied West Bank – videoIt was the latest series of attacks in a deadly campaign of Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in recent months, violence which has drawn accusations of “ethnic cleansing”, including from the British government.In the town of Abu Falah, near Ramallah,at least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.View image in fullscreenTeargas fired by Israeli forces.Photograph: Léo Corrêa/APThe Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that the facts surrounding the attack on Levine were “unclear”, suggesting the attack was the fault of “200 Arabs and far-left activists” who confronted Israeli youths. The office added that it condemned “violence against anyone”.View image in fullscreenLevine speaking to journalists in hospital after the attack.Photograph: Ali Sawafta/ReutersThere has been asurge of settler violenceagainst Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but there has been a rise in violence this year as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.At least four Palestinians had been killed and more than 100 others injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.View image in fullscreenPalestinians and activists collecting olives after the attack on Friday.Photograph: Léo Corrêa/APThe new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without the approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.‘They have total impunity’: West Bank settler violence surges after Gaza ceasefireRead moreThe rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited, for the purpose of preventing settler violence, from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026.The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers razed trees.Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well-documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop it.Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelWashington PostJournalist safetyMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the world
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the world
Content: A scene from NAZA, which interviewed military insiders anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night.Photograph: NAZA/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA, which interviewed military insiders anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night.Photograph: NAZA/The GuardianNAZA‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentaryFilm interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the worldSammy GecsoylerFri 16 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCritics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentaryNAZAas a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, wasreleased in UK cinemas this weekand will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.44:17NAZA: the film Israel does not want you to see - videoThe Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an exposé” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.When the film opened in Italy last month, ittopped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.1:55NAZA - official trailerThe film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.Various organisations, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went onto win the special jury prize.Explore more on these topicsNAZAIsraelGazaIsrael-Gaza warPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15 | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups
Author: Tom Levitt
Headline: Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups
Content: The supreme court has reportedly upheld Youssef al-Manasif’s death penalty for offences committed as a minor. Last year Saudi Arabia put to death 356 people.Photograph: HandoutView image in fullscreenThe supreme court has reportedly upheld Youssef al-Manasif’s death penalty for offences committed as a minor. Last year Saudi Arabia put to death 356 people.Photograph: HandoutRights and freedomSaudi ArabiaSaudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groupsSupported byAbout this contentTom LevittFri 16 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 05.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA young man faces imminent execution inSaudi Arabiafor attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes includingjoining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funeralsthat the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.The charity Reprieve says Manasif was tortured and coerced into signing a false confession and only met his state-appointed lawyer for the first time in 2022 – five years after his arrest.Manasif’sdeath sentence has now reportedly been upheldby the Saudi supreme court, which was likely to be his last hope of avoiding execution.His family have not spoken in public about the case and could face harassment or arrest if they do so. “There is nothing they can do now but wait,” said Duaa Dhainy, a consultant for Reprieve and the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights.Saudi Arabia has seen what activists describe as a“horrifying” surge in executionsunder the rule of the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. Last year saw a record356 people put to deathin the country. Most of those executed areforeigners convicted of minor and non-violent drug crimes.At least 17 people, who were children at the time of their alleged offences, have been executed in Saudi Arabia since 2015, according to Reprieve.Saudi Arabia issued a royal decree abolishing thedeath penalty for childrenin 2020, stating that individuals would not be sentenced to death for crimes committed when they were minors.However, it has since upheld the death penalty in a number of cases involving child defendants. In April, itexecuted Ali al-Subaiti, along with his uncle, Mustafa al-Subaiti,for non-lethal “terrorist” offences committed when he was 12 years old.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTheUN’s independent human rights expertshave previously expressed concerns about Manasif’s case. It said Saudi Arabia should immediately halt planned executions of people convicted of offences allegedly committed when they were under 18.“They are using execution as a tool to show how powerful they are and how they can threaten anyone who does not follow their rules,” Dhainy said of the Saudi regime. “We think he should be treated as a minor and not sentenced to death as his charges relate to when he was under 18.”Human Rights Watch said executing Manasif for a non-violent crime committed as a minor would be “an unconscionable new low”.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaRights and freedomMiddle East and north AfricaCapital punishmentHuman rights (Global development)Human rights (Law)Mohammed bin SalmanYouth justicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Future of western security is at stake in Yemen civil war, says country’s former PM | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed says Iran-backed militia’s use of drones represents ‘new era of radical terrorism’
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed says Iran-backed militia’s use of drones represents ‘new era of radical terrorism’
Content: Houthi supporters gather in the militia’s stronghold city of Sana’a, Yemen, earlier this month.Photograph: Mohammed al-Mahdi/ReutersView image in fullscreenHouthi supporters gather in the militia’s stronghold city of Sana’a, Yemen, earlier this month.Photograph: Mohammed al-Mahdi/ReutersYemenFuture of western security is at stake in Yemen civil war, says country’s former PMMaeen Abdulmalik Saeed says Iran-backed militia’s use of drones represents ‘new era of radical terrorism’Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthroughPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 16 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 05.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said.Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost.Appealing for more western help, Saeed said he had no doubt that theHouthisintended to seize control of all of Yemen, and claimed their goal was “to help Iran to expand the chaos”.View image in fullscreenHouthis ride in a funeral procession for their fellow fighters in Sana’a, Yemen, in September.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPASaeed admitted the lack of coordination among government-backed troops, competition between Gulf states and a slowness to appreciate the implications of Yemen acquiring long-range drone technology had contributed to the pressure facing his government, and its chief backerSaudi Arabia.“We only have light weapons and Saudi Arabia did not plan at an early stage for this escalation, but it is never too late to regain our position,” he said.Saeed called on the west to think through the implications of allowing the Houthis to take control of Yemen, arguing the country would never be secure with Houthis on the land.‘We expect war to reach the city soon’: Yemenis stockpile as Houthis advance on TaizRead moreSaeed is not only an adviser to the Yemeni president, Rashad al-Alimi, he was prime minister between 2018 and 2024 and a former negotiator with the Houthis.He said: “The battle around Taiz is not just a battle for Taiz, but a broader battle that involves the whole of the western world, and one of the most important maritime straits. The Houthis know controlling Taiz is controlling the straits and it’s the highlands before the straits and the coastal city of Mocha and the Gulf of Aden. If Taiz is lost, access to the strait will be lost. The rest of the country will come later. The Houthi plan is to control the whole of Yemen.”Taiz has become the new frontline in the war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces after the Houthis launched a military campaign last month to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast, ending four years of relative calm in Yemen after aUN-brokered ceasefire froze the frontlines in 2022.He said existing intelligence showed the Houthis were already seeking to control parts of the south, including the former Soviet camp at al-Sabiha, in the Lahij governorate, and eventually Aden. “The Houthis bleed a lot,” he said, “they suffer a lot, but they always want quickly to use their gains or any collapse to gain more land.”With some Houthi leaders offering safe passage to armed groups to leave the city, he said for now the Houthis were allowing some fuel and commodities into the urban area of Taiz which houses more than 500,000 people, but in the meantime they were expanding their control of rural areas and smaller major cities.Saeed said: “In a matter of days there will be a full siege and they will try to enter the city. I know the Houthis. They will show some flexibility until they are ready to control. It will be much worse than the siege of 2015. It will be catastrophic.”He described Taiz as a modern democratic city untied to tribal culture, and predicted the Houthis would try to impose their Zaydi education, financial and tax systems very quickly, but the citizens would continue to resist. “The loss of Taiz would have a very significant symbolic impact on the idea of the modern state in Yemen and of resisting the Houthi project which relies on tribal networks and extremist religious education.”View image in fullscreenDisplaced Yemeni families from al-Kadha, west of Taiz, at al-Akdaf refugee camp toward the end of last month.Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/APSaeed admitted Taiz only had light weapons and the government had not been prepared for the loss of the west coast, allowing the Houthis to attack Taiz from four different axes.“We have good troops,” he said, “but the problem is the coordination. We needed more communication between the National Shield Forces, National Resistance Forces and the Giants Brigades. It’s been a wake-up call inside the government and the army because not enough happened between the truce of 2022 and the restart of the fighting this year to reorganise the troops. The Houthi ideology solely is to fight.”He added: “I hope now that the knife has come to our neck, and the Houthis represent a critical threat, the priority would be to come together to defeat the Houthis, and then to discuss other demands and guarantees.”The exiled leader of the southern secessionist force, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, on Tuesday called for a mobilisation of southern troops against the Houthis, but coupled this with a demand for a referendum on secession within two years. He brought tens of thousands on to the streets in support on Wednesday, but his return would be a bitter pill for Riyadh to swallow.Saeed said it was not a coincidence that the Houthi attack along the Red Sea coast in September had come when Iran was under heavy pressure.“Its airplanes and airports cannot operate, 90% of the oil was coming out of Hormuz. That is why they attacked the Saudi east-to-west pipelines. The Houthis, by talking about a Saudi blockade, have found a reason to hit the Saudi oil installations, airports and they want to do it now because the only thing Iran can do is to keep expanding the consequences of the war for America.”He said Houthi military capability and negotiating power had been transformed over the last decade leading to its ability to target key sites in Saudi Arabia now. “In 2017, the Houthis had nothing but blind missiles to fire at us that missed their targets.” By 2020, he said intelligence existed that Iranian experts operating from the Houthi capital Sana’a were training Houthis and in December of that year, in a devastatingly effective attack, they fired ballistic missiles at Aden airport. The attack left 28 dead and 107 injured, including Saeed himself, newly installed as prime minister. The missile travelled 186 miles (299km).He explained: “We thought even then they did not have that many missiles, but since then the Iranians have expanded their manufacturing lines.” In January 2022, using missiles, the Houthis attacked Abu Dhabi oil tanker trucks more than 900 miles away.In October 2022, inside Yemen, they struck the Nushayma oil terminal and al-Dhabba port, severely damaging government finances. By the time the US attacked Yemen in March 2025, he said “it was clear the Houthis had dozens of targeted missiles, land sea missiles and drones. They had become a unified front with Iran, and developed their missile base.”He warned: “This is a new era of radical terrorism. It is not the old chaotic one of Isis and al-Qaida. It is semi-state actors and militias threatening powerful states with cheap technologies, and smuggled third-party components. The way Iran has invested in the Houthis could become a model for threatening navigation elsewhere. It is a new model of war, without traditional armies, needing different air defences. Gulf countries have to reshape and rethink their defences”.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricaDrones (military)Saudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthi missiles strike Yemen presidential palace, killing five | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Attack was the first on Aden’s Al-Maashiq palace ⁠in the latest fighting between ​the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Attack was the first on Aden’s Al-Maashiq palace ⁠in the latest fighting between ​the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia
Content: Smoke billows from the presidential palace following an attack by the Houthis, according to government officials, in Aden, Yemen, on Thursday.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke billows from the presidential palace following an attack by the Houthis, according to government officials, in Aden, Yemen, on Thursday.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersYemenHouthi missiles strike Yemen presidential palace, killing fiveAttack was the first on Aden’s Al-Maashiq palace ⁠in the latest fighting between ​the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi ArabiaGuardian staff and agenciesThu 15 Oct 2026 20.27 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’sHouthisfired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing five people, the government said, as the Saudi-led coalition listed dozens of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure in ⁠recent weeks.The attack was the first on Aden’s Al-Maashiq palace ⁠in the current conflict between ​the Iran-aligned Houthis andSaudi Arabia. The palace is the seat of Yemen’s Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government.Yemen’s prime minister, Shaya al-Zindani, ⁠and cabinet members were safe following the attack, Yemeni information minister Moammar al-Eryani said. Witnesses told Reuters they heard loud booms near the palace. Yemen’s cabinet said the attack involved missiles and drones.Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthroughRead moreYemen’s health minister, Qasim Buhaibeh, said five people were killed and 16 wounded in the attack, with casualties including guards and civilian employees.Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said its fighters had bombed what he described as ​the Saudi military operations headquarters in Aden, as part of the group’s declared policy ‌of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.Agence France-Presse reported that a Yemeni government minister said on condition of anonymity that the palace attack had hit a command centre for the Saudi-led coalition. The official added that the command centre was hit by three missiles, and the headquarters of the coalition forces at the presidential complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.Fighting has escalated between the Houthi rebels and a Saudi-led coalition as part of clashes linked to the US and Israeli war onIran, and aid agencies have warned of rapidly worsening conditions in Yemen.The clashes have complicated efforts to end the wider Iran war and further rattled global markets as Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s top oil exporters, faces repeated attacks. Regional aviation is affected, too, as the rebels have warned airlines about their use of Saudi airspace for attacks. Thousands of flights across the kingdom have been disrupted.The UN security council issued a joint statement on Thursday condemning the “escalatory” attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia, including “reckless strikes” on Riyadh’s airport.The Saudi capital’s international airport has been targeted by strikes 20 times since the beginning of the month, with an attack last weekend killing 13 people and wounding more than 300.In a joint statement shared by the security council “condemned in the strongest terms continued and escalatory Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” as well as “continued Houthi attacks and threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab [strait]”.Earlier on Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted a cruise missile over the province of Medina. Flightradar24, a tracking platform, said dozens of flights were canceled or delayed at Jeddah’s airport.The coalition statement did not assign blame for the attack. The Houthis’ military spokesperson denied the rebels carried it out. The group previously pledged not to attack airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia.Saudi Arabia also said it destroyed a drone over the country’s eastern province, a major oil-producing region, and intercepted a drone in Khamis Mushait, near a major military airbase.Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia said theheadquarters of the oil giant Saudi Aramco were hit by Houthi attacks, and reported damage to the building.Inside Yemen, the fighting has revived a devastating civil war after four years of relative calm. One focus of alarm is the Houthi-besieged city of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where residents were running short of basic necessities.With Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaIranUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s Cockroach Janta party leader detained amid crackdown on protests | India | The Guardian
description: Abhijeet Dipke was arrested before planned anti-government demonstrations in Delhi
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Abhijeet Dipke was arrested before planned anti-government demonstrations in Delhi
Content: Abhijit Dipke called on supporters to protest after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow Cockroach Janta party leaders.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersView image in fullscreenAbhijit Dipke called on supporters to protest after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow Cockroach Janta party leaders.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersIndiaIndia’s Cockroach Janta party leader detained amid crackdown on protestsAbhijeet Dipke was arrested before planned anti-government demonstrations in DelhiHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiFri 16 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in centralDelhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of themost substantial challengesto the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused ofoverseeing a revisionof India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.11:32India’s Cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown - The LatestThe authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They weresentenced to five daysin jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and showNarendra Modi“that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streetsRead moreDespite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.Explore more on these topicsIndiaNarendra ModiSouth and central AsiaProtestDelhiActivismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarks | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Alan Feeney, who sat on Solihull and Birmingham councils, said there was ‘no excuse’ for his comments
Author: Sinéad Campbell
Headline: Alan Feeney, who sat on Solihull and Birmingham councils, said there was ‘no excuse’ for his comments
Content: Alan Feeney was revealed to have made racist comments about Asian homeowners in secretly recorded footage.Photograph: ITVView image in fullscreenAlan Feeney was revealed to have made racist comments about Asian homeowners in secretly recorded footage.Photograph: ITVReform UKReform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarksAlan Feeney, who sat on Solihull and Birmingham councils, said there was ‘no excuse’ for his commentsSinéad CampbellFri 16 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlan Feeney has resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after backlash overracist comments that were capturedin an undercover investigation.In aFacebookpost on Friday, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”Earlier this week, anITVinvestigation revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.Feeney has apologised for his comments. “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said,” he wrote in a Facebook post.“The comments do not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report. These are communities I have supported countless times in my personal and professional life over many years, many of whom I have been lucky enough to call friends.”Earlier this year, Feeney won seats in the Shard End ward ofBirminghamcity council and the Castle Bromwich ward of Solihull metropolitan borough council, and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull.Following the ITV investigation, which is part of a longer series onReform UK, Feeney announced on Facebook that he was leaving Reform for “personal reasons”, but kept his seats as an independent councillor before resigning.In a Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “Byelections will be held on a timescale laid out by those councils in the due course. I hope that in time these councils, and the communities they serve can heal and move on.”Secretly filmed footage showed Feeney making racist remarks alongside two other Reform candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, while canvassing during May’s local elections. Both Campbell and Whelan have also resigned after the fallout from the investigation.Nigel Farage has repeatedly pledged to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots”. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.The clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Feeney calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.In a Facebook post Feeney wrote: “I understand that my words have caused hurt and anger, particularly among those from the communities I serve. For that, I am deeply sorry. I will be undertaking intensive personal analysis to understand how these sentiments could have taken root, and ensure they can never do so again.”Alan Feeney and Reform UK have been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsReform UKLocal politicsHate crimeBirminghamLocal governmentITV NewsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Healey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issue | Heathrow third runway | The Guardian
description: Chancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Chancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’
Content: Heathrow has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenHeathrow has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAHeathrow third runwayHealey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issueChancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’Heather Stewartin BangkokFri 16 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow despite the prime minister declining to back it.Healey’s predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves, put approval of the long-planned runway at the heart of her “growth speech” last year, saying it would“make Britain the world’s best-connected place to do business”.However, since arriving in No 10 in July,Andy Burnhamhas ducked the issue of whether the runway should go ahead, suggesting it should be “a matter for London and Londoners”.A recent Sunday Times report suggested the prime minister had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was “unconvinced” by arguments for the megaproject.Asked for his views in Bangkok this week, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation, which recently closed. He appeared to strike a markedly more positive note than Burnham, however.“I think in recent decades, and this is true in Heathrow and airports right across the UK, that they have been a big part of jobs and growth. And the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth,” he said.Healey has insisted economic growth is his and Burnham’s “number one mission” in government.Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support.“Our shareholders would like to do this,” he said earlier this week. “They do think that things are taking a long time, and so far they have decided to be OK with that … But of course we cannot wait for ever.”The airport’s owners include Qatar’s investment authority; the French private equity firm Ardian; Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission.Healey voted in favour of the third runway when the question was put to the House of Commons in 2018.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe chancellor was in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund annual meetings but has returned toLondonto put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.The UK was praised by the IMF this week for taking action to cut its deficit, while other large economies have opted not to do so. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged Healey to “stay the course” in his budget.On Thursday, official figuresshowedthe UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August.Explore more on these topicsHeathrow third runwayHeathrow airportAirline industryJohn HealeyAndy BurnhamAir transportTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Well-known individual’ tries to secure permanent injunction against Guardian and ITN | The Guardian | The Guardian
description: Lawyers tell high court that client could harm himself if serious allegations against him are made public
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Lawyers tell high court that client could harm himself if serious allegations against him are made public
Content: The Guardian’s investigation concerned serious allegations about an individual’s conduct over a period of years, a judge said.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s investigation concerned serious allegations about an individual’s conduct over a period of years, a judge said.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe Guardian‘Well-known individual’ tries to secure permanent injunction against Guardian and ITNLawyers tell high court that client could harm himself if serious allegations against him are made publicMichael SavageMedia editorFri 16 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA “well-known individual” is trying to secure a permanent injunction against the Guardian andITNto prevent them from publishing details of serious allegations made against him.At a high court hearing on Friday, the claimant’s legal team said there was a serious risk that he could harm himself should the allegations be made public.They have told the court publishing the claims would breach articles two and three of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), the former of which relates to the right to life.A trial is due to take place later this month to examine whether an injunction preventing reporting of the allegations should be made.An earlier ruling by the judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said the case included two media organisations that had “conducted a journalistic investigation into allegations concerning the claimant’s conduct towards a number of individuals”.“The proposed publications concern serious allegations about the claimant’s conduct over a period of years,” it stated.“The matters alleged are said to have arisen in a variety of professional and personal contexts.”The judge explained that the claimant had given a broad denial of the allegations which the defendants propose to publish.In a submission to the court, the claimant’s legal team, led by Sara Mansoori KC, said he was “a well-known individual who suffers from very serious mental health problems”.The submission stated he had attempted to take his own life on two occasions and remained seriously ill.ITN and the Guardian are opposing the injunction sought.In their own written submission to the court, their legal team set out their position on the questions that fall to be decided at trial.In a skeleton argument, they said the relevant duties under the ECHR were not triggered and should not prevent publication, and in any event, mitigations could be put in place to protect the claimant.Nicklin said on Friday that it was important to have the proceedings as open as possible, adding: “This case is going to be controversial either way it is decided.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsThe GuardianNational newspapersNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesITNnewsShareReuse this content

title: Met police investigating row over founding of Your Party | UK news | The Guardian
description: Inquiry said to have been launched after force received report ‘relating to alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database’
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Inquiry said to have been launched after force received report ‘relating to alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database’
Content: Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana founded the leftwing Your Party in 2025.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenJeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana founded the leftwing Your Party in 2025.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyUK newsMet police investigating row over founding of Your PartyInquiry said to have been launched after force received report ‘relating to alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database’Alexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice are carrying out a criminal investigation into a row over the founding of Your Party, which split the leftwing party as it was established last year.A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan police said they had launched an investigation after they received a report in September 2025 “relating to the alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database”, the Politico website reported.Your Party was founded in summer 2025 by the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and the former Labour MP Zarah Sultana, both of whom now sit as Your Party MPs in the House of Commons.But relations between the different factions in the party have been strained since its creation in July last year. That September Sultana revealed a new membership portal on X, and encouraged members to become paying members for £55.Corbyn described the site as a “false membership system” and told supporters to ignore an email requesting funds. Sultana said her only aim had been to “safeguard the grassroots involvement that is essential to building this party”, and later accused the party of being run by a“sexist boys’ club”.Officers had now arrested a man on suspicion of an offence under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act, a police spokesperson told Politico. The man was released pending further inquiries and has not been charged.Officers also previously interviewed a woman in her 30s under caution in connection with the same investigation. The spokesperson added: “The investigation continues.” The police spokesperson did not name any political party in their statement, and the spokesperson did not confirm which political party their investigation was related to.Sources told the Guardian that the investigation was linked to the long-running dispute connected to the establishment of Your Party. Neither the man arrested nor the woman interviewed by police are MPs and neither have been charged with an offence. Neither Corbyn nor Sultana were accused of wrongdoing, Politico reported.In January, it emerged that the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) advised the party that while it was taking no further action over the Your Party membership portal launch,it may have involved “serious criminal activity”and should be referred to the police.A Your Party spokesperson said: “It would not be appropriate to comment any further about ongoing police investigations.”They also said: “We can reassure our members and supporters that our systems are secure and that this was an isolated incident.”Your Party has struggled to make a widespread national impact since it was founded, while the Green party of England and Wales, rebranded as an eco-socialist party, has seen its membership quadruple.In February, Corbyn won a comprehensive victory to become thede facto leader of the leftwing startup party. He said Your Party would work with the Green party and others to push for a “coordinated left-flank offensive” against Reform and Labour. Sultana was also voted on to the party’s leadership committee under its collective leadership model.Corbyn-backed candidates took 14 of the 24 available places on the party’s central executive committee (CEC). Sultana-backed candidates took seven of the seats and three went to independents.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK national security adviser under pressure over wife’s comment on supporting Palestine Action | Palestine Action | The Guardian
description: Author Sarah Helm, married to Jonathan Powell, wrote to back novelist Sally Rooney’s support of proscribed direct action group
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Author Sarah Helm, married to Jonathan Powell, wrote to back novelist Sally Rooney’s support of proscribed direct action group
Content: The author Sarah Helm is a former Sunday Times journalist and diplomatic editor at the Independent, and spent many years covering the Middle East.Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe author Sarah Helm is a former Sunday Times journalist and diplomatic editor at the Independent, and spent many years covering the Middle East.Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianPalestine ActionUK national security adviser under pressure over wife’s comment on supporting Palestine ActionAuthor Sarah Helm, married to Jonathan Powell, wrote to back novelist Sally Rooney’s support of proscribed direct action groupRobyn VinterandRachel HallFri 16 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, is under pressure to distance himself from a comment made by his wife, the award-winning writerSarah Helm, in support of Palestine Action.The post was made in defence of the critically acclaimed Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who said she had been forcedto pull her books from shelvesin the UK after pledging proceeds from their sales to Palestine Action.Helm, a former Sunday Times journalist and diplomatic editor at the Independent who spent many years covering the Middle East, wrote on X indicating support for the direct action group, which was proscribed last year.Under terror laws, this could constitute a criminal offence, carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years in prison. The ban has so far resulted in more than 3,700 arrests for backing the group, with more than 2,250 people formally charged as terrorists.In response to comments by the broadcaster Adam Boulton that Rooney’s support for Palestine was “anti-Jewish”, Helm wrote: “God help us authors who support Palestine andPalestine Action. Sounds like Adam would have all our books swept off the shelves in a jiffy.”Police said the post was “in the process of being assessed” to determine whether an investigation was required.Downing Street distanced itself from Helm’s post on Friday, with a spokesperson saying: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”Helm’s works include a bookabout the women imprisoned by the Nazis at the Ravensbrück concentration camp, andLoyalty, a play about the Iraq war, inspired by her husband’s decade as the chief of staff to the then prime minister, Tony Blair.The author, who is writing a book about Gaza, married Powell in 2007. He was appointed in 2024 as a national security adviser under Keir Starmer.View image in fullscreenJonathan Powell.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesAccording to government guidance, being married to a suspected or convicted terrorist would normally result in the revocation of security clearance. Under the vetting framework for a job as national security adviser, being married to someone tied to a proscribed terrorist organisation is viewed as creating an automatic, unmitigated national security risk.Responding to questions about Powell’s position after his wife’s comments, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”A spokesperson for Defend Our Juries, a free speech group which supports the right for people to protest peacefully, thanked Helm for “defying this absurdly authoritarian ban”.“How can Andy Burnham’s government possibly defend this banin the supreme court next monthwhen his own national security adviser’s wife has openly defied it? This unprecedented attack on free speech in our country is plainly unsustainable,” they said. “We know of 36 people who have been arrested and had their homes raided for similarly expressing support for Palestine Action on social media.“We hope Sarah will not face the same treatment for standing up for free speech and Palestinian lives. But her defiance further exposes the absurdity of a ban that cannot be enforced against everyone who challenges it. There are simply too many of us who will continue to defy this unjust law until the government is forced to see sense and abandon it.”However, the Campaign Against Antisemitism called for Helm to “face the full force of the law”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA spokesperson said: “This is gobsmacking. Clearly, the police need to investigate and Sarah Helm must face the full force of the law, just like others who appear to express support for any proscribed terrorist organisation.“But this raises extremely serious questions forJonathan Powelland the government. Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country’s national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post.”A Met Police spokesperson said: “We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action. It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required.View image in fullscreenSally Rooney has been supported in her stance by an open letter signed by hundreds of writers.Photograph: Kalpesh Lathigra/ FaberHundreds of writers have signed an open letter in support of Rooney, whose books includeNormal PeopleandConversations With Friends, warning that “a country that bans its writers for speaking out is not a free country”.The letter has been signed by 419 novelists, poets, editors and illustrators including Ali Smith, Kamila Shamsie, Robert Macfarlane, Daisy Johnson, Eliza Clark, Jeanette Winterson, Alice Oseman, Derek Landy, Louise O’Neill, AM Dassu and Nikesh Shukla.The letter states: “As authors, illustrators, poets, and editors, we stand withSally Rooneyand Faber Books, and condemn a government whose actions, and inactions, have led to her books being pulled from sale in the UK.“Writers already face book bans worldwide and at home. It is unconscionable that a government can now effectively ban a single author for protesting that government’s own conflation of protest with terrorism. What future governments might do with this power should frighten us all.”Rooney said she had made the decision to withdraw from the UK market with her publisher, Faber, after learning that passing earnings on to her for the sale of her books in the UK could constitute a serious criminal offence. In a letter shared with the Guardian, Rooney said she was “wholly prepared to accept the consequences”. Faber will continue to sell Rooney’s books in other countries.Explore more on these topicsPalestine ActionJonathan PowellUK security and counter-terrorismSally RooneyProtestFreedom of speechActivismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brush fires set homes ablaze in southern California as it braces for more hot weather | California | The Guardian
description: Hot, windy weather stokes fires in southern California as utilities shut off power to 150,000 customers as precaution
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: Hot, windy weather stokes fires in southern California as utilities shut off power to 150,000 customers as precaution
