Content: Firefighters work to save structures on Via La Mirada during the Norte fire in San Clemente.Photograph: Paul Bersebach/The Orange County Register/APView image in fullscreenFirefighters work to save structures on Via La Mirada during the Norte fire in San Clemente.Photograph: Paul Bersebach/The Orange County Register/APCaliforniaBrush fires set homes ablaze in southern California as it braces for more hot weatherHot, windy weather stokes fires in southern California with mandatory evacuation orders in place for manyLois Beckett,Gabrielle Canon,Eline Gordtsin Dana Point, and agenciesFri 16 Oct 2026 19.21 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 09.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fast-moving fire spread into neighborhoods in southernCaliforniaon Fridayas the region braces for more hot, windy weather that will amplify fire dangers through Saturday.Several structures could be seen ablaze in video footage captured by local news helicopters as firefighters worked to wrangle the more than 465 acreNorte fire, which erupted in Orange county on Friday.At least six homes were destroyed, according to Mark Backoff, a division chief with the Orange county fire authority (OCFA). “Due to topography features and the weather, this fire rapidly grew,” he said in a video update Friday afternoon. “We continue to be engaged in the firefight and we have additional resources coming.”Photos taken by the local TV news station showed a row of houses at the end of a cul-de-sacreduced to blackened debris. Others were coated red by fire retardant.Roughly 16,000 people in the coastal communities of San Juan Capistrano and San Clemente were under mandatory evacuation orders by Friday afternoon. Flames aggressively ripped across the brush-covered hillsides, shrouding the sky in thick smoke. Sirens wailed through the city streets, as the hum of helicopters and aircraft echoed from above.Nine schools in the area dismissed early, as the OCFA urged all residents under the order to leave quickly.In a Friday evening press conference, officials said two firefighters were injured battling the blaze due to heat exhaustion. While the fire continued to burn out of control; authorities said the objective was to limit its further spread and keep the fire within its current footprint.Just to the south, a blaze dubbed the Henderson fire, which erupted in San Diego Marine Corps training base Camp Pendleton on Thursday, swept across more than 2,000 acres by Friday afternoonEvacuation orders in place after wildfire breaks out in California - loopVideos of the incident shared by the California department of forestry and fire protectionshowed a wall of flamesthat thrashed in the strong winds alongside the Interstate 5. The major highway was closed in both directions by California Highway Patrol for part of the afternoon,as plumes of thick black smoke clouded visibility. The blaze was 20% contained by Friday evening.A blaze in Malibu, west ofLos Angeles, covered roughly 146 acres and was 39% contained on Friday evening. Evacuation orders and warnings for a large swathe of the Santa Monica Mountains were still in effect.Facing daytime highs of up to 92F (33C) with wind gusts reaching up to 65mph, fire officials said “crews will continue to protect structures and build containment” in a Fridaymorning update, adding that fire progression and flare ups could occur under increasing winds.More than 7,200 structures remained under threat, but none have been reported damaged or destroyed by the Bryson fire.Map of the Bryson and Peak fires in the LA area that have prompted evacuation orders and warnings in the area.Lindsey Horvath, the Los Angeles county supervisor, thanked firefighters “who held the line to make sure that despite these challenging winds, no lives or structures were put in harm’s way” by the blaze. Local residents were asked to keep roads clear to make it easier for emergency responders to operate.There were “only minor injuries” to the more than 400 firefighters working to contain the Bryson blaze, Anthony Morrone, the Los Angeles fire chief, said during a press conference held on Friday morning.The blazes broke out during a high wind event that has increased fire risks across southernCalifornia. Dry, warm and gusty north-east winds known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior of southern California toward the coast and offshore, could continue through Saturday, according to the National Weather Service, and the potential for extreme fire behavior and rapid spread may still rise.As the firefight continues, California governor Gavin Newsom secured a Fire Management Assistance Grant from the Federal Emergency Management agency to help support crews working to suppress Orange county’s Norte fire.“By securing this federal assistance, we are ensuring our local and state partners have the critical resources they need,” he said in an issued statement.In anticipation of the extreme weather event, California’s office of emergency services also pre-positoned resources statewide.View image in fullscreenFirefighters battle the Bryson fire, a wind-driven wildfire in the hills east of Malibu, California, on Thursday.Photograph: David Swanson/Reuters“It’s a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.Fire hazards typically rise in southern California during this time of year, and risks are expected to remain high into November. If there aren’t significant rains, they could extend longer.Evacuations issued as multiple wildfires ignite in hot, windy CaliforniaRead moreBecause some of the state’s worstwildfiresin recent years have been sparked by power equipment, utilities proactively shut off power to more than 150,000 customers across the state.In Los Angeles, the mayor, Karen Bass, who faced criticism for her city’s response to deadly fires in 2025, directed the fire department to deploy personnel and equipment ahead of the winds. The fire department also requested assistance from the state’s office of emergency services.Schoenfeld said the Santa Ana winds are not going to be as strong as those that fueled a deadly firestorm in early 2025, that destroyed thousands of homes and killed more than 30 people when gusts reached up to 100mph.A map showing the Henderson fireBut she still urged residents to be ready.“We are still in red flag conditions through 8pm [Saturday] evening,” Horvathsaid. “It’s important that we stay vigilant and stay prepared.”Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaCalifornia wildfiresUS weatherWest CoastWildfiresLos AngelesExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Shooter in fatal Bend, Oregon, school shooting was former student there | Oregon | The Guardian
description: One teacher and three children killed after Griffin J John II, 16, barged into elementary school and began shooting
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: One teacher and three children killed after Griffin J John II, 16, barged into elementary school and began shooting
Content: A person places flowers at a makeshift memorial to the victims in Bend on Friday.Photograph: Haven Daley/APView image in fullscreenA person places flowers at a makeshift memorial to the victims in Bend on Friday.Photograph: Haven Daley/APOregonShooter in fatal Bend, Oregon, school shooting was former student thereOne teacher and three children killed after Griffin J John II, 16, barged into elementary school and began shootingOregon elementary school shooting: what we know so farDani Anguianoin Bend, Oregon,Uwa Ede-Osifo,Anna BettsandAbené ClaytonFri 16 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 16-year-old who barged into an elementary school in Bend,Oregon, and unleashed a barrage of gunfire that killed a teacher and three children was a former student at Silver Rail elementary, officials confirmed in a Friday press conference.The heavily armed shooter, identified as Griffin J John II, climbed over a fence and onto the school’s property before shooting through a set of locked doors to enter the building.The shooter, a former special needs learner, beelined toward a special education classroom left of the entrance doors, firing as many as 15 rounds.All of the victims from Thursday’s shooting were in that room: five-year-old Rhoam Summer, two other students, aged eight and 11, whom authorities have not identified, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert.Lambert, from central Oregon, had regarded Silver Rail as a “dream job”, her family said in a statement read by police. “She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs.”The shooting also left a seven-year-old in serious condition, police said, and 54-year-old educator Becky Drury with serious, but non-life-threatening, injuries.A 36-year-old Silver Rail parent,identifiedby relatives as Kaylub Giamanco, heard the gunshots as he was driving by and entered the school.He saw an educator in a scuffle with the shooter, at which point he intervened, shooting and killing the teen.Police say the teacher threw her phone at the shooter before tackling him, as she fought to disarm him.Oregon elementary school shooting: what we know so farRead more“She almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” Bend police chief Mike Krantz said.Authorities recovered 44 more rounds of ammunition in the shooter’s backpack.Police have not offered a motive, citing the continuing investigation.Candlelight vigils and memorials have sprung up around Bend, as the city has been thrust into a gruesome, but tragically familiar American story.Outside the school on Friday, a steady stream of people arrived to deliver flowers in front of the campus.They left dozens of bouquets, teddy bears, Minnie Mouse stuffed animals and a pumpkin. Most people stopped by for just a moment to pay their respects. Some sat, and parents held their children and cried together.It was eerily quiet at a time when the campus would normally be teeming with activity, said Joe Camarlinghi, father of a third grader at the school.View image in fullscreenChildren draw with chalk during a candlelight vigil in Bend on Thursday.Photograph: Eli Imadali/Oregon Public Broadcasting/APFabiola Caseres, who runs a local preschool and came by to deliver flowers, said the sadness was palpable all around the close-knit city.“It just feels so heavy,” she said. “Everybody is looking like deer in the headlights. It’s so sad, and you can’t stop thinking about the kids. They’re supposed to come home.”Thursday’s events mark the most deadly school shooting since the September 2024 mass killing at Apalachee high school in Georgia, where a 14-year-old shooter killed two teachers and two students.Although a motive in this school shooting remains unclear, the age of the shooter points to a troubling pattern.Some of the most recent high-profile shootings on and off school campuses have been carried out by teenagers and young adults, many of whom are a part of nihilistic online communities where posters praise, and seek to emulate, prior shooters like those who carried out attacks at Columbine high school, in Christchurch in New Zealand and at Virginia Tech.In May, two teenagers who met and were radicalized online shot and killed three people at a mosque in San Diego before shooting themselves. In their manifesto, theyexplicitly named the Apalachee high school shootersas their inspiration.View image in fullscreenA woman cries during a vigil for the victims in Bend on Thursday evening.Photograph: Eli Imadali/Oregon Public Broadcasting/APThe city of Bend, home to about100,000 residents, held acandlelit vigilon Thursday night. Hundreds of people gathered in Bend’s Drake Park as the sun set. Oregon governor Tina Kotek and Bend mayor Melanie Keblerattendedthe vigil.“There is power and love in this park tonight,” Kotek said. “On behalf of everyone who lives in Oregon, I am so sorry for what you are experiencing today. No parent, no family, no community should have to have this kind of day.”All schools in Bend and La Pine, a neighboring city,were closedon Friday.Explore more on these topicsOregonUS school shootingsWest CoastUS gun controlnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump in Georgia falsely claims election of Jon Ossoff was illegitimate | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President appears at rally for struggling Mike Collins, dismisses critics and touts ‘most successful’ two-year run
Author: George Chidi
Headline: President appears at rally for struggling Mike Collins, dismisses critics and touts ‘most successful’ two-year run
Content: Trump speaks at a campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia. Trump is campaigning for Mike Collins for US Senate and Rick Jackson for governor.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump speaks at a campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia. Trump is campaigning for Mike Collins for US Senate and Rick Jackson for governor.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump in Georgia falsely claims election of Jon Ossoff was illegitimatePresident appears at rally for struggling Mike Collins, dismisses critics and touts ‘most successful’ two-year runGeorge Chidiin Dalton, GeorgiaFri 16 Oct 2026 18.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 21.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt a rally in north Georgia,Donald Trumpagain claimed that the 2020 election in Georgia was fraudulent, alleging that the election of US senator Jon Ossoff was illegitimate.Ossoff, who faces US congressman Mike Collins in November, does not represent Georgia’s values, Trump said.“And he was never elected,” Trump added.Ossoff has maintained a consistent lead against Collins, with most recent polling showing him with a nine-point lead against his Republican rival.Trump claimed he was about to complete the “most successful” two-year run of a president in history, touting stock market gains, low unemployment and poverty rates and the establishment of “Trump accounts” for newborns. Trump again said that American voters would receive a $5,000 government check if Republicans hold the US House of Representatives, claiming that $21tn in foreign manufacturing investments pledged on his watch would offset the trillion-dollar cost.Most of those pledges remain unfulfilled.Trump also touted his immigration record and the overthrow of the Venezuelan government.“Forty-eight hours, and that war was done,” Trump said.He described the early days of the war on Iran from the perspective of Oval Office meetings and damage reports, particularly of strikes against Iranian leadership.“They’ll blow up Israel, they’ll blow up the Middle East,” Trump said of Iran and the imperatives of launching attacks. “Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president.”The Iran war has caused a spike in gasoline and diesel prices. Trump was dismissive of critics citing the increased cost of living on his watch, describing the term “affordability” as Democratic propaganda.“In the past 17 months, zero illegal aliens have been admitted into the United States,” he said.An undocumented migrant is rarely “admitted” in any official way.Trump returned to his regular themes at the rally, which began at about 2pm. About 1,200 people packed grandstands at Dalton municipal airport. Trump took the stage at about 4.20pm, 80 minutes after his scheduled start, with about 300 people standing unshaded in the Georgia afternoon sun. His supporters were undaunted.“Donald Trump is the greatest president of all time,” said Tracy Spencer of Chattanooga, Tennessee, as she awaited the president’s arrival in Marine One. Asked how she addresses the increasing criticism of the president from disillusioned conservatives, she scoffed.“Well, none of my friends and family are expressing that to me, because they know better,” she said. “But I have heard the rumors that there are some people that think that, and I would say to those people that growth doesn’t happen overnight and that there are growing pains.”Trump obliquely discussed his administration’s attacks on anti-discrimination policies he terms “DEI” while describing the “handsomeness” of a US soldier he encountered at the White House.“Everything is based on merit,” Trump said. “I really have my difficulties with the supreme court, but … our country now is based on merit.”Two protesters briefly unfurled a banner with an anti-ICE slogan. They were hustled out of the grandstands quickly by security. The assault of a protester in Ohio by Trump supporters in the stands on Monday was not repeated.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS politicsJon OssoffGeorgiaUS SenateUS CongressDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Family of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventable | Georgia | The Guardian
description: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after reportedly ‘passing out’ and falling off Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia while beside niece
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after reportedly ‘passing out’ and falling off Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia while beside niece
Content: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem in an undated photo. Kariem died after he was thrown from his seat while riding a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday.Photograph: Kelvin Johnson/APView image in fullscreenHassan Jihad Ibn Kariem in an undated photo. Kariem died after he was thrown from his seat while riding a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday.Photograph: Kelvin Johnson/APGeorgiaFamily of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventableHassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after reportedly ‘passing out’ and falling off Goliath rollercoaster in GeorgiaMarina DunbarFri 16 Oct 2026 18.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe family of a man who was ejected from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park inGeorgiaanddiedhas publicly questioned whether the death could have been prevented.Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was riding the Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia nearAtlantaalongside his niece during a family trip to celebrate her birthday when he was thrown from the ride. His niece witnessed her uncle’s death, a relative told the Atlanta ABC News affiliateWSB-TV.“A large part of me does believe, you know, it was a freak accident, but the other part of me questions … could this have been prevented?” Joshua Nelson, Kariem’s brother-in-law, told the outlet.Nelson, whose daughter was seated beside Kariem, shared her account of the terrifying moments leading up to her uncle’s death.Man who died in Six Flags rollercoaster fall in Georgia was a father and educatorRead more“She said he fainted, or passed – her words were ‘he passed out,’” Nelson said. “And then they went up and down, up and down, up and down – and she said it went up again and his latch, I guess, snapped or came loose and he fell,” Nelson remarked.During the celebratory family outing, Kariem had expressed his excitement about riding the Goliath, which was one of his favorite attractions, according to Nelson.Nelson said that he hoped Kariem did not experience pain during his final moments.Kariem was an educator and a father to a 10-year-old daughter. According toAtlantapublic schools, Kariem started his career at Wesley International Academy as a technology teacher before being promoted to an information technology manager.Georgia authorities as of Friday werestill investigatingthe circumstances of Kariem’s death at Six Flags Over Georgia, which opened its gates Friday evening for the first time since the incident. Cobb county police department’s major crimes unit haslaunchedan investigation.Since Kariem’s death, Six Flagstemporarily closednine rollercoasters across six amusement parks around the US.Deaths such as Kariem’s are rare. But his death has prompted some to call for federal oversight of amusement parks, which in the US has been left to individual states, asthe New York Times reported.Explore more on these topicsGeorgiaAtlantaTheme parksnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People’s dignity, and democracy, is at stake’: meet the economist ditching ideology for reality | Economics | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Isabella Weber prescribes a common-sense solution to poverty, inequality and fascism – making life’s essentials affordable for all
Author: Michael Segalov
Headline: Exclusive: Isabella Weber prescribes a common-sense solution to poverty, inequality and fascism – making life’s essentials affordable for all
Content: In Anti-Fascist Economics, Isabella Weber calls on governments to defeat fascism by making life’s necessities more affordable.Photograph: Steffen Roth/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIn Anti-Fascist Economics, Isabella Weber calls on governments to defeat fascism by making life’s necessities more affordable.Photograph: Steffen Roth/The GuardianEconomicsInterview‘People’s dignity, and democracy, is at stake’: meet the economist ditching ideology for realityMichael SegalovExclusive: Isabella Weber prescribes a common-sense solution to poverty, inequality and fascism – making life’s essentials affordable for allFri 16 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 08.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe trouble with economists, Isabella Weber believes, is they do not behave like dentists. They obsess over ideological purity and are inflexible when searching for solutions, regardless of society’s symptoms. Dentists have no such pretensions – patients have little patience for dogma when in insufferable pain.John Maynard Keynes, Weber clarifies in the canteen of theWissenschaftskolleg zu Berlin(Berlin’s Institute for Advanced Study), was the first to draw this dental comparison – and she is running with it. As she sees it, the symptoms could not be more severe. “The status quo for the majority is entirely unbearable,” while extreme inequality and corporate concentration has reached levels “simply incompatible with democracy” worldwide. This is exacerbated by a climate crisis that “generates massive windfall profits” for big business as the “ecological foundations of our lives disintegrate”. All the while the far right is making hay.This analysis echoes much mainstream liberal and left-leaning thinking. But Weber is concerned that her peers in the economic establishment act as if they are oblivious. “What’s common sense to most people is not to economists,” she says, and as such our economic system has “promised but not delivered”. She reels offdisturbing statisticsthat highlight the growing disparities between haves and have nots. “As economists, we should do better. People’s dignity, and democracy, is at stake.”In progressive circles, Weber, 38, is quickly becoming one of the most sought-after economists of her generation. An associate professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and an associate at Harvard’s Fairbank Center, she advises policymakers in the US, Europe and Latin America. She popularised the term “greedflation” to describe profiteering during recent cost of living crises. Her new book,Anti-Fascist Economics, is the culmination of years of research into inequality and inflation, and a lifelong commitment to fighting fascism. As she writes: “If we understand economics as the study of the material foundations of society, then economics is key to averting the catastrophes in front of us.”View image in fullscreenIsabella Weber in Berlin’s Institute for Advanced Study in September.Photograph: Steffen Roth/The GuardianWeber is calling on fellow economists to “abandon ideology” and develop a “big tent economic policy” that can counter anascendant far right. Their gains, she argues, are not the result of a particularly compelling offer, but a direct consequence of traditional political parties refusing to acknowledge the endemic hardship facing their constituents, and the absence of a coherent economic vision from progressives, liberals and the centre right. “Currently, only the extreme right is willing to say yes, something is broken, and a different present and future is possible,” Weber says. “We can’t leave an alternative to this dystopia to them.”In Anti-FascistEconomics, she pitches a solution: make life’s necessities affordable. That is housing, transport, food, water, energy, healthcare: the stuff humanity depends on. “Fascism is rising from frustration, born out of a crisis of livelihoods,” says Weber. “So, we need to reclaim these essentials now.”Progressive politicians are already heeding her instructions. At a meeting of city mayors last month, the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, outlined how Weber’s work, which he had followed for years, had informed his affordability agenda in the city: free buses, universal childcare, rent caps, public groceries. Weber has consulted with other US politicians – Elizabeth Warren, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders – and UK ministers including Ed Miliband. The speech of the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, to Labour conference last month was Weberesque in its messaging. “Homes. Water. Energy. Transport. Care. Broken up and sold off,” hedeclared from the lectern. “Economic control diminished by selling off essentials.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham’s Labour conference speech was distinctly Weberesque in its messaging.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersWhile it is a simple slogan, making the essentials affordable is a complex policy challenge. Each sector has unique properties, and functions differently from place to place. Weber argues that any and all levers should be pulled in pursuit of putting this floor under livelihoods, from novel approaches to centuries-old thinking. “The goal isn’t more state intervention,” she clarifies, “it’s just a tool, as are profits and markets to ensure affordability. In economics, we tend to have these overarching models and an inclination for silver bullets. I’m arguing not for universal solutions but nitty gritty detail.”Take food, for example. At every stage of the value chain from source to table, she is urging governments to identify and implement interventions to keep prices down. At one end, four multinationalscontrol between 70% and 90%of global grain trading (with profits that “thrive on volatility”). This does not optimise affordability. Her proposal? Create public buffer stock systems – publicly owned entities that can buy and sell grain into its market, not with the goal of maximising profits, but stabilising prices to protect producers and consumers. Keynes made this case a century ago.A global public option would be a diplomatic nightmare, so Weber champions an orthodontist’s approach. She advised the South African government to pool regional buying power. “If the African Union developed its own buffer stock system, already this joint procurement would get them better terms.” Then, when prices are low, it could purchase; during peaks, it could sell to stabilise its market and provide regional insulation to shocks.At the other end of the chain is retail. Weber cites the Mexican government’scanasta básicapolicy, through which retailers voluntarily cap the total price of a basket of two-dozen essential goods. In return, the government offers advantageous tariff rates and tax relief, “and at a weekly press conference lauds those who do a good job and calls out those who don’t”. In Mexico’s 2024 presidential election, the governing Morena party increased its vote share from 55% to 61%.View image in fullscreenZohran Mamdani has followed Weber’s work for years, informing his affordability agenda in the city.Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockThe environment sits at the core of Weber’s thinking: a policy that does not factor in climate is incompatible with her anti-fascist economics logic, she says. As Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor outline in theirnew book, End Times Fascism, powerful populists are embracing environmental destruction. “When these people say climate change is of no concern, they know it’s not true,” says Weber, “but they allow the planet to burn because they benefit from the fallout. If we don’t start acting effectively, significant parts of the global population will be sacrificed.”In her book, Weber argues that fossil fuel dependency fans the flames of fascism: “Keeping essentials tethered to fossil fuels [leaves] ordinary people exposed to the price volatility of oil and gas that generates the economic insecurity on which authoritarian politics feeds.”She is arguing for the stabilisation of a “basic allowance” of fossil fuels for individual consumption to ensure affordability, but warns that unless this happens alongside major public investment in green infrastructure, it is a zero-sum game. In 2022, publicly listed oil and gas companies raked in $916bn in global net income. “In research we conducted on the United States we showed 50% of those profits go to the top 1% of households. The bottom 50% of households only got a 1% share.”View image in fullscreenClaudia Sheinbaum, president of Mexico. Her Morena party increased its vote share after implementing acanasta básicapolicy.Photograph: Isaac Esquivel/EPA“People can’t afford things, see the rich get rich, and become angry,” says Weber. If profits stream into shareholder pockets, Weber argues, inequality will continue to propel the far right. “There are dynamics and patterns in economics,” says Weber, “but how we shape and steer them is a political question.”It is late August when we meet, just days before the Saxony-Anhalt state election in which Alternative für Deutschland (AFD) secured amilestone electoral victory. It is a “textbook example”, suggests Weber, of the far right’s success. Saxony-Anhalt is one of Germany’s poorest regions according to several metrics. “And with all its beautiful castles and villages,” says Weber, “it’s the perfect setting for the glorification of a mythical Germany of the past.” (This is one cornerstone of fascism, Weber suggests.)The AFD’s campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was “alles ist möglich” – everything is possible. As is often the case, the far right promises something better, while traditional parties of government offer stasis.Weber has been sitting on the CDU-led German government’scommission on reforming fiscal rules. Tasked with looking at mechanisms to allow higher levels of borrowing to fund public investment, it should have concluded last autumn. “I can’t say too much while it’s ongoing,” she caveats, before adding: “We aren’t getting anywhere. Meanwhile our government is implementing severe social [security] reforms against the will of voters.” Witnessing the far right succeed, while her economist peers act as “a major blockage to economic policies that would rehabilitate faith in democracy? It’s made me desperate to hold my ground.”View image in fullscreenDemonstrations against the far-right AfD party in Magdeburg, Germany, this month.Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAFascism is not an abstract concept to Weber. She was raised in Nuremberg, once a focal point of Third Reich propaganda. Family legend is that her grandfather, a priest in the Ruhr Valley, refused to hang a swastika in his church. As a small child, she realised “something so terrible happened that the only way to resolve it was to bomb our city to the ground”. During the 90s, resurgent neo-Nazis regularly marched through the medieval city. Weber and her grandmother would take to the streets in opposition. “I grew up with the threat of fascism,” she says, “and learnt that being anti-fascist and preventing its return is my first civic duty – in Germany, our democracy exists only becausewe defeated it.”Weber is keen to point out there is precedent to much of her agenda, and not just the Covid-era policies that tore up the economic rulebook to safeguard livelihoods. Many post-war countries operated a “mixed economy with public ownership as a vital component … Neoliberalism has made us think this is the exception, but it wasn’t for decades.” Or look to Switzerland, which avoided privatisation in sectors such as telecommunications, water, energy and transport. While inflation across the OECD hit anaverage of 9.5% in 2022, in Switzerland itonly reached 2.8%.What advice would she offer Burnham in Britain? “Renationalise water,” she says. “Invest in the NHS where people experience the state every day. Some form of rent controls. The proud history of council houses reimagined as models for affordable, climate-friendly living. The affordable food basket. Make public transportation very cheap, free even, in overcrowded cities.”Much of this sounds common sense to a progressive 2026 audience, but even a few years ago, these ideas were on the fringes. In December 2021, Weber tentatively floated the ideain the Guardianthat price controls could be used to stabilise the price of essentials. “It completely exploded with a hysterical reaction,” says Weber, “as if I was a physicist discounting the laws of gravity.” She became, as the New Yorker put it, “the most hated woman in economics”, mocked and ridiculed by her contemporaries. The Nobel laureate economist and New York Times columnist Paul Krugman said her argument was “truly stupid”, though he later apologised.“It was a horrible time in my life,” Weber says. “But what I was saying is now being proved right. This experience has given me a calm confidence. These are intellectual battles worth the fight.”At the New School in New York, Weber studied 20th-century socialism. “So much was utopian and up in the sky: nice ideas, but so removed from lived experience.” And so we return, again, to the economist-as-dentist: “In this movement, common sense must be the starting point to rehabilitate democracy.”Anti-Fascist Economics: In Defence of Affordability, Dignity and Democracyby Isabella Weber is published by Allen LaneExplore more on these topicsEconomicsThe far rightIncome inequalityCost of living crisisInequalityPovertyHousinginterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands | Mining | The Guardian
description: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia
Author: Stefano Valentino
Headline: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia
Content: Deforestation in Indonesia linked to nickel mining.Photograph: Didi Hardiana, NGO PuspahamView image in fullscreenDeforestation in Indonesia linked to nickel mining.Photograph: Didi Hardiana, NGO PuspahamMiningRevealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous landsMines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in IndonesiaStefano Valentinoin Sulawesi andAjit NiranjanFri 16 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolkswagen, Ford andTeslaare among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot inIndonesiathat houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”View image in fullscreenWadimula: ‘Destroying [the forest] means destroying our own life.’Photograph: Stefano ValentinoElectric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.View image in fullscreenMorowali industrial park on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary.Photograph: Stefano ValentinoPublic filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a reportfoundlithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communicationsfoundlast year.The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests.View image in fullscreenA track cut through forest in the Hengjaya concession.Photograph: Stefano ValentinoSulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo,Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits.Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain.Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.”Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.”Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.”Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.”Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.”General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.”Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.”Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.”CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment.This investigation was supported byJournalismfund EuropeandThe Pulitzer Center. Lorenzo Di Stasi and James Jackson contributed reporting.Explore more on these topicsMiningDeforestationElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsAutomotive industryTravel and transportTrees and forestsIndonesianewsShareReuse this content

title: Hall of Famers v bunch of gamers: the Dodgers’ exit proves money can’t buy everything | MLB | The Guardian
description: The Brewers turned LA’s stars into ghosts during their four-game NLCS sweep, destroying the ‘team that destroyed baseball’ and revealing the sport’s hard truth
Author: David Lengel
Headline: The Brewers turned LA’s stars into ghosts during their four-game NLCS sweep, destroying the ‘team that destroyed baseball’ and revealing the sport’s hard truth
Content: Superstar Shohei Ohtani and the Dodgers were swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLCS.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APView image in fullscreenSuperstar Shohei Ohtani and the Dodgers were swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLCS.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APMLBHall of Famers v bunch of gamers: the Dodgers’ exit proves money can’t buy everythingThe Brewers turned LA’s stars into ghosts during their four-game NLCS sweep, destroying the ‘team that destroyed baseball’ and revealing the sport’s hard truthDavid LengelFri 16 Oct 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMilwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy had just watched his club dismantle Los Angeles for a fourth straight National League Championship Series game. Standing with his team in the Dodger Stadium clubhouse, he was ready to celebrate. But before popping his champagne and setting off a stream of celebratory suds, Murphy had a message.“They got a bunch of Hall of Famers. We got a bunch of gamers.”Murphy had nailed the Dodgers to the wall, ending the season of a juggernaut who came into 2026 with eyes on becoming the first NL team to win three straightWorld Seriestitles.He also nailed the postgame speech.Brilliant Brewers reach first World Series since 1982 as Dodgers blow 4-0 leadRead moreThe Dodgers are dead, and instead, it’s Milwaukee who made history, becoming the first team to avenge an NLCS sweep by returning the favor against that very same team, the very next season.Making history, it seems, is a theme with these Brewers, who racked up a franchise-best 103 wins during the regular season, and have now dethroned a team who seemed a shoo-in to become baseball’s first true dynasty since the millennium.Milwaukee transformed LA into a team of ghosts, and no more so than in Game 4. With the desperate Dodgers bidding to wake up the echoes with a 4-0 lead, the Brewers went to work. And again, it was Jake Bauers who broke LA’s back. In Game 2, Bauers tortured Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto with an epic 12-pitch walk that sparked a key rally. In Game 3, there was an epic 11-pitch at-bat, this time against two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell, concluding with a franchise-defining home run. In the fourth inning of Game 4, Bauers struck a double against starter Tyler Glasnow, cutting the Dodgers’ lead in half. An inning later, Bauers – the journeyman infielder who paused his retirement and returned this season because he needed health insurance for his soon-to-be newborn – drew a bases-loaded walk to tie the game. Garrett Mitchell’s sixth-inning solo home run gave Milwaukee a lead that would hold up. An old-school, three-inning save by Aaron Ashby was the chef’s kiss.Now Milwaukee will head to their first World Series since 1982. There will be plenty of time to ply the Brew Crew with pixelated plaudits as they await their American League opponents, the Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians. First, though, comes the funeral.The tight, young, dynamic and fundamentally sound Brewers made Los Angeles’s best look old, flat and incapable. And while it all seems somewhat sudden, perhaps the writing was on the wall all along.The Dodgers, the team who have everything, lack for nothing and have more money than Davy Crockett, won 100 games this season, but were just 38-37 against teams above .500 and hit into an MLB-worst 128 double-plays. In ways, they looked more like another expensive but deeply flawed coastal superpower: the New York Yankees.The Bronx bombsalso beat up on lesser opponents all season long while struggling against higher-end teams. It’s no coincidence that both teams are now out; baseball has a way of weeding out the suckers, even in what some believe is a “crap shoot” of a postseason.Perhaps the most shocking spectacle was the undoing of the sport’s most prolific figure, Shohei Ohtani. The best two-way player in baseball, inside his category of one, showed signs of breaking down in the latter portion of the season. First injuries forced him to stop pitching. Then he went homerless from late August until Thursday. Ohtani said it was only his ability, not injuries, holding him back, but he was dropped to sixth in the batting order for Game 3, and that doesn’t happen to an elite player in his prime unless there are issues. In the seventh inning of Game 4, with Kiké Hernández 90ft away from tying the game at five, Ohtani waved at an Ashby slider that was closer to Fresno than the Dodger Stadium home plate. Ohtani, the four-time MVP, wasn’t alone. Former MVP Mookie Betts hit light; former MVP Freddy Freeman hit even lighter. The lineup, collectively, hit for a .590 OPS in the series, while the pitching was uneven at best.View image in fullscreenMookie Betts, Max Muncy, Kiké Hernández and Freddie Freeman made up one of baseball’s most expensive rosters.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APAfter the game, manager Dave Roberts, who was out-skippered by Murphy all series, told Fox that “the great thing about what we do is, you can try as much as you want, want it as bad and there’s nothing you can do about it. There’s nothing guaranteed.”And that, it seems, gets to the heart of where we are with the Dodgers and where we may be with baseball: nothing, at all, is guaranteed. Not even after signing Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz in the offseason for a combined $309m. Not even after trading for Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal at the deadline. And not after writing $340m worth of checks. The Dodgers’ payroll is more than the combined payroll of the Rays, the Guardians, and the Brewers, the club that sent home“the team that destroyed baseball”.And so the Dodgers, always in the headlines, leave us with all sorts of questions. The most straightforward: how will they respond and retool? The bigger questions: can critics say they destroyed baseball when the Brewers and their19th-ranked payrolljust destroyed them? Is baseball, a game that involves both skill and luck and always keeps us guessing, really some kind of utopian paradise where paupers can actually compete for prizes against princes? Are high payrolls and all-star laden rosters the most important metrics when it comes to who can compete for a title? How much can a smart, deliberate team brass make up for small budgets? In other words: who can find the gamers, when they can’t afford the Hall of Famers?Explore more on these topicsMLBLos Angeles DodgersBaseballUS sportsMilwaukee BrewersWest CoastWorld SeriesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: WNBA finals 2026 predictions: Is Angel Reese about to win a Dream title? | WNBA | The Guardian
description: The Valkyries and Dream tip off the WNBA finals on Saturday at Ballhalla. Our writers give their verdicts with a first-time champion set to be crowned
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: The Valkyries and Dream tip off the WNBA finals on Saturday at Ballhalla. Our writers give their verdicts with a first-time champion set to be crowned
Content: Golden State’s Kiah Stokes drives to the basket against Atlanta’s Angel Reese during the second half of their June game at Chase Center in San Francisco.Photograph: Thearon W Henderson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGolden State’s Kiah Stokes drives to the basket against Atlanta’s Angel Reese during the second half of their June game at Chase Center in San Francisco.Photograph: Thearon W Henderson/Getty ImagesWNBAWNBA finals 2026 predictions: Is Angel Reese about to win a Dream title?The Valkyries and Dream tip off the WNBA finals on Saturday at Ballhalla. Our writers give their verdicts with a first-time champion set to be crownedElla Brockway,Bryan Armen Graham,Stephanie KaloiandAndrew LawrenceFri 16 Oct 2026 08.09 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Valkyries are here because ...… of big dreams, excellent defense and smart roster construction.This franchise aimed big when it entered the league and has been more than rewarded. (An $850mvaluation, $100m inrevenue… next a championship?) After reaching the postseason in year one, they made the right offseason additions, trusted in players written off elsewhere, and put together what may have been the greatest defensive season in WNBA history.Ella Brockway… they’ve made a mockery of the conventional expansion timetable.Built around abest-in-class defensive efficiency, positional versatility and an unusually deep rotation, Golden State have become far more than the sum of their parts. Gabby Williams supplies the star power, Veronica Burton the steady hand and Natalie Nakase the uncompromising identity.Bryan Armen Graham… the entire organization believed in this team before they even had a team.The Valkyries did so much correctly – they built the facilities, they hired Nakase, they showed the team and fans that they were all in. The players have wholly embraced playing for Golden State, and they’ve fought their way to this achievement with the backing of an organization that understands that two-way relationship.Stephanie Kaloi… they share the ball beautifully, play exceptional team defense, have a coach who will wring every ounce from them and herself – and they think patience is for losers.Andrew LawrenceQuick GuideWNBA finals 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. All times Eastern.Sat 17 OctGame 1: Atlanta at Golden State, 3.30pm (NBC)Mon 19 OctGame 2: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm (USA/CNBC)Wed 21 OctGame 3: Golden State at Atlanta, 8pm (USA/CNBC)Sat 24 OctGame 4: Golden State at Atlanta, 1pm (NBC)Mon 26 OctGame 5: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm* (USA/CNBC)Thu 29 OctGame 6: Golden State at Atlanta, 8pm* (USA/CNBC)Sat 31 OctGame 7: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm* (USA/CNBC)*-if necessaryHow to watchIn the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Dream are here because ...… of elite rebounding, a strong backcourt and smart roster construction.Atlanta made two personnel moves this year that, if they win the title, will go down as some of the most astute decisions in this era of the W: theysplashed for Angel Reese in the offseasonand then added DeWanna Bonner mid-season. They knew the pieces that they were missing and completed their puzzle.EB… Reese has given Atlanta a ferocious presence on the glass, complementing a talented backcourt featuring Rhyne Howard, Allisha Gray and Jordin Canada. Karl Smesko’s team can score in bunches but have reached another level defensively, overwhelming the Liberty in a three-game semi-final sweep.BAG… they’ve earned it.Atlanta have also done so much correctly: hiring Karl Smesko was a surprise, but a welcome one. Signing Reese gave the team the puzzle piece they needed, and the ironclad support from fans and the team’s belief in themselves pushed them here today. The Dream have truly been a marvel to behold this season.SK… they were smart enough to make a deadline deal for DeWanna Bonner– a Hall of Fame-caliber veteran with extensive championship experience whose steadying influence on this young team cannot be understated. That and coach Karl Smesko has challenged Reese to expand her shooting range, and the dividends are beginning to show.ALView image in fullscreenThe Valkyries have turned their home court, nicknamed Ballhalla, into one of the WNBA’s most formidable venues.Photograph: Kavin Mistry/Getty ImagesHave the Valkyries changed the blueprint for building a WNBA champion?Yes, with a caveat.They are proof that you don’t need to have one standalone superstar or spend years stacking draft picks to contend. But they’ve also shown the importance of an ownership group willing to buy all the way in. Joe Lacob, who also owns the NBA’s Warriors, wasclearin his ambition to make the Valkyries a champion. Not every WNBA-NBA owner has historically shown that kind of interest or enthusiasm. As we return to the days of most W teams sharing ownership groups with their NBA counterparts – that will be the case in Houston, Philadelphia, Detroit and Cleveland – watch who follows through.EBPerhaps, although they still have four games to win. Golden State have demonstrated that expansion teams need not spend years stockpiling lottery picks or chasing marquee free agents. Shrewd drafting, identifying undervalued veterans and international talent and a clearly defined system can accelerate the process. Their rapid success challenges the league’s star-driven orthodoxy.BAGYes.Golden State began shredding expectations with the 2024 expansion draft, and have doggedly proven that newcomers need not be defined by the past. The Valkyries haven’t just raised the bar for expansion franchises; they’ve raised it for the entire league. On the court, the players have shown what can be accomplished through collective effort rather than reliance on a single superstar. Off it, the front office and ownership took risks without knowing whether they would pay off. The Valkyries are proof of what’s possible when an entire organization believes in a shared mission.SKYes.Not only have they shattered the long-held notion that it takes at least two superstars to make a title run; they’re showing just how badly the rest of the league slept on Gabby Williams and Veronica Burton. And yet: I get the sense that teams will still feel like they need a big name to pour in the buckets and keep the seats filled. It may take dynastic run to truly flip hearts and minds.ALThe coaching advantage goes to ...Nakase, but it’s close. In a postseason where some teams have been … let’s say …less-than-complimentaryof their coaches, it’s been refreshing to see two teams who share a genuine trust and connection with theirs. I’ll give the edge to Nakase because of her finals experience (two trips as an assistant on the Aces).EBNakase, just. Smesko has transformed Atlanta into a genuine contender, but Nakase’s ability to extract championship-level performances from a roster assembled almost from scratch is extraordinary. Her defensive schemes dismantled former boss Becky Hammon’s Aces and her willingness to trust the entire rotation gives Golden State a crucial tactical advantage.BAGNakase, because she’s been here before as an assistant coach with Hammon. I’m not discrediting Smesko at all, because he’s one of the smartest in the game. Nakase has an experience edge that will help her, but both teams have something even more special: the full trust of their entire roster.SKMark me down as a push.I love how in sync Smesko is with his locker room, both from a vibes and Xs and Os standpoint. And I’ve been following Natalie Nakase since her NBA emergence as the Clippers’ top tape grinder. This stage isn’t too big for either of these finals head coaching rookies.ALskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenValkyries coach Natalie Nakase has transformed an expansion franchise into a championship contender in just two seasons.Photograph: San Francisco Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesUnheralded player to watch ...Naz Hillmon, Atlanta.Rhyne Howard calls Hillmon the backbone of the Dream. Their starting five is so stacked - four of their five expected starters average more than 13 points per game – that Hillmon (5.2 ppg) flies under the radar. She does the dirty work that doesn’t show up in the box score. Atlanta have beaten Golden State just twice in their past six meetings; both times (last season), Hillmon had big games.EBKiah Stokes, Golden State.The veteran center’s contributions rarely register in the scoring column, but her rim protection and rebounding were instrumental in neutralizingA’ja Wilsonduring the semi-finals. With Reese dominating the offensive glass, Stokes faces another formidable assignment. Her ability to limit second-chance opportunities could decide the series.BAGKiah Stokes, Golden State.Though after the last two weeks it’s a little hard to argue she’s unheralded. For the Dream, I think it’s Jordin Canada. Both played crucial roles in their teams’ semi-final series wins.SKKaitlyn Chen, Golden State.Unheralded is a label that only fits Chen so much. She was the straw that stirred UConn’s 2024 NCAA title team. And now here she is again, playing big relief minutes in the backcourt for Golden State. I suppose the underdog element comes from her being selected in thethirdround of the 2025 draft. What a steal that turned out to be for the Valkyries.ALView image in fullscreenAngel Reese has emerged as a driving force behind Atlanta’s run to the WNBA finals, their first appearance in the championship series since 2013.Photograph: Stacy Revere/Getty ImagesThe finals MVP will be ...Gabby Williams, Golden State.Lacob may have been biased when he called Williams the best player in the world after the Valkyries’ Game 1 semi-final win over A’ja Wilson and the Las Vegas Aces, but she has a solid case as the best all-around player in these finals.EBGabby Williams, Golden State.The French international has elevated her game spectacularly in the postseason, averaging 22.7 points through the semi-finals while providing her customary defensive disruption. On a team without a conventional superstar, Williams has become the closest thing to one. Expect her two-way brilliance to define the championship series.BAGAngel Reese, Atlanta.I’d bet on the Dream’s third-year star if Atlanta can pull it off. She’s electric right now. If the Valkyries win, I think it could be Gabby Williams, Kiah Stokes, Veronica Burton or Tiffany Hayes. To me, having four options is a sign that the team plays to its collective strengths instead of relying on one or two players to win.SKGabby Williams, Golden State.Her production is giving prime Napheesa Collier, and I don’t see it dipping against the Dream’s imposing frontcourt.ALView image in fullscreenValkyries guard Gabby Williams drives past  Dream guard Jordin Canada during the second quarter of their July game at Gateway Center Arena in College Park, Georgia.Photograph: Brett Davis/Getty ImagesThe winner will be ...Golden State in seven.I was the contrarian in ourpre-playoffs predictionsand chose the Valkyries to win it all. I’m sticking with that pick now. They’re deep, they’re in good form, they have the best home-court advantage in the league and they know how to beat the Dream. (They did it three times this season.) I’ll say it again: if my preseason prediction of WNBA All-Star Veronica Burton couldn’t come true, then I will settle for WNBA champion Veronica Burton.EBGolden State in six.Atlanta have the individual talent and defensive chops to make this a fascinating series, particularly if Reese controls the glass and Howard finds her shooting touch. But Golden State swept all three regular-season meetings and have demonstrated an extraordinary ability to win in different ways. Their defensive versatility, superior depth and home-court advantage should prove decisive. Two years after entering the league, the Valkyries will complete one of the most remarkable championship runs inWNBAhistory.BAGAtlanta in six.I’ll go with the Dream, but please don’t think this is anything other than an excruciating question to answer. These WNBA finals are so special because two underdogs are fighting it out and either could win. Both teams are enormously talented and both bring compelling emotional stories to the table. What the Valkyries have done and continue to do is extraordinary, while what the Dream are accomplishing would have been unimaginable even last season. Golden State beat the Atlanta in all three regular-season meetings, but the teams haven’t faced each other since early July. I think the series will go six games, each close and exciting, with the Dream ultimately closing it out on their home floor.SKGolden State in six.I just think they’re so good, so deep and – unlike the Minnesota Lynx just ahead of them in the standings – they haven’t really lost form this season. I think the matchups definitely favored the Dream in their playoff run, but they meet their match in the Valkyries. The hope is that they can at least give Atlanta fans their money’s worth after heaven and earth were moved for the Dream to maintain a real home court advantage at State Farm Arena. Still, I like the Valks in six games.ALExplore more on these topicsWNBAGolden State ValkyriesAtlanta DreamAngel ReeseBasketballA’ja WilsonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Real Madrid demand La Liga president resign over Goebbels comparison | Real Madrid | The Guardian
description: Real Madrid have demanded the ‘immediate resignation’’ of Javier Tebas after he compared the club’s efforts to discredit referees with the propaganda techniques of Nazi Germany
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Real Madrid have demanded the ‘immediate resignation’’ of Javier Tebas after he compared the club’s efforts to discredit referees with the propaganda techniques of Nazi Germany
Content: ‘The executive of Real Madrid has an orchestra of mouthpieces,’ said Javier Tebas, the president of La Liga.Photograph: Arnold Jerocki/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The executive of Real Madrid has an orchestra of mouthpieces,’ said Javier Tebas, the president of La Liga.Photograph: Arnold Jerocki/Getty ImagesReal MadridReal Madrid demand La Liga president resign over Goebbels comparisonJavier Tebas accuses Madrid of ‘propaganda techniques’Club want ‘immediate resignation’ for ‘constant attacks’AgenciesFri 16 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madrid have again demanded the resignation of the president of La Liga after he compared the club’s efforts to discredit referees with the propaganda techniques of Nazi Germany.Javier Tebas lashed out at Madrid on Friday on social media with a long post that criticised how its club television channel says referees hurt its chances of winning. The channel regularly runs reels of what it considers gross errors by match officials who are set to work upcoming games for the 15-time European champions.Tebas compared the tactic with those used by Joseph Goebbels, the minister of propaganda in Nazi Germany during the second world war.Vinícius claims he is targeted by referees and says flair players need protectionRead more“The executive of Real Madrid has an orchestra of mouthpieces and Real Madrid leads the way,” Tebas wrote. “Its script is always the same: select plays that favor it, repeat the alleged affront, increase suspicion and name enemies. It reminds one of the propaganda techniques that Goebbels used.”Tebas added: “The comparison is with the techniques, not with the ideology or, of course, with Madrid fans.”Madrid responded by saying in a statement that Tebas, who has clashed several times over the years with the club president, Florentino Pérez, was unfit to hold his job representing Spain’s top clubs. Madrid also demanded his “immediate resignation”.“Javier Tebas’s repeated conduct demonstrates a lack of neutrality, respect, and impartiality incompatible with his institutional responsibilities,” it said. “His constant attacks on Real Madrid and those demanding transparency and regeneration represent, in our club’s view, a genuine scourge for Spanish football.”The head coach, José Mourinho, has also voiced complaints that Madrid, who hold a record 36 Spanish league titles, are regularly hurt by referees.View image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho watches Real Madrid in action.Photograph: Ivan Romano/Getty ImagesIn September, Madriddemanded Tebas step downafter he criticised the club for attacking the refereeing team in the2-1 loss at Atlético Madrid.In Friday’s statement, Madrid repeated the complaint that Tebas has not done enough over the ongoing judicial probe into Barcelona’s alleged payments to an official on the refereeing committee of the Spanish soccer federation.Meanwhile, Spain’s football federation will take its ⁠case to the court of arbitration for sport after Fifa rejected its appeal against sanctions imposed over Islamophobic chants by supporters during a match against Egypt ⁠in March.Fifa fined the ⁠federation $20,000 (£15,000) and ordered ​it to close at least 15% of the available seats for Spain’s next home friendly. The sanctions relate to incidents at the RCDE Stadium near Barcelona, home ⁠ofLa Ligaclub Espanyol, where some Spain fans chanted, “If you don’t jump, you’re a Muslim” during a World Cup warm-up match that ended in a 0-0 draw.The RFEF argued that the word Muslim was “neither insulting nor pejorative”, adding the fans’ conduct should be assessed under Fifa’s article 17, which covers political, ideological, religious or offensive messages, rather than article 15, which deals with discrimination and racist abuse.However, Fifa’s disciplinary committee rejected that argument, saying article 15 does not require the explicit use of a ‌slur and that a term can be discriminatory when used in context as “an insult, taunt or marker of inferiority”.Explore more on these topicsReal MadridLa LigaEuropean club footballSpainnewsShareReuse this content

title: Game, set and tache: Carlos Alcaraz joins growing trend for a stylish top lip | Men's hair | The Guardian
description: Tennis superstar is latest celebrity to sport a ‘refined’ moustache which owes little to bushy Tom Selleck look
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: Tennis superstar is latest celebrity to sport a ‘refined’ moustache which owes little to bushy Tom Selleck look
Content: Carlos Alcaraz at the Shanghai Masters: ‘I always wanted to step on the court at least once with the moustache.’Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPAView image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz at the Shanghai Masters: ‘I always wanted to step on the court at least once with the moustache.’Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPAMen's hairGame, set and tache: Carlos Alcaraz joins growing trend for a stylish top lipTennis superstar is latest celebrity to sport a ‘refined’ moustache which owes little to bushy Tom Selleck lookEllie Violet BramleyFri 16 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe tennis superstarCarlos Alcarazmight have been knocked out of the Shanghai Masters in straight sets earlier this week, but he did so sporting a moustache that became almost as remarked upon as his aptitude for a sneaky drop shot.“I always wanted to step on the court at least once with the moustache,” Alcaraz said. The Spaniard and his team had all agreed to take the facial-hair plunge if he won the Japan Open, which he did for a second straight year.“¡Bigotes para todos!”or “moustaches for everyone”, they apparently cheered at the end of the match.At Milan fashion week last month, the Wuthering Heights starJacob Elordisported a thin strip of hair on his top lip as he watched his girlfriend, Kendall Jenner, model for the Bottega Veneta show.A moustachioed Harry Styles is roughly halfway through his record-breaking 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York. The actorTimothée Chalamet, who kept his Marty Supreme ’tache on throughout awards season, has been playing around with his facial hair again, adding a goatee.View image in fullscreenNcuti Gatwa poses for photographers at the Albie awards in London.Photograph: Scott A Garfitt/APOn TikTok, gen Z men with moustaches are plentiful, as are tutorials for how to grow and style them – alongside almost as many videos from older generations questioning them.High street barber shops are seeing evidence of it, too. AtCitadel in Sheffield, more young men are asking for moustaches, and a large number are asking specifically for thin ones, which the owner, Marie Williams, describes as “[a] low maintenance, easygoing moustache that’s attainable to most”.According to Jay Byrne, a barber atDog House barbers in Birminghamand a formerBritish barber of the year: “The moustache is certainly making a comeback, particularly among younger men.”The moustaches appearing on young men’s faces are a long way from the bushier ones seen in the 1970s and 80s, epitomised by Tom Selleck in Magnum PI.They seem more to hark back to the Hollywood stars of the 40s and 50s such as David Niven and Clark Gable. “We’re seeing a move away from the heavier, traditional moustaches … towards a much more refined, deliberately styled look,” says Byrne.“Achieving the look is all about precision, proportion and understanding what suits the individual’s facial structure. It’s not simply a case of growing a moustache and leaving it alone. The shape, thickness and detailing are what make the difference.”View image in fullscreenJacob Elordi sporting a moustache at Milan fashion week.Photograph: Luca Bruno/APAccording to Dr Ashley Morgan, a masculinities scholar at Cardiff Metropolitan University: “Skinny moustaches are a sign of difference, especially from men who keep beards.”Given the rise of the manosphere and the complicated state of masculinity at the moment, Morgan thinks these skinnier moustaches could be intended to steer clear of signalling alpha masculinity. “Young men want to demonstrate a carefully curated form of ‘manliness’,” she says.For these young male celebrities in particular, Morgan thinks it could be “an expression of ageing”.“Timothée Chamalet is 30, Jacob Elordi is 29 … it could well be a sign that they want to show that they are mature, they have entered a new phase of life, and want to be seen as more ‘manly’ while remaining youthful.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor 34-year-oldNcuti Gatwa, who starred in the most recent series of Doctor Who, it has certainly been a way to lean into his age after making his name while playing a schoolboy in the hit TV drama Sex Education.‘You look like an Agatha Christie villain!’ The moustache is back – but should it go away again?Read moreGatwa told theRadio Times: “I’d spent the last four years playing a child [in Sex Education], at the age of 30, so I said: ‘Let me have my moustache back.’”The fashion historian Tony Glenville once had a curly moustache but, he says, “like many men, [I] got rid of facial hair during the mask-wearing times of Covid”. He says it is a trend “among young men who’ve not really seen it around so much recently”. Facial hair, as with all things, “has huge fashion phases for men”.Movember, which launched in 2003 and has grown into a global movement, sees men grow moustaches for the month of November to raise money for charity and has arguably made facial hair more popular again.For such a small slither of hair, the moustache is historically and culturally freighted. It can symbolise freedom and has long held a central position in gay culture.While the moustache might be a “trend” in western culture, in other cultures it is much more of a constant. From romance to war, religion to masculinity and sexuality, moustaches connote different things in different contexts.Luckily for anyone wanting to give a thin moustache a whirl, according to barber Williams, it is a style that “requires minimal upkeep; just a few snips with the scissors to maintain”.Explore more on these topicsMen's hairMen's fashionCarlos AlcarazTimothée ChalametJacob ElordiNcuti GatwaBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From the Octagon to Quantico: UFC teaching the FBI to fight is its latest tie to Trump world | UFC | The Guardian
description: The mixed martial arts organization has had links to the US president for years. Now it could be involved in training federal agents
Author: Karim Zidan
Headline: The mixed martial arts organization has had links to the US president for years. Now it could be involved in training federal agents
Content: Justin Gaethje was among the UFC fighters present at a training seminar for the FBI.Photograph: Chris Unger/Zuffa LLCView image in fullscreenJustin Gaethje was among the UFC fighters present at a training seminar for the FBI.Photograph: Chris Unger/Zuffa LLCUFCFrom the Octagon to Quantico: UFC teaching the FBI to fight is its latest tie to Trump worldThe mixed martial arts organization has had links to the US president for years. Now it could be involved in training federal agentsKarim ZidanFri 16 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the lead-up to UFC Freedom 250 –the cagefighting spectaclethat took place on the South Lawn of the White House to mark Donald Trump’s 80th birthday this past summer – the FBI announced that a handful of UFC fighters would visit the bureau for an exclusive training seminar for federal agents.Taking place at theFBISpecial Agent Academy in Quantico, Virginia, the March seminar put roughly 300 federal agents and academy students through specialized hand-to-hand combat training with seven past and current UFC fighters, including former middleweight champion Chris Weidman, who was pictured giving attendees advice on warding off attackers.The two-day seminar included photo-ops with the fighters, whoworebranded UFC-FBI training gear. FBI director Kash Patel also posed for photos with federal agents, and appeared to behanding out signed headshotsof himself.“[UFC CEO] Dana White has changed the game in the mixed martial arts industry and we’re extremely honored to be partnered with him, the professionals, and the UFC,” Patel said in the UFCpress release. “We are grateful for their shared love of our nation, so that we can better defend her.”Now, six months after the initial seminar, the FBI appears to be in the process of awarding the UFC an exclusive contract to train agents in mixed martial arts, further cementing the relationship between the fighting organization and theTrump administration.In September, the bureau filed aSole Source Justificationform, a document that allows the government to award contracts without considering bids from other companies. The bureau claimed that the UFC was “uniquely qualified” to provide these services, noting in the form that “the trainers provided by UFC have the skills necessary to instruct striking techniques, grappling/takedowns, weapon defense, ground control, as well as conditioning to the standard that the FBI expects and requires.”The document says that the exclusive contract would be limited to a single year, while a potential long-term contract would be open to competitive bidding following “market research.” The exact sum that the FBI plans to pay theUFCis not disclosed.The FBI claims the UFC collaboration is part of an initiative to provide innovative training for its agents, but it also appears to be a part of the sustained consolidation of the UFC-Trump alliance.Over the past decade,the UFC has emergedas one of Trump’s most influential and reliable partners. The promotion’s owner, Ari Emanuel, was once Trump’s agent and has helped steer the UFC’s rightward shift. Whiteis a close friend of the president, andhas stumped for himover the course of three presidential campaigns.
