Author: Jack Snape
Headline: Jillaroos defeat Fetu Samoa 40-0 in Sydney as Jocelyn Kelleher kicks six conversions on her debut
Content: Australia celebrate their win over Samoa in the Women's Rugby League World Cup Group A match in Sydney.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenAustralia celebrate their win over Samoa in the Women's Rugby League World Cup Group A match in Sydney.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPWomen's Rugby League World CupAustralia cruise past Samoa in women’s Rugby League World Cup openerJillaroos defeat Fetu Samoa 40-0 in SydneyJocelyn Kelleher kicks six conversions on her debutJack SnapeFri 16 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 17.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Jillaroos’ World Cup defence began with a comprehensive 40-0 victory over Samoa at Commbank Stadium in Sydney, even if they eased off in the second half with just two tries after the break.Jocelyn Kelleher was assured by boot and hand on her debut at five-eighth, vindicating the decision by coach Jess Skinner to leave Ali Brigginshaw out of the squad and Jesse Southwell out of the matchday 18.Women’s Rugby League World Cup shapes as tightest yet as gap closes on hosts Australia | Megan MauriceRead moreKelleher kicked six from seven conversion attempts, and had a hand in two tries, earning her the player of the match award. She said her debut was “amazing” and the team is “having so much fun in camp, we’re training well together”.View image in fullscreenJocelyn Kelleher kicked six out seven conversions on her Australia debut.Photograph: Mark Evans/AAPKelleher’s comfort was aided by the Roosters’ NRLW premiership-winning connections running throughout the team. No 7 Tarryn Aiken played second receiver outside Kelleher, and the halves were supported by their clubmates Olivia Kernick at lock and Keely Nizza at bench hooker, as well as Millie Elliott in the front row and both centres in Jess Sergis and captain Isabelle Kelly.The captain said after the match her side has plenty of improvement in them. “It was a bit scrappy from us in bits there,” she said. “But it’s the start of the tournament, a new team playing together, so I’m excited to see what comes next.”Australia quelled a spirited opening from Samoa, who were playing their first World Cup match since 2008. Their side included two players – Taliah Fuimaono and Evania Isa’ako – who had played for the Jillaroos. The latter even ran out for the Jillaroos in the 2022 World Cup final,scoring the final try. The team also featured Queensland State of Origin centre, Ivana Lolesio, and premiership-winning prop Amber Hall, who scored in theRoosters’ victory over the Broncos two weeks ago.For a brief early moment, it looked like the contest could deliver an upset. A penalty and a handling error handed the Fetu Samoa repeat sets at the Australian line. They even resisted the urge to take the two points from a pair of subsequent penalties. But a dropped ball from fullback Destiny Mino-Sinapati let the Jillaroos off the hook.The Samoans would be left to rue that mistake. Within minutes Australia had crossed through Jaime Chapman off a simple spread left. A cut-out pass from Tamika Upton handed the winger enough space to finish easily. Minutes later it was Aiken on the right lofting it out to Julia Robinson to score. The Broncos winger ignored the path to the corner, instead coming inside and taking three tacklers over the line.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJulia Robinson in action against Samoa.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPKelleher opened her international career with a masterful fading conversion from the sideline, before a trademark bomb forced a handling error from Samoa. It set up the attacking set which saw Jillaroos’ backrower Shaylee Bent cross untouched.The Samoans were getting stretched, and the Jillaroos began to run through the gears. Nizza streamed through the middle, thanks to a dummy and a fend, to score Australia’s fourth. Just before halftime, Kelleher breezed through the Samoan line and found Kernick. Early in the second period, it was Kernick who put Keilee Joseph over with a short-ball.From there the Jillaroos’ momentum slowed, as minds wandered towards the next pool match against England in Perth next week. The Samoans had their moments in defence, keeping out the Jillaroos on multiple occasions in a heroic second half effort. Prop Laikha Clarke came within millimetres of scoring with ten minutes to go before knocking on. The highlight of the evening might have been the crunching tackle on Tiana Penitani Gray by teenage winger Freedom Crichton Ropati, although Sergis crossed late to put the icing on the result.On an evening that also included the men’s Samoa side beating France 78-4 in a try-fest, the biggest disappointment was the size of the crowd at Commbank Stadium. The passionate Samoan community in western Sydney was noisy but the turnout was ultimately low, and tens of thousands of empty seats highlighted that the interest in this tournament – like the Jillaroos’ form – has room for improvement.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Rugby League World CupRugby League World Cup 2026Australia women's rugby league teamSamoa rugby league teamWomen's rugby leagueRugby leagueAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia 40-0 Samoa: women’s Rugby League World Cup – as it happened | Women's Rugby League World Cup | The Guardian
description: The Jillaroos got their title defence off to a good start with a convincing win at CommBank Stadium
Author: Megan Maurice
Headline: The Jillaroos got their title defence off to a good start with a convincing win at CommBank Stadium
Content: 14h ago07.09 EDTSummaryMegan MauriceWell, what an opening game for the women’s tournament! While it didn’t have the close scoreline of the men’s opener last night, there was so much heart and passion on the field and some truly incredible defence from Samoa. I’m looking forward to seeing how they build throughout the tournament – they have so much talent and some very smart players – in particular Freedom Crichton Ropati and Destiny Mino-Sinapati – who will only get better as they go on.The Jillaroos will take a lot out of that game as well – while they’ll be heartened by the strong win, they will want to cut down their error rate, especially when they come up against New Zealand and England. They made 10 errors and conceded five penalties – many of them at crucial times. I wouldn’t be surprised to see coach Jess Skinner look to mix up some combinations and see if that reduces the error rate.However, they will be pleased with their 519 post-contact metres and nine line breaks – they are always making things happen out on the field and when they can hold on to the ball they will have the chance to score even more tries.Both teams have a week off now – Samoa will come up against Wales next Friday back at CommBank Stadium, while the Jillaroos take on England in Perth next Saturday.I hope you enjoyed this great battle tonight and keep on watching the incredible women playing in all the teams at this tournament. Until next time, go rugby league!Australia cruise past Samoa in women’s Rugby League World Cup openerRead moreShareUpdated at07.36 EDT

title: Brilliant Brewers reach first World Series since 1982 as Dodgers blow 4-0 lead | MLB | The Guardian
description: Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning, Milwaukee’s bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning, Milwaukee’s bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4
Content: The Milwaukee Brewers celebrate reaching the World Series.Photograph: Mark J Terrill/APView image in fullscreenThe Milwaukee Brewers celebrate reaching the World Series.Photograph: Mark J Terrill/APMLBBrilliant Brewers reach first World Series since 1982 as Dodgers blow 4-0 leadNLCS Game 4: Brewers 6-4 DodgersDefending champions swept out of playoffsMilwaukee roar back from four runs downBrewerswill face Rays or Guardiansin World SeriesAgenciesThu 15 Oct 2026 23.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 00.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJake Bauers started the Brewers’ comeback with a two-run double and Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead home run to deliver a 6-4 victory ⁠over theLos Angeles Dodgerson Thursday and send Milwaukee to their first World Series appearance in 44 years.Bauers added a bases-loaded walk to tie the game in the ⁠fifth inning as the Brewers ⁠rallied from an early ​four-run deficit to sweep the National League Championship Series in four games. The dominating performance came after Milwaukee were swept out of the NLCS by Los Angeles ⁠last season.“We got down early tonight and we were like, it’s going to be a great story,” Brewers veteran Christian Yelich said. “We’re going to come back and win this. Like, stay together, start chipping away. And that’s exactly what they did.”Dodgers manager Dave Roberts had few complaints at the loss, saying the 2024 and 2025MLBchampions had been comprehensively outplayed.“At the end of the day, we got beat,” Roberts said. “We got outplayed in all facets. Those guys played flawless. Defensively they pitched better than we did, they hit better than we did, they slugged more than we did. You’ve got to sometimes just tip your cap.“I personally told our guys that there’s no apologies, there’s no sorries. We gave it everything we had, and it wasn’t good enough. That’s part of life.”Catcher William Contreras guided the Brewers’ pitching staff in a bullpen game, and four pitchers held the Dodgers scoreless over the final seven innings. JoJo Romero tossed two innings, and Aaron ⁠Ashby handled the final three frames for his second save of the postseason.“Playing with that chip on our shoulder,” Ashby said. “You don’t ever know what to expect going into a series like that last year. You don’t know how bad it can be, and then it was as bad as it was. And we came out and we survived, and we came back this year, and those guys played their tails off.”Petey Halpin’s two-run homer lifts Guardians past Rays for 2-1 ALCS leadRead moreThe Brewers will open the World Series at ​home on 23 October against the winner of the ‌American League Championship Series between ‌the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays. The Guardianshold a 2-1 leadafter winning 3-2 on Thursday.Milwaukee made ‌their only previousWorld Seriesappearance as an AL team in 1982, falling in seven games to the St Louis Cardinals.Shohei Ohtani hit a three-run homer in his return to the leadoff spot but also struck out three times while playing with knee and biceps discomfort that will be addressed in the offseason.Dodgers starter Tyler Glasnow gave up four runs on three hits and two walks over 4.1 innings. He struck out six. Tanner ‌Scott gave up Mitchell’s go-ahead home run in the sixth inning.“I’ve always dreamt of moments like these as a kid,” Mitchell said.The Dodgers appeared to be all business in the second inning when Andy Pages delivered a one-out RBI single and Ohtani added ​a towering three-run blast with two outs for a 4-0 advantage.Bauers continued his impressive series in the fourth inning with a two-run ground-rule double to cut the Milwaukee deficit in half.David Hamilton cut the Dodgers’ lead further when he made it 4-3 in the fifth inning with an RBI single, ending Glasnow’s night. Dodgers reliever Evan Phillips subsequently loaded the bases with two outs on a pair ⁠of walks. Alex Vesia replaced Phillips and walked Bauers on four pitches to tie the ​game.Milwaukee went up for good in ​the sixth at 5-4 when Mitchell, ​a Southern California native and UCLA alumnus, greeted Scott with a leadoff home run.The Dodgers wasted ​a one-out double from ‌Kyle Tucker in the ​sixth inning and a leadoff ​double from Pages in the seventh. Another double combined with an error in the eighth put Will Smith on third base as the tying run with one out. Ashby then retired Tucker on a shallow fly ball and struck out Teoscar Hernandez to end the threat.Hamilton sealed the victory with a two-out home run in the ninth inning against Edwin Diaz. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.Explore more on these topicsMLBMilwaukee BrewersLos Angeles DodgersWest CoastBaseballUS sportsWorld SeriesShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk reveals ‘world’s first flying car’ at Tesla event | Tesla | The Guardian
description: The Tesla Roadster 2 drove up a curved ramp before using SpaceX rocket thrusters to fly, flip and land
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: The Tesla Roadster 2 drove up a curved ramp before using SpaceX rocket thrusters to fly, flip and land
Content: Tesla's redesigned 'flying car' Roadster performs a ramp-assisted mid-air flipTeslaElon Musk reveals ‘world’s first flying car’ at Tesla eventThe Tesla Roadster 2 drove up a curved ramp before using SpaceX rocket thrusters to fly, flip and landMark SweneyFri 16 Oct 2026 07.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Musk has revealed Tesla’s latest model, which he claims will be the world’s first flying car, using technology from his aerospace company SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”.The billionaire, who hosted a demonstration of the Tesla Roadster 2 at theSpaceXrocket development and testing facility in Texas, said the sports car could go from 0 to 60mph in a record time of less than a second and had thrusters.Avideo of the eventshows the Roadster, which he said was controlled remotely “to make sure we don’t kill anyone”, driving up a curved ramp using suction to grip upside down, before using thrusters toflip, fly and land.Later in the demonstration the Roadster is seen using the jets toleap over a line of Tesla’s existing modelsand then accelerate to 60mph in record time.“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk said in a post on his social media site, X, accompanying a video from the event.Speaking at the event on Thursday, Musk said: “Flying cars are real. It’s got altitude controls, thrusters and main thrusters in the rear. So it can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics.”“I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions,” Musk said, adding that the prototype was “not necessarily a safety optimised car but it takes the fun meter to 11”.In 2014 Musk expressed hisscepticism about a future with flying vehicles.However, three years later he announced the development of the Roadster 2, which will go into production in 2028 and is priced in excess of $200,000, (£150,000), to create an electric sports car “to give a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the event, aTeslareservation website for expressing interest in the two-seater Roadster 2 showed that a “performance” version of the vehicle would require a £50,000 deposit. A “thrust” version would require a $250,000 deposit.Meanwhile, a one-seater “rocket” variant with “full flight system” was labelled as being available only by invitation. The car company added that flying it was not permitted on public roads.Explore more on these topicsTeslaAutomotive industryElon MuskSpaceXTechnology sectorAeronauticsMotoringnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pornography with strangulation and incest to be banned in England and Wales next month | Pornography | The Guardian
description: Campaigners welcome legislation which follows recommendations by 2025 review into pornography regulation
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Campaigners welcome legislation which follows recommendations by 2025 review into pornography regulation
Content: Pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation, and sex between people who are related or pretending to be related will be illegal from 6 November.Photograph: Tero Vesalainen/AlamyView image in fullscreenPornography depicting strangulation or suffocation, and sex between people who are related or pretending to be related will be illegal from 6 November.Photograph: Tero Vesalainen/AlamyPornographyPornography with strangulation and incest to be banned in England and Wales next monthCampaigners welcome legislation which follows recommendations by 2025 review into pornography regulationJamie GriersonFri 16 Oct 2026 03.09 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 02.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePornography that depicts strangulation and incestuous relationships will be banned in England and Wales from early November, the government has announced.The content will be outlawed from 6 November after cross-party pressure prompted ministers to announce new legislation earlier this year.Online pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation, sex between people who are related or pretending to be related, or when somebody is pretending to be a child under 16, will be illegal.The justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said: “This isn’t about criminalising harmless sexual preferences. But porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people.“Content that normalises, or even glorifies, violence against women is dangerous and can blur the line with what is acceptable in real life.”The Conservative peer Gabby Bertin made the recommendations in her review into pornography regulation which reported in 2025.Her report found pornography that shows women being choked can have “devastating” real-world consequences. It highlighted “disturbing” role-play, including incest and adults portraying children. Both will be banned.The report said there had been a “total absence of government scrutiny” of the pornography industry.Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence in its own right, but it is not illegal to show it online.Reacting to the announcement, Lady Bertin said: “It is very good news these offences will come into force, and not a moment too soon.“This change in law alongside better enforcement and stronger regulation will send the unequivocal signal not only to the companies that host and facilitate porn but also to wider society that extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable.”The End Violence Against Women Coalition campaign group welcomed the ban, urging ministers to ensure it is enforced.Its interim director, Janaya Walker, said: “This is an important step towards tackling the normalisation of violence against women and girls, and the result of years of campaigning by EVAW and other experts who have raised concerns about the impact of violent pornography.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolice routinely failing to investigate ‘revenge porn’, research revealsRead more“Strangulation can cause serious, lasting harm and even death, yet its widespread portrayal in pornography risks normalising this violence in sexual relationships, particularly among young people.“The introduction of this offence is an important recognition of the harm caused by violent pornography and the need to hold an industry accountable for content that depicts and profits from violence against women and girls.“The government must now ensure the ban is effectively enforced, and update the Online Safety Act so that online platforms are required to remove this content.”This article, including the headline, was amended on 16 October 2026. The legislation applies to England and Wales, not the UK as stated in an earlier version.Explore more on these topicsPornographyViolence against women and girlsInternet safetynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis | Transport | The Guardian
description: Protest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licences
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Protest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licences
Content: Wayve robotaxis leave the depot on the day the company launched autonomous passenger rides in London via Uber last month.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersView image in fullscreenWayve robotaxis leave the depot on the day the company launched autonomous passenger rides in London via Uber last month.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersTransport‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxisProtest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licencesGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 16 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor passengers in Britain who want to try the latest ride, robotaxis are eagerly awaited: more than 100,000 are on Uber’s waitlist inLondonafter the first UK services started in September.Others view them with trepidation. “I think we should all be worried,” said Florentina Ghiuzan, an Uber driver from Essex. “I was shockedTfL approved it so soon. I knew change would come. But I thought it would come with a solution for us.”London’s rollout is facing mounting opposition, from drivers fearing for their future and the capital’s politicians, with a critical report demandingTransportfor London (TfL) is given full powers to permit or suspend operations.Drivers will this weekend protest outside the headquarters and depot of Wayve, which has partnered with Uber to supply London’sfirst autonomous cabs for hire.The direct action marks the latest salvo between unions and the global tech companies, whose driverless cars trials expanded this week to Manchester, with fears that hundreds of thousands of driver jobs could be lost.Although only a handful of driverless cars now ply the streets, Uber has announced plans to deploy 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis worldwide starting next year, and its senior executives have talked about all new cars being autonomous by 2040. In San Francisco, Waymo’s fully autonomous cars already operate more than a quarter of all rides.The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, and bosses atTfLhave expressed unease, and the London assembly’s transport committee has called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services.In a report published this week, the committee said there was “considerable uncertainty around many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers.The chair, Caroline Russell, said they were not convinced that London should welcome robotaxis. “Rather than just accepting the autonomous passenger service model proposed by operators, London should be looking at the transport problems it is trying to solve and then considering what solutions this technology could provide,” she said.TfL is understood to see little benefit in theaddition of robotaxi services to its crowded city streets, even if the numbers turn out to be relatively few in comparison to the wider traffic.For the robotaxi companies, London is a tempting challenge to crack. Commercially, it is one of the biggest private hire markets in the world and a foothold in Europe; logistically, it is a tricky test bed to prove their vehicles are viable anywhere. Compared with the grid system of US cities in particular, it presents narrower, twisting and unruly streets, without the kind of rules on jaywalking that give cars priority on the road.Wayve autonomous vehicles added to Uber app in LondonUnder current rules, TfL licenses passenger services, but the government decides whether autonomous vehicles can operate. TfL has approved the start ofUberand Wayve’s limited robotaxi services, which retain a human safety driver in the front seat.As it stands, when it comes to fully autonomous passenger services, the Department for Transport would issue permits for robotaxis with TfL only able to grant or refuse consent, rather than regulate their usage on London’s streets.That has alarmed TfL, which sees parallels with when Uber first started business in London, creating problems few had considered, and was twicerebuffed in licence renewalsas not a “fit and proper” operator. Quite how driverless cars will affect the capital’s transport ecosystem is unknown – and TfL wants to retain the power to intervene.City hall is also concerned about the social implications of more than 100,000 licensed drivers losing income or a living. Those at the frontline in the App Drivers and Couriers Union (ADCU) are planning protests outside Wayve’s London base from this Saturday.Their members include Ghiuzan, 42, who started working as a driver four years ago after going back to college. She said: “Our earnings are the same or even lower since I started – and with the robotaxis on the market it could get even worse.”Ghiuzan said she was notified of the start of autonomous services as an Uber customer – but received no notification as a driver. She thinks people will switch to robotaxis: “Young people like them, it’s new, and you don’t have to pay the driver … I might have other skills, but for lots of drivers who are older and have done it their whole life, it’s going to be quite a challenge.”View image in fullscreenUber driver Faisal Osman said robotaxis would ‘decimate the livelihoods of many people including me’.Photograph: Faisal OsmanFaisal Osman, 51, from east London, has been an Uber driver for 12 years, after switching from a long commute to an IT engineering job to allow him to work nights when he had children. He knows four other engineers who joined Uber: “We all used to talk about AI taking our jobs in IT. We thought, we’re not earning as much driving but we’ll be safe for a while, support the family, pay the bills. But robocabs are a massive concern.“People might be interested but it will decimate the livelihoods of many people including me – I really wanted some authorities to say no.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenUber driver Abdurzak Hadi said he was thinking about safety as well as the threat to his job.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianAbdurzak Hadi, an Uber driver and theLondon chair of the ADCU, said Saturday’s protests would follow a similar action held at Waymo’s base in Park Royal in August. He said: “For me as a driver, I’m thinking about competing with a machine that’s not going to get tired, and could work 24 hours a day.“But as a Londoner with family, I’m thinking about safety. As licensed drivers we’re taught by TfL about safeguarding, looking out for a vulnerable child, or for abuse. Or looking after passengers who can only read your lips. We’re a safety net. But losing my job – that’s also losing a safety net for my family.”A recent report from the Centre for British Progress thinktank said more than 400,000 UK drivers (121,000 in London) would soon find “much of this work obsolete”, andurged the government to tax autonomous vehiclesto help pay for the social consequences and economic losses.TheGMB unionhas demanded a “just transition” to help drivers reskill and find new work. Speaking at the Labour conference last month, the GMB’s Mark Betteridge said the union was not against change but added: “The people who do these jobs will know the reality far better of what change will look like … Drivers tell us they want some sort of transition plan to get through this.”The roads minister, Justin Madders, told the meeting that autonomous vehicles could bring “opportunities for well-paid and unionised jobs” and the government wanted Britain to be a “world leader” in the technology. But, he added: “Sometimes government hasn’t worked on the impact on workers … We’re absolutely committed to making sure that doesn’t happen that time.”An Uber spokesperson said: “Drivers and AVs [automated vehicles], which we believe will also offer considerable benefits to cities, are both expected to grow side by side for quite some time. That said, we shouldn’t hide that autonomous mobility will impact workers, riders, and the communities they live in.“We are in conversations with the government and local stakeholders to ensure we can realise the promise of AVs while not leaving drivers and communities behind.”Uber said it had not significantly increased its share of fares in London but VAT changes meant drivers were keeping less of the fares customers paid, and it said it was the only private hire operator in the UK recognising its drivers as workers with employment protections.View image in fullscreenWayve said that with Uber it was taking a ‘deliberately phased approach’.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersWayve said that with Uber it was taking a “deliberately phased approach”, and had engaged extensively with political leaders, community organisations and accessibility advocates. A spokesperson said its robotaxis could “make a positive contribution to London’s transport system, helping to improve road safety, expand connectivity and give people more ways to travel.“There is clear excitement in the potential for this technology to support safer, more accessible journeys, provided it is introduced responsibly and in partnership with the city. We have a positive, constructive relationship with TfL and we’re working pragmatically together to ensure any future services meet its expectations.”A spokesperson for Khan said the mayor was committed to ensuring that Londoners benefitted from the opportunities new technologies could bring but shared “concerns about potential impacts on safety, congestion and jobs”, as any changes needed to “work for our world-leading transport system – including taxi and private hire services, and those who drive them”.Explore more on these topicsTransportSelf-driving carsRoad transportWaymoUberTfLLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals
Content: Meta says its new open-weight AI model rivals and in some cases outperforms Chinese equivalents.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta says its new open-weight AI model rivals and in some cases outperforms Chinese equivalents.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI modelMeta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivalsAgence France-PresseThu 15 Oct 2026 20.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them.‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cutenessRead moreChinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.“Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.Muse Spark Open is also “optimized” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signaling an unusual partnership between the two tech companies.Muse Spark Open requires significant computing power. Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said.The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model, which it said rivalled the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude.Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)MetaChinaComputingShareReuse this content

title: The ultra-rich are spending one million dollars a day fighting California’s proposed billionaire tax | The super-rich | The Guardian
description: Tech billionaires have raised more than $340m to defeat Prop 40, a one-time 5% wealth tax that will fund healthcare and education
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Tech billionaires have raised more than $340m to defeat Prop 40, a one-time 5% wealth tax that will fund healthcare and education
Content: ‘A few controversial billionaires like Sergey Brin would rather spend millions … than simply pay their fair share in taxes so millions of their fellow Californians don’t lose their healthcare.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘A few controversial billionaires like Sergey Brin would rather spend millions … than simply pay their fair share in taxes so millions of their fellow Californians don’t lose their healthcare.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesThe super-richThe ultra-rich are spending one million dollars a day fighting California’s proposed billionaire taxTech billionaires have raised more than $340m to defeat Prop 40, a one-time 5% wealth tax that will fund healthcare and educationDara KerrFri 16 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTShareTech billionaires have been dumping hundreds of millions of dollars into the fight against a wealth tax inCalifornia. They’ve raised more than $340m, and the campaign they’re funding is spending more than $1m a day to defeat the measure, according to state financial disclosures.With the election less than a month away, those funds are being spent at a stepped-up pace. During the first 19 days of September, according to the most recent campaign filings, the opposition campaign plowed through at least $21.2m to fight the billionaire tax – surpassing $1m per day. Voters are being inundated with robotexts, mailers and advertisements that warn a tax on billionaires would “expose all Californians to higher taxes”, as one ad reads.Californians will vote on the ballot measure, Proposition 40, in early November. If passed, it wouldrequire a one-time 5% taxon the state’s billionaires, with the proceeds mostly funding healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance. The measure has divided Democrats in the state, with some giving enthusiastic support and others rejecting the proposal because it’s just a one-time levy and the bulk of it would only fund certain healthcare programs.The state’s major unions and progressive politicians like the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders and California congressman Ro Khanna back Prop 40. But both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, as well as organizations like Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, a lobbying branch of the healthcare group, oppose it. Among its fiercest critics, however, are the tech billionaires it would most directly apply to.The donors to the no campaign area who’s who of Silicon Valley, including the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, crypto magnate Chris Larsen and several prominent venture capitalists.The biggest donor, by far, is the Google co-founderSergey Brin, who has contributed at least $102m to fight the tax, according to campaign finance filings. The runner-up is Schmidt, who has donated more than $42m. For comparison, the yes on 40 campaign has raised a total that’s just shy of $33m, mostly from the healthcare union sponsoring the measure.Proponents and opponents alike are casting the billionaire tax as a potential first step toward wealth taxes in more states. While those against the measuresee it as populist contagion, those in favor connect it to the top issue of the midterms – affordability. And with California having more billionaires than any other state, Prop 40 is seen as setting the stage for more referendums on wealth inequality throughout the country.“There’s a lot of volatility among the electorate surrounding a pushback against Marie Antoinette and her tech friends,” said David McCuan, a political science professor at Sonoma State University who studies ballot measures. “And that’s what the ‘yes’ forces are relying on.”Recent polling on Prop 40 shows that it’s favored to pass, but its lead has shrunk over the last few weeks as the opposition campaign has increased spending. Alate-September pollby the University of California shows 45% of voters likely to vote yes on the tax with 42% voting no. Just a month earlier, the proposalenjoyed a 7% lead.View image in fullscreenPeople attend a rally against Proposition 40 at the Iron Workers Apprenticeship Training center on 5 October in La Palma, California.Photograph: Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesComplicating matters aretwo separate countermeasuresthat Prop 40’s opponents successfully placed on the November ballot, Proposition 41 and 42. Prop 41 directly targets the billionaire tax, while Prop 42 is more of a general proposal to protect individuals from certain new taxes. If either of these measures receives more yes votes than Prop 40, they will stop the billionaire tax from taking effect – even if it passes.“Props 41 and 42 have poison pills in them to destroy 40,” McCuan said. “And when voters are confused, when they are uncertain … it’s much easier to get a no vote.”Will Trump’s economy sink Republicans in the US midterm elections? Our reporters answered your questionsRead moreBig tech’s strategyEarlier this month, the campaign fighting the billionaire tax placed an ad on television, digital and streaming platforms across the state. It starts with quiet, foreboding music and the president of the California Medical Association, René Bravo, dressed in a white lab coat, saying: “The people pushing Prop 40 say it’s supposed to improve healthcare. That’s not true.”The campaign has debuted similar ads saying teachers, carpenters and firefighters also oppose the wealth tax, saying it’s “a dangerous experiment”.The messaging around the campaign centers on how the tax would hurt “doctors, teachers, small businesses, working families and public safety”, without mention of the state’s billionaires. The no on Prop 40 campaign calls it “an everyone tax”.Likewise, the campaigns for the two measures that would pre-empt the billionaire tax argue these proposals promote transparency and have the backing of small businesses and taxpayers. One of the measures says its coalition includes retirees, blue-collar workers, seniors and veterans.The three campaigns against the wealth tax, however, draw nearly all of their funding from Super Pacs loaded withSilicon Valleymoney, according to campaign finance filings. Since July, the committees opposing Prop 40 and supporting Props 41 and 42 have received a total of more than $297.8m, most of that from a Super Pac called Building a Better California.The billionaires have found themselves in alliance with several healthcare, education, construction and public safety unions and associations. Governor Gavin Newsom has decried the billionaire tax, as have gubernatorial candidates, Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton. Katie Porter, a former Democratic Congresswoman known for taking corporate executives to task, has become one of the main faces of the opposition campaign – writing op-eds, speaking at rallies and being quoted in ads and mailers.The three campaigns are spending much of their fortunes on an army of consultants tasked with everything from lobbying politicians to working on media strategy. The consultants include the Republican-leaning law firm Nielsen Merksamer, known forfighting on behalfof tobacco companies, and the political consultancy PCI Campaigns, known forbattling propositionsthat sought to repeal the death penalty and require condom use in pornographic films.Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California is also listed as a paid contractor in campaign filings and has been one of the no campaign’s most vocal endorsers.State filings show that the campaigns donated tens of thousands to the California Democratic party, along with the Democratic parties of San Diego, Orange county and Los Angeles county. Despite the donations, all of these Democratic parties have backed the billionaire tax, urging a yes vote on Prop 40.Opponents of the wealth tax have also explicitly targeted the Latino community, placing ads, articles and op-eds in Spanish-language news outlets throughout the state. Onearticlein San Diego’s El Latino is headlined: “No a la Proposición 40: Una Buena Idea, Mal Construida” (“No on Proposition 40: A good idea, poorly executed”).When asked about the no on Prop 40’s spending strategy and donations it has received fromSuper Pacs, a spokesperson for the campaign emailed a comment from Bravo: “The more Californians learn, the more they see Prop. 40 for what it is – a harmful tax scheme that permanently damages the state’s budget and economy with zero accountability or safeguards to ensure funding actually improves care or lowers costs for patients.”Brin and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California didn’t return requests for comment. The Building a Better California Super Pac declined to comment.Yes on 40’s strategyLast week, Sanders, the progressive senator from Vermont,traveled to Californiato stump for Prop 40 alongside state politicians. The longtime advocate of wealth taxes announced to a crowded rally of supporters that the measure was “the most important ballot initiative in the country”.View image in fullscreenRo Khanna introduces the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders at the Ballots over Billionaires event in downtown Los Angeles on 5 October.Photograph: Jackson Tammariello/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock“The whole country, and frankly people from around the world, are paying attention to what is happening here,” Sanders said to wild applause. “It is not easy running a campaign where you’re going to be greatly outspent. But that is what you are doing, and the entire country is proud.”The billionaire tax wasfirst proposed late last yearby the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), which says the one-time tax is necessary because of huge federal healthcare funding cuts under Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The union says the funding would preserve healthcare for 3.4 million Californians.Since then, the campaign has garnered momentum through its partnerships with unions, community leaders and progressive politicians, including Khanna, a Democratic congressman who represents the district that includes Silicon Valley, the powerful California Federation of Labor Unions AFL-CIO, the California Teamsters union and the state’s Democratic party. Besides the SEIU-UHW, one of the campaign’s biggest donors is Saikat Chakrabarti, a former tech engineer who ran for Congress earlier this year but lost in the primary.“A few controversial billionaires like Sergey Brin would rather spend millions to fund shady opposition campaigns than simply pay their fair share in taxes so millions of their fellow Californians don’t lose their healthcare,” said Debru Carthan, a spokesperson for the yes campaign and vice-president of SEIU-UHW. “No amount of billionaire spending is going to intimidate us or turn us back.”Instead of relying on more expensive traditional media, the yes campaign has turned to Instagram, Snapchat and YouTube to create viral moments and target younger audiences. Campaign finance disclosures show campaign expenditures have gone to consultants, mailers and social media ads.“Dolly Parton could have died a billionaire and she didn’t,” said an unnamed influencer in a yes on Prop 40postlast month. “And the one reason that she didn’t is that she spent decades of her life giving away her money to charity and to philanthropy … There’s a really simple question that I want to ask the billionaires of California: how much is enough?”The no on Prop 40 campaign has also paid for ads on Google, Instagram, Yahoo, X and Taboola, according to campaign filings. It has additionally paid $3,000 for its Instagram posts to be amplified – a practice that gives an inorganic boost to social media.“Billionaires are pouring hundreds of millions into deceptive commercials to confuse voters about Prop 40 because the truth is, they know that taxing the rich is popular,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions. “We cannot let them buy our elections and choose who gets to live or die.”McCuan echoes the idea that the vote on Prop 40 is bigger than this election. How voters come down on the ballot measure will signal whether the issue will spill over to more states and even nationally, he said.“That is about testing the broader issue of wealth inequality and affordability in a wide-open presidential election in 2028,” McCuan said. “And if you’re a zillionaire or on the no side, you want to nip this thing in the bud so it doesn’t go to other places.”

title: How to dress a tech oligarch: The Social Reckoning’s costume designer on Zuckerberg’s style evolution | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters
Content: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning (2026), directed by Aaron Sorkin.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenJeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning (2026), directed by Aaron Sorkin.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyFashionHow to dress a tech oligarch: The Social Reckoning’s costume designer on Zuckerberg’s style evolutionSusan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweatersHannah MarriottFri 16 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first Aaron Sorkin Facebook movie, 2010’s The Social Network, helped cement the early aughts image ofMark Zuckerbergrebelling against corporate norms in rumpled hoodies and T-shirts.The follow-up, The Social Reckoning, is carbon-dated from 2019 to 2021. This is “post-hoodie”, as the movie’s costume designer, Susan Lyall, describes it, “post-thumbing his nose” to formality. It is also peak robot. Zuckerberg’s reserved wardrobe of suits or interchangeable long-sleeved shirts echo his chilling composure throughout, even as fury simmers under the surface.The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet ZuckerbergRead moreThe costume was based on deep research by Lyall and also by actor Jeremy Strong who, she says, is “very into costume”. Having worked together before, on the Sorkin movies Molly’s Game and The Trial of the Chicago 7, they would text a lot during the preparation process.“He reaches out before I even get to reach out to him. It’s my third movie with him, so I’m pretty used to it. He’s very proactive. He’s one of my favourite actors because of that. He would know exactly where [Zuckerberg] wore what. He wanted the exact Nike shoe – the footwear was very important to him – and the exact Brunello Cucinelli T-shirt and sweater, and so on,” she says.Strong has become notorious for method acting, and method dressing, too, seems to be part of his process. “It’s sort of the first step in the performance. That and the haircut,” says Lyall.The conversations went deep. “It’s actually kind of nerdy, you know, to sit there and talk about the color of the shoelaces. There aren’t that many people who want to talk about that. I always joke with him, if the acting thing doesn’t work out, you can have a position in my department!” she says.Lyall found those Nikes – to be specific, the 2018 Nike Flyknit trainer in black anthracite – on Grailed. For the sweaters, it was Strong, she says, who worked out how to reach the eye-wateringly expensive Italian luxury brand Brunello Cucinelli, in order to buy specific pieces, “because we don’t want the latest. We want stuff from five or six years ago, and they were very helpful at procuring it. And that was because of him. He was really proactive.”Lyall has spent a lot of hours thinking about how tech oligarchs dress. Not only Zuckerberg but Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and others too, who were partial inspiration for another of her recent credits, the 2025 Jesse Armstrong movie Mountainhead about four devilish plutocrats.View image in fullscreenA still from Mountainhead (2025), directed by Jesse Armstrong.Photograph: HBO/2025 Home Box Office Inc. All Rights ReservedThey, too, wore a lot of Brunello Cucinelli. That brand sells cashmere cardigans for $16,500 and ribbed sweaters for $4,600. Amusingly, it currently has the Immanuel Kant quote “beauty is the symbol of the morally good” in prime place on its website homepage.In Lyall’s view, Brunello Cucinelli is a “safety net for people like Mark Zuckerberg. If they’re not sure about what they’re wearing, if they pay a lot for it, they feel a little better about it. You know, if this little sweater is $2,000, it must be good. It’s kind of a security blanket, or just an affirmation of your own success. You’re going to be OK if you’re wearing this tasteful thing.”double quotation markI think [tech billionaires] have discovered a new way to flexSusan LyallThe Zuckerberg of The Social Reckoning had moved on from the earlier antifashion stance that prompted him to declare, in 2014, that he was “not a cool person”, and only wore grey T-shirts because he wanted to make “as few decisions as possible … I feel like I’m not doing my job if I spend any of my energy on things that are silly or frivolous.”By the period captured in the movie, says Lyall, “I believe Zuckerberg was trying to be relatable, but also starting to understand Silicon Valley’s obsession with taste and the cost of things.” He was also more buff than he had been. In her interpretation, he seemed to be thinking: “My fit physique looks very nice in this clingy but expensive sweater. And ‘if you know, you know’ – I think there’s a bit of that. But I also think, he’s nouveau riche without being gaudy. It’s not without taste.”Since then, Zuckerberg’s outward presentation has graduated to outright peacocking.For the tech billionaires, in general, says Lyall: “I think something happened. I think they have discovered a new way to flex. And it’s not quiet luxury. It’s loud.”For Zuckerberg specifically – whose makeover came suddenly with ostentatious gold chains, Loewe shorts and Alexander McQueen suits embellished with dragonflies in around 2024 – it could not feel much more strategic.View image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect conference on 25 September 2024 in Menlo Park, California.Photograph: Godofredo A Vásquez/APDabbling with fashion allows Zuckerberg to look like a different guy from the one we have seen so many times sweating in a suit in front of Congress. It also provides a distraction from the reality of his products and work, giving him something soft and harmless to talk about.Zuckerberg has even used the classic fiction writer’s trick of embedding backstory within his jewellery. In 2024, when he started wearing a large, gold pendant necklace over his T-shirt, he claimed it wasn’t just because he wanted to look like a hip-hop star, as the internet understandably concluded.When finally asked about his pendant in an interview (“oh this?” he said, with an approximation of spontaneity) he explained that it was embossed with a Jewish prayer he sings to his kids every night at bedtime, thus reminding the public of his humanity – his faith, and the importance he places on being there for his children.This year, asMetahas recruited fashion stars such as Kylie Jenner to market its smart glasses, he has spent yet more time courting fashion, attending Prada shows and the Met Gala.Last month, he gave the New York Times an interview purely about clothing, claiming that he buys almost all of his wardrobe on Instagram himself – which sounds extremely decision-requiring and time-consuming for a person of his workload.Many of the labels he mentioned were more contemporary, less oligarch-coded, among them Mike Amiri, a purveyor of $400-ish T-shirts, with whom he has worked on bespoke items including the “Building is my love language” he wore to present Muse at a Facebook conference. Online, too, when he buys something of the $200-ish, rather than $2000-ish price tag, he may even pop into the comments, when complimented on that item, to draw users’ attention towards it (“It’s@johnelliottco– I’m loving their stuff recently”).Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?Read moreJust as the new personal AI assistant Muse has been fashioned to look utterly adorable – surely such a cute fluffy Labubu-like creature could never spark an apocalypse! – Zuckerberg’s own continuing makeover appears conceived to make him a more friendly and, ideally, more human.In fashion, though, it’s not as simple as ticking the box to confirm you are not a robot. When he explained his interest in style tothe New York Times, for example, he said, “I think the company is an instantiation of my values” and claimed he wanted to “be intentional about how I program that”.A turn of phrase that suggests that, under his vibrant new clothing, the cashmere-clad machine depicted in Sorkin’s movie may not have been properly deactivated.Explore more on these topicsFashionMark ZuckerbergMetafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors | Games | The Guardian
description: This odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appears
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: This odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appears
Content: One of 2026’s boldest, most original games … Penguin Colony by Origame Digital.Photograph: Origame Digital/Fellow TravellerView image in fullscreenOne of 2026’s boldest, most original games … Penguin Colony by Origame Digital.Photograph: Origame Digital/Fellow TravellerGamesReviewPenguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrorsPC; Origame DigitalThis odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appearsLewis GordonFri 16 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleANazi kneels down on frozen snow, staring at an endless Antarctic horizon. Another holds a gun to his head, ready to end his own life. I direct a small waddling penguin up to them, trying to imagine what it could be thinking. Dismay, perhaps. Likely bewilderment. But then a faint smile seems to break out across its beaky face, as if amused by these silly humans and their misguided belief that they could ever best this howling, harsh landscape.For most games, the idea of playing as a penguin observing Nazis losing the plot near the south pole would be weird enough. But Penguin Colony, developed by Origame Digital, pushes further. This is an audacious, frequently brilliant retelling of HP Lovecraft’s 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness, in which eldritch horrors are just as common as Nazis. Further weirdness abounds: the many collectibles scattered about this place are not shiny gold objects à la Super Mario or Sonic. Rather, they are words. So tottering about as a semiaquatic bird, you have a unique mission: collect human language.View image in fullscreenUnnerving, discordant … Penguin Colony.Photograph: Fellow TravellerBut let’s zoom out for a moment because playing Penguin Colony is more straightforward than this description suggests. First and foremost, it is a semiopen world exploration game in which you direct a penguin to the same unearthly entity that the Nazis are chasing. You hop, swim and glide about tummy-first, chewing up miles of frozen wasteland like an indefatigable snowboarder. Tapping a button next to another penguin lets you swap into its body. Some of these, like the rockhopper penguin, are nimble movers, capable of jumping especially high. Fluffy penguin chicks, meanwhile, can squeeze through tiny gaps.At first, the game’s polar levels are straightforward: snow drifts and ice floes peppered with the remnants of human habitation such as fishing huts. But your surroundings quickly grow stranger: supersized stone labyrinths whose architectural splendour evokesDark Souls, alien-looking obelisks and abyssal crevasses. Everything in the world is rendered in jagged, low-poly graphics, looming from the screen like a hallucinated PlayStation 2 game.View image in fullscreenLow-poly nightmares … Penguin Colony by Origame Digital.Photograph: Origame Digital/Fellow TravellerAs you navigate these spaces, a deep-voiced narrator relays the expedition of a scientist from decades before. It’s clear he is driven by the same hubris and racism as his Nazi successors.The layering of space, time and narrative is terrifically unsettling. At one point, having just hopped my way through a challenging platform section, I came across a Nazi cannibal feasting on his fellow soldier as a researcher delivered yet another verbose pontification on his God-given right to plunder Earth’s southernmost tip. At times, jarring cuts to archive footage and what seem to be Indigenous art interrupt the low-poly action. My head was often spinning, trying to reconcile all these conflicting, contrapuntal elements. Better, I found, to let go and soak up the unnerving, discordant whole.Penguin Colony is a little uneven technically: I experienced a small number of audio glitches and, at times, bugs with the controls. Yet this does not overly detract from an experience that builds to an incendiary conclusion: a takedown of Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism while also, intriguingly, inviting the player to see the world in newly reenchanted terms.This latter point is made with aplomb at the game’s end: a spectacular cosmological map that details everything you discovered on that playthrough. More tantalisingly, it shows you all the things you missed. This reveal is liable to induce a feeling of vertigo and wonder: Penguin Colony, one of 2026’s boldest, most original games, is far bigger than it first lets on. To access all of its secrets and excavate all of its meaning, one must think and act less like a human mainlining towards their objective. On the contrary, you must embrace the spirit of a renegade penguin, waddling carefree towards whatever piques your interest: atrocity, beauty and all.Penguin Colony is available now onPC, with PS5 and Nintendo Switch versions planned for 2027Explore more on these topicsGamesAdventure gamesIndie gamesPCGame playPlatform gamesHP LovecraftreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Of course Trump is helping Russia in Ukraine – he’s a master of the art of betrayal | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: The old certainties have gone. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in this new and dangerous world, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The old certainties have gone. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in this new and dangerous world, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago, Florida, 28 December 2025.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago, Florida, 28 December 2025.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpOf course Trump is helping Russia in Ukraine – he’s a master of the art of betrayalJonathan FreedlandThe old certainties have gone. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in this new and dangerous worldFri 16 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.37 EDTShareDonald Trump must find it oddly frustrating. He keeps showing the world exactly who he is, and yet the world keeps refusing to believe it. As clearly as he can, he is announcing that he is not the leader of the free world, that he is not even a reliable member of the democratic west, that he is in fact an ally of its enemies – but the west, including Britain, either doesn’t fully get the message or can’t quite bring itself to draw the obvious conclusion.Trump had another go this week, finding multiple ways to declare that in the war between Russia and Ukraine, he is no mediator or peace broker but a partner of Vladimir Putin. In fairness to him, the US president had loudly issued that declaration within weeks of his return to the White House when, in February 2025, he delivered anon-camera dressing down of Volodymyr Zelenskyyin the Oval Office, seeking to humiliate the Ukrainian leader by telling him “you don’t have the cards”, even as JD Vance demanded their visitor show gratitude. That should have made Trump’s position sufficiently plain, but in the past few days he has all but put it up in lights.Earlier this week Ukrainian forces found thatan essential piece of kit– a version of Elon Musk’s Starlink system used by Kyiv to guide its drones – was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph. That meant not only a sudden shrinking of Ukraine’s ability to strike behind the frontlines, but also the hobbling of an air defence system vital in protecting the capital from Russian jet-propelled drones. This was no technical hitch. Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, is owned and controlled by the US government – and,as Reuters reported, the order to limit its use in Ukraine came from the White House. Put simply, Trump actively intervened in the war to weaken Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. “The decision will bring a lot of human losses,” Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan. “Of course, people will die.”Trump’s move was hardly a bolt from the blue. This same week,Ukraineendured at least two nights of Russian bombardment without the usual advance warnings from the US of when or where Moscow was about to strike. Trump denied that he had broken off long-established intelligence sharing with Kyiv, but that’s exactly what it looked like.All this followed the US president’s decision to break the international sanctions regime on Moscow, by agreeing tobuy $4bn worth of Russian diesel oil. That volume will barely make asplash in the US market, where high diesel prices are imperilling the Republicans’ midterm chances in several rural states that rely on the stuff, but it will come as a welcome cash infusion for Putin’s war machine. Just asRussia’s military position was looking precarious, Donald Trump has come riding to the rescue. Throw in theUS invitation to Putin to attend December’s G20 meetingat one of Trump’s golf clubs in Florida, and you have a US president who might as well be skywriting his support for Russia and his betrayal of Ukraine.In Trump’s first term, much energy was spent trying to work out what dark secret lay behind this apparent affinity with Moscow. I tend to the view advanced by my expert colleagueLuke Harding, who, when asked if Trump is a tool of the Russian intelligence services, answers with a question of his own: if Trump were a Russian asset, in what way would he behave any differently from the way he behaves now?Whatever the motive, or whether, as Harding suggests, it’s some combination ofgreed, ideology, dictator envy andkompromat, the facts are unarguable. The most powerful member of the western alliance is, at best, an unreliable partner and, at worst, in league with the alliance’s chief enemy. Why this matters should not need spelling out, least of all in the week when the head of MI5 described Russia as“aggressor number one”. For years now, the Kremlin has demonstrated its willingness to attack Nato member states, usually in the form of hybrid or “grey zone” operations that are not overt acts of war but come instead with a patina of deniability. One study found that there have been than no fewer than“151 confirmed Russian-directed industrial sabotage incidents in Europe between February 2022 and February 2026”, while last weekend broughtcredible reports of a Russian intention to assassinate executivesof key European defence firms.What should the US’s erstwhile allies do about this new reality? The first task is to keep supporting Ukraine, all the more energetically given that Washington has, in effect, switched sides. The second is to avoid an error that is looming. The midterm elections, which are little more than a fortnight away, are expected to deliver big gains for the Democrats and a big blow to Trump. If Democrats retake one or both houses of Congress, plenty of European leaders will be tempted to exhale deeply, conclude that the orange storm has passed and that normal transatlantic service is about to resume. That would be a grave mistake.For one thing, while the US president has been unbound by congressional restraint for most of the past two years, it’s not certain that a constrained Trump will be a tamed Trump. On the contrary, one Washington hand warns that he could become a “cornered animal”, even more extreme in the area where a president is freest to act, namely foreign affairs. Of course, Trump will be gone eventually, but there too lies the danger of false comfort. “This shift is permanent,” one former UK cabinet minister tells me. If nothing else, Trump has proved that Trump and Trumpism can happen: now we know that the western alliance is neither guaranteed nor unshakeable, but vulnerable to a change in the US political weather.All of this means we are living in a newly dangerous world. Witness the richly reported new bookWar is Interested in Youby Gideon Rachman, which lays bare quite how seriously leading policymakers rate the risk of a third world war. It’s an age in which we can no longer rely on others to defend us. The chilling lesson of the Starlink episode for those who depend on US hardware or software is that the US always retains an off switch. In other words, Britain and the rest of Europe have to be able to defend ourselves, with our own armies and our own arms.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe best time for governments to have made this case was the night of that shocking Oval Office scene with Zelenskyy last year. But the second-best time is now. When John Healey delivers his first budget on 28 October, this is the argument he needs to set out. As a former defence secretary, he is especially well placed to do it. The Labour manifesto of 2024 was written before Trump was re-elected, before anyone knew that in the great clash of our time the US was about to align itself with authoritarianism against democracy. Things have changed and that document can no longer be treated as holy writ. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in a changed and perilous world. Trump is telling us that in a crude, loud voice. We must listen.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistUS midterms: Trump, war and America’s futureOn Thursday, 5 November join Jonathan Freedland, Devika Bhat, Professor Adam Smith in London and David Smith and leading US commentator Tara Setmayer live from the US to discuss the results and their implications for the future of Trump, the US and global politics.Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUkraineTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: No Nobel again for Trump but he looks a cert to retain Fifa peace prize | John Crace | The Guardian
description: With his war in Iran and siding with Russia, it’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place
Author: John Crace
Headline: With his war in Iran and siding with Russia, it’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place
Content: The US president is put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe US president is put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersDigested weekDonald TrumpDigested week: No Nobel again for Trump but he looks a cert to retain Fifa peace prizeJohn CraceWith his war in Iran and siding with Russia, it’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer placeFri 16 Oct 2026 06.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.40 EDTShareMondayIt might have been more, shall we say, diplomatic if Donald Trump had taken some deep breaths after finding out he had been overlooked for the Nobel peace prize for the second year running before virtually declaring war on Norway. But maybe we should just be grateful he refrained from rubbishing the South African human rights activist Navi Pillay,who picked up the award, and shelved his plans to livestream the execution of the Norwegian prize committee. There again, you can understand his frustration. It’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place. Where would we be had not The Donald started a war with Iran which he shows no sign of knowing how to finish and which has forced up the price of global energy? And it was so good to see him intervening so positively in Russia’s war with Ukraine by appearing to side with the aggressor. These are just the things everyone is looking for in a Nobel peace laureate. The president is also put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts; though it would be helpful if he could let us know which ones. Are they ones he has personally started – Trump appears disappointed that Argentina hasn’t invaded the Falklands again – or ones that only he knows about. During a press conference at Chequers in 2025, he claimed to have brought about a lasting peace between Albania and Azerbaijan. Maybe there are other wars going on we just don’t know about. Perhaps Australia and New Zealand have been bombing each other for years with neither side noticing. And perhaps the border between France and Italy has been a no-go zone ever since the fight between Zinedine Zidane and Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final. Still, Trump looks a cert to retain Gianni Infantino’s Fifa peace prize –if only because it seems likely to be scrapped, making him the only winner.TuesdayWe may be facing higher levels of global threat and energy costs, but the political outlook isn’t all bleak. You’d need to have a major sense of humour failure not to be enjoying Reform sliding in the polls and falling out with one another. Things seemed to start going wrong when the Guardian exposed Nigel Farage’s £5m bung fromthe Thai-based crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne. Nige has still not come up with a convincing explanation of how the money would be spent. Other than maintaining an expensive lifestyle. Then there was the Channel 4 sting when two of Farage’s closest political allieswere caught allegedly trying to take an illegal overseas donation. Nige’s excuse? He wasn’t listening to his conversation with the donor. Who hasn’t dozed off when there’s £500,000 at stake? Since then everyone in Reform appears hell-bent on being the worst versions of themselves as the party loses support by tacking ever further to the right. On Monday, Robert Jenrickdeclaredhe would personally be happy to give the order for the Royal Navy to blow every small boat crossing the Channel out of the water. This was too much for Zia Yusuf. Zia is widely loathed within the Reform elite but no one has found a way of saying no to his money, so he gets to call himself the bogus title of shadow home secretary. His main objection to Honest Bob’s plan is that he wasn’t the one to think of it first. Meanwhile, Nige just sits back and pockets the money. Seemingly unable to stop his party collapsing around him.View image in fullscreenMeghan: ‘I hope I’m not upstaging the – what’s she called? – the Princess of Welsh.’Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersWednesdayAfter several years of consultation,the Bank of England has announced the four animals, insects and birds that will appear on the new banknotes. What goes on what denomination has yet to be decided, but the ones chosen are the European hedgehog, the barn owl, the buff-tailed bumblebee and the Atlantic puffin. And while I’d have quite liked to have seen my much-missed dog Herbie, who died last year, on one of the notes, they all seem reasonable choices to me. I guess the last thing the Bank wanted was to start a war between cat and dog lovers. But not everyone is happy. Partly because they are mad but mostly because they don’t apparently understand how the selection process worked. It was the public who got to choose both the theme of the banknotes and the actual creatures. Needless to say, leading the charge against the new notes are Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, who see the hedgehog and the puffin as some kind of woke symbols. A country going to the barn owls and the bumblebees. They have moaned, what was wrong with having Winston Churchill? Are we now ashamed of our past? No, you halfwits. You don’t have to plaster Churchill’s face on everything to prove you are British. Most of us are secure enough in our identity not to need countless flags and symbols as a reminder. It’s just nice to have a change from time to time. And how many people used to see Churchill’s face on a £5 note and feel a well of pride every time you wanted to buy a sandwich? For that matter, how many people even use cash these days? Mind you, once AI has mined all our data from our emails and bank accounts we could be back to a cash and letter-writing society.ThursdayIn one of his last conversations with a close friend,Jeffrey Archerwas asked if he had any regrets. While he admitted to having some flaws, Archer went on to say that there was nothing he would change. I find that remarkable. I’m not expecting him to apologise for having invented so much of his life – a fantasist is going to fantasise – and he had every right to be proud of his book sales. But not to feel a tiny bit of regret about having lied on oath and being sent to prison. Or feel guilty for the lives he ruined as a result of his lies. That feels borderline sociopathic. Isn’t it human to wish you had done some things differently? I’ve been thinking about this now I’ve turned 70. There’s a lot about my life that I love – family, friends, job – but I have a lasting sadness and guilt about my 20s that I find hard to forgive. The waste, the self-destruction, the damage I did to myself and others. Many of those who knew me had doubts I would even live to 30. I had those doubts, too. And sometimes didn’t much care either way. So yes, I have a whole decade I would love to have done differently. The repair job has been a lifetime’s work and it’s still ongoing. It will probably always be thus.View image in fullscreenBurnham to Zelenskyy: ‘Oh. I was hoping you might have some money for our armed forces.’Photograph: Alastair Grant/APFridayThe Celebrity Traitors continues to be addictive television. A class above the civilian version, partly because we all know something about the celebs, but mainly because the game is different. The civilians are playing for money, the celebs are playing for screen time. That’s why Amol Rajan was gutted to be banished inside 24 hours. The one exception was Richard E Grant, who didn’t care one way or the other. Since his wife died he’s become more disinhibited. The worst has already happened to him. Halfway in, Maya Jama and James Acaster are making great traitors. Maya because she’s so hard to read as her face doesn’t move, James because he genuinely believes he’s too nice to be a traitor while stabbing his friends in the back. I’m amazed Jerry Hall is still in. Not because she’s particularly suspicious but more because she’s incredibly annoying. And why has no one asked her what it was like being married to Rupert Murdoch? The faithful who is playing a blinder is Sharon Rooney. So far she has said and done nothing to attract the film crew, which means she’s likely to be around for a while yet. Being boring is not a bad strategy. I’d like to see a version ofThe Traitorsfor politicians, and in my forthcoming shows (Birmingham MAC on 31 October, Huntingdon theatre in Worcester on 26 November) I will be inviting the audience to offer suggestions for possible contestants. So please come along and let’s see if we can make it happen.View image in fullscreenPrince William: ‘Couldn’t Harry have done this one?’Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAOn Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026.
