title: Since my daughter moved out of home, my household has shrunk. A yearly tradition brings us together | Nova Weetman | The Guardian
description: Since my mother died, I have tried other jams – Seville orange, apricot, rich plum – but there are no memories to the taste
Author: Nova Weetman
Headline: Since my mother died, I have tried other jams – Seville orange, apricot, rich plum – but there are no memories to the taste
Content: ‘Making cumquat jam is a tradition I inherited from my mum. Along with her recipes for plum pudding, broad bean falafels and tomato relish.’Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Making cumquat jam is a tradition I inherited from my mum. Along with her recipes for plum pudding, broad bean falafels and tomato relish.’Photograph: Getty ImagesOpinionJams, preserves and spreadsSince my daughter moved out of home, my household has shrunk. A yearly tradition brings us togetherNova WeetmanI wait each year for my cumquat tree to fruit. Then I make Mum’s jamFri 16 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTShareIt’s citrus season, and the trees of my streets are heavy with the bright balls of fruit. My son sometimes picks me a lemon or two on his way home from school, and I help myself to the basket of limes that hang from the fence of a nearby house. The potted plant on my balcony fruited early this season, and for weeks I watched as the hundreds of small green cumquats slowly ripened. I finally picked them when they were fattened with juice and seeds and colour, the cat squatting on the ground to watch. When I dropped a cumquat she sniffed at the skin and turned away, as if sensing the sharpness of its flesh.When life gives you cumquats or kumquats make a marmalade and mezcal cocktail – recipeRead moreSince my daughter moved out several years ago, my household has shrunk. It is now only my son and me. And the cat. A scratchy, sullen creature who delights in ignoring us both unless we are sitting in the seat she believes is hers. My son has begun cooking for himself, and so I find my services in the kitchen required less often. Except for the yearly making of cumquat jam.The jam is a tradition I inherited from my mum. Along with her recipes for plum pudding, broad bean falafels and tomato relish. When I was a kid, Mum would scavenge each year in her friends’ gardens for cumquats and then spend close to two days chopping, deseeding, soaking, boiling and jarring the fruit to fill our cupboards with the stained glass orange jam. Years later, when I had children, Mum introduced them to the tart taste, and they were hooked too. When she died, 15 years ago, winter came and went without our usual jars to see us through. We tried eating jam made from other fruits. Seville orange, apricot, rich plum, but there were no memories to the taste, and the jars would sit unfinished in the fridge for months.Witnessing my grief at losing my mum, some friends bought me a baby cumquat tree in a large yellow ceramic pot that proved itself hardy enough to survive my limited gardening skills. The first year that it flowered with delicate white buds, we watched, delighting in the growth of the cumquats, waiting until they were large enough to pick. My kids helped strip the tree of fruit. It was nothing like the haul Mum used to make jam with, but it filled a bowl. I hacked up the cumquats, not neatly like Mum did, but fast and furious, not bothering to remove the pips because I’d read somewhere they would float up during boiling and you could scoop them from the top with the scum. Impatiently, I didn’t follow the ratio of sugar or simmer for the correct amount of time, and that first batch was overcooked. The jam was too dark in colour, and the texture was all wrong, but we ate it anyway, the taste taking me immediately back to my childhood home, where I’d perch up at the bench each morning before school and work my way through rye toast smeared with jam.View image in fullscreen‘Witnessing my grief at losing my mum, some friends bought me a baby cumquat tree in a large yellow ceramic pot.’Photograph: Nova WeetmanThe following year, I channelled Mum’s patience and made two large jars of jam. They were the perfect amber-colour, rich and bright, with chunks of rind and the occasional pip. It wasn’t enough to squirrel away in the cupboard like a true survivalist, but it saw us through a month or two of breakfasts. This year, I managed six jars, enough to spare for giving one to a friend, and another to my daughter when she came for dinner one night. She took half our loaf of fresh sourdough bread with her too so she could replicate the favourite breakfast of her childhood.My son and I are now down to our last jar of jam, and we have started rationing it without discussion, eating it on toast weekly instead of daily, to make it last as long as we can. I do sometimes buy cumquat jam if I see it at a market, but it never quite tastes the same. There is something treasured in waiting each year for the tree to grow the fruit to make the jam. It is ritual that connects us to the jam that Mum once made.My cumquat tree still lives in the same yellow pot. It has moved house twice with us, requiring four people to lift it on to a trolley, and it now grows in the strip of sun on our apartment balcony. It is not much to look at it until the flowers come and the fruit arrives, but then it brings with it all the promise of the taste of my childhood.Nova Weetman is an award-winning author of books for children and young adultsExplore more on these topicsJams, preserves and spreadsOpinionFruitFamilyAustralian food and drinkcommentShareReuse this content

title: We are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently?  | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: The education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculator, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: The education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculator, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: ‘Lucy Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Lucy Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamyOpinionEducationWe are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently?Simon JenkinsThe education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculatorFri 16 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 05.54 EDTShareAt last the fourth R is born. Articulation – speaking – is to join reading, writing and arithmetic in the education canon. What has become the mighty struggle against the dictatorship of the screen can begin in earnest. The spoken word, human-to-human communication, must finally be recognised by the gods of reactionary schooling. The pundits call it oracy.On Thursday, the education secretary, Lucy Powell, called the academics’ bluff. She wants a radical reform of the national curriculum in England to reduce “desktop” working in favour ofverbal fluency and practical skills. This will take courage. For decades, education’s senior leaders have been ramming easily forgotten “subjects”, such as maths and French,into children’s brains so they can be judged and measured in league tables. These tables have grown ever more dominant as ministers seek to climb “global rankings”.After the second world war, an “academic” secondary education was shaped by the increased demand for a university-educated workforce. Higher education was expanded, but Britain’s technical and vocational schools and colleges wererelegated out of sight. Teaching became enslaved to exam quantification and lost contact with the real world.But the act of excluding communication skills from this academic orthodoxy has come home to roost. Artificial intelligence and mobile phones are progressively distancing young people from adults and each other. I notice gatherings of young people who used to chatter, laugh and banter. They now stand gazing at their screens or they just shout at each other. Conversation – sharing, informing, discussing, sympathising – seems on the way out.Speaking itself is going out of fashion. Research suggests that in the past two decades the number of words people say each day has shrunk bynearly a third. They prefer texting. A quarter of young people now say theynever even answer the phoneunless pre-arranged. They fear a phone call means bad news.Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage. It is about conveying what one means clearly; listening, debating and handling disagreement. Speaking well means using eye contact and appropriately adjusting your tone of voice. It means politeness and tolerance. Above all, it enables young people to present themselves to others effectively, whether in work, play, argument or friendship.To the Greeks and Romans, oracy was the towering skill of rhetoric. It was central to citizenship. The New Education movement of Steiner and Montessori in early 20th-century Europe stressed building on the qualities of the individual child rather than imposing rote learning from above. It is significant that the movement has seen a revival in theWaldorf schoolsnow favoured by California’s AI executives in Silicon Valley.That such ideals of progressive education have long been drummed out of the English curriculum is outrageous. The aversion to the spoken word has corresponded with the increasing prominence of maths in the curriculum, its skills beyond foundational arithmeticirrelevant to all but a tiny minorityof adults. Children need to master elementary maths in primary school. But after that they only need to know how to use a calculator. I wonder how many readers remember being able to answer this question fromlast year’s GCSE paper: “The volume of a sphere is 4/3πr³ whereris the radius. Work out the volume of a sphere with diameter 20cm in terms of π.”It is extraordinary that passing this exam isstill required for most apprenticeships. Yet while he was prime minister, Rishi Sunakwanted maths to be compulsoryuntil the age of 18. Small wonder it has long headed the list of“most hated” school subjects.Quite how the teaching profession will react to Powell is not clear. The hyper-centralisation of British government has meant ever more school time spent on exams. This has led to cutting back on individualised learning and creativity, which typically flourishes in teaching of the arts. Teachers are pressed to “teach to the test”, at peril of damnation from Ofsted. These days, only the private sector dares resist.Winchester collegedevotes an hour a day to its form of oracy: “div” and “forum” sessions, when pupils discuss contemporary topics not covered by the examination syllabus: scientific ideas, philosophy, politics, music, critical thinking and the acceptance of others’ opinions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch speech-centred concepts as group learning and peer tutoring are being pursued in some universities, and the cause was taken forward in the 2024oracy commission report. But the catch is always resources. The essence of teaching people how to speak must lie in personal contact. It is in the human relationship of tutor and pupil, which was once the essence of teaching as a profession, not a mechanical skill.One key might lie in killing maths. Leave it to its enthusiasts. For the rest, school should be about the world outside, a world of other human beings. It is about how to go about handling them that young people have most to learn.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEducationOpinionLucy PowellGCSEsExamsSchoolsEnglandMathematicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t work | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: The current system is unable to quench the public thirst for locking people up – and certainly doesn’t ensure proper care once they are released, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: The current system is unable to quench the public thirst for locking people up – and certainly doesn’t ensure proper care once they are released, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: A former inmate leaves HM Prison Liverpool on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA former inmate leaves HM Prison Liverpool on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionPrisons and probationBritain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t workPolly ToynbeeThe current system is unable to quench the public thirst for locking people up – and certainly doesn’t ensure proper care once they are releasedFri 16 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 08.53 EDTSharePublic services need more investment across the board. Every day, another wretched story. Look at the Institute for Government’s (IFG)Public Services Performance Trackerfor a plain assessment of A&E corridor care, councils struggling to meet the demands of social care and the Send system, the courts backlog, GP caseloads or families lost in temporary accommodation. A chancellor approaching a budget is besieged by need. It’s easy for us journalists to pick out shock stories and claim each one is an absolute priority, but how should a chancellor choose?Today it’s the probation officers, whoseconference in Newcastleis launching a ballot for industrial action. Their caseloads overflowed long ago, but now thousands of prisoners released early –2,000 this month– have been thrust upon them. The responsibility is overwhelming, with officers blamed for crimes their clients commit.The probation story is told in scores of reports: the National Audit Office found the servicerunning on half the staff neededto cover released prisoners. It also reportedfailures in electronic tagging, echoed by the IFG reporting only 55% oftags were fitted in time. Napo, the probation officers’ union, blames the problems on awarding contractsto the lowest biddersat prices that mean the job isn’t done properly.The number of offenders charged withserious further offences while on probationhas increased, with the public accounts committee blaming staff shortages. Vacancies leave probation services25%-30% below target levels. The government is training another 1,300, but that’s not enough, says Napo, considering thehigh dropout rateonce recruits discover the abuse, threats and stress of the work, alongside the fact that the most common cause of staff sickness ismental ill health.The sheer impossibility of their caseloads caused the government to abandon any attempt to say what their caseload should be, so the “workload measurement tool” wasabruptly ditched in Septemberjust before the October raft of new prisoner releases. There is no point in stating an official workload standard that can’t be met.Eleven hostels and seven halfway houses, places that help probation officers supervise released prisoners, havejust closed for repairs and because of a lack of staff. Drug addiction and mental health problems untreated in prisons, coupled with cuts to education, training and rehabilitation, make prisoners even less prepared for release.The probation system was broken by adisastrous privatisationwhen Chris Grayling (whobanned the sending of books to prisoners) split it apart into 21 private companies, with the workforce organisationally divided in two. Private companies only handled offenders judged low to medium risk, while the most serious offenders remained under the control of the state. Companies under-invested, experienced staff left, and none of the innovation promised was delivered. Afterthis ideological privatisation was abandoned in 2021, the probation service never recovered.The lord chancellor is set to address the probation officer’s conference. “But please,” says Napo chair Ben Cockburn, “no bullshit. Don’t tell us how well we do an exceptionally difficult job. We know that.”. Napo rejected a 5% pay offer on the grounds it falls far behind equivalent offers to workers in local government, police and social work. Under planned industrial action, Cockburn says probation officers will work to contract and refuse unpaid overtime. That, he says, will cause collapse.What probation officers need immediately is reduced workloads, pruned to the riskiest cases, leaving less serious cases unallocated. “Put the service into special measures,” Cockburn says. He also wants the courts to stop piling on more cases until there are enough staff to cope. “We are firefighting from one emergency to another,” he says – or called away to someone in a police cell, or to a paedophile found dating a woman with a child, or a domestic violence case.Cutting workloads for probation officers is only a short-term solution, one that avoids the real question. Why is there an ever-rising prison population, despite the sustained, multi-decade fall in crime rates?“We are addicted to prison,” Cockburn says. In his view, probation works when officers have time for long-term working relationships with offenders. “It’s the best job in the world,” he says, recalling the journey of one prisoner who had committed a terrible crime as a young man. “I saw him in prison, knew him for 15 years, with time for therapeutic work.” But, these days, that’s so rare. “Someone now might see eight different officers, retelling their story over and over, creating no trust.”Why build more prison cells? An inspection of a brand new private prison,HMP Millsikein East Yorkshire, found it unsafe due to a lack of experienced staff, as well as chronic staff shortages.Even at its opening, it was “chaotic”, lacking basic processes for important things like locking doors and counting prisoners. Hundreds of cells are still empty because of a lack of officers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPublic pressure to lock up more prisoners and supervise them when released will never be matched by a willingness to pay the taxes needed to cover the cost of attracting people to work in this sector. That’s the truth Cockburn wants politicians to be brave enough to tell. This country is not alone in wrongly believing crime is ever-rising when all across Europe it hasfallen for decades. But no one believes it. A news and drama fixation on horrific crime stirs primal fears that belie these facts. Politicians everywhere score points with a frightened public by clamouring for more punishment.When I last visited a hard-pressed prison, I asked the governor what she most needed, and was astonished when she said she wouldn’t invest here, but “right at the start, before the damage is done, in early years”.Asking where every pound spent does most good is the kind of mega-question budgets don’t answer. But a brave chancellor would cut prison funding down to housing only the most dangerous, and spending better on what works, such as well-funded probation officers.Keep telling this fact: all crime is horrible – sex crime is at last reported more often – but the overall drop in neighbourhood-level crime in England and Waleshas been about 80%since its peak in 1995. Meanwhile,prison numbers have risen significantly. In his upcoming speech at the probation officer’s conference, it would take unprecedented political bravery for the lord chancellor to dare end the pretence that prison works.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionUK criminal justicePublic sector cutsCrimeStaff shortagescommentShareReuse this content

title: The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win | Frances Ryan | The Guardian
description: The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Content: People rallying against disability benefit cuts in Parliament Square last year.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople rallying against disability benefit cuts in Parliament Square last year.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianOpinionWelfareThe right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and winFrances RyanThe prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the momentFri 16 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.02 EDTShareBack in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: alandmark reportpromising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”.The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them. They’ve even providedan interactive map(in the yellow and black colours of a road hazard sign, no less) so members of the public can type in their postcode to see if their neighbourhood is “a welfare hotspot”.This is not just another ugly social policy report from a politically sidelined former minister – it is a gauntlet being thrown down ahead of Britain’s big benefits debate.Next month, the government is expected to release two major reports into the social safety net:the Timms reviewon personal independence payments (Pip), which pays for some of the extra costs of disability in England and Wales, and theMilburn reviewinto young people who are out of work.It wouldn’t be overstating the importance of Westminster reviews to say their recommendations could shape the future of our welfare state for decades to come. With almost1 millionyoung people not in education, employment or training (Neet) and the disability benefits bill rising in cash terms, Andy Burnham will face immense pressure to use the proposals to launch a once-in-a-generation overhaul of the social security system.An overhaul in itself is no bad thing. Disabled people applying for benefits face a debilitating mess of bureaucracy and barriers, while too many young people have been abandoned, facing greater obstacles and fewer services. The question is, will the overhaul actually improve conditions for the people who rely on it, or buckle to the anti-benefit sentiment that’s been bubbling up for months?That the right is not currently in power won’t stop it from wielding significant influence on what’s to come, in large part thanks to its dominance of Britain’s media ecosystem. Legacy media are not even hiding their attempts to shape November’s reforms before they are announced, with the Times this week launching a “welfare inquiry” to investigate the impact of the benefits “crisis” on public finances.Some of this is made up of concrete policy proposals, such as the Daily Mail’s pitch toradically means-test Pip. But increasingly much of it is just vibes, a vague sense that this disability problem is getting out of control (or having one isbecoming “cool”, as the Telegraph recently put it), and that disabled people – particularly the young – are somehow grifting “perks” while everyone else struggles with rising bills.The changes in how people consume media since the last major benefits reforms in the early 2010s mean the risks of misinformation and outright bigotry are even greater. Last week, Nigel Farage announced plans for a new video studio in Westminster for thelaunch of Reform TV on YouTube, with the party’sproposed £50bn benefits cutspresumably being lined up as viral content.Keep an eye out too for a revival of the striver v scrounger rhetoric asenergy and housing costsare set to lead to the worst living standards in modern times by 2029-30. There are few easier ways to convince workers that the unemployed should go hungry than when they’re cutting back on their own food shop. It is telling that the CSJ study includes a section directly comparing “economically inactive claimants” with workers: someone on minimum wage would have to work six days a week to match “the security, cash and ease” a disabled person gets from a package of state benefits, it proclaims. About 1.4 million foreign nationals receive working-age benefits, it ominously adds. Divide and conquer never gets old.A Labour government is no guarantee these divisions – worker v claimants, old v young, migrant v citizen – won’t be espoused from the cabinet table. No recommendations by Timms or Milburn have been confirmed yet, butWhitehall sources saythere are potential plans to scrap a key part of universal credit for under-25s and replace it with a multi-billion pound package to get people back into work.Sure, it’s depressing if ministers are tempted to bow to the prevailing political winds by pulling cash from young people, but it’s not exactly surprising. For decades, the right has set the boundaries for what Britain’s safety net can be, resulting in little more than subsistence-level benefit rates, an ever crueller culture of testing and a sicker population.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe conventional wisdom has always been that change can only go one way: the benefits system can repeatedly become more punitive and error-strewn, but never more compassionate or accurate. For a leader who has defined himself as someone unafraid of large-scale change, Burnham is well placed to challenge that orthodoxy – if he wants. The opportunity to transform the benefits system does not come up often, and it is rarer still for a Conservative prime minister not to be at the helm.It’s unfashionable to say it out loud but the truth is that Labour has the power to radically improve the disability benefits system: introduce moreevidence-based assessmentsand reduce the need for mass appeals against incorrect decisions; stop using public money to line the pockets of private companies; and endunnecessary reassessments for lifelong disabilities. Similarly, ministers can address why more people need disability benefits in the first place: by investing in threadbare mental health support; addressing NHS waiting times and poor preventive health services;fixing Access to Work; and tackling employer attitudes to disabled candidates.The right has long believed it has a monopoly on Britain’s benefits system, as if it were still paternalistic Victorians punishing and pitying the lower orders. But check the calendar and it is 2026. There is aLabourgovernment in office and two big wads of research coming that can at last lay the groundwork for remaking our safety net. The millions who rely on it must hold their breath to see whether that chance will be grabbed or thrown away.Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsWelfareOpinionBenefitsDisabilityLabourAndy BurnhamUniversal creditcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween | Television | The Guardian
description: The comedy smash is back – and now the standups aren’t allowed to laugh or shriek! Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Phil Wang and more reveal what made them crack – and what happened when they went too far
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The comedy smash is back – and now the standups aren’t allowed to laugh or shriek! Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Phil Wang and more reveal what made them crack – and what happened when they went too far
Content: Paranormal obsessive … Daisy May Cooper on Last One Laughing HalloweenPhotograph: Prime VideoView image in fullscreenParanormal obsessive … Daisy May Cooper on Last One Laughing HalloweenPhotograph: Prime VideoTelevision‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: HalloweenThe comedy smash is back – and now the standups aren’t allowed to laugh or shriek! Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Phil Wang and more reveal what made them crack – and what happened when they went too farBrian LoganFri 16 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat could be more disorientating for a comedian than not being able to laugh – for nine hours! – nor elicit laughter from anyone else in the room? I’ll tell you. Try all of the above on a sunny summer weekend while pretending it’s Halloween. Then force the comics to return to the scene of what one of their number, Phil Wang, calls “a cross between a gameshow and a psychological experiment”, and relive the whole ordeal for a man from the Guardian. Is it any wonder Wang, Lou Sanders, Tom Allen and others come across as a little punch-drunk 24 hours after emerging from televised captivity on the smash comedy hit Last One Laughing?It’s the day after filming, at Elstree Studios, the show’s Halloween special which sees a unique tweak to its winning formula: contestants must not only refrain from laughter but from screaming. “Which I thought might be a non-event,” says Wang, “but it’s actually harder. I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am.” The participating comics – including paranormal obsessive Daisy May Cooper and that maestro of comedy-horror, Reece Shearsmith – seek not only to amuse each other but spook them too. Which makes sense, says hostJimmy Carr. “Laughs and screams come from the same place. There’s surprise in a joke, and there’s surprise in a jump scare. Comedy and horror mess around in the same area. It’s the same bit of your brain.”View image in fullscreenThe cast of Last One Laughing HalloweenPhotograph: RAY BURMISTONNot that Last One Laughing is making serious moves into chiller territory: after all, why tamper with a format that’s given Prime Video such a huge hit? With over 2m people tuning in per episode, series one was the platform’s biggest ever UK launch. The show later won a Bafta for Best Entertainment Programme. “I don’t want to overplay the jump scares,” says Carr – who first persuaded the channel to develop a UK version of what was originally a Japanese hit. “There’s nothing that would trouble anyone. It’s not that kind of show. It’s just fun. It’s ‘event TV’ – especially when it’s tied around something like Halloween – that’s great for bringing people together.”And for bringing comedians together too – the more so now LOL has joined Taskmaster as the shop windowpar excellencefor standups making the leap from fringe to mainstream. Alongside national-treasure veterans (Bob Mortimer in series one; Mel Giedroyc in series two), Last One Laughing reserves places for up-and-coming acts – see recent Edinburgh comedy award winner Harriet Dyer here. Getting involved, she says, was “a whirlwind, to be honest. But it was a dream come true.” All the participating comics agree, mind you, that you can’t treat LOL like a career opportunity. “You can’t play it like that,” says Tom Allen. “You have to engulf yourself in the moment. And that reveals people’s true character. There’s something very vulnerable about laughing. We feel very open when we do it.”View image in fullscreen“Laughs and screams come from the same place” … host Jimmy Carr on Last One Laughing: Halloween.Photograph: AmazonFew comics are more oversharingly their own self than Lou Sanders, a late casualty (red-carded by Carr in episode six) in series one, now returning for series 2.5. There’s a strict embargo on spoilers today, but when I ask Sanders if previous experience gave her an advantage in the Halloween outing, her response does not suggest a triumphant comeback. “I thought I would be better,” she says. “But I was immediately on the back foot. And Reece got into my head early on.” Then there’s the knowledge that millions are watching. On series one, “Joe Wilkinson said to me ‘no one’s going to watch this,’ and I believed him. And then it did well. This time, you know there’s going to be eyes on it.”Sanders has been charged with giving me a tour of the LOL house, a bar cum living room cum art deco theatre, like a prefab 1920s ocean liner constructed in a ginormous Elstree hangar. Here is the fruit machine that’s used to prompt new challenges. There the stage on which contestants perform their ‘joker’ party pieces – around which more strictures circulate than you’d expect. (“I thought it would be funny to have a fire on my head,” says Harriet Dyer. “But I was told: no fire. Then I wanted long arms, but I wasn’t allowed them … ”) There are also creepy dolls, just for Halloween. Does it get claustrophobic in here, I ask Sanders? “I wasn’t in here long enough to know” comes her doleful reply.View image in fullscreenStraight face … Lou Sanders in Last One Laughing: Halloween.Photograph: AmazonBut if Sanders’ tactics proved inadequate, others enter Last One Laughing with sophisticated strategies all mapped out. “My tactic was to channel Dame Maggie Smith in Downton Abbey,” says Tom Allen. “Very aloof, very lofty. So I channelled everything through my eyebrows, rather than a lot of people, who try not to laugh by biting the inside of their mouth.” Wang had a more attacking approach. “My mantra was: a good defence is a good offence. Get on the front foot, try to get to people. Focus on those you know at first, because you know what makes them tick. And while doing that, watch the people you don’t know, to see what makes them laugh.”Dyer entered the house with an idea of whatnotto do. “I think Sam Campbell said on series two that he thought about, like, kids dying to stop himself laughing. So I thought: should I focus on the worst thing that’s ever happened to me? But I’m not sure watching someone be traumatised with what life’s thrown at them makes for very good telly.” Campbell is the maverick Aussie comic who tested the show’s conceit to breaking point last time around, by staying po-faced from start to finish. He eventually lost in a tie-break to David Mitchell. “We nearly broke David,” says Jimmy Carr. “At the end he was going, ‘I don’t think I’ll ever laugh again. I’ve lost that part of myself for ever’.”View image in fullscreenSerious matter … Reece Shearsmith competes in Last One Laughing: Halloween.Photograph: AmazonSeries two’s other breaking point was reached when – great controversy, this – the comic Amy Gledhill was red-carded by Carr for smiling rather than laughing. My own household can’t have been alone in its outrage at this disregard for the show’s core conceit. But Carr is unrepentant. “I mean, we’d got to that stage of the day,” he says: something had to give. “And it’s that water cooler thing: as long as people are arguing about it and having fun, so much the better.”To Carr, the show is as much sports as entertainment: the key, he thinks, to its success. “There’s a narrative to sports, whereby you’ve got to watch to the end because you don’t know what’s going to happen. And that’s the same thing with this show: it’s competitive, and you want to know who’s going to win.” “And each episode ends on a really effective cliffhanger,” adds Phil Wang, “which is quite hard to achieve with comedy.”The other clincher, for Carr and the comics, is how rigorously LOL is produced. Says Carr, “the other countries don’t do the set pieces we do”: the guest appearances, the challenges, the props and tricks contestants can bring to the table – much to Lou Sanders’ dismay. “Reece Shearsmith is Mr Halloween, isn’t he? He’s got all that stuff at home! It’s not fair. I haven’t got a severed hand at home, have I?”According to Wang, “shows that prepare more than they need always prosper. And this show definitely prepares more than it needs.” Every contestant has a camera trained on them throughout, and a dedicated “spotter” hanging on their every smirk. “I presented it in the room yesterday for nine hours,” says Carr. “But I haven’t seen it all yet. When you get in the edit, there’s a whole other show there. There’s all the conversations people have on the screens I’m not watching. I remember on series two discovering all these incredible moments with Diane Morgan we just didn’t know were there.”The lineup has already been announced for LOL series three, which broadcasts next year. Harry Hill, Katherine Ryan and Lee Mack all feature. What advice – or warnings – would the Halloween participants impart? “You end up in there for so long,” says Wang – lucky for some! – “that your mood goes from giddy and excited to paranoid and nervous. I was doing a lot of pinching, a lot of breathing, a lot of meditation and mindfulness.” It was, says Tom Allen, “an intense experience, trying to withhold two emotions and not let them out of the bag. It’s exhausting.”But it’s all in the service, says Allen, of something much needed in our not-always-joyful times. “The series speaks to a childlike sense of play, one that reminds us of being in assembly or in class at school and not being allowed to laugh. There’s nothing more exquisite than that burning desire to laugh while having to keep a lid on it, the steam cooker pressure that brings. Last One Laughing returns us to that youthful joy. I think it’s something people really crave.”Last One Laughing: Halloweenis onPrime Video from Friday.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionJimmy CarrfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the top | Music | The Guardian
description: Adored by Madonna and Charli xcx and buoyed by finding true love, the Londoner is branching out into rock and breaking the mainstream. She explains how her working class upbringing made her so fearless
Author: Simran Hans
Headline: Adored by Madonna and Charli xcx and buoyed by finding true love, the Londoner is branching out into rock and breaking the mainstream. She explains how her working class upbringing made her so fearless
Content: ‘I work hard, but I really prioritise chilling’ … Shygirl in 2026.Photograph: Jessica MadavoView image in fullscreen‘I work hard, but I really prioritise chilling’ … Shygirl in 2026.Photograph: Jessica MadavoMusicInterview‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the topSimran HansAdored by Madonna and Charli xcx and buoyed by finding true love, the Londoner is branching out into rock and breaking the mainstream. She explains how her working class upbringing made her so fearlessFri 16 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaving the important stuff to chance isn’t Shygirl’s style. First aid kit, wind-up radio, batteries: earlier this morning, the singer filled her online shopping basket in preparation for impending disaster. She had read a news article advising households to put together an emergency kit. “I’m that kind of person,” she says, grinning. She woke her boyfriend, who was asleep in bed next to her. “I was like: babe, we’re sorted! I’ve got the water purifying tablets, everything!”It’s a sticky September afternoon in east London, and the singer, whose real name is Blane Muise, introduces herself as “Shy” and slides into the booth opposite me at an Italian trattoria. She first burst on to the club scene with the naughty, pulsating Want More in 2016, and in the decade since, the singer, rapper and DJ has applied the same rigour to her career as she has to her emergency prepping, going from cult underground artist to rising pop star, opening arenas for Beyoncé and Charli xcx, winning a Mobo award in 2024, and appearing in Madonna’s recent Confessions II – The Film, in which she shared a toilet stall with Arca and Richard E Grant.She has also grafted hard at falling in love and entering a long-term relationship, which is the subject of her forthcoming second album, Swallow!. An epic, soaring rock record, with more than a touch ofWilliam Orbit-era Madonna, it is an ode to intimacy, vulnerability and mutual devotion. Love, she says, is “scary, exciting and big”. The 33-year-old’s particular mix of hard and soft, of brash swagger, blunt humour and slippery feminine desire has found an exhilarating new form of expression.View image in fullscreenBrash swagger and blunt humour … Shygirl.Photograph: Jessica MadavoIn December 2022, Shygirl was preparing to go on tour. Her debut album Nymph had received rave reviews and she was finally earning enough money from music to rent her own place. “I felt good about the reception, but there’s always that anticlimactic feeling when you get what you wanted. You’re like: OK, now I have it. Now what?” she says, tossing her tangerine corkscrew curls. “Then I met George.”Go on, I say, tell me the story. “It was on Raya,” she says conspiratorially. She was hungover from a night out while browsing the members-only dating app. When they matched, she asked him to send a voice note: “I don’t like meeting up with people unless I can hear what they sound like and their cadence.” Satisfied, she invited him over to watch one of her favourite films, Alien. “Then we got Thai takeout and hooked up,” she says matter-of-factly.She was leaving for Australia later that week, but they kept talking for almost two months. When she decided to extend her trip and add a visit to Japan, “I was like: fuck it. Do you wanna come to Tokyo?” She flew him out – “in economy”, she says, laughing – and she and actor George Smale have been together ever since. “We had 10 days there and one other date in London when I got back before saying, ‘I love you.’” By the summer, they’d moved in together. Unlike previous relationships, she says, “I didn’t feel like I was all of a sudden so enamoured with someone that I didn’t know where my footing was.”View image in fullscreen‘Love is scary and exciting’ … Shygirl and George Smale at British Vogue’s Forces For Change at The Maine Mayfair, London, 23 November 2023.Photograph: Mike Marsland/WireImageThat contentment and calm was a source of inspiration. “When I made Lucky, I sat in the room with the mic. I didn’t write anything down, I just said how I felt,” she says of the album’s lead single. “It’s me saying: I am an active participant because of the choices that brought me here.” Like many of the tracks on Swallow!, Lucky[Hymn] is an indie song. “It had more of a classic tone to it because I felt like I was in a classic part of my life,” she says.With its dreamy, moody guitars and anthemic, crashing drums, Swallow! is a different sound for an artist whose previous records have flirted with hyperpop, UK garage and electronica. As a millennial, Shygirl came of age when guitar-driven pop music was dominating the charts. “It was very prevalent in all the pop I grew up listening to: Keane, Madonna, random shit like the Rasmus,” she says. In the 2010s, when she was a teenager, musical discovery was serendipitous: “We had HMV, where you could just walk in and put the headphones on.” Her curiosity, she says, was encouraged by her parents. “I’m not from a family where they would just give you answers.”Shygirl is the eldest of three children born to young parents in south-east London, and spent her early years bouncing between Downham, Catford and Lee Green. “My life has shown me that you are never entitled to anything,” she says. “You can be deserving but not receive.” When has she felt like that? “I grew up with that experience. My parents worked really hard. They didn’t have everything.”Her dad, who is of Grenadian origin, worked for the UK government’s Welsh office and later as a club promoter in Notting Hill. She didn’t see him much when he was working nights. Meanwhile, “my mum used to work as a cleaner, a toilet attendant, a receptionist, a dinner lady,” she says. “She’s always had a job.” So has Shygirl, who as a teenager worked at a restaurant her mum managed.Her parents are no longer together, though she is quick to clarify that hers was a happy childhood. “I wanted for nothing,” she says. “But I’m of the mindset that if you want something, you have to go get it. I’m only the one to blame if I don’t.” That determination runs through new songs such as Live the Life You Like, a stomping, Prodigy-esque anthem. “And then I’m pushing / It’s not enough,” she purrs.In Amsterdam, in 2018, she booked her first show before her debut EP, Cruel Practice, had even been released. “I was like: I don’t even have any music out and someone’s taken a chance on me,” she remembers. Soon afterwards she handed in her notice as a booker at a modelling agency. “I’m about to quit a day job that had holiday pay, sick pay, and I’m gonna go be a musician? But because I used to do contracts with the model agency, I knew how to push a rate up.” She negotiated requests from brands who wanted to use her music in their adverts, until one came in from Rihanna, for Fenty Beauty, and she got overexcited – “not as sharky as I usually am” with making the deal. She got a manager, the money came in and Shygirl paid off her credit card. She likens herself to a gambler: “My money was up from being, like, two grand in debt. I’d owed my housemate money for rent.”She signed a record deal in 2020; this year, she bought a house. She hadn’t even entertained owning one, “because I was so busy thinking I need to pay my rent and bills. My dad still doesn’t own a house. My mum just got one.” Her drive to make music, she says, “has always been to make my life better than my origins, and to prove to my family that their sacrifice is worth something”. But “living an experience they have never lived” has been accompanied by a dose of “mad guilt”.She played New York’s Madison Square Garden with Charli xcx and Troye Sivan as2024’s Brat summerraged on into Brat autumn. Seeing how Charli, a peer and friend, was able to maintain her sense of self even as everything became “as big and stressful as it gets” made pop domination feel more achievable. Although, “we definitely have different intentions for our day to day”. Charli, she stresses, works incredibly hard. “I work hard, but I really prioritise chilling,” she laughs.View image in fullscreen‘All of us are trying to open doors for each other’ … Charli xcx and Shygirl at Madison Square Garden, New York, 2024.Photograph: Rich Fury/MSG/Getty Images for MSG Entertainment HoldingsSpending an afternoon hanging out with Shygirl, as she radiates self-possession, grace and plenty of gossipy wisdom, one gets the sense that she is something of a girl’s girl. “All of us are trying to open doors for each other – all the female artists that I’ve worked with.” Being a woman, she says, is her biggest barrier as an artist. “In my experience, that is the most prevalent block at the moment.” She gives the example ofBeyoncé’s Grammy win for best country albumwith Cowboy Carter, which prompted the Recording Academy to create two separate categories for best country album: traditional and contemporary. “The rules shift, and the doors’ locations change,” she says.Realising there might be a ceiling for her ambition, one imposed on her by others, has meant she is now “only interested in working with people who want different-ness. Who are not comfortable with the status quo, because I can’t relate to that. It’s not an experience I’ve had in any avenue of my life.” And, she adds, “it’s usually men” upholding that status quo. “Not to be a man hater: I love my boyfriend!”Shygirl and Smale have been collaborating creatively, too. He provided background vocals on album opener Alyse and they have worked together on the interconnected videos for the new album, which she co-directed and which form an elliptical thriller narrative based around a kidnapping. “You’re dropped into a situation the same as The Bourne Ultimatum or Tell No One. You may have been an ordinary person; you’re now in extraordinary circumstances: what do you do?” she says. Her character ends up tied to a chair. She seldom even thinks of not acting in any situation, she says, so it was a challenge to play someone barely able to move.But her character screams, shouts, cries and thrashes as she’s held captive, giving Shygirl an outlet for emotions she didn’t realise she needed to express. “I never raise my voice,” she says. “To shout at someone who has made you angry? To show that you’re affected by them in that way? I would never do that.” An eldest daughter, she describes herself as a protector who feels responsible for everyone else in her life.“I feel like every child gets to a point where they see their parents as human beings, not just as their caregivers. That happened for me when I was very young.” How young? “Ten, 12.” It meant she never had idols. “I don’t really look up to anyone in that way,” she says. “I see everyone with faults.”‘I lost a $3m brand deal. I was like: OK, losers!’ Swedish pop provocateur Zara Larsson on fame, fun and fighting the powerRead moreIn the video’s final shot, Shygirl looks directly into the lens, “accepting that this is a contrived environment”. She wanted to break the fourth wall, even if that movie trope is a bit of a cliche: “Sometimes cliches are cliches for a reason, you know?”Of course, falling in love is the biggest cliche of all, I add. “Exactly!” Once you’ve said “I love you” a million times to your partner, she says, “you’re looking for other ways to express it”. Her smile is beatific thinking about it all. Playing the new album to her boyfriend made her cry; the delicate, intensely vulnerable ballad Real allowed her “to revisit the memory of when we were in Japan, and recognise that now as falling in love”. It has an incredulous, awestruck quality, as though she can’t believe her own good fortune. “We’re always choosing each other,” she says. “I’m always choosing what’s happening in my life.”Swallow! is released on 6 November via Because Music. Shygirl’s 2027 world tour begins 13 March at Columbiahalle, BerlinExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockDance musicIndieElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Some Woman review – Anne-Marie Duff is wholly believable but this twisty drama is not | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The far-fetched plot turns and some underdeveloped characters undermine the powerful messages about prejudice in Helen Edmundson’s play
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: The far-fetched plot turns and some underdeveloped characters undermine the powerful messages about prejudice in Helen Edmundson’s play
Content: Moving, harrowing … Anne-Marie Duff in Some Woman at Dorfman theatre, London.Photograph: Ellie KurttzView image in fullscreenMoving, harrowing … Anne-Marie Duff in Some Woman at Dorfman theatre, London.Photograph: Ellie KurttzTheatreReviewSome Woman review – Anne-Marie Duff is wholly believable but this twisty drama is notDorfman theatre, LondonThe far-fetched plot turns and some underdeveloped characters undermine the powerful messages about prejudice in Helen Edmundson’s playArifa AkbarFri 16 Oct 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 09.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpposing forces tug against each other in this new drama asAnne-Marie Duffis magnificent amid playwright Helen Edmundson’s implausible plotting. The result is a failed suspension of disbelief yet a convincing central performance.Duff plays Julie, a mother, ex-wife and working woman whose already over-burdened life is turned upside down by an incident at a tube station when an 11-year-old boy randomly and aggressively insults her. She challenges him, reasonably, and in a series of unconvincing plot turns, winds up facing a legal battle and potential prison sentence.As a story of an ordinary middle-aged woman being buffeted by patriarchal forces around her, this play is stuffed full of important issues. We hear stories of casual sexual abuse, laughed off by those around Julie. Now we see her life virtually destroyed by the boy’s allegation.There is mention of CCTV footage and you wonder if an Adolescence-style video reveal is to come. But the plot makes clear that there is no incontrovertible evidence against her, yet she stands to lose everything.View image in fullscreenPotential brilliance … Ioanna Kimbook (left) and Anne-Marie Duff in Some Woman at the National Theatre, London.Photograph: Ellie KurttzThe points about everyday misogyny come through loud and clear, especially that the legal system is rigged to distrust women and believe men (or an 11-year-old boy in this instance). The West End dramaPrima Facie, recently adapted for the screen, showed us just that in relation to sexual violence against women. But this is not a courtroom drama and the alleged crimes on which it turns are simply not believable.Directed byBlanche McIntyreand staged without an interval, there is potential brilliance here, if only the plot were better crafted and so many unfocused issues not thrown at us – from the eating disorder of one daughter (Grace Doherty) to Julie’s difficult relationship with another (Hannah Onslow), both barely explored, as well as Julie’s experience of infidelity and divorce. Each of these issues gets its moment, briefly, with characters around Julie too flimsy to feel true.View image in fullscreenConfrontation … Stephen Wright in Some Woman.Photograph: Ellie KurttzThe structural failings of the script aside, there are many individually moving and harrowing scenes. They culminate in a confrontation between Julie and the boy’s father (Stephen Wight). Again, this plot-turn challenges the bounds of believability but this time you can brush that aside because the forces of threat, anger and fear feel horribly, sadly real.Julie seems pushed towards victimhood yet she refuses this foisted powerlessness in a society where toxic masculinity is chillingly in plain sight: men openly express loathing of women, boys spit obscenities at female strangers. Truth is all Julie has and upholds, whatever the legal repercussions. She is not only the everyday victim of misogyny but an everyday female hero too. This message has its own power, however bad the plotting may be.At theDorfman theatre, National Theatre, London, until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreNational TheatreAnne-Marie DuffBlanche McIntyreViolence against women and girlsWomenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sweet nothings, urinal cakes and headless dogs: 10 artworks worth seeing at Frieze | Frieze art fair | The Guardian
description: There’s plenty that stands out at Regent’s Park this year, from antidepressant pens and an ibuprofen-dolling robotic arm to Miriam Cahn’s 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture and a 150m-year-old dinosaur skull – still with embedded tooth
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: There’s plenty that stands out at Regent’s Park this year, from antidepressant pens and an ibuprofen-dolling robotic arm to Miriam Cahn’s 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture and a 150m-year-old dinosaur skull – still with embedded tooth
Content: Take note … Carolyn Lazard, Portrait IV.Photograph: courtesy the artist/Trautwein HerlethView image in fullscreenTake note … Carolyn Lazard, Portrait IV.Photograph: courtesy the artist/Trautwein HerlethFrieze art fairSweet nothings, urinal cakes and headless dogs: 10 artworks worth seeing at FriezeThere’s plenty that stands out at Regent’s Park this year, from antidepressant pens and an ibuprofen-dolling robotic arm to Miriam Cahn’s 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture and a 150m-year-old dinosaur skull – still with embedded toothFrieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tentEddy FrankelFri 16 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElla Fleckat Ehrlich SteinbergThe raised platform in the middle of British artist Ella Fleck’s installation vibrates under your feet to the sound of a male voice. He’s whispering sweet nothings, intoning sexual fantasies. It’s all based on third-party agencies that manage OnlyFans accounts, interacting with users, creating fictional relationships that horny guys spend thousands on. It’s a greasy, gross, uncomfortable exploration of sex work on an industrial scale.Yuli Serfatyat Xxijra HiiYuli Serfaty’s headless metallic dog sculptures guard this booth, their claws sharp, their heavy teats dragging on the floor. It’s a surreal symbol of femininity pushed to an extreme, a body devalued and exploited. A video shows the creature trying to escape the booth, and succeeding. The whole installation looks like HR Giger meets Wolfenstein 3D, but with a nasty, satirical edge.Rirkrit Tiravanijaat David ZwirnerView image in fullscreenRepetitive, meaningless … Rirkrit Tiravanija, untitled 2026 (a bitter pill).Photograph: Jack Hems/courtesy the artist/David ZwirnerFinally, something to help you get through Frieze. Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija’s sculpture here is a robotic arm that carefully hands visitors a little red-and-white ibuprofen pill. If you don’t reach out, it just drops it on the floor. The robot does its job, over and over, regardless of if you’re there to receive it. It feels futile, obscene, repetitive, meaningless. Quite the comment on modern life.Carolyn Lazardat Trautwein HerlethIt might look like a display of pens, and that’s because it is. But each one is a promotional item from a pharmaceutical company, given out as gifts to American medical professionals. Lazzard bought them in estate sales from real doctors. They become a portrait of selling out, of how healthcare in the US can be bought by corporations. There are pens with branding for antidepressants, ADHD meds, Viagra: corporations are keeping you going, keeping you productive. When it clicks, it’s an incredibly grim conceptual vision of how our bodies are treated as commodities.Gray Wielebinskiin the toiletsThe urinal cakes in the Frieze bogs this year aren’t just there to keep whiffs at bay – they’re art. This is urinal cake as sculptural intervention, thanks to artist Gray Wielebinski, who has designed each one with a custom scent and encased them in metal cages. They sort of look like little chastity devices, glistening lumps of odorous chemicals for you to wee on. They’re weird, almost erotic sculptures. You can hear the anguished cry of thousands of artists wishing they’d thought of it first.Miriam Cahnat Galerie Jocelyn WolffView image in fullscreenStanding out … Miriam Cahn.Photograph: courtesy Galerie Jocelyn WolffThere is such an overwhelming amount of (usually very bland) painting at Frieze that it really takes a special painter to stand out. But Swiss artist Miriam Cahn’s installation is a proper diamond among the swill. It’s a whole booth filled with 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture. Each one plumbs new depths of anxious, monstrous introspection. She grins and screams, stands and falls, all in blurred, messy washes of colour. Psychologically intense, overwrought, emotional stuff.William-Adolphe Bouguereauat Stair SaintyMy love for 19th-century French academic painter William-Adolphe Bouguereau verges on a sickness. I mean, I have a Bouguereau tattoo. So finding this little gem among the Dutch flower paintings and Egyptian busts of Frieze Masters was a genuine thrill. It’s a weird, yellowed little thing – based on a Tintoretto – of a man lying prostrate on the ground. The ropes that bind him have been snapped, wood is splintered. Here is the aftermath of violence, the shocking silence after a traumatic event. This is one of the great things about Masters: getting to spot art historical gold hidden away on the back wall of some booth. This gallery also had a gorgeous James Tissot portrait. It’s 19th-century art nerd heaven.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLuce Turnierat Harlesden High StreetView image in fullscreenLuce Turnier, Nude Woman in Chair (1977).Photograph: Courtesy the artist/ Harlesden High StreetThere are some amazing narratives to discover in the Frieze Masters spotlight section, especially the work of Haitian modernist Luce Turnier, who lived between Paris and Haiti but has largely been forgotten by art history. This small display of stark portraits – like a more sombre Alice Neel – and vitrines is a little glimpse into a lost period of international modernism from an artist who feels ripe for a museum show.View image in fullscreenCamarasaurus supremus skull with embedded allosaurus tooth, 145-155 million years old.Photograph: David Brunetti/courtesy David AaronCamarasaurus supremus skull at David AaronYou eventually go antiquities and Flemish art blind walking around Frieze Masters, so finding the fossilised dino skulls that David Aaron Gallery has lugged to the tent is always a bit of Jurassic relief. This year they’ve brought an enormous triceratops skull and an awesome camarasaurus supremus with the tooth of an allosaurus embedded in it. Absolutely brutal, and possibly the only thing my four-year-old would like in either fair.Sohrab Huraat ExperimenterThere’s death and fear written into all of Sohrab Hura’s paintings here. They’re grotesque expressionist scenes of everyday violence: a man kicked to the ground, a crow pecking at a bleeding carcass above a figure staring aghast at a newspaper. It’s like Edvard Munch but with way more blood and guts. The painting of the woman in the dust storm isn’t good, but the rest are great, angry things.Explore more on these topicsFrieze art fairLondonArtExhibitionsPaintingInstallationMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting | Film adaptations | The Guardian
description: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation
Content: What a novel idea … The Shining, The Godfather and The Silence of the Lambs.Illustration: Guardian Design/Maximum Film/Alamy; Allstar Picture Library/Alamy Stock Photo; Channel 5View image in fullscreenWhat a novel idea … The Shining, The Godfather and The Silence of the Lambs.Illustration: Guardian Design/Maximum Film/Alamy; Allstar Picture Library/Alamy Stock Photo; Channel 5Film adaptationsAn open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to TrainspottingNot every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptationLouise WillderFri 16 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey this summer, buying my ticket into the popular conversation along with everyone else. This year’s other divisive adaptation, Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights, had the world and his wife arguing about it before they had even watched the film. No doubt the makers of the recentSense and Sensibility movie werealso hoping for lots of people to go and see it to discover whether they hated it.After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: “That’s exactly how I pictured it in my head.” Or even less likely: “That was better than the book.” We’re more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year’s Thursday Murder Club debacle.But what makes agoodadaptation? Like Odysseus himself, and as every Nancy Meyers fan knows: it’s complicated. I have just written a book about the towering heights and profane depths of adaptation, The Book Was Better, for which I subjected myself to some of the worst viewing experiences possible, including the soft rock opera musical Heathcliff; 1996’s freakishly bad The Island of Dr Moreau; and a horrible three-part version of Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged. But I also saw plenty of masterpieces that equalled or sometimes surpassed the originals. Here’s what I learned.View image in fullscreenAll aboard … Trainspotting.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyThe first thing to say is that the quality of the source is irrelevant. I went into my research with some pretty fixed ideas: for instance, that “the brilliant adaptations are nearly always of fiction of the second or third class”, as Anthony Burgess wrote; that some works are “unfilmable”; that classics have more “room to breathe” on TV. Soon Irealised none of these were true. Yes, sometimes workmanlike novels, such as the late 60s and early 70s triumvirate Jaws, The Godfather and The Exorcist, can be tuned to a level of genius on screen. But great books can make great films, too: Trainspotting, The Go-Between, The Leopard and Burgess’s own A Clockwork Orange are just a few examples. And sometimes, in the case of The Da Vinci Code and Fifty Shades of Grey, a deeply silly book becomes a deeply silly film.double quotation markDon’t be too reverential ... an adaptation should never be a greatest hits albumIt is true that certain books lend themselves to the screen more readily.Jane Austen’s immaculate plots of love impeded are templates that can be dressed up in the clothes of any age, like the computer template Cher Horowitz uses to plan her outfits at the start of Clueless– thene plus ultraof free-handed adaptations. Austen’s novels contain the DNA of all romcoms, just as Robinson Crusoe is found in The Martian, the gothic novel in horror films, or A Christmas Carol in every single Christmas movie. Short stories, with their twisty shocks and rush towards the end point, seem made for cinema; my favourite film,Don’t Look Now, is based on a Daphne du Maurier novella. The murky origins and elasticity of myths and their close cousins, folk and fairytales, make them ceaselessly adaptable, because they leave gaps for a film-maker to fill with their own imaginations.Being unfaithful is usually helpful. Some of the best adaptations flirt with the source material, taking frightful liberties and then abandoning it like a tabloid love rat. “Steal the parts that you need, and then run as fast as you can,” advised Paul Thomas Anderson; Hitchcock claimed he read The Birds once before making his version, and never thought about it again. (One screenwriter I spoke to told me he was once asked not to read the novel he was adapting as the production company thought it would be a hindrance). Books and films are entirely different beasts, “apples and giraffes”, as author-screenwriter Dennis Lehane once said. Adaptation is an act of translation from the verbal to the visual. A film-maker needs to find their own language.View image in fullscreenYou’ve come a long way, baby … Children of Men.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyOne of my most beloved unfaithful adaptations is Alfonso Cuarón’s 2006 Children of Men, and not just because it stars Clive Owen at the peak of his physical perfection. It manages to transform a cerebral, theological novel by the Conservative peer PD James into a dystopian thriller about populism, terror and how we treat immigrants, one which – although now two decades old – feels fresher each year. (James was delighted with it.) Cuarón used the novel as a jumping-off point, then left it behind to follow his own adventure. What remained was the central conceit: what if we lived in a world without children? The “what if” high concepts of science fiction and speculative fiction are perfect for playing fast and loose with: a vessel into which a film-maker’s own preoccupations, and the anxieties of their age, can be poured.When writer-director Sally Potter reinvented Virginia Woolf’s time-travelling fantasia Orlando, she treated it “as if the book never existed”, turning it into a lavish nose-thumb to a UK establishment that had just passed section 28. She was, she said, cruel to the novel to be kind to the film. It’s the destruction-as-creation mantra. In the hands of the right writer and director, a source can, and should, be made to submit to their will: Stanley Kubrick betrayed Stephen King’s vision of The Shining but made a tour de force. Heart of Darkness mutated into a war epic with Apocalypse Now; Red Dragon became, well, a Michael Mann film, the hypnotic Manhunter. An adaptation should never be a hollow greatest hits album. Being too reverential towards a literary source can kill it, which is why I suspect films such as The Hunger Games and The Road, lovingly and stylishly made with few changes, felt slightly bloodless on screen to me.Can anything really be faithful anyway, and to what? No story is 100 per cent original. (As Alienscreenwriter Dan O’Bannon said: “I didn’t steal from anybody. I stole fromeverybody!”) I don’t even think you can be “true to the spirit” of a text, because the spirit is different for everyone. We all have our own little films running in our heads when we read. Many see The Great Gatsby as a death knell for the US; adapters tend to think: “parties!”. I think Heathcliff is a psychopath who likes to hang little dogs; successive directors clearly didn’t. I loved discovering that Jodie Foster lobbied hard for the part of Clarice Starling in The Silence of the Lambs because, for her, the novel was about a woman saving the life of another woman while “all these fucking men” get in the way. An adaptation may just be a glimpse into another mind’s eye, but their pictures seldom match the ones we had imagined.View image in fullscreenUp to date … Renée Zellweger as Bridget Jones.Photograph: Working Title/Sportsphoto/AllstarPerhaps the most obvious example of this is casting. As sure as night follows day, Hollywood casts a better-looking actor than strictly necessary, although not always reaching “Denise Richards in hotpants as a nuclear physicist in The World is Not Enough” levels. This can be deliberate: in Robert Bloch’s novel Psycho, Norman Bates is physically repellent; Hitchcock wanted the sweet-faced Anthony Perkins for the part to wrongfoot the audience. More often it’s because, as the critic Roger Ebert observed, cinema is a machine for generating empathy, so the thinking goes that leads should be “likable” – which backfired horribly when Bruce Willis was cast as a desiccated English journalist in the notoriously disastrous adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s The Bonfire of the Vanities. But sometimes an actor who is wrong on paper can make a role their own, whether it’s Margaret Rutherford as Miss Marple, Renée Zellweger as Bridget Jones or Michael Caine as Harry Palmer in The Ipcress File (in Len Deighton’s novels he’s a northerner and doesn’t have a name). Charisma goes a long way.Perhaps in the end, adaptation all comes down to emotions and sensations. “You’ve drunk the drink, and the taste that’s left in your mouth is what you go with,” as Anthony Minghella described adapting The Talented Mr Ripley. Irvine Welsh said you must smell the books. Hossein Amini, who reinvented The Wings of the Dove as “noir in costume”, wanted to recapture that ecstatic moment when “nobody else in the world understood or experienced that book exactly like I did”.Returning to The Odyssey, I wonder why, even though Nolan did the right things, subordinating it to his worldview and faithlessly reinventing it for our age by turning a wily trickster into a traumatised veteran, the film just made me feel as if I’d been in a war: long periods of boredom and waiting punctuated by violence. Perhaps, ultimately, he overthought it and should have felt it instead? Or maybe, as the late Hilary Mantel said of adaptation, you must “put down the text, and dream it”.The Book Was Better by Louise Willder (Oneworld, £14.99).
