title: Sod’s law: what can two turf swaps 40 years apart tell us about Britain’s biodiversity crisis? | Art and design | The Guardian
description: In 1983, David Nash dug up a section of Kensington Gardens and swapped it with Welsh grassland. Four decades later, Mike Perry’s reverse swap revealed a striking reversal in the fortunes of urban and rural nature
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: In 1983, David Nash dug up a section of Kensington Gardens and swapped it with Welsh grassland. Four decades later, Mike Perry’s reverse swap revealed a striking reversal in the fortunes of urban and rural nature
Content: ‘When you make work outside, things happen’ … the results of Reverse Sod Swap in Springfield Park, London, in 2025.Photograph: Mike PerryView image in fullscreen‘When you make work outside, things happen’ … the results of Reverse Sod Swap in Springfield Park, London, in 2025.Photograph: Mike PerryArt and designSod’s law: what can two turf swaps 40 years apart tell us about Britain’s biodiversity crisis?In 1983, David Nash dug up a section of Kensington Gardens and swapped it with Welsh grassland. Four decades later, Mike Perry’s reverse swap revealed a striking reversal in the fortunes of urban and rural naturePatrick BarkhamFri 16 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1983, an open-topped truck unloaded an unusual cargo in Kensington Gardens: 83 hunks of turf cut from Cae’n y Coed, a wooded hillside in the Ffestiniog valley. The ring of turf measuring eight metres in diameter that was removed from the park beside the Serpentine Gallery in west London to make space for the Welsh sods was then trucked from London to north Wales.So began Sod Swap, a piece of sculptural defiance byDavid Nash, which has had an unexpected and epic afterlife. More than 40 years later, photographic artist Mike Perry restaged the work asReverse Sod Swap, exchanging exactly the same amount of turf between Springfield Park in Hackney, east London, and pastureland in Pembrokeshire, with strikingly different results. With twin works acquiring new relevance in a time of extinction and climate crises, the sod swapping is now the subject of a new book.It all began, says Nash, who is 80 and still working with wood and trees, with his own “bloody-mindedness”. He was invited to contribute to a new Serpentine gallery show of British sculpture. He submitted an idea of some wood sculptures for an indoor gallery because he felt too many outdoor sculptures were “like UFOs, they came and they went”, as he puts it. “But the gallery said: ‘Oh, David, you’re an outside artist, so we’d like you to participate in the outdoor space.”Nash, who made his very outdoorsyAsh DomeandWooden Bouldera few years before, bristled. He’d actually created an outdoor piece for a Serpentine show when he was a postgrad student at Chelsea Art School in 1970. When he tried to secure it in the ground he was told he couldn’t touch the Kensington Gardens turf because it belonged to the queen.View image in fullscreenMaking the cut … David Nash’s original Sod Swap being installed at the Serpentine gallery in west London in 1983.Photograph: © David NashSo this time, he plotted to rough up the manicured London park’s immaculate lawns by installing a ring of wild grassland from north Wales while also challenging definitions of “sculpture”. There was a lot of “bright red metal” around in the early 80s, says Nash wryly. “I wanted to create something that didn’t need to be cleaned.”Sod Swap, he says, was a declaration of his identity. “I was very keen that what I put in had a sense of where it came from, which was where I was, which was north Wales.” When he realised he would have to dig up a load of Kensington turf, he decided to take that back to Wales. “That became the swap, and I liked the connotation of being a sod. It was nothing to do with the environment, really, but it turned out to be.”Nash was anticipating a reaction and he got one. After several worried meetings about the dig, and head-scratching from council officials about the risk of “invasive” Welsh plants contaminating Kensington Gardens, Sod Swap went ahead. “He’s very subversive, David,” saysPerry. “He doesn’t look it, but he is. The Serpentine expected him to bring in a big wooden sculpture. And he said: ‘No, I’m going to cut up your lawn.’ He wanted to show who he is as a person but also what sculpture could be – it doesn’t have to be a solid object on a plinth. It can be an ephemeral piece of organic material.”In 2023, when Perry started a rewilding and art project on 4.9 hectares (12 acres) of farmland in west Wales, he wondered if he might revisit Nash’s concept, four decades on. Slightly nervously, he contacted Nash, and was relieved when the sculptor gave an enthusiastic “yes”. A week later, Perry drove over to north Wales, where Nash took him to see the site of the Kensington Garden sods. Amazingly, 40 years on, they could still detect a faint circle in mossy grass now punctuated by mature trees.View image in fullscreenThe grass is always greener … Reverse Sod Swap, Ffynnonofi, West Wales, 2024Photograph: Mike PerryThe Welsh turf hadn’t lasted so long in London. After the show ended, the gallery planned to simply to remove the turf but, thankfully for Nash, the “archangels of art outside”, Sue Clifford and Angela King, stepped in. The two co-founders of environmental arts charityCommon Groundhurriedly found another unlikely London home for Nash’s Welsh sods: in the lawns of Kenwood House on Hampstead Heath.Clifford and King also had the bright idea of convening ecologists to count the species in each turf circle. The Welsh sods held 28 different species, including grasses, wildflowers, brambles and even nettles, while the manicured sods cut from Kensington Gardens were made up of a meagre three different species of grass. Suddenly, Nash’s little challenge to the art world held an ecological message, highlighting the biodiversity to be found in rural meadowlands and the sterile quality of urban parks.While Nash’s little piece of Wales acclimatised to Hampstead Heath, the artist conscientiously watered the London turf at Cae’ny Coed, even buying a secondhand mower so he could keep it in the condition to which it was accustomed. The original plan was to return it to Kensington Gardens, but Nash says the Arts Council told him they had run out of project money and couldn’t afford to transport it back. Sod Swap became permanent.Eventually, after 10 years at Kenwood House, English Heritage removed the Welsh sods. “The London turf stayed in Wales,” remembers Nash. “Chestnut trees I planted grew and grew and shaded the turf, and moss came in. There were daisies from London which came up for about five years but then disappeared. I kept up mowing it as if it was in London for 20 years until it was virtually all moss and then I thought I would let it go.” Over the years, artists, curators and students made a pilgrimage to visit it.View image in fullscreenGrass-roots movement … David Nash with Mike Perry in one of Nash’s shelters in Cae’n y Coed, north Wales, in 2023.Photograph: Cornelia ParkerReverse Sod Swap was “a kind of biographical piece for me,” says Perry. He lived in London for 20 years before moving to an old farm by the sea in north Pembrokeshire. “My parents retired down here so I’ve always been going between east London and west Wales,” he says. The landscape and seascape of the Pembrokeshire Coast national park still looks gorgeous but “it’s a very melancholy thing walking down to the sea because there’s nothing in the hedges. They’re stripped right back and the grass is just mown 24/7 by so many sheep. The chair of the RSPB [Royal Society for the Protection of Birds] said national parks are where wildlife goes to die.”Perry had hoped Reverse Sod Swap would be an ecological statement, but he couldn’t have anticipated just how much of a statement it would make. In Wales, he took the turf from pasture still heavily grazed by sheep belonging to a tenant farmer. At the London end, he was given “a really poor” plot in Springfield Park with “bad bits of soil from everywhere and a little bit of grass out of all sorts of rough material. But I quite liked it because there were giant burdocks and ‘weeds’ and thistles. I liked that mix.”Perry’s first challenge was to replicate the dimensions. Nash couldn’t remember the exact size of his 1983 turf circles but Perry dug out the old catalogue statement, which noted that there were 83 sods measuring 90x30cm (35x12in) in size. He then followed Nash’s idea of making little wooden “stretchers” to carry each sod from the ground to the waiting lorry. On the journey to Wales, they twice stopped at motorway services to water the precious sods.In the two-and-a-half years since Reverse Sod Swap, Perry has been surprised by how the project has continued to transfix him. “David put his hand on my shoulder and looked me in the eye and said: ‘Mike, when you make work outside, things happen.’ I didn’t really know what he meant. But what’s amazing is that the work is living and changing all the time – it keeps giving me new images and new findings.”View image in fullscreenNatural exchange … Mike Perry marking out Reverse Sod Swap, Ffynnonofi Farm, West Wales, 2024.Photograph: Mike PerryAfter the reverse transplant, botanists surveyed the transplanted turfs and, strikingly, found the reverse of Nash’s 1983 swap. The turf taken from Springfield Park contained 39 species in total, whereas the Welsh sheep-grazed turf contained just four species. And so, across four decades, the two works starkly illustrate the loss of rural biodiversity – a loss often disguised by the superficially unchanging character of the British landscape, with its patchwork of hedges, fields and woods. But Reverse Sod Swap also reveals a more hopeful trend in London, where species have been revived by urban rewilding efforts, from creating wildflower areas in parks to building new sustainable urban drainage areas.Perry is encouraged by what he sees when he returns to London and walks down the Grand Union canal. “It feels like there’s butterflies, there’s rough stuff. It’s not scientific because there are obviously areas in Wales that can’t be farmed and there’s amazing biodiversity, but I was just really trying to make a point through art.”Nash is touched by the longevity of his Sod Swap, and the ecological message it has taken on. “What Mike has done is an amazing bonus,” he says. “My Sod Swap highlighted the paucity of plant species in London, not that that was my main intention. Reverse Sod Swap is much more pertinent environmentally because it’s highlighting the paucity of rural land. We artists put work out there and hope people will see it and make something of it – be stimulated or take it on as part of their awareness.”Reverse Sod Swap by Mike Perry and David Nashis published by Little Toller on 16 October (£25). title: Calling the shots: what NAZA says about perpetrator cinema | NAZA | The Guardian
description: The documentary detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza is the latest film to give a voice to those who carry out atrocities – confronting viewers with some of the most difficult questions of all
Author: Danny Leigh
Headline: The documentary detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza is the latest film to give a voice to those who carry out atrocities – confronting viewers with some of the most difficult questions of all
Content: In NAZA, anonymisedmembers of Israeli intelligence discuss their remote execution of the assault on Gaza.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenIn NAZA, anonymisedmembers of Israeli intelligence discuss their remote execution of the assault on Gaza.Photograph: The GuardianNAZACalling the shots: what NAZA says about perpetrator cinemaThe documentary detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza is the latest film to give a voice to those who carry out atrocities – confronting viewers with some of the most difficult questions of allDanny LeighFri 16 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 09.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAre we still talking about the banality of evil? When that overworked phrase was first used by philosopher Hannah Arendt, it described the blank persona of Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann. Now, inNAZA, anonymisedmembers of Israeli intelligence discuss their remote execution of the assault on Gaza. The comparison to Hitler’s Germany, while understandably controversial, is made by a subject themselves. If they are banal, it is a modern, oddly familiar kind. These are articulate, middle-class millennials. They say they are leftwing and non-racist. Put differently, they could be Guardian readers.And yes, one remarks,they have been conducting a genocide.The work of directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor is shattering. But we have been shattered before by the firsthand accounts of people who carry out atrocities – sometimes called perpetrator cinema. In 2013, director Joshua Oppenheimer releasedThe Act of Killing, an astonishing film involving members of 1960s right-wing Indonesian death squads. It was lavishly acclaimed.Since then, it has only kept feeling painfully relevant.View image in fullscreenThe Act of Killing (2012).Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyBefore that, documentary wild card Errol Morris madeStandard Operating Procedure, interviewing US soldiers who abused Iraqis at the notorious Abu Ghraib jail. Edging into drama, you might even include Jonathan Glazer’sThe Zone of Interest, where the commandant of Auschwitz lives happily with his wife and children. (Glazer is an executive producer of NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian.)Joshua Oppenheimer: ‘You celebrate mass killing so you don’t have to look yourself in the mirror’Read moreQuestions gnaw through them all. To begin: who is it that commits crimes against humanity? The answer can feel inconclusive. NAZA is filled with Tel Aviv high-fliers, some citing as justification the horrific attacks of October 7. But the American troops of Standard Operating Procedure are ordinary grunts in the “war on terror”. Meanwhile, inThe Act of Killing, ageing street thugs recreate their murders of trade unionists and teachers as the action movies they imagine them being. Flamboyance blooms in the abyss.In every case, what we see won’t leave our heads, even as we flail for an adequate response. The late critic Roger Ebert famously called movies “empathy machines”. But these films short circuit the machinery. How can we empathise with people who seem to show no remorse?For some,NAZApresents a bigger problem than that. The Israeli government has floated stripping Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, among other threats. But even for audiences far from the Middle East, the film is hard to deal with. We may feel anguished just as we are reminded how safe our anguish is. We might even think about that most unfriendly word: complicity.But perpetrator cinema is about more than complicity. It is about the attempt to fathom the perpetrator. Discussing NAZA on theJewish Currentspodcast, Oppenheimer spoke to that task. “To understand a crime as a human activity, we have to look at the human beings who undertake that activity.”View image in fullscreenIn Killing Anna (2026), Syrian army officers were catfished into discussing civilian massacres.Photograph: Keo Films/ DogwoofOr do we understand mass murderers enough through what they do? In 2013, The Act of Killing also met pungent criticism. One influential figure in British documentary publiclycalledit a “snuff film”. (Oppenheimer next madeThe Look of Silence, about the victims.) And NAZA has faced pre-emptive criticism from Palestinians, including poet Mosab Abu Toha, arguing that the last three years in Gaza have already been documented by Gazans. “It’s all there,” he posted on social media. “So what will this film add?”In this reading, NAZA is accused of privileging the perpetrator – giving literal voice to those for who the best platform, perhaps, would be a trial at the Hague. And yet another question is both obvious and uncomfortable. What’s in it for them anyway?In this year’s documentaryKilling Anna, former Syrian army officers were catfished into discussing civilian massacres by an academic posing as a loyalist of Bashar al-Assad. But most perpetrators are wholly aware they are being recorded. As such, we might expect a sobbing confessional. Not quite.The torturers of Standard Operating Procedure came close now and then, but only amid a lot of evasion. As further ethical complication, they were also paid for their interviews. With The Act of Killing, though, Oppenheimer found a still more disturbing truth – his butchers were gleefully unrepentant. (They also believed that, as an American, he would approve of garrotting leftists.) And in NAZA, Yuval Abraham has said some of his interviewees spoke from “the opposite of shame”. That word complicity comes up again. Should a film-maker be doing this?‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead moreThe thing is, though, lack of shame has a price.“War crimes are defined by the winners,” an Indonesian gangster says in The Act of Killing. “I’m a winner, so I can make my own definition.” In these films, that definition changes hands. Brilliantly, Oppenheimer did it by granting his subjects the freedom to reveal their nightmare psyches. In NAZA, journalism of the highest quality draws out a guilty plea with a seemingly howling lack of conscience.Palestinian accounts of the assault on Gaza have been wrongly ignored. The response, to this Israeli version, of the Netanyahu government is telling. Aside from menacing the directors, amimicking rebuttal, Naza: The Real Story was recently launched, desperately trying to reclaim control of the story.View image in fullscreenStandard Operating Procedure (2008).Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyAnd a director’s “complicity” is often indispensable. In 2017, the scalding Adriana’s Pact saw Chilean documentary maker Lissette Orozco interview her aunt, rumoured to have worked for the secret police of dictator Augusto Pinochet. When it turned out she had, the aunt’s berserk response to what she saw as a family betrayal was crucial to the story. Now the exposures of NAZA come from interviewees who would presumably never have talked to Abraham and Szor were they not Israeli too.But more than that – the fact they are is also proof that Israelis can still say no to this Israel. Vital as they are elsewhere, the real power of these films is in the societies they portray. Official Indonesian history echoed the gangsters’ tales of bravely ridding the country of communists. Oppenheimer made the film available free there. Now NAZA confronts the belief that atrocities are only ever down to far-right “bad apples”. In perpetrator cinema, a common thread is directing us to unseen hierarchies – the politicians and generals whose lies to their own people are now laid bare.View image in fullscreenSandra Huller in the 2024 Auschwitz drama The Zone of Interest.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyPut like that, hope almost glimmers. Still. These films advise caution. Hollywood movies are delivery systems for catharsis. Here, it is elusive. Near the end of The Act of Killing, the most naggingly sympathetic of the subjects starts to retch, as if his body is trying to expel his own past. But nothing comes up. And now we watch NAZA, and know what has happened in Gaza still happens today.No, what hope perpetrator cinema gives us is specific. Appearing with Oppenheimer on the Jewish Currents pod, Palestinian film-maker Rami Younis recalled meeting a giant of his country’s cinema, director Hany Abu-Assad, whose movies had been accused of humanising Israeli police. “What do you think happens when you keep demonising your enemy?” Abu-Assad said. “What happens toyou?”Usually “humanising” implies a soft focus. But NAZA and The Act of Killing remind us being human involves being capable of evil. They also offer the chance to fight back. The perpetrator of genocide refuses to see their enemy as like themselves – to truly look at them. With perpetrator cinema, though, we can look hard at people with whom we would like to share nothing – and say we are both human, however monstrous that also makes us.NAZAis in cinemas worldwide and will screen on the Guardian’s website from late NovemberExplore more on these topicsNAZAThe Act of KillingThe Zone of InterestPalestineMiddle East and north AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Quentin Tarantino makes a rare appearance on Graham Norton’s sofa | Television | The Guardian
description: The director talks about his new West End farce starring Sacha Baron Cohen. Plus: a squad of boozy miscreants target the Empire State Building in The Walking Dead. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The director talks about his new West End farce starring Sacha Baron Cohen. Plus: a squad of boozy miscreants target the Empire State Building in The Walking Dead. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Quentin Tarantino, who is on the Graham Norton Show to talk about his farce, The Popinjay Cavalier.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenQuentin Tarantino, who is on the Graham Norton Show to talk about his farce, The Popinjay Cavalier.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Quentin Tarantino makes a rare appearance on Graham Norton’s sofaThe director talks about his new West End farce starring Sacha Baron Cohen. Plus: a squad of boozy miscreants target the Empire State Building in The Walking Dead. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Jack Seale,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellFri 16 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Graham Norton Show10.40pm, BBC OneIt has been more than a decade since director Quentin Tarantino was on Graham’s sofa, and now he’s back to rave about his new Sacha Baron Cohen-starring West End farce, The Popinjay Cavalier. Taking a seat with him are US chat host Ellen DeGeneres; Colin Farrell, with a moving documentary about his friend; and Gemma Chan, who stars opposite Channing Tatum in the film Josephine. Suede provide the uplifting live music from their latest album, Antidepressants.Hollie RichardsonGardeners’ World8pm, BBC TwoA glimpse of GW’s future: Frances Tophill takes the lead this week, rather than soon-to-depart presenter Monty Don. She’s planting garlic in containers, and perennial vegetables, the sort that should provide bounty year after year with minimal maintenance, in her borders.Jack SealeThe Walking Dead: Dead City9pm, Sky OneMore post-apocalyptic splatter from a very rotten Big Apple. To shore up New York’s power grid, Maggie and Negan must recruit a squad of boozy miscreants – including a fireman, a chef and a porn star – for a high-risk raid. Their target? The zombie-infested Empire State Building.Graeme VirtueWar9pm, Sky AtlanticView image in fullscreenMessy divorce … Sienna Miller as Carla in War.Photograph: Miya Mizuno/Sky/HBOThe classy divorce is quickly becoming seedy as Carla (Sienna Miller) and Morgan (Dominic West) build their cases. When Carla tells her son, he is devastated and goes to Morgan for answers (“Your mum, she farts in bed – I just can’t take it any more”). Meanwhile, is junior lawyer/mole Johnny (Archie Renaux) in over his head?HRThe Last Leg10.05pm, Channel 4Josh Widdicombe is a very busy (and probably tired) man. The night before Strictly, he’s back on his old late-night hosting spot with Adam Hills and Alex Brooker. Now in its 35th (!) season, the show’s first guests chewing over the week that has been are comics Ellie Taylor and Tim Minchin.HRGrimsburg12.45am, Sky OneSeason three of the offbeat animated copcom continues with jaded detective Marvin Flute (voiced by Jon Hamm) bonding with his jittery son Stan over competitive hobby-horse riding. Elsewhere in town, Wynona gets brain surgery to simplify her love life. Could this be heartsick cyborg Greg’s big chance?GVFilm choiceMasterplan (Thomas Vincent, 2026), Prime VideoView image in fullscreenGentleman thief … Stanley Tucci as the scheming Roger in Masterplan.Photograph: Amazon MGM Studios/PASettle back and let the estimable Stanley Tucci work his charms on you … just like his gentleman thief, Roger Cavendish, who lures his long-lost children – hacker Chiara (The White Lotus’s Simona Tabasco) and explosives expert Jay (Victor Belmondo) – into a preposterous plot to steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in this heist comedy. The restored criminal family’s tentative bonding is mere window dressing for the main business of gadgetry, disguises and uncertain motives. Much of this is from the Mission: Impossible playbook, but with Tucci in charge it often sparkles.Simon WardellMoss & Freud(James Lucas, 2025), HBO MaxDerek Jacobi has already portrayed, superbly, one titan of post-second world war British art, Francis Bacon (in 1998’s Love Is the Devil). Now, in Lucas’s fascinating snapshot of the early 2000s, he has a good stab at late-period Lucian Freud. The true story of supermodel Kate Moss (a well-cast Ellie Bamber) sitting for a painting by him is a study in similarity and contrast: she’s the hard-partying doyenne of British fashion; he’s the austere old master. But he has his own wild side to reckon with, while she finds a kind of stability through their regular meetings.SWExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Make Me Well by Xand van Tulleken – an eye-opening takedown of wellness myths | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: The engaging TV doctor dismantles the spurious science behind modern day snake oils, from collagen to turmeric
Author: Simon Usborne
Headline: The engaging TV doctor dismantles the spurious science behind modern day snake oils, from collagen to turmeric
Content: Are supplements really benficial to our health?Photograph: Viktoriya Skorikova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAre supplements really benficial to our health?Photograph: Viktoriya Skorikova/Getty ImagesBook of the dayScience and nature booksReviewMake Me Well by Xand van Tulleken – an eye-opening takedown of wellness mythsThe engaging TV doctor dismantles the spurious science behind modern day snake oils, from collagen to turmericSimon UsborneFri 16 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Xand van Tulleken set off on a journey into the wild west of wellness, he didn’t expect to discover anything new about vitamin D. Of all the supplements that line our shelves and social media feeds, it ought to be the least controversial; even the NHS website, which is hardly a wellspring of quackery, advises that everyone should consider taking a daily dose during autumn and winter, when we risk becoming deficient (D is the vitamin we get mostly from sunlight, and which helps keep our bones strong).The tiggerish TV doctor and twin brother to Chris (he’s the one who wroteUltra-Processed Peopleabout the food industry) qualified at a time of high excitement in vitamin D circles; in the early 2000s, big studies were linking it not just to bone health but cancer, heart disease and dementia. “The range of potential problems to be solved was dizzying,” Van Tulleken writes in Make Me Well.But – spoiler alert – it turns out evidence even of the benefits of the most medically endorsed supplement shrivels under scrutiny. After immersing himself in decades of trials and speaking to a professor who had devoted his career to what he now views as the false promise of vitamin D, Van Tulleken finds no justification for its routine consumption for all but a tiny proportion of the population who are genuinely deficient.View image in fullscreenXand van Tulleken.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverThe vitamin D chapter follows what becomes a familiar and compelling pattern in Van Tulleken’s first proper solo book, in which he combines the rigour of an investigative journalist with medical expertise and the bouncy bedside manner that makes him such a natural broadcaster. He’s also the best kind of science writer, leaning into complexity while making it as easy to digest as a fish oil gummy (another thing you might want to stop forking out for).As well as vitamin D, he goes deep on collagen, testosterone, multivitamins, turmeric and krill oil supplements, as well as the burgeoning markets for personalised nutrition, glucose monitoring, wearable tech and private blood screening. In each case, he finds a troubling blurring of the lines between wellness and healthcare – and yawning gaps between hype and the evidence. He also uncovers the harm that wellness fads can do to our bodies, our relationship with food and the environment.In a chapter devoted to collagen, Van Tulleken travels to China to learn how a messy byproduct of the meat industry has been marketed as a modern elixir with a mark-up of as much as 1,000%. Ejiao, a premium kind of donkey-derived collagen, has become such a coveted source of “ingestible beauty” that manufacturers have exhausted Chinese supplies of donkey hides; soon rural communities in countries across Africa were finding that their animals were being slaughtered for export so that their skins could be boiled up and turned into expensive gummies and powders.He also explores the history and booming business of supplements, from the literal snake oil of the late 19th century to an unwholesome contemporary market driven by podcasts, influencers and a scientific publishing industry that appears to have striking deficiencies of its own: “The more research I do, the more I see the same patterns repeatedly: conflicts of interest, industry-funded trials, industry-­owned journals and an entire system designed to exploit people.”He concludes that, for the generally healthy person, wellness requires things that it’s hard to package and sell to supermarkets or via a subscription: a diet rich in whole foods and fruit and vegetables, for example, and a hobby that involves the achievable yet challenging mastery of some kind of rewarding skill. (The scientific evidence for the health benefits of, say, becoming a potter or learning the piano is far more robust than that for knocking back testosterone or vitamin D.)“The right people to make you well won’t be health gurus,” Van Tulleken says at the end of a book that deserves to prompt some kind of industry reckoning. “They might be dance instructors or librarians or martial arts teachers or the person who runs your local choir.” While I consider resuming reacquainting myself with my own piano, I have no plans to dust off my bottle of vitamin D pills as the nights draw in.Make Me Well: A Quest to Understand the Confusing World of Wellness by Xand van Tulleken is published by Cornerstone (£22). title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup | Crime fiction | The Guardian
description: The Heights by Ian Rankin; The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier; Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings; The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West; Inheritance by Gillian Slovo
Author: Laura Wilson
Headline: The Heights by Ian Rankin; The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier; Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings; The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West; Inheritance by Gillian Slovo
Content: Ian Rankin … The Heights is his first standalone thriller in almost two decades.Photograph: Robert Ormerod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIan Rankin … The Heights is his first standalone thriller in almost two decades.Photograph: Robert Ormerod/The GuardianCrime and thrillers roundupCrime fictionReviewThe best recent crime and thrillers – review roundupThe Heights by Ian Rankin; The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier; Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings; The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West; Inheritance by Gillian SlovoLaura WilsonFri 16 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenThe Heightsby Ian Rankin (Orion, £25)Luxury tower blocks, those potent symbols of hyper-gentrification, the increasing wealth gap and the displacement of existing communities, are a gift to novelists. Rankin’s first standalone thriller in almost two decades centres on The Heights, 18 storeys high and facing London’s Hyde Park, where DS Gillian Gish is investigating the suspicious death of night-shift security guard Dwayne Hogarth. The high-net-worth individuals who live there, including a young singer, a gangster’s wife, a man who “made a mint in post-glasnost Russia” and the daughter of a very well-connected Zimbabwean, are either uncontactable or tight-lipped, and it soon becomes clear that the developer, despite his bravado, is in financial trouble. Everyone, it appears, has something to hide – and then a second corpse is discovered. Rankin is a superb storyteller, and this is well up to his usual high standard, while DS Gish – less complex, but considerably more relatable than John Rebus – is worthy of her own series.View image in fullscreenThe Mortonsby Scott Westerfeld & Justine Larbalestier(Viking, £18.99)There are shades of both The Sopranos and Wednesday Addams in this tale of a powerful old American family whose trade is murder, blackmail and financial fraud. As the Mortons’ great hope, Jessica, puts it, “Give your child a strong hand, a sharp knife, and a big family, then teach them loyalty without care.” The children are given pet rabbits on which to prove their lack of compassion; the family are as ruthless with their own as with everyone else, their graveyard being full of youngsters who failed to make the grade. Jessica, who achieved her first kill aged 20, looks set to take on the murderous mantle, but a summer internship leads to a train of events that culminate in the discovery of a conscience. The Mortons is vivid and exciting, with a nice vein of mordant humour, but there’s a lot of world-building to get through, some of it lacking in internal logic; it’s hard to keep track of the many characters, and the violence towards innocent people and animals may leave some readers feeling queasy.View image in fullscreenMurder Most Crypticby Alys Cummings (Michael Joseph, £16.99)Cummings’s entertaining debut begins with a man walking into a meeting of people in recovery, announcing that his name is Laurence and he’s an alcoholic, then dropping dead. The group, who spot a handwritten cryptic crossword clue that’s fallen out of Laurence’s pocket – answer: Murder – are quicker to suspect foul play than the police, and when the same clue appears in the following day’s newspaper, they decide to figure out what’s going on. Told from the points of view of people trying, with varying degrees of success, to remain sober, this book involves a fair amount of unreliable narration – not least because of the memory gaps of the blackout drunk. The emergence of pertinent backstories lends rather more emotional depth than is found in the average cosy, while the discovery of further cryptic crossword clues provides an ingenious puzzle element (answers given at the end for non-cruciverbalists).View image in fullscreenThe Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonaldby AJ West (Orenda, £20)West’s latest historical mystery is a re-imagining of real events: actor William Terris was stabbed to death outside London’s Adelphi theatre in 1897 by deranged and destitute fellow performer Richard Archer Prince, who was subsequently found “criminally insane” and sent to Broadmoor. The action here takes place in 1917, against the backdrop of the first world war, as Everest Macdonald’s father, brother of William, hands her a packet of papers and charges her with finding out the truth about her uncle’s death. What follows is a fascinating journey that takes us back to the Indian sepoy rebellion of 1857 and encompasses “blackmail in all directions, secret love affairs, loyalties, vendettas, even phantoms and tribal curses”, as well as a plethora of hysterical thespians including real-life stars of the turn-of-the-century British stage such as Herbert Beerbohm Tree and Seymour Hicks. Well-researched, atmospheric and suitably melodramatic, this is a rip-roaring read-at-one-sitting historical mystery.Inheritanceby Gillian Slovo (Peepal Tree, £12.99)The eponymous inheritance of Slovo’s latest novel involves political and financial corruption in a South Africa still emerging from the long shadows cast by apartheid. Novelist Deborah Harrison’s younger sister Gail killed herself after denouncing Deborah’s latest book – a re-imagining of the family tragedy that blighted their childhood – as a misrepresentation. Deborah has always accepted the official version of events, that her mother killed her father in 1984 and went to prison for it, but Gail, whose adulthood was blighted by addiction issues and escalating paranoia, maintained that this was not the case. Now she has left a will tasking her sister with finding their now-released mother, with whom they have had no contact for over 40 years, and Deborah discovers that the truth is far more complicated than she has been led to believe. This is a suspenseful and moving tale about generational trauma, the complex nature of memory, making peace and letting go.Explore more on these topicsCrime fictionCrime and thrillers roundupThrillersFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums? | Fontaines DC | The Guardian
description: Once scrappy post-punk poets, they’re now one of the biggest bands in the world. As they release new album Dopamine Chamber, fans including Kneecap and Shame explain their sensational rise
Author: Kate Solomon
Headline: Once scrappy post-punk poets, they’re now one of the biggest bands in the world. As they release new album Dopamine Chamber, fans including Kneecap and Shame explain their sensational rise
Content: Fontaines DC, with frontman Grian Chatten, centre.Photograph: Ewen SpencerView image in fullscreenFontaines DC, with frontman Grian Chatten, centre.Photograph: Ewen SpencerFontaines DC‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums?Once scrappy post-punk poets, they’re now one of the biggest bands in the world. As they release new album Dopamine Chamber, fans including Kneecap and Shame explain their sensational riseKate SolomonFri 16 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Irish rockers Fontaines DC emerged in 2019, they were a bunch of post-punk poets making abrasive guitar music at a time whenDance Monkey,Drakeand The Greatest Showman reigned supreme. But today, as their fifth album Dopamine Chamber is released, the quintet are looking towards a 2027 filled with gigs in UK stadiums, US arenas and headline slots at big European festivals – plus rumours of topping Glastonbury’s Pyramid stage. It’s quite a trajectory.Their rise has been strangely traditional for a time when social media has culture in a chokehold. Ever more ambitious albums, the support of radio and institutions such as the BBC, and a lot of touring have all played parts. Beyond that, “fact is, they’re one of the best bands in the world,” says fellow countryman Mo Chara, one third ofKneecap.Fontaines DC formed at the BIMM Music Institute in Dublin in 2014. The school’s dean, Alan Cullivan, describes them as having had “an absolute focus. It was all about writing a better song after a better song after a better song.” They’d apparently play to 30 people in a dive bar one week, then come back three weeks later and half the songs would be new.That caught the attention of Trevor Dietz, who became their manager and was described by Fontaines as “the sixth member of the band” when he died earlier this year. “He brought this unwavering sense of self-belief, and that was very contagious,” says Jeff Bell, who’d end up signing the band to Partisan Records.Dietz’s connections brought Fontaines into orbits outside the Dublin gig circuit. By 2017 the band had released the single Liberty Belle and Dietz introduced them to south London bandShame, who were playing their first headline Dublin shows. “We went on this tour together for our first album,” remembers Shame singer Charlie Steen. “It felt like they had their own crowd even with just a few songs out – it’s one thing to have that in Dublin, but it’s another thing to have it in Leicester.” He adds that Fontaines’ frontman Grian Chatten “gave me aYeatsbook to read on that tour”: typical of the singer’s unashamed poetic leanings.BBC Radio 6 Music’s Steve Lamacq was an early champion of the band around the same time. “They sent us the self-released seven-inch of Hurricane Laughter, and we played that a couple of times – it had a power and an atmosphere that a lot of records around at the time didn’t really have,” he recalls.In March 2018 the band played the Victoria in Dalston, east London, a tiny pub backroom. In the crowd was Lamacq, enthralled by Chatten’s stage presence, and Bell, who flew to Dublin the next week to sign them. “As soon as I met them, it was clear that they were the biggest band in the world,” Bell says. “It just hadn’t happened yet.”The label developed a clear gameplan with the band. “There were two guiding principles: authenticity and urgency,” Bell says. “If the mixes weren’t right, start again. If an edit didn’t feel right, it didn’t go to radio. If a writer didn’t get it, don’t do the interview. We also made a point of showcasing the lyrics wherever we could; that was a real point of access for a lot of people.” After their 2019 debut album Dogrel went Top 10 in the UK and Ireland, the Covid lockdown could have scuppered them, like it did so many small acts on the rise. But instead of cancelling releases as others did, they pressed ahead with the release of their second album, A Hero’s Death, which was nominated for a Grammy.View image in fullscreenFontaines DC pictured in 2026.Photograph: Elizaveta PorodinaThe enormous crowds that Fontaines DC now command are not a result of pandering to the TikTok algorithm, though, even mid-lockdown. The band has a presence on social media, but they haven’t done viral video series such as Hot Ones,Chicken Shop DateorSubway Takes. “They are one of those artists that has very quickly become contrarian to the rule, where they’ve taken a less-is-more approach,” says Liam Ward, founder of music-focused social media marketing agency Something Something.That doesn’t stop Fontaines having hardcore fans who film entire shows for social media and, in Ward’s opinion, this fan activity online is organic (as opposed to manufactured by legions of fake accounts,as deployedby some of their indie peers). “I have not even heard rumours or whispers [of that],” he says. “They put out what they put out, and all of that craziness and noise happens around them.”Their previous album, 2024’s Romance, which came with DayGlo artwork and rave-adjacent new looks for the members, was derided by some early fans as too pop but became their first platinum seller in the UK and Ireland and earned another couple of Grammy noms. Dopamine Chamber,raved about in a five-star review in the Guardian, is just as strange and arresting. “Arctic Monkeys, in a way, have done a brilliant job setting up a space for Fontaines by being a really interesting rock band who have evolved a lot since the early days,” Lamacq says. “There’s a new, younger audience who are perhaps more lyrically led. They like the vocabulary as well as the music.”Kneecap’s Mo Chara says Fontaines’ political leanings, citing a homelessness benefit show the band curated, and their stance against the genocide in Palestine, further endeared the group to him and many others. He adds: “If you’re making music as good as they are, the mainstream can’t ignore it, but it feels like they were making music their own way and not to appeal to the masses. The mainstream has come to them rather than the other way round.”Fontaines DC: Dopamine Chamber review – gloomy, gorgeous and a gargantuan triumphRead moreThere are plenty of bands making amazing music who don’t reach the upper echelons of commercial success, though. For Abel González, who is on the booking team for Barcelona’s Primavera festival, “it’s all about feelings”. Fontaines first played the festival on a small stage in 2018, but next year they’re among the big-name headliners. “Every time they’ve come back to the festival, they’ve had new things to say, and we’ve wanted to hear them.”The true reason for Fontaines DC’s dizzying rise likely lies somewhere in the middle of a complex Venn diagram: a once-a-generation confluence of talent, commitment, good people and luck. The consensus seems to be that there’s no limit to how massive they could become. Bell agrees, still rabidly enthusiastic about the band even after they’ve moved from Partisan to current label XL Recordings. “They still haven’t reached the top of their mountain. I’m excited to see where it keeps going.”Dopamine Chamber is out now on XL RecordingsExplore more on these topicsFontaines DCPop and rockIndiePunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the buzzy bildungsromans of boy wonder Superfan and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Kali Flanagan was handpicked by Julian Casablancas to support the Strokes – now, at 21, he’s writing songs full of the rushing emotions of youth
Author: Archie Forde
Headline: Kali Flanagan was handpicked by Julian Casablancas to support the Strokes – now, at 21, he’s writing songs full of the rushing emotions of youth
Content: Hand-spun emotion … Superfan.Photograph: courtesy of Grace Anthony SchmidtView image in fullscreenHand-spun emotion … Superfan.Photograph: courtesy of Grace Anthony SchmidtAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the buzzy bildungsromans of boy wonder Superfan and the week’s best new tracksKali Flanagan was handpicked by Julian Casablancas to support the Strokes – now, at 21, he’s writing songs full of the rushing emotions of youthArchie FordeandBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 16 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromNew YorkRecommended if you likeCameron Winter, Adrianne Lenker, Alex GUp nextMy Piledriver Heart album out now; UK tour beginning 4 NovemberMaking coming-of-age music as a young person can feel strange after a pandemic. So here are a few more curveballs. Imagine the breezy, youthful indie you post online in your early teens gets you a record deal. Covid happens. You move to New York, change your artist name, and then Julian Casablancas eyes you at an open mic and invites you to open for the Strokes in Colorado, aged 18, solo.This pinball game of life is the music career of Superfan, AKA Kali Flanagan, who is now 21 and whose latest album, My Piledriver Heart, offers up a codex of miniature bildungsromans worth the buzz.Flanagan’s primary tools are some of the simplest: drop-tuned, condensed acoustic guitars (which he calls “acousticellos”) and quietly strong vocals reminiscent of Elliott Smith or Alex G. Roomy drums and distortion on tracks such asIn the Gold Roomor Keeping Your Smile add a welcome noisy edge.The album’s true power is Flanagan’s ability to hand-spin emotion out of simple melodies, phrases or builds, thanks in part to deft cello work by Omeed Almassi (who has also played with Bar Italia): take the way the strings mimic an unfurling guitar line at the climax ofMiss W Jones, or the bassy Nick Drakeian outro toOde to Hum (I Want It to Rise). Even so, when you think Flanagan lands on something concrete, he doesn’t: this is music that conjures up new feelings on every listen. Isn’t that what growing up is all about?Archie FordeThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreen@’s Victoria Rose and Stone Filipczak.Photograph: Ingmar Chen@​ – Love in the DarkThePhiladelphia duo, who in a previous generation might have been dubbed freak-folk, release their album Autosmile today, and it’s one of the year’s very best. This particular track has a riveting blend of innocence and experience, with hymnal yet careworn vocals.Snoh Aalegra – KarmaAn utterly stunning, minimalist R&B ballad with shades of Maxwell to its chorus and mk.gee to its guitar, as Aalegra lacerates herself over the way she betrayed a lover.​Blondie – Spectral EyesThough Johnny Marr wrote it and plays the big, simple riff, the lead single to the New York legends’ first album in nine years is all about Debbie Harry, rhythmically chattering through the chorus with a rough, time-worn grade to her voice.Carissa’s Wierd – I Don’t Feel Like I Feel RightIn the 25 years since their last album, the US indie duo have amassed a huge audience on streaming who will no doubt flock to this new single, a romantic tussle whose tension is kept taut even as the epic drums kick in.Marla Kether – Libera (ft Margaridas)Her day job is being Little Simz’s bassist, but Kether’s own music is well worth seeking out: Libera is a propulsive Latin-house track with delicate, chirrupping vocals by Margaridas – and, predictably, a killer melodic bassline.Teri Rini – Behind Every MirrorYou can reliably smash “buy now” on anything Melbourne label Efficient Space puts out, spanning contemporary artists and crate-digging comps. This, a spellbinding 1981 song from an overlooked US jazz singer, is from an upcoming example of the latter, entitled Nothing Ever Was.Post Common – Check AtomiserGuitars are rarely as gorgeously distorted as they are here, with tones like a wind-assaulted microphone shifting through the Brighton trio’s otherwise melodic post-hardcore.Subscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistIndiePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Worldpeace DMT: Stick Around for Tea review – ‘laptop twee’ duo keep things goofy but strengthen songs | Indie | The Guardian
description: Bringing back the hyperliterate sound design of their acclaimed 2025 debut, the London duo explore childhood with whimsical humour and terrific musicality
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Bringing back the hyperliterate sound design of their acclaimed 2025 debut, the London duo explore childhood with whimsical humour and terrific musicality
Content: Devastatingly contemporary … Leo Fincham and Rowan Miles, AKA Worldpeace DMT.Photograph: Thomas ConnollyView image in fullscreenDevastatingly contemporary … Leo Fincham and Rowan Miles, AKA Worldpeace DMT.Photograph: Thomas ConnollyIndieReviewWorldpeace DMT: Stick Around for Tea review – ‘laptop twee’ duo keep things goofy but strengthen songs(WPDMT)Bringing back the hyperliterate sound design of their acclaimed 2025 debut, the London duo explore childhood with whimsical humour and terrific musicalityShaad D'SouzaFri 16 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of last year’s surprise highlights was The Velvet Underground & Rowan, the debut album by the wacky, hyperliterate London duo Worldpeace DMT. That irreverent album title summed up their approach to their references: Leo Fincham and Rowan Miles – also of theFemcels– buttressed nods to Fleetwood Mac and the Beach Boys with a palette straight out of NME circa 2011. If it isn’t a coup to make the sound of Grouplove and Darwin Deez sound cool and urbane in 2025, I don’t know what is.View image in fullscreenStick Around for Tea album artwork.Photograph: PRThis year, Worldpeace DMT have changed tack, perhaps in response to suggestions that they’re at the forefront of an emergent genre called “laptop twee”. The duo’s August mixtape Flowers Powers mostly eschewed plunderphonics and heavy sampling in favour of live instrumentation that ran the gamut from Spiritualized to outlaw country; Stick Around for Tea, their second album, brings back a shade of the goofy,Sung Tongs-esque sound design that made their debut such a joy, while pulling Fincham and Miles’ songwriting to the fore.Stick Around for Tea seems, loosely, to be a concept album about childhood. The inherent whimsy of the Worldpeace DMT project suits these songs, which wring dry humour from lyrics about spiders, tigers and anthropomorphised guitars. Fincham and Miles sing in a self-consciously childish way that belies their taut musicality: a lush, almost Van Dyke Parks jauntiness on Munich Gyaru, for example, or a knack for bulletproof pop structure on the title track. The result is the kind of devastatingly contemporary record that even arch classicists couldn’t possibly turn up their noses at.Explore more on these topicsIndiePop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: PatKop & Say album review – playfulness and beguiling delicacy in mix of new and old  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Compositions by both musicians themselves frame works by Szymanowski and Prokofiev
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Compositions by both musicians themselves frame works by Szymanowski and Prokofiev
Content: Complementary … Patricia Kopatchinskaja and Fazıl Say.Photograph: borggreve/Courtesy of Marco BorggreveView image in fullscreenComplementary … Patricia Kopatchinskaja and Fazıl Say.Photograph: borggreve/Courtesy of Marco BorggreveClassical musicReviewPatKop & Say album review – playfulness and beguiling delicacy in mix of new and oldPatricia Kopatchinskaja and Fazil Say(Alpha)Compositions by both musicians themselves frame works by Szymanowski and ProkofievErica JealFri 16 Oct 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatricia KopatchinskajaandFazil Sayhave recorded Say’s music together before, but this is their first recording to feature Kopatchinskaja as a composer as well, but this is no vanity project: Say’s and Kopatchinskaja’s pieces make good complements to Szymanowski’s three Mythes and Prokofiev’s Violin Sonata No 1.View image in fullscreenAlbum artwork for Patkop & Say.Photograph: Courtesy of Marco Borggreve for Alpha ClassicsSay’s Lost Screams Sonata is driven by repeated piano rhythms, its fierceness tempered by an episode in which Kopatchinskaja plays low, ghostly harmonics and Say gently plucks the strings of the piano so it almost sounds like a second violin. Kopatchinskaja’s three-movement piece UniSolo is an impish work with a searching, thoughtful playfulness that comes from the parallel world to the Kurtág miniatures she plays so well.These two frame a haunting performance of Mythes that embraces the strange sumptuousness of these pieces, with playing of beguiling delicacy from both musicians. With an even bigger scope, Prokofiev’s wartime Sonata No 1 has moments in which Kopatchinskaja turns her tone almost ugly, even in places where other violinists might choose to soar heroically. Each of these works pushes at the edges of what the violin can do, and casts the instrument in a kind of narrative role: Kopatchinskaja, who always looks to play the storyteller, seizes upon these qualities with relish.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Cocktail of the week: Àclèaf’s PX martini – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: Like a classic espresso martini, but with the addition of vanilla vodka
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Like a classic espresso martini, but with the addition of vanilla vodka
Content: Àclèaf’s PX martini.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenÀclèaf’s PX martini.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Àclèaf’s PX martini – recipeLike a classic espresso martini, but with the addition of vanilla vodkaAndréa NuningerFri 16 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is our twist on the much-loved classic. It takes inspiration from a classic espresso martini, with the addition of vanilla vodka bringing with it an oaked edge that cuts the sweetness of the sherry.PX martiniServes150ml vanilla vodka– we useAbsolut Vanilia35ml pedro ximénez35ml freshly brewed espresso– we useJamaican BlueFill a cocktail shaker with ice, then add the vodka, PX and espresso – for the best texture, measure in the espresso last, so the ice doesn’t melt too quickly and over-dilute the cocktail. Shake vigorously for at least 20 seconds, so the mix emulsifies and produces that classic, creamy, frothy, off-white layer on top. Fine strain into a chilled martini glass or coupe and serve.Andréa Nuninger, restaurant manager,Àclèaf, Plympton, DevonExplore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodWineCoffeerecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for baked oats with morello cherries and almond  | Breakfast | The Guardian
description: This moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfast
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: This moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfast
Content: Helen Goh’s baked oats with morello cherries and almond.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s baked oats with morello cherries and almond.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotBreakfastHelen Goh’s recipe for baked oats with morello cherries and almondThis moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfastHelen GohFri 16 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been making versions of these baked oats ever since discovering Heidi Swanson’s recipe inSuper Natural Every Day. This is my favourite store-cupboard version, for when stone fruit and berries have slipped out of season. Morello cherries are a dark, tart variety of sour cherry, with an intensity of flavour and bright acidity that stand up particularly well to baking. I love them here paired with almonds and coconut drinking milk (the light kind sold in cartons, not the rich tinned variety). The cherries I use are whole fruit in syrup, which I drain and dot over the oats – they remain distinct while becoming deliciously jammy as they bake. Almost any fruit compote or jam will work here, though, so choose your favourite.Baked oats with morello cherries and almondJarred cherries come in many forms, so if yours is more like a compote or jam, simply add it in small teaspoonfuls instead.Prep10 minCook45 min, plus coolingServes4-630g unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly, plus extra for greasing210g jumbo rolled oats1 tsp baking powder1 tsp ground cinnamon½ tsp fine sea salt1 large egg60ml maple syrup, plus extra to serve500ml coconut drinking milk1 tsp vanilla extract100-120g morello cherries in syrup, drained, or cherry compote or jam30g flaked almondsIcing sugar,for dusting (optional)Yoghurt or cream,to serveHeat the oven to 195C (175C fan)/385F/gas 5½ and lightly grease a 26cm ovenproof dish that’s about 5-6cm deep – the oat mixture will form a fairly shallow layer.Put the oats, baking powder, cinnamon and salt in a medium bowl, mix well, then tip into the greased dish. In a large jug, whisk the egg, maple syrup and melted butter, then add the coconut drinking milk and vanilla, and whisk again to combine. Pour this evenly over the oats, then gently press down any oats that remain dry.Dot the drained cherries evenly over the oats. If using a thicker compote or jam, drop small teaspoonfuls over the surface, then use the tip of the spoon to drag each one out slightly, creating ripples rather than deep pools. Scatter over the flaked almonds.Bake for about 30 minutes, until golden on top and just set in the centre. Leave to stand for five to 10 minutes before serving, dusted with icing sugar if you like, and with yoghurt or cream and a little extra maple syrup alongside.Explore more on these topicsBreakfastThe sweet spotFoodDessertBakingFruitAutumn food and drinkCereals and grainsrecipesShareReuse this content
